papers.abstract: Images reveal appearances, but counting often asks about physical objects. A single entity may be visible directly, in several reflections, or through glass, so detecting every visible occurrence does not determine how many entities are present. Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate these two operations. We introduce PhysCount, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can distinguish what appears in an image from what physically exists in the scene. PhysCount contains 546 real-world images and 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups. For each group, annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed, and identify appearances of the same entity. Four complementary question families test the enumeration of appearances, the enumeration of physical entities, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance--entity correspondence. We measure both accuracy on each family and the proportion of groups answered entirely correctly. Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them. Even the strongest model answers every question correctly in only 13.36\% of groups. Performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes. Higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement. These results expose a gap between recognizing what is visible and correctly recovering the physical entities behind those observations.
authors: Lidong Lu, Jiaxin Lv, Liangrui Dong, Xinyi Mao, Lidong Zou, Zhenquan Li, Tong Lu, Guo Chen
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 546 real-world images and 4,595 questions across 651 target-specific groups.
Tests appearance counting, physical-entity counting, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance–entity correspondence.
Evaluates 40 MLLMs; the strongest model answers all questions correctly in only 13.36% of groups.
Performance worsens when one entity creates multiple appearances or appearances span different observation modes.
Higher resolution offers limited gains in complete-group accuracy, while jointly answering related questions helps substantially.

Figure 2 summarizes the construction of PhysCount in three stages. First, we build the image set through automatic candidate filtering followed by human selection. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Qwen Team (2026b) filters natural images from Common Canvas Gokaslan et al. (2024), GPIC Chandrasegaran et al. (2026), and other public collections for mirror and glass scenes in which reflections or glass change the apparent count. Human annotators then inspect these candidates and select images with localizable targets, distinguishable direct, reflected, or through-glass appearances, and counts that can be resolved through careful inspection. The selected images contain salient appearance duplication or interactions between reflected and transmitted content.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark probing MLLMs' ability to distinguish visual appearances from physical entities; directly relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: PhysCount: Do MLLMs Count Visual Appearances or Physical Entities?
papers.tldr: PhysCount shows that MLLMs can count visible appearances more easily than they can infer the underlying physical entities they represent.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot generalization but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing adversarial fine-tuning methods often use pre-trained model guidance to preserve image--text alignment while improving robustness. Our analysis of visual representation drift reveals complementary limitations of two representative forms of guidance. Matching visual features provides broad coverage by constraining all directions equally, but lacks semantic emphasis. Matching prediction distributions prioritizes semantically relevant directions, but remains limited by the candidate texts and prediction probabilities. These limitations can hinder preservation of pre-trained image--text relationships and degrade zero-shot performance. To address these issues, we propose Textual Response-Aware Guidance (TRAG), which constrains visual representation drift using the pre-trained text encoder's responses to local variations in input embeddings. Specifically, TRAG constructs anchor-level constraints from the response directions and magnitudes around semantic anchors, then aggregates them using pre-trained image--anchor relevance, yielding an image-adaptive constraint. Extensive experiments across architectures and tasks demonstrate state-of-the-art clean and robust performance. Further analysis shows that TRAG helps preserve pre-trained image--text relationships.
authors: Yubo Cui, Xianchao Guan, Zheng Zhang
bullets: VLMs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, while robustness fine-tuning can damage pretrained image–text alignment and zero-shot performance.
Feature matching covers visual directions broadly but lacks semantic focus; prediction matching is semantic but limited by candidate texts and probabilities.
TRAG builds anchor-level constraints from the text encoder’s response directions and magnitudes to local embedding variations.
These constraints are aggregated using image–anchor relevance, producing image-adaptive guidance.
Experiments across architectures and tasks report state-of-the-art clean and robust performance, with better preservation of pretrained image–text relationships.

papers.selection_reason: Method for preserving image-text alignment in vision-language models under adversarial fine-tuning; directly relevant to multimodal foundation model robustness.
papers.title: Textual Response-Aware Guidance for Zero-Shot Adversarial Robustness of Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: TRAG improves zero-shot adversarial robustness in vision-language models by constraining visual representation drift according to text-encoder responses around semantic anchors.

papers.abstract: We revisit advantage estimation in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and observe that any token-level advantage admits a two-stage factorization: a \emph{sample-level baselining} step that converts scalar verifier rewards into a comparable sequence-level signal, and a \emph{token-level credit assignment} step that distributes that signal over the trajectory. Existing estimators typically address only one of these stages: affine baselines preserve the shape of each task's reward law, so heavy tails and binary cliffs propagate into the gradient, while token-level credit rules tie the size of each token's update to raw confidence scales and need not conserve the total credit issued by the verifier. We propose \textbf{TACE} (Two-stage Advantage and Credit Estimation), a two-stage estimator that addresses both stages. At stage~(S1), we replace linear standardization with a one-dimensional optimal-transport map to a standard normal, which gives a common population reward law across tasks and caps finite-sample outliers deterministically. At stage~(S2), we rank-calibrate a stop-gradient evidence contrast within each trajectory and renormalize the clipped token weights to have mean one, so credit is redistributed across tokens while its total mass and sign are conserved. We prove population-level inter-task moment equity, a deterministic tail bound, and mass-conservation, boundedness, and sign-anchoring properties that affine baselines and unnormalized token weights do not satisfy. On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE obtains the strongest results on a majority of the benchmarks but does not dominate every setting.
authors: Lang Chen, Zongxin Xu, Borui Wang, Anran Liu, Shitong Chen
bullets: Existing GRPO advantage estimators can propagate heavy-tailed or binary reward scales across tasks.
TACE uses optimal transport to map scalar rewards to a standard normal, aligning reward distributions and deterministically capping finite-sample outliers.
It rank-calibrates within-trajectory evidence contrasts and normalizes clipped token weights to conserve total credit.
The method provides inter-task moment equity, tail bounds, mass conservation, boundedness, and sign anchoring.
On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE performs best on most benchmarks but not in every setting.

Stage (S2), ours (starting from the evidence ratio of Yang et al., 2026): runs πθ under non-privileged (PS) and privileged (PT ) contexts, rank-calibrates the per-token log-evidence within the trajectory, and applies a sign-anchored, mean-one (mass-preserving) magnitude weight wi,t. The composed token advantage Âi,t = Ai · wi,t plugs into the standard GRPO clipped surrogate.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-time reward-calibration and credit-assignment method for multimodal RLVR, directly relevant to multimodal foundation-model training.
papers.title: Distributional Reward Calibration and Budget-Neutral Credit Assignment for Multimodal RLVR
papers.tldr: TACE calibrates reward distributions and redistributes token credit in GRPO while preserving total credit and its sign.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are now used as zero-shot judges of image quality, but their color judgments are rarely tested with colorimetric ground truth. We present a five-task benchmark based on the CIE colorimetric framework: AWB pair judgment, skin-tone bias direction, CCT estimation, CIE Delta E 2000 pair ordering, and color naming under changing illuminants. We test eight MLLM endpoints, including four Qwen3-VL variants, GLM-4.5V, GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-4.7, and Gemini-3.1-Pro. The models often solve coarse binary AWB judgments, but they remain weak on numeric CCT estimation and on some fine color-difference judgments. On ColorChecker-24 stimuli, the three closed-weight frontier models reach CCT MAE of 715-1056 K, compared with 1358-2133 K for the five open-weight models. A non-ColorChecker control shows that this advantage is partly template-dependent. The results suggest that current MLLMs have useful color words and coarse visual priors, but their color judgments are not reliably calibrated to CIE-computable color differences.
authors: Shuwei Yue, Kaida Xiao, Zhihua Wang, Qiao Chen
bullets: Introduces five tasks covering white-balance judgment, skin-tone bias, CCT estimation, Delta E 2000 ordering, and color naming under changing illuminants.
Evaluates eight MLLM endpoints, including Qwen3-VL variants and several closed-weight models.
Models often succeed on coarse binary AWB judgments but struggle with CCT estimation and fine color-difference comparisons.
Closed-weight frontier models show lower CCT errors than open-weight models on ColorChecker-24, though the advantage is partly template-dependent.
Overall, useful color vocabulary and visual priors do not ensure reliable calibration to CIE-computable color differences.

papers.title: Benchmarking color judgment in multimodal LLMs with CIE-computable ground truth
papers.tldr: A CIE-grounded benchmark finds that MLLMs handle coarse color judgments but remain poorly calibrated for precise color differences and numeric color-temperature estimation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can now process hour-long videos, making extended multi-turn dialogue over a single video a natural mode of use. Sustaining such a dialogue requires more than answering each question in isolation: the model must retrieve and reuse information established earlier in the conversation, both what it has seen and what it has said, an ability we term in-context video memory. Existing video QA benchmarks leave this ability unmeasured: their questions are mutually independent, never reference one another, and each is answerable from the video alone, so nothing ever requires carrying information across turns. We introduce VideoMemBench, in which each sample pairs a single video with a long multi-turn dialogue, whose turns are connected by typed cross-turn dependencies: an Episodic Dependency refers back to a visual episode described in an earlier turn, probing memory of what the model has seen, while an Answer Dependency builds on the model's own earlier answer, probing memory of what the model has said. Every dependency is verified considering two properties: 1) necessity, meaning the question cannot be answered without its earlier turns, and 2) non-leakage, meaning the question does not restate the information from its earlier turns. To enforce these properties, we design a construction pipeline with three LLM roles: a planner, a generator, and a judger, with each dialogue reviewed by human experts. VideoMemBench comprises 326 videos with 2,476 turns, of which 1,387 depend on earlier turns, including multi-parent dependencies and long-range call-back. Among over 20 evaluated open- and closed-source MLLMs, Claude Opus 5 performs the best with an overall score of only 45.7\%, highlighting the challenge of in-context video memory. Our dataset and evaluation are released.
authors: Zhengdong Hu, Chao Wang, Kaituo Feng, Huanjin Yao, Mingfei Lu, Hehe Fan, Yi Yang
bullets: Evaluates in-context video memory rather than independent video question answering.
Tests two dependency types: recall of earlier visual episodes and reuse of the model’s own prior answers.
Ensures dependencies are necessary and non-leaking, using planner, generator, and judger roles plus human review.
Contains 326 videos and 2,476 dialogue turns, with 1,387 turns dependent on earlier turns.
Across 20+ open- and closed-source MLLMs, the best reported overall score is only 45.7%, underscoring the difficulty.

figures.caption: Figure 2 The VideoMemBench construction pipeline. Starting from a curated video pool, a planner specifies turn intents and a typed dependency graph. A generator constructs the dialogue turn by turn, while a judger checks necessity, non-leakage, and visual grounding, returning failed turns for regeneration. Completed dialogues are checked against the plan and reviewed by human experts.

Figure 1 Example of VideoMemBench with cross-turn dependencies: Independent turns (e.g., T1, T8) establish visually grounded facts; dependent turns refer back to earlier turns through expressions such as “the scene from T1” or “the target from T1”, without restating earlier content. An Episodic Dependency (e.g., T2) requires recalling what the model has seen: the model must recover which scene T1 described before answering the question. An Answer Dependency (e.g., T3, T4) requires recalling what the model has said : each builds on the answer produced at an earlier turn.

Figure 4 Analysis of factors affecting in-context video memory. (a) Accuracy on dependent turns by dependency distance, measured from the current turn to its earliest parent; the dashed line shows the mean across all evaluated models. (b) Accuracy on dependent turns by the number of parents. (c) Independent- and dependent-turn accuracy by dialogue position for two models: the light segment shows dependent-turn accuracy, the full bar height shows independent-turn accuracy, and the dark segment represents their difference. (d) Accuracy on answer-dependent turns under self-rollout and oracle histories. Oracle histories replace previous model responses with ground-truth answers.

Figure 3 Dataset statistics of VideoMemBench. (a) Category distribution across four major domains and their finegrained subcategories. (b) Distribution of videos by duration. (c) Distribution of the number of dialogue turns per video. (d) Distribution of question dependencies, including independent questions, episodic dependencies, and answer dependencies. (e) Text-length statistics for questions, answers, and answer choices, reported as mean ± standard deviation.

Figure 6 A soccer dialogue example from VideoMemBench. Seven dialogue turns cover player identification, spatial tracking, and match events, with later questions referring to previously discussed players. Reference answers are shown in red, and model responses marked correct at the turn level are shown in green.

Figure 7 A basketball dialogue example from VideoMemBench. Selected video frames are shown above, followed by eight dialogue turns with reference answers and responses from five models. Reference answers are shown in red, and responses marked correct are shown in green.

Figure 5 The expert review interface. For each dialogue, the expert replays the video in the top panel, where the evidence window of the current turn is marked on the timeline, and reads the dialogue turn by turn, where the parent turns and the type of each dependency are highlighted. The expert answers the current question before the reference answer is revealed, then marks the turn as correct, answer wrong, dependency not required, wording leaks a parent, or duplicate, and edits the question, the options, or the answer in place. A dialogue is retained only after every turn has been marked correct or revised, and the interface records each decision together with the time spent on the turn. Referent here means episodic dependency. Please zoom in to see the details.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long multi-turn video conversations and in-context video memory in MLLMs; fits video understanding and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: VideoMemBench: How Well Do MLLMs Remember in Video Conversations?
papers.tldr: VideoMemBench introduces a benchmark showing that MLLMs struggle to remember and reuse information across long, multi-turn video conversations.

papers.abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) are tested for fine-grained understanding with image--text matching probes, a model must prefer the correct image or caption over handcrafted negative. In retrieval, the correct item must beat thousands of alternatives. We measure how these two evaluation methods relate by using two probing benchmarks, \svo{} and SugarCrepe, for retrieval tasks. For 100 image and caption queries we judge the top-10 retrievals from full dataset of six VLMs, with human annotators and an LLM assessor. We than compare how well models rank pool of items on the same queries, while changing only where the negatives comes from: the benchmark, a random draw, or the judged-incorrect retrievals of other models. On \svo{} the accuracy of retrieving a positive over handcrafted negatives is significantly higher than for retrieved ones (the correct item is preferred in 85\% against 77\% of the time). Using pool of ten retrieved negatives leads to same accuracy as when one uses pool of 200 to 430 random negatives. On SugarCrepe the order is reversed: its handcrafted negatives are harder than the retrieved ones. Incomplete relevance labels explain most of the low retrieval scores on \svo{}, where the top-ranked item is correct for 54--90\% of the queries under human labels against 6--21\% under the benchmark's labels. However, we detect no association between passing the probe for a query and retrieving a correct item first. The LLM assessor o3 agrees with individual annotators ($\kappa$ 0.57--0.61) slightly less than they agree with each other (0.64--0.68).
bullets: The study compares two probing benchmarks, SVO and SugarCrepe, with retrieval over full datasets for six vision–language models and 100 image/caption queries.
On SVO, handcrafted-negative accuracy is higher than accuracy against retrieved negatives (85% vs. 77%); ten retrieved negatives are as challenging as 200–430 random negatives.
On SugarCrepe, handcrafted negatives are harder than retrieved negatives, showing that probe difficulty depends on negative construction.
Incomplete SVO relevance labels substantially depress retrieval scores: human labels identify the top result as correct for 54–90% of queries, versus 6–21% under benchmark labels.
Passing a probe does not predict retrieving the correct item first; the LLM assessor shows moderate agreement with human annotators.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models can both generate and understand images within a single set of weights, offering an opportunity to use image synthesis as training supervision for visual comprehension. However, existing visual chain-of-thought methods rely on human-annotated helper images during training and require slow image generation at test time. We present SelfThinker, the first self-evolving framework that turns a unified model's self-generated visual thoughts into stronger understanding without human image annotations. Given a visual problem, SelfThinker samples candidate helper images from its generation pathway and uses its frozen understanding pathway to score each candidate via conditional pointwise mutual information. High-utility visual thoughts then refine the generator via flow matching and serve as privileged teacher context for on-policy self-distillation. At inference, SelfThinker reasons directly from the original image in text without generating intermediate images. Although trained only on small synthetic visual-search and navigation datasets, SelfThinker transfers broadly to natural-image and spatial benchmarks, raising the seven-benchmark average of ThinkMorph-7B from 52.7 to 64.0 (+11.3 points). Controlled image-perturbation probes further show that SelfThinker surpasses ThinkMorph-7B by up to 40.4 points and its pretrained BAGEL-7B backbone by up to 23.2 points across fine-grained and spatial perception tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhangquanchen/SelfThinker.
bullets: Addresses reliance on human-annotated helper images and costly image generation at test time.
Samples candidate visual thoughts and scores them with the frozen understanding pathway using conditional pointwise mutual information.
Uses high-utility thoughts for flow-matching generator refinement and on-policy self-distillation.
Trained on small synthetic visual-search and navigation datasets, it transfers to natural-image and spatial benchmarks.
Raises ThinkMorph-7B’s seven-benchmark average from 52.7 to 64.0, while inference avoids intermediate image generation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of SelfThinker . The upper-left Self-Evolution panel summarizes the closed loop of imagining candidate visual thoughts, verifying reliable ones, and evolving into a stronger model. Imagine: a shared UMM with Generation and Understanding pathways produces candidate visual thoughts and decoded answers. Verify: the frozen Understanding pathway scores each candidate by its log-likelihood utility, calibrates the acceptance threshold against thoughts from other problems, and selects the top verified thought under the ground-truth answer or majority vote. Evolve: the verified thought is distilled into the Student Understanding pathway via on-policy token-level JSD distillation from the EMA Teacher (SelfThinker), supported by flow-matching generator refinement (SelfThinker -Gen). No human image annotation is used

Fig. 5 Verified visual thoughts on diagnostic items. papers.abstract: Tumor delineation is required for radiotherapy planning, yet automatic segmentation is limited by errors, predominantly false positives, that distort dose and increase editing time. The radiology report accompanies the scan and localizes disease at the suborgan level, but existing text-promptable models condition on short referring phrases, and most operate in 2D. We present RepConTUR, a single native-3D early-fusion multimodal model that conditions volumetric abdominal tumor segmentation on the narrative report. We extend AbdomenAtlas 3.0 to a suborgan-level promptable segmentation dataset and generate report-based VQA pairs, yielding four report-derived tasks on the same annotations: referring segmentation (RES), report-grounded segmentation (GSEG), report generation (RRG), and visual question answering (VQA). We train RepConTUR, comprising a 3D CT encoder, an early-fusion language model, and a native-3D segmentation module, jointly on the four tasks. Across liver, kidney and pancreas, RepConTUR attains the highest Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), instance-wise precision, and detection F1 among the text-promptable baselines, and adding the report raises mean precision while leaving recall comparable. Against two vision-only specialists, nnU-Net and the report-supervised R-Super, RepConTUR attains the highest value on every in-domain metric for liver and pancreas and the highest mean DSC, recall, precision, and detection F1 over the four out-of-distribution public cohorts. Ablations indicate that conditioning on the narrative report raises detection F1 from 0.499 to 0.528 within the same model, that joint GSEG training raises RES F1 from 0.450 to 0.482, and that the native-3D segmentation module raises GSEG F1 from 0.139 to 0.528 over its 2D counterpart. Code is available at https://github.com/Oncosoft-Research/RepConTUR.
authors: Seunghwan Lee, Sangjoon Park, Jongmin Lee, Yoon Jo Kim, Wonyoung Cho, Jin Sung Kim, Han Joo Chae
bullets: Addresses false-positive tumor delineation errors that increase radiotherapy-planning dose distortion and editing time.
Combines a 3D CT encoder, early-fusion language model, and native-3D segmentation module, jointly trained on segmentation, report generation, and VQA-related tasks.
Extends AbdomenAtlas 3.0 with suborgan-level report-promptable annotations and four report-derived tasks: RES, GSEG, RRG, and VQA.
Outperforms text-promptable baselines on DSC, instance precision, and detection F1 across liver, kidney, and pancreas; report conditioning improves mean precision with comparable recall.
Ablations show gains from report conditioning, joint GSEG training, and native-3D segmentation; evaluation focuses on abdominal tumors and specified public cohorts.

papers.abstract: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.
authors: Subhashini Venugopalan, Jenny Tan, Taylor Roper, Jimmy Tobin, Anton Kast, Alicia Martin, Sam Sepah, Amy Pavel
bullets: Targets inline audio descriptions that must fit naturally into existing video silences, including diverse user-generated content.
MTG-AD contains 36 hours of professionally annotated video and more than 8,000 descriptions created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals.
MTG-AD-Eval provides fine-grained, actionable metrics, including rendered-audio assessment of speech overlap and timing.
Frontier MLLMs describe visual events well and reduce overlaps, but still show weaknesses in narrative pacing and flow.
Automated metrics correlate significantly with human ratings; users narrowly prefer human descriptions but find MLLM outputs highly beneficial for comprehension.

papers.abstract: Medical diagnostic reasoning requires verifiable links between visual evidence and clinical knowledge, yet current medical vision language models are aligned with objectives that reward the wrong behavior. Uniform supervised fine tuning lets easy cases dominate updates while clinically critical boundary cases saturate prematurely. Sparse rewards based only on final-answer correctness cannot assess anatomical grounding or clinical logic, inviting reward hacking through answer shortcuts. We propose MedCBR, a two-stage alignment framework coupling boundary-aware preference optimization with rubric-grounded reinforcement learning. First, we construct counterfactual boundary preferences at the model's capability frontier using empirical pass rates and preference pairs that share reasoning prefixes but diverge at decisive diagnostic branches. Difficulty Weighted Boundary Preference Optimization (DBPO) concentrates learning on this calibrated boundary region. Second, we distill reusable clinical rubrics from boundary trajectories and activate them according to prediction entropy. Entropy Gated Grounded Policy Optimization (EGPO) rewards answer correctness, anatomical grounding, and reasoning fidelity while suppressing rubric noise on reliable samples. A reference policy anchored to the boundary-aligned model couples population-level boundary priors with instance-level uncertainty, making diagnostic reasoning more accurate and clinically grounded. Experiments on six medical benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong general, specialized, and reinforcement learning baselines, reaching 61.2% average accuracy with the largest gains on challenging differential diagnosis tasks. Ablations show super-additive gains: combining the two stages exceeds the sum of their individual improvements.
authors: Hongyu Bai, Jiaqi Zeng, Chunzheng Zhu
bullets: Targets two alignment issues: easy cases dominate supervised updates, while answer-only rewards miss anatomical grounding and clinical reasoning.
Uses DBPO to learn from counterfactual preference pairs at the model’s empirical capability frontier, emphasizing decisive diagnostic branches.
Uses EGPO to activate distilled clinical rubrics based on prediction entropy and reward correctness, anatomical grounding, and reasoning fidelity.
Across six medical benchmarks, MedCBR reaches 61.2% average accuracy and shows its largest gains on challenging differential-diagnosis tasks.
Ablations indicate the two stages provide super-additive benefits when combined.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding is crucial for robots to understand language instructions with visual observations. This paper addresses the problem of visual grounding uncertainties, where a robot uses a black-box vision-language model (VLM) to ground free-form natural-language instructions to target objects. Prevailing methods derive uncertainty from the VLM itself. Yet, outputs of the VLM, e.g., generated uncertainties, are from the same parameters and structures producing the predictions, and inherit the bias. We give a formal Bayesian definition of the problem that treats the VLM prediction as an observation. An external surrogate Bayesian model then quantifies per-query uncertainty over a local neighborhood of a held-out calibration set, decomposed into aleatoric and epistemic components. A hierarchical retrieval across input modalities realizes a compact joint-space neighborhood, mitigating the curse of dimensionality. The estimator further integrates with conformal prediction or model-based planning for active visual grounding, where robots are allowed to take verbal or physical actions to ground targets. Across grounding benchmarks and state-of-the-art VLMs, it consistently improves both calibration and task performance. On a real Fetch robot under open-world instructions, it enables principled trade-offs between confident action and information gathering, substantially improving robustness.
authors: Hanbo Zhang, Tianrun Hu, Cedar Site Bai, Anxing Xiao, David Hsu
bullets: Targets biased uncertainty estimates produced internally by black-box vision-language models (VLMs).
Treats each VLM prediction as an observation and decomposes local uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components.
Uses hierarchical cross-modal retrieval to construct compact joint-space neighborhoods from held-out calibration data.
Integrates with conformal prediction and model-based planning for active visual grounding through verbal or physical actions.
Improves calibration and grounding performance across benchmarks and VLMs, including more robust behavior on a real Fetch robot.

papers.abstract: Thinking vision-language models reason for thousands of tokens, yet still miss small details in high-resolution images. Zooming methods pay for extra inference passes, and outcome rewards never tell the model where to look at. In Qwen3.5-4B, we find that the bottleneck is selection, not seeing: a few attention heads, which we call localization heads, pick the evidence out of thousands of visual tokens; ablating four of them costs 13.2 points more than ablating four random heads, and their focus fades as the reasoning grows. We therefore propose Localization-Head Alignment (LHA), which makes attention a training signal: whenever the reasoning states a visual fact, these heads learn to look at the focal region rather than the background, as an auxiliary loss in both SFT and RL training. On benchmarks of V*, HR-Bench 4K and TreeBench, LHA lifts Qwen3.5-4B from 74.1% to 76.6% accuracy, the best single-pass 4B result we evaluate, ahead of multi-pass zooming and released 7B models. Alignment alone adds 1.8 points over otherwise identical training while shortening reasoning by 20%, and the gains carry over to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
authors: Yuan Wang, Wei Wu, Hongning Wang
bullets: The main bottleneck is selecting visual evidence, not processing high-resolution images.
A small set of localization heads identifies relevant regions; disrupting four causes a 13.2-point larger accuracy loss than disrupting random heads.
LHA uses an auxiliary attention-alignment loss whenever reasoning states a visual fact, and supports both supervised and reinforcement learning.
On V*, HR-Bench 4K, and TreeBench, LHA improves Qwen3.5-4B from 74.1% to 76.6% accuracy and reduces reasoning by 20%.
The approach also transfers to Qwen2.5-VL-3B, but its scope is evaluated on the reported benchmarks and models.

papers.abstract: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently fail to recognize culture-specific concepts, especially from underrepresented regions. Effectively injecting this long-tail knowledge into existing models remains a challenge. In this work, we investigate knowledge editing as a targeted alternative by introducing CulturalBind, a benchmark comprising 3.2K images of 1K concepts from 6 domains, designed to evaluate culture-aware cross-modal knowledge as well as concept-level knowledge editing in VLMs. Pre-edit evaluation reveals that textual and visual knowledge is decoupled: models often demonstrate text-based knowledge of cultural concepts but fail to identify them from images. We then evaluate editing methods in single and sequential scenarios. Although current methods successfully correct individual visual recognition errors, they exhibit low cross-modal portability, failing to integrate edits into the model's broader parametric knowledge. Furthermore, performance degrades rapidly under sequential editing, highlighting the need for comprehensive adaptation approaches that better consolidate multimodal knowledge over time.
authors: Malvina Nikandrou, Georgios Pantazopoulos, Ioannis Konstas, Alessandro Suglia
bullets: Cultural knowledge from underrepresented regions is often poorly recognized in images despite being known textually.
CulturalBind benchmarks 3.2K images covering 1K concepts across 6 domains for cross-modal knowledge and editing evaluation.
Current editing methods can fix individual visual recognition errors but have limited cross-modal portability.
Sequential editing causes rapid performance degradation, revealing weak knowledge consolidation.
The findings motivate more comprehensive methods for sustained multimodal adaptation.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn conversations with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reuse input context, but long multimodal inputs increase time to first token (TTFT). Query-aware hard pruning reduces prefill tokens but permanently excludes information that later questions may require. We propose Raincheck, a framework for deferred multimodal prefill that decouples initial token selection from later information availability. An existing pruning method selects tokens for initial prefill; Raincheck preserves and progressively prefills unselected tokens in source order using unused compute capacity during decode. Unfinished prefill continues after answer return during available scheduling gaps. Attention visibility control and affine state mapping enable context updates after generation begins in full-attention and hybrid recurrent models. Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B with 30% initial multimodal-token retention. Across both models and four pruning methods, Raincheck recovers on average 77.7% and 60.4% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on MultiVerse and ConvBench, respectively. On MultiVerse, the SGLang implementation reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill, with less than 0.5% increase in mean time per output token (TPOT).
authors: Wenjie Huang, Jun Zhang, Hongyaoxing Gu, Haoyang Huang, Tianqi Xu, Xinyue Hao, Xinyi Hu, Xinle Du, Jun Dai, Shuang Ge, Chen Lei, Yue Li, Mingcheng Wan
bullets: Targets high time to first token caused by long multimodal inputs and hard pruning’s irreversible information loss.
Uses initial token pruning, then progressively prefills omitted tokens during decode or scheduling gaps.
Supports full-attention and hybrid recurrent models through attention visibility control and affine state mapping.
Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads.
With 30% initial token retention, recovers 77.7% and 60.4% of hard-pruning quality loss on MultiVerse and ConvBench; TTFT falls by up to 24.1% on MultiVerse with under 0.5% TPOT increase.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in test-time optimization have shown that the multimodal reasoning performance of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) can be improved during inference without modifying backbone model parameters. However, existing approaches primarily operate at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process largely uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation. To address this limitation, we propose LatentWeave, a test-time framework that treats multimodal reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory. LatentWeave performs structured Latent Weaving, progressively refining intermediate hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations, and further introduces Reasoning Anchors via lightweight WEAVE tokens to stabilize reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. These mechanisms are designed to enable fine-grained, step-aware intervention in the latent reasoning process while keeping the main MLLM backbone parameters fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines; the contribution of latent optimization, anchor training, and additional test-time computation is analyzed separately in the ablation and efficiency studies. Our code is available at https://github.com/jins7/LatentWeave.
authors: Fanci Meng, Kun Wang, Guibin Zhang, Xinlei Yu, Jiaming Zhang, Ming Li, Yang Wang
bullets: Targets error accumulation and limited control in autoregressive latent reasoning.
Applies structured, segment-wise refinement to intermediate hidden states through Latent Weaving.
Uses lightweight WEAVE tokens as Reasoning Anchors to stabilize and guide answer-oriented generation.
Reports improvements over evaluated baselines across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Ablation and efficiency studies separately examine latent optimization, anchor training, and added test-time computation.

papers.abstract: View- and target-specific echocardiography AI models capture useful but complementary information and may not achieve sufficient predictive performance in isolation. A learned ensemble is a natural way to combine these outputs, but heterogeneous models typically require each output to be converted into a binary decision, probability, confidence score, or fixed-length feature vector. We developed a supervised large language model (LLM)-based late-fusion module that directly aggregates view-specific predicted finding statements and predicted measurements in language space and learns a case-level fusion function. In patient-level three-fold cross-validation of 859 examinations from 646 patients, the proposed method integrated heterogeneous outputs within a single framework, performed comparably to the best-performing reference strategy evaluated, and outperformed a general-purpose LLM without task-specific training. These results suggest that a supervised LLM can combine multiple upstream models without model-specific output conversion or feature engineering that requires medical knowledge.

papers.abstract: We present Youtu-Parsing-Omni, an omni-modal parser that converts documents, images, audio, and video into structured records grounded in space and time, providing a perception layer for agents that read, locate, and cite evidence across modalities. Its design rests on one encoder for every modality and one schema for every task. Youtu-Omni-Encoder, initialized from a pre-trained language model to strengthen text reading, encodes all modalities with shared weights in a unified space-time coordinate system, and a few fusion layers let video frames attend to concurrent audio, bringing cross-modal fusion and temporal alignment into perception itself. OmniSchema unifies the outputs of all ten parsing tasks, allowing a single self-evolving post-training procedure, OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD), to provide a shared token-role-based objective across tasks. In each round, the model is trained on its own rollouts against token-level targets from a reference-conditioned copy of itself, which is then refreshed with the trained weights, so that the parser and its supervision co-evolve. With a single 5 B-parameter checkpoint, Youtu-Parsing-Omni achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench v1.6 (96.96 Overall) and leads all open-weight models on OmniParsingBench (75.08 Avg.), with its advantage concentrated on audio and video. It also achieves the best overall chart-parsing score (95.02) and the highest exact chemical-fingerprint agreement among compared systems, and matches a dedicated optical-music model in character-level transcription of typeset sheet music while staying far ahead of general-purpose systems. Code and model weights are publicly available.
authors: Yunhang Shen, Zhangquan Chen, Xiaotian Li, Zhongpeng Cai, Qing Zhou, Zekai Zhang, Kun Zhang, Zezhong Wu, Jian Hu, Haihan Gao, Heting Gao, Xin Li, Yinsong Liu, Deqian Jiang, Di Yin, Haoyu Cao, Xing Sun, Bing Liu, Yanqiu Qu, Yunfei Wu, Kun Yin, Zhixiang Wei, Yongxiang Hua, Qianyu Li, Xiaoxing Hu, Peiyuan Zhang, Lijiang Li, Dong Xu, Zhenchuan Yang, Yiliang Jiang

OSAD uses self-generated rollouts and refreshed reference models for self-evolving post-training.
A single 5B-parameter checkpoint reports leading results on OmniDocBench v1.6 and among open-weight models on OmniParsingBench, especially for audio and video.
It also performs strongly on chart parsing, chemical fingerprints, and typeset sheet-music transcription; code and weights are public.

We compare how visual and audio inputs are encoded before reaching the language model in the conventional design and in Youtu-Parsing-Omni. (a) Existing omni-modal parsers encode pixels and audio with two separately pre-trained towers, whose streams first meet inside the language model. (b) Youtu-Parsing-Omni replaces both towers with a single encoder, Youtu-Omni-Encoder. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful tool for improving multimodal reasoning. However, standard outcome supervision suffers from credit assignment ambiguity, as a model may receive positive rewards by exploiting language priors or dataset shortcuts rather than grounding its reasoning in the requisite visual evidence. This makes high-quality negative responses critical, since effective negatives should remain plausible under the current policy while exposing the shortcut that should be suppressed. In this paper, we propose EVAN, a multimodal reinforcement learning framework utilizing EVidence-Ablated Negatives to train LMMs against their own language-prior failures. EVAN first identifies highly visually dependent examples using a scaled image information gain metric and preserves data diversity with a mixed-ranking strategy. It then constructs evidence-ablated images by masking the most discriminative image patches, eliciting plausible but visually ungrounded responses from the current policy. During policy optimization, these negative responses are incorporated as bounded auxiliary signals under the clean image, penalizing shortcut learning while maintaining RL stability. Experiments across challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that EVAN mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/DawnLIU35/EVAN.git.
authors: Chenxi Liu, Tianyi Xiong, Yanshuo Chen, Heng Huang
bullets: RLVR outcome rewards can miss whether reasoning is grounded in images, allowing language-prior shortcuts.

These negatives are used as bounded auxiliary penalties during policy optimization to suppress shortcut learning while preserving stability.
Experiments on challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks show improved modality balance and performance over strong RLVR baselines.
Scope: the approach targets multimodal reasoning settings where visual evidence is necessary.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have led to significant progress in visual reasoning capabilities. However, existing benchmarks curate image-question pairs pertaining to object categories with few instances, enabling trivial object referencing and limited visual ambiguity. In this work, we introduce MIMO-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs in a Multi-Instance per Multi-Object categories (MIMO) setting. Each image-question pair in our benchmark pertains to instances belonging to object categories with multiple instances. The presence of such similar feature distractors causes hindrance in basic visual reasoning tasks, necessitating the referring expression to be composed of multiple visual subtasks to uniquely and unambiguously identify the target object. MIMO-Bench comprises 3,802 image-question pairs across attribute binding and numerical counting tasks. Despite impressive performances on existing benchmarks, both SOTA open-source (InternVL, QwenVL) and proprietary (Gemini, GPT-5) models exhibit substantially lower performance on MIMO-Bench, highlighting their limitations in the MIMO setting. The benchmark will be made publicly available.
authors: Saumya Mundra, Ajoy Mondal, Vineeth N Balasubramanian, C. V. Jawahar
bullets: Existing visual-reasoning benchmarks often contain few object instances, allowing relatively easy object reference.
MIMO-Bench introduces 3,802 image-question pairs involving multiple instances across multiple object categories.
Tasks cover attribute binding and numerical counting, requiring multi-step referring expressions to disambiguate targets.
Both open-source models such as InternVL and QwenVL and proprietary models such as Gemini and GPT-5 perform substantially worse in this setting.
The benchmark is intended to be publicly available.

papers.abstract: Gardening in the backyard implies living there, while checking into an Airbnb more likely means staying for a few days. Such duration judgments are important for understanding human mobility, travel behavior, and social context. However, duration is rarely stated explicitly in social media posts and must instead be inferred from noisy textual, visual, and contextual cues. In this paper, we investigate whether vision-language models possess such duration commonsense. We create a new corpus of geotagged tweets co-annotated by humans and LLMs to serve as a testbed for this task. We find that state-of-the-art models struggle with duration inference, even when guided by multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting. Error analyses further reveal that models often fail to integrate critical contextual information, or they overly rely on prominent visual details while overlooking subtle hashtags and semantic nuances. These findings underscore the significant challenges remaining in context-aware multimodal understanding.
authors: Chenyang Yu, Zhaomin Xiao, Yan Huang, Eduardo Blanco
bullets: Introduces duration commonsense reasoning as a task for interpreting human mobility and social context.
Builds a geotagged-tweet corpus co-annotated by humans and LLMs.
Evaluates vision-language models, including with multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Models often miss important context, hashtags, and semantic nuances while overemphasizing salient visual details.
Results highlight persistent challenges in context-aware multimodal understanding.

papers.abstract: Visual rule reasoning asks whether multimodal models can recover an abstract concept from a few examples. Existing studies either infer rules from visual examples but evaluate only classification or verbalization, or supervise executable generation with rules provided as input. Consequently, the relationship between visual rule understanding and reliable rule instantiation remains insufficiently explored. We present Bongard-Forge100k, a controlled benchmark, together with RuleForge, a backbone-agnostic framework that jointly learns visual rule understanding and rule-conditioned executable generation. The benchmark contains 108,797 problems: 86,000 for training, 19,297 for testing familiar rules, and 3,500 for testing held-out rule compositions. The framework progresses through rule-understanding training, joint understanding and scene-program supervision, and refinement via execution-grounded reinforcement learning with Understanding Replay. Executing generated programs under multiple random seeds provides verifiable feedback on executability, rule satisfaction, diversity, and robustness. With UniLIP as the primary backbone, RuleForge improves multiple-choice accuracy over the base model by 20.93 percentage points on familiar rules and 28.42 percentage points on held-out rule compositions, while increasing scene-level rule satisfaction on familiar rules from 2.91% to 70.99%. Additional experiments on InternVL3.5, Qwen3-VL, and Show-o2 demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed training data and framework across diverse multimodal architectures.
authors: Weifeng Xu, Yaxiong Wang, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Introduces Bongard-Forge100k, a 108,797-problem benchmark covering familiar rules and held-out rule compositions.

With UniLIP, improves multiple-choice accuracy by 20.93 points on familiar rules and 28.42 points on held-out compositions.
Raises familiar-rule scene satisfaction from 2.91% to 70.99%; results extend across several multimodal backbones.

papers.abstract: Human handwriting is produced as an ordered sequence of pen movements, but an offline image keeps only the final ink. Handwriting trajectory recovery aims to restore the ordered stroke points and their pen-up/pen-down transitions. Existing image-trajectory pair datasets are recorded with digitizing tablets under controlled conditions, which limits writer coverage and stylistic diversity. Moreover, there is no benchmark that measures the visual grounding capabilities of general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for the stroke trajectory recovery task. In this work, we introduce inkGround, a benchmark for stroke trajectory recovery from full-page, camera-captured handwriting. inkGround pairs 537 page images (~18.7k words, ~163k strokes) with reference trajectories produced by a pretrained offline-to-online model, filtered by OCR agreement, and verified by human raters. Because these references are pseudo-labels that represent one plausible pen trajectory, we also evaluate VLMs on the IAM-OnDB dataset, which provides recorded pen trajectories. We cast the task as text-conditioned point grounding: given a page image and a target word, the model must locate the word and output its ordered stroke points. Outputs are scored by trajectory fidelity (DTW, Chamfer distance), readability of the rendered strokes (Accurate Rate, Correct Rate), and style similarity. We benchmark four open-source and three frontier closed-source VLMs with a shared in-context prompt. Closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produce legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also holds on IAM-OnDB.

Evaluates trajectory fidelity, rendered-stroke readability, and style similarity across four open-source and three closed-source VLMs.
Closed-source models—especially Gemini-3.1-Pro—generate legible trajectories close to references, with the ranking replicated on IAM-OnDB.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.
authors: Lu Wang, Zhuoran Jin, Longxiang Wang, Junhong Chen, Yupu Hao, Yao Xu, Daojian Zeng, Yubo Chen, Kang Liu, Guang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Existing systems often assume complete information, risking endless waiting or hallucinated answers when video or user intent is unclear.

Models remain substantially challenged: the strongest reported model reaches 52.18% on the Ask-F1 metric.
The benchmark covers both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, emphasizing proactive information seeking.

papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) can process speech directly, but it remains unclear how well they use the non-lexical acoustic information that speech carries. We study this question through pain, using TAME-Pain, which contains pain-neutral Harvard sentences and spoken pain ratings recorded at different self-reported pain levels. We introduce HEAR, a four-stage diagnostic framework that traces pain-related information from the speech signal to the model's prediction, and apply it to seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs. On the Harvard sentences, where pain can only be inferred from the voice, all models perform at chance level, and same-speaker references or few-shot examples improve balanced accuracy by no more than six points. On the spoken ratings, the same models reach 87.5-99.7% balanced accuracy. Layer-wise probing of open-weight LALMs shows that pain can be decoded from early audio representations (74.1% balanced accuracy for binary prediction and 45.0% for three-class severity), but that this information, along with most pain-associated acoustic cues, decreases in deeper layers. In an acoustic perception test, weaker models cannot distinguish even large changes in these cues, whereas stronger models can but still fail to infer pain. Finally, we recover pain-related acoustic cues and directly reinject them as structured text into the prompt, which improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points. These results indicate that current LALMs encode paralinguistic information in early layers that is largely unavailable when the model produces its answer.
authors: Wenqi Li, Xiangjue Dong, Sulaiman Vesal
bullets: On pain-neutral Harvard sentences, where pain is conveyed only through voice, all seven LALMs perform at chance; references and few-shot examples help by at most six balanced-accuracy points.
On spoken pain ratings, models achieve 87.5–99.7% balanced accuracy, suggesting performance depends strongly on task and available linguistic information.
HEAR traces pain information from audio to prediction: pain is decodable in early representations but declines in deeper layers, along with most associated acoustic cues.
Stronger models can perceive large acoustic changes yet still fail to infer pain; reinjecting recovered cues as structured text improves pairwise prediction by up to 32 points.

papers.title: Do Audio LLMs HEAR Pain? Tracing Acoustic Evidence from Speech to Language Reasoning

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.
authors: Yu Liu, Youxing Li, Yuedong Tan, Zhiwei Yang, Zihan Su, Hanqi Feng, Shaojie Zhang, Libin Liao, Zihao Wan, Chenxu Wu, Cong Cao, Fangfang Yuan, Yanbing Liu, Ziheng Chen, Pei Fu, Radu Timofte, Zongwei Wu, Nicu Sebe, Barnabas Poczos, Jian Luan
bullets: Addresses when to introduce fresh experience, complementing methods that focus on what experience to generate.
Uses reward variation and training accuracy to detect declining learning signals without validation or test scores.
Generates multimodal questions from a static library of model-authored programs with independently checkable answers.
Automatically verifies task properties and refresh rules, while separately auditing generated answers.
Raises average performance from 57.77 to 61.05 using 800 fresh tasks.

papers.abstract: The large-scale digitisation of medieval manuscripts creates a growing need for automated iconographic indexing. We evaluate two complementary paradigms for this task on 9,735 full-folio images annotated with 2,333 TIMEL concepts: generative Vision-Language Models (VLM) and supervised discriminative classifiers (SDC). The VLM experiments evaluate fine-tuning, structured JSON decoding, taxonomybased candidates generation, and deterministic reranking. The discriminative experiments evaluate flat, hierarchy-aware, and patch-attention heads over a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Our results highlight key functional differences: ML-Decoder (SDC) achieves the strongest overall retrieval performance (precision@1 of 0.696, MRR of 0.806), with loss calibration (Asymmetric Loss) serving as the primary performance lever. While SDCs provide superior precision and reliability within a closed vocabulary, VLMs offer strong semantic generalization and broad taxonomic coverage, particularly through structured JSON targets and verify-calibrate reranking (hierarchical F1 of 0.559). Furthermore, model behavior strongly depends on concept abstraction: SDCs excel at perceptually grounded descriptive concepts, whereas VLMs provide useful hypotheses for complex interpretative scenes. Finally, we find that enforcing explicit hierarchy within model architectures limits coverage compared to spatial feature aggregation. Overall, rather than competing approaches, SDCs and VLMs emerge as complementary components for future hybrid indexing systems combining structured retrieval with exploratory annotation assistance. As a methodological contribution, we define the soft F1 metric to provide a taxonomy-aware evaluation that credits semantically close predictions based on lowest common ancestors.
authors: Vincent Jolivet (ENC, CJM), Lucas Terriel (ENC), Chahan Vidal-Gor{\`e}ne (CJM, ENC)
bullets: Evaluates generative VLMs and supervised discriminative classifiers on 9,735 folio images annotated with 2,333 TIMEL concepts.
ML-Decoder achieves the strongest retrieval performance, with precision@1 of 0.696 and MRR of 0.806; Asymmetric Loss is the main performance lever.
VLMs show broader taxonomic coverage and semantic generalization, especially with structured JSON targets and verify-calibrate reranking.
Classifiers perform best on perceptually grounded concepts, whereas VLMs better support hypotheses for complex interpretative scenes.
The approaches are complementary: the study proposes hybrid systems and introduces taxonomy-aware soft F1 evaluation.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs), which can process and generate diverse modalities within a single framework, have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm. However, when these models undergo continual learning on multiple tasks across different modalities, their learning and forgetting dynamics remain poorly understood. In this paper, we systematically investigate how architectural design and adaptation method shape intra-modal learning and cross-modal interference between the generation and understanding sides. Specifically, we report three findings. First, the severity of cross-modal interference decreases with the degree of modality-specific parameter isolation. Second, a within-model asymmetry: the generation side of a UMM is markedly more fragile than its understanding side. Third, what post-training adds is the first to be forgotten: purely post-training capabilities such as personalized generation collapse by 84\% to 90\%, while pretraining capabilities remain stable. Together, these results clarify how parameter isolation and post-training fragility shape UMMs' learning and forgetting dynamics, offering a starting point for developing continually evolving UMMs.
authors: Xinrui Wang, Zhihao Chen, Jia Tang, Alexandra Gomez-Villa, Bartlomiej Twardowski, Joost van de Weijer, Songcan Chen
bullets: Greater modality-specific parameter isolation reduces cross-modal interference.
The generation side is substantially more fragile than the understanding side.
Post-training capabilities, such as personalized generation, are forgotten first, while pretrained capabilities remain stable.
The findings provide design guidance for building continually adapting multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Humans routinely consume multimodal content, where textual and visual information is naturally interleaved. Although Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) can jointly generate text and images, multimodal interleaved generation remains largely underexplored. Progress in this area is hindered by two key limitations: (1) the lack of well-defined interleaved generation tasks and corresponding training data, and (2) the absence of fine-grained evaluation protocols that can reliably diagnose model performance across different capability dimensions. To this end, we present IntReal, comprising two complementary components: IntReal-100K, a real-world dataset of multimodal interleaved samples spanning four major categories, and the IntReal Evaluation Suite, which evaluates model performance across seven complementary dimensions using specialized expert models, enabling coarse-to-fine diagnosis. Extensive experiments validate our evaluation suite through low inter-metric redundancy (max pairwise absolute Spearman's $\rho \leq 0.42$ ), high agreement with human judgments (83.3% accuracy), and strong consistency across different expert evaluators (Spearman's $\rho > 0.9$ ), supporting the complementarity and reliability of our metrics. By benchmarking four families of UMMs, we show that IntReal Evaluation Suite reveals distinct strengths and weaknesses across models. Post-training experiments demonstrate the utility of IntReal-100K for improving interleaved generation and further show that training unimodal generation can also benefit interleaved generation. These findings suggest that interleaved generation can benefit from modality-specific optimization, rather than requiring joint text-image training at every stage.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) show strong performance in radiology report generation (RRG) and medical visual question answering (Med-VQA), producing free-form clinical descriptions and answers from medical images. However, they may generate clinically meaningful statements that lack visual evidence or contradict image content. We refer to these errors as visually irrelevant hallucinations and investigate them at the phrase level. We propose CLEAR (Counterfactual Localized Evaluation of Alignment and Response), a model-agnostic post-hoc framework for phrase-level hallucination risk estimation. CLEAR decomposes generated responses into visually assessable clinical phrases. For each phrase, phrase-conditioned grounding identifies a candidate visual region, which is selectively perturbed by a localized counterfactual intervention. CLEAR characterizes the intervention using two complementary auditing cues: response cues, capturing semantic and clinically meaningful changes in the generated response, and alignment cues, measuring changes in image-phrase compatibility. These cues are normalized and jointly modeled to estimate phrase-level hallucination risk. Across four datasets spanning RRG and Med-VQA, CLEAR outperforms state-of-the-art hallucination detection baselines across multiple medical and general-purpose VLMs. On MIMIC-CXR, CLEAR improves AUPRC from 85.10% to 90.23%. Its effectiveness is further validated on a GT-derived controlled VIH benchmark. These results establish visually irrelevant hallucination as an important fine-grained reliability failure mode in medical VLMs and demonstrate the value of model-agnostic visual-support auditing for more trustworthy multimodal clinical generation.
authors: Ke Zou, Nan Zhou, Tao Yang, Meng Liu, Linchao He, Zehui Liao, Ling Huang, Guangren Huang, Yidi Chen, Yi Zhang, Hu Chen, Huazhu Fu
bullets: Medical VLMs can produce clinically meaningful statements that are visually unsupported or contradict the image.

It grounds each phrase to a candidate region, perturbs that region, and combines response-change and image–phrase alignment cues to estimate hallucination risk.
Across four radiology report generation and Med-VQA datasets, CLEAR outperforms existing detection baselines across multiple VLMs.
On MIMIC-CXR, CLEAR raises AUPRC from 85.10% to 90.23% and is additionally validated on a controlled benchmark.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are advancing in multimodal understanding and reasoning, accelerating medical model development. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to determine disease location and nature, differentiate syndromes and guide treatment. This diagnostic process constitutes a complete chain of reasoning. We present Fu-TCM, a multimodal TCM LLM trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples derived from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and publicly available datasets. The model was further optimized using Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which explicitly targets syndrome differentiation through rewards for response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B led all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, achieving a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% and surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results across all six benchmarks by 7.13 percentage points. Its largest margin was 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Case-level analyses further showed a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models. These findings suggest that TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable and that structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.

Fu-TCM-27B achieved a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% across six benchmarks, leading all evaluated benchmarks.
Case analyses found that more accurate intermediate reasoning fields were generally associated with better final syndrome selection.

papers.abstract: Short video platforms have become a primary channel for black and gray industry operations in internet finance, where inducements such as prompts to like, follow, join private chat groups, or click external links frequently steer users toward fraud. Because such videos are short, dynamic, and often convey intent through fleeting visual cues rather than stable text, a moderation system must guarantee detection recall and localize the offending segment so reviewers inspect only the relevant clip. Existing OCR+LLM pipelines transcribe on-screen text frame by frame and classify the transcript, but exploit only textual information. Many inducements are conveyed through visual cues OCR cannot observe, and keyframe-based localization cannot recover precise temporal boundaries. We explore OCR+MLLM, which augments the text pipeline with a Multimodal Large Language Model, and compare three routes: OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a large zero-shot MLLM, along detection, latency, token consumption, and deployment complexity. OCR preserves the text signal that guarantees recall, while the MLLM jointly performs OCR-grounded discrimination and temporal grounding, localizing both textual and non-textual inducements. We construct a dataset of 2,419 internet finance short videos (66.49 hours) with 3,194 annotated events across four categories, and study reward design for RL-based grounding under class imbalance. We report two findings: auxiliary reward terms are exploited through reward hacking, and stronger localization rewards degrade class-balanced detection. We therefore design a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling. Experiments show OCR+MLLM localizes better than the keyframe OCR+LLM baseline (mIoU 26.52 vs. 14.49) and detects non-textual inducements that text-only pipelines miss, while maintaining 67.0 percent macro recall.
bullets: Targets prompts to like, follow, join private groups, or click external links that may lead to fraud.
Combines OCR with a multimodal LLM for joint discrimination and temporal grounding of textual and visual cues.
Evaluates OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a zero-shot MLLM across detection, latency, token use, and deployment complexity.
Uses a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling after finding reward hacking and detection–localization trade-offs.
On 2,419 annotated videos, OCR+MLLM raises mIoU to 26.52 versus 14.49 for keyframe OCR+LLM and detects non-textual inducements missed by text-only methods.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

papers.selection_reason: Open MoE hybrid Mamba-Transformer LLMs with long-context training, multimodal capabilities, and efficient deployment.
papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
papers.tldr: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning are open hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE models optimized for efficient reasoning, long-context, multimodal, and agentic AI workloads.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) ground language in visual evidence, yet their semantic reasoning can be exploited through transferable black-box adversarial attacks. Existing attacks typically allocate perturbations using surrogate-model saliency, which may not reflect how an unseen MLLM semantically interprets or relies on different image regions. We introduce VISTA (Vulnerability-Informed Semantic Transfer Attacks), a black-box framework that identifies semantically vulnerable visual regions from an MLLM's responses without access to gradients, logits, parameters, or internal representations. VISTA supports two attack settings: (i) VISTA-Proxy, a pure-transfer setting that probes an open-source MLLM and transfers the resulting adversarial examples to unseen commercial MLLMs without querying them; and (ii) VISTA-Victim, a query-assisted setting that probes the target MLLM to capture model-specific semantic vulnerabilities. VISTA builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior (UBMB) map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts, then uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing and a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions. Across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, VISTA achieves up to 97 % attack success rate (ASR) while maintaining a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) above 30 dB. Notably, VISTA-Proxy achieves up to 93 % ASR without querying the final victim, demonstrating that response-derived semantic vulnerability can enable effective transfer across heterogeneous MLLMs.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between surrogate-model saliency and how unseen MLLMs actually interpret visual regions.
Builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts.
Uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing with a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions.
Supports pure-transfer VISTA-Proxy and query-assisted VISTA-Victim attack settings.
Reports up to 97% ASR with PSNR above 30 dB; VISTA-Proxy reaches up to 93% ASR without querying the final victim across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6.
