papers.abstract: Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. However, quantization error is widely assumed to cause unavoidable semantic loss, fundamentally limiting the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and positioning continuous visual representations as an intrinsic upper bound. Using multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, we revisit this assumption and find quantization error unreliable, as discrete representations with substantially larger errors can achieve better understanding. Instead, the effective bit budget of discrete indices emerges as a key determinant of downstream performance. However, existing quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute progressively less semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this saturation, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization, which quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks. It continues to improve at larger bit budgets, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Trained on industrial-scale multimodal data, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, outperforming UniAR and Emu3-Chat by 22.8% and 59.2%, respectively, on a nine-metric average. To our knowledge, it is also the first discrete-representation model competitive with strong continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR tasks. We further identify the key principles and a practical recipe enabling this competitiveness. These results and insights support the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models. Code and models are available at https://github.com/hustvl/FVQ
bullets: Quantization error is not a reliable predictor of semantic fidelity; larger-error discrete representations can perform better.
Effective bit budget, rather than quantization error alone, is a key driver of downstream understanding.
Existing quantizers saturate as added codebooks provide diminishing semantic information.
Factorized Vector Quantization uses complementary fixed-dimensional feature views with symmetric parallel codebooks to reduce this saturation.
The resulting model matches continuous-representation performance, including fine-grained OCR, and reports strong gains over prior discrete-representation models.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of FVQ. During quantizer training, multiple dense projections produce complementary views of the same visual feature, which are quantized in parallel by independent codebooks. The selected codewords are combined through tight-frame synthesis for feature reconstruction. In the subsequent VLM training stage, the quantizer is frozen, and only the resulting discrete indices are mapped to newly initialized token embeddings for multimodal understanding. The nine-metric average is computed over MMMU, MathVista, MMStar, OCRBench/10, ChartQA, CharXiv-DQ, CharXiv-RQ, DocVQA, and InfoVQA.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Tongkun Guan, Zhibo Yang, Mingkun Yang, Haocheng Wang, Wei Shen, Xiaokang Yang
bullets: Targets perception degradation during MLLM post-training, where subjective dense captions make reliable rewards difficult.
Perception RL converts verified caption errors into fixed-label QA pairs with rule-based rewards, using chain and multiple-choice formats.
Perception Agentic RL handles unresolved dense cases through multi-turn tool use, with Coordinate Injection and grounding-aware process rewards to reduce spatial errors.
Uses shared cold-start SFT followed by single-turn and multi-turn perception RL.
Achieves 71.6% average accuracy across seven benchmarks, exceeding the same-tool base model by 15.7 points and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 5.2 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Perception RL: from perceptual errors to rewardable QA. (01) Perception tree construction: A hierarchical capability map and model probing reveal perceptual weaknesses, guiding specialized and general data-construction routes. Appendix ?? expands the displayed tree with additional skills and associated failure modes. (02) Rewardable QA construction: A multi-agent pipeline mines and verifies errors in the base model’s captions, then composes them into questions with unambiguous answers. MCQs combine unrelated errors, while chain QA connects correlated errors. (03) Rule-based reward for RL: The resulting QA pairs provide exact-match rewards for training the model’s visual perception. The error distribution and example errors are illustrative.

Fig. 1: PERCEPTRL: making real-world perception rewardable, and training it at two levels. Center: How it becomes rewardable. Open-ended captions contain useful perceptual information but are difficult to score with direct rule-based rewards. We extract and verify perceptual facts from these captions, then formulate QA pairs with fixed answer labels for rule-based training (top). The pipeline organizes tasks from multiple perception families (e.g., color, spatial position, counting, functional state, orientation), using a perception tree to guide data construction (Section 3.2). The difficulty axis is what divides the two levels. Level 1: Perception RL. A single look suffices here, so we train single-turn visual QA under a rule-based outcome reward. The left panel shows what this must fix: an error entering at the perception level is inherited by an otherwise correct reasoning chain, so the answer is wrong for a purely perceptual reason. Level 2: Perception Agentic RL. This tail, where objects are small, scenes are cluttered, or details require magnification, resists a single look, so the model inspects the image over multiple grounded turns with a code interpreter. The right panel illustrates how a grounding error, where a predicted crop or annotation misses its target, can affect subsequent observations. Its propagation and accumulation across successive tool interactions constitute coordinate drift. Coordinate Injection corrects these grounding errors during data construction, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity (Section 3.3).

Fig. 3: Perception Agentic RL: correcting and supervising spatial grounding during multi-turn visual inspection. (01) Coordinate drift. A misplaced annotation changes the visual evidence available to later turns. Subsequent spatial operations can inherit this error, leading to repeated or missed counts. (02) Coordinate Injection (CI). During trajectory construction, CI identifies the intended target of each spatial operation, corrects its coordinates using a VLM judge or the LocateAnything detector, and re-executes the code before the next turn. The corrected trajectories provide cold-start SFT data. (03) Grounding-aware process reward. During RL, a fidelity judge evaluates the predicted boxes and points against their intended targets in the original image. The resulting per-turn rewards complement the final-answer reward and supervise intermediate spatial accuracy (Equation 17).

papers.selection_reason: Improves MLLM fine-grained visual and spatial perception via RL and tool-use supervision.
papers.title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
papers.tldr: PerceptRL improves fine-grained visual perception in MLLMs by turning verified caption errors into rewardable QA tasks and training multi-turn visual inspection with grounding-aware feedback.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) to solve complex visual problems, but also exposes them to CoT hijacking: an adversary implants a backdoor through poisoned fine-tuning so that a visual trigger induces a hijacking turn, redirecting an otherwise faithful reasoning chain to an attacker-chosen answer. However, since the hijack acts within the reasoning chain, existing multimodal backdoor defenses designed for MLLMs that answer directly struggle to detect it. Moreover, inspecting the chain itself does not reliably expose the hijack, since the hijacking turn can resemble honest self-correction in form. In this paper, we find that honest reasoning tends to revise its answer at high-entropy "aha moments", whereas a hijack can overturn a confident answer through a near-deterministic turn. To quantify this contrast, we formalize this phenomenon as belief inertia, the cumulative next-token entropy of a reasoning span minus the answer-belief revision it induces, with markedly lower values for hijacked spans than for honest reasoning spans. Since hijacking tokens are also image-dependent, we further improve detection by restricting the measure to image-dependent spans, yielding visual belief inertia (VBI). Building on this, we propose InertiaGuard, a training-free, test-time detector that flags a trace when its VBI falls below a threshold calibrated on a small set of clean traces. Across various attacks and benchmarks, InertiaGuard achieves higher detection performance than existing baselines, while generalizing to different model architectures and trigger types.
bullets: CoT hijacking redirects a model’s reasoning and answer after an attacker implants a backdoor triggered by an image.
Existing defenses struggle because hijacks occur inside reasoning chains and can resemble honest self-correction.
The paper defines belief inertia as reasoning-span token entropy minus the resulting answer-belief revision.
Visual belief inertia (VBI) focuses this measure on image-dependent spans, improving sensitivity to visual hijacks.
InertiaGuard is a training-free, test-time detector calibrated on a small set of clean traces and performs better than existing baselines across attacks, benchmarks, architectures, and trigger types.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CoT hijacking combines low belief inertia with strong image dependence. Each dot is a reasoning step (gray: clean; red: hijacking) sampled from a validation set. (a, b) Hijacking steps induce large belief revisions B at low entropy cost H , resulting in lower belief inertia than clean reasoning. (c, d) Because hijacking steps also exhibit strong image dependence, adding this criterion filters out most low-inertia clean steps while retaining hijacking steps.

Figure 2: Illustration of INERTIAGUARD. Although the model initially recognizes the stop sign, a trigger-induced hijacking turn redirects its answer from (b) to (a). To detect this redirection, INERTIAGUARD first identifies image-dependent steps, then compares the belief revision across spans containing these steps with their cumulative entropy. Because the hijacking span induces a large revision at little entropy cost, its belief inertia falls below the calibrated threshold, causing the trace to be flagged.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes InertiaGuard, a test-time detector for backdoored multimodal reasoning models, utilizing 'visual belief inertia' (VBI) to identify hijacking turns based on entropy differences in reasoning chains.
papers.title: Detecting Chain-of-Thought Hijacking in Backdoored Multimodal Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: InertiaGuard detects visual trigger-induced chain-of-thought hijacking by identifying unusually deterministic answer revisions in multimodal reasoning traces.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are deployed as zero-shot judges of image aesthetics, and panels of several models are recommended, on thin evidence, as the way to make such judges reliable. On two human-rated datasets, EVA and PARA, we find that a panel of holistic judges never significantly beats its best member, whether the verdicts are averaged or fused by a learned combiner. What a panel is worth depends on what it is fed. We therefore have each model score each image on the five dimensions of a frozen, human-written rubric and fuse those scores, alongside each model's verdict, across model families with an out-of-fold combiner. The dimension scores measure what their labels claim: with the overall human score partialled out, a dimension prompt carries more attribute-specific information than the holistic prompt in 28 of 30 model-attribute cells. Fused, they beat the best single VLM in all ten three-family panels on EVA (against that best single model, +0.07 Spearman rho for the strongest trio and +0.10 for the pre-declared one, and +0.06 and +0.07 when averaged over twenty fold partitions; against the panel mean, the primary test gives +0.118 on its EVA design set), and on PARA they reach parity under Spearman rho and a small, non-significant loss under Kendall tau-b, where one model already captures 85% of the human noise ceiling. It is not a feature-count artefact: giving the same combiner an equal number of pure holistic columns, split from the same repetitions, does not reproduce it. The gain costs a few hundred labels, which do not transfer between datasets, and 4.8x the API calls on EVA; we report it with paired bootstraps and Kendall tau-b, alongside a failed pre-registration and the configurations that lost.
bullets: Holistic judge panels never significantly outperform their best member on EVA or PARA.
Models score five frozen, human-written rubric dimensions, and an out-of-fold combiner fuses these scores with holistic verdicts across model families.
Dimension prompts provide more attribute-specific information than holistic prompts in 28 of 30 model–attribute comparisons.
Dimension-aware fusion beats the best single VLM across all ten EVA three-family panels, while reaching parity or a small non-significant loss on PARA.
The approach requires a few hundred dataset-specific labels and 4.8× more EVA API calls; labels do not transfer between datasets.

papers.selection_reason: Studies vision-language model behavior and proposes a transferable rubric-based fusion method for VLM evaluation.
papers.title: Feed the Panel Dimensions, Not Verdicts: Rubric-Decomposed Fusion of Vision-Language Aesthetic Judges
papers.tldr: Feeding VLM panels rubric-based aesthetic dimensions—not just holistic verdicts—makes fusion reliably improve on the best individual judge on EVA, but offers little benefit on PARA.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.
authors: Shilong Li, Xingyuan Bu, Hao Shi, Yun Xing, Weixin Feng, Qiangpeng Yang, Shilei Wen
bullets: Addresses the weakness of language-only reasoning traces, which can lose access to relevant video evidence.
Constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments instead of relying only on coordinates or pasted crops and frames.
Uses visual token prediction over an input-video-derived vocabulary to unify visual reconstruction and text generation.
Supports interleaved text and visual latent states, with a reinforcement-learning extension that jointly optimizes visual and text token actions.
Improves performance across multiple video benchmarks, particularly on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of VideoLVR. (a) A teacher MLLM synthesizes evidence-grounded reasoning trajectories through rejection sampling and trajectory polishing. (b) Visual tokens from regions supporting the same reasoning step are grouped and ordered by timestamp to form latent targets. VideoLVR jointly trains text generation with next-token prediction and latent visual evidence generation with visual token prediction over the input-video visual vocabulary. (c) At inference with the supervised model, each decoder hidden state is projected into a latent visual state and fed back as the input for the next decoding step, enabling autoregressive reasoning over latent visual evidence without additional visual observations.

papers.title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
papers.tldr: VideoLVR lets multimodal models revisit compact latent visual evidence during video reasoning, reducing visual forgetting without greatly expanding context.

papers.abstract: For reliable deployment, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) should recognize when an image provides insufficient evidence to answer a question and withhold unsupported answers. Yet refusal alone is not necessarily evidence of such recognition: models may refuse because of unrelated safety constraints or without identifying the missing evidence. We study how refusal on visually unanswerable questions is shaped by three sources of control: inference-time instructions, post-training, and internal activation interventions. Across three MLLMs on the MoHoBench benchmark, we systematically manipulate the meaning and placement of refusal instructions, compare supervised and preference-based post-training, and intervene on a refusal-related activation direction derived from naturally answered and refused examples. We find that refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with model-specific changes at the sample level that are obscured by aggregate refusal rates. Evidence-aware and general refusal instructions have stronger effects than an intentionally mismatched safety instruction. Post-training produces larger increases in refusal, but can also induce responses that combine refusal language with attempted answers. In contrast, activation intervention produces smaller yet transferable changes across prompt conditions, without evidence of indiscriminate refusal on tested visually answerable samples. These findings show that refusal is jointly shaped by external instructions, post-training, and internal representations, highlighting the need to disentangle evidence recognition from a model's learned propensity to refuse.
authors: Ananth K Suresh, Aveen Dayal, Gouthaman KV, Aditya Pola, Vineeth N Balasubramanian
bullets: Refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with effects that vary across individual samples and models.
Evidence-aware and general refusal prompts influence behavior more than a mismatched safety instruction.
Supervised and preference-based post-training increase refusal more strongly, but may produce responses that refuse while still attempting an answer.
Intervening on a refusal-related activation direction yields smaller but transferable changes across prompts without indiscriminate refusal on tested answerable images.
The study evaluates three MLLMs on MoHoBench and emphasizes separating evidence recognition from general refusal tendencies.

papers.title: When Visual Evidence Is Insufficient: How Instructions, Post-Training, and Internal Activations Shape Refusal in Multimodal Language Models
papers.tldr: Refusal on visually unanswerable questions reflects a mix of evidence recognition, instructions, post-training, and internal representations—not necessarily genuine awareness of missing visual evidence.

papers.abstract: When a multimodal model computes 17+35 from text or 91-39 from a rendered image, it produces the same answer, 52. Does it use one internal concept of number for both, or separate machinery for each path? Similarity metrics such as RSA or CKA cannot settle this question. They give the same score to identical and to rotated directions, and two representations can look alike only because both prepare the same output digits. We therefore use causal interventions. For four conditions (text or image, addition or subtraction), we learn a small subspace of Gemma4-12B-it's residual stream in which swapping coordinates swaps the model's answer. The subspaces answer three questions. First, do the conditions write numbers along the same directions? They do not. Reusing a subspace from text in an image on the same operation recovers only 53.2% of its causal effect. A single rotation and rescaling maps one subspace onto the other and raises recovery to 91.4%, so the conditions share one geometry expressed in different coordinates. Second, does this shared geometry only reflect the digit the model is about to print? To test this, we split each subspace into 9 directions that the output layer reads to choose the next digit and 13 directions that it cannot see. The 13 hidden directions still carry the number, yet changing them barely alters the digit being written. Third, what are these hidden directions for? A model must emit a multi-digit answer one digit at a time, so it can compute the full result early and keep it in reserve. When two numbers share their first digit, swapping the number in the hidden directions leaves the digit being written intact and redirects the next digit in 77.6% of cases. The model thus forms an abstract numerical concept upstream and unfolds it across time: multimodal representations share meaning through relational geometry across distinct coordinate frames.
authors: Oriol Juan Sabater, Alex Ferrando de las Morenas, Pau Rodr\'iguez, Xavier Suau
bullets: Text and image arithmetic use distinct subspaces, but a learned rotation and rescaling aligns them, recovering 91.4% of the causal effect.
Similarity measures alone cannot distinguish shared numerical concepts from representations that merely support the same output digits.
Numerical information exists in hidden directions not directly read by the output layer, beyond the directions controlling the next digit.
Swapping hidden numerical states redirects later digits in 77.6% of cases while preserving the current digit, indicating early computation of the full answer.
The evidence is limited to four conditions: text/image inputs paired with addition/subtraction in Gemma4-12B-it.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the experimental framework. Crossing input modality (T, I) with operation ( , ) yields four conditions reaching the same number. In each condition, we learn a 22-dimensional causal subspace Ri that governs generation (Section 3). While direct reuse fails across modalities, scaled rotations αQ restore causal control to 91.4% (Section 4). Decomposing Ri into a 9-dimensional readout subspace D and a 13-dimensional latent subspace L reveals that numerical geometry survives outside the digit readout and synchronizes into a single shared latent frame (Section 5). Finally, latent numerical identity in L is scheduled across time, redirecting the token emitted at the subsequent autoregressive step (Section 6).

papers.title: Beyond the Readout: A Latent Numerical Frame Shared Across Modality and Operation

papers.abstract: This report presents the implementation and validation of two end-to-end multimodal adaptation pipelines for 3D-aware visual question answering on a custom spatial dataset. The first pipeline fine-tunes HiSpatial-3B, which augments RGB observations with metric-scale 3D point maps; the second adapts Qwen3-VL through memory-efficient QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning. The completed engineering stack covers dataset conversion, image-annotation alignment, monocular geometry preprocessing, instruction construction, mixed-domain training, checkpoint management, batch inference, and automated evaluation. On the target spatial benchmark, HiSpatial adaptation increases overall accuracy from 1.73% before fine-tuning to 79.89% at 3,600 steps. On a separately collected styled split, accuracy improves from 14.9% to 55.1%, indicating transfer beyond the original training set. The Qwen3-VL pipeline is likewise implemented end-to-end for both 8B- and 32B-scale models using mixed-domain QLoRA adaptation. The resulting accuracy improves from 20.74% to 45.27% for Qwen3-VL-8B and from 30.79% to 47.60% for Qwen3-VL-32B. Together, these results establish two complementary and reproducible adaptation pipelines for geometry-aware and general-purpose multimodal spatial reasoning. These results establish a reproducible engineering foundation for subsequent work on metric 3D reasoning, spatial grounding, and domain-adapted multimodal systems, while also identifying training-data composition as a central factor in preserving general multimodal capability during specialization.
authors: Yu Zhang, Xiaogang Wang, Yuhang Cheng, Jingrui Li, Wenbo Chen
bullets: Fine-tunes HiSpatial-3B with RGB images and metric-scale 3D point maps, raising target-benchmark accuracy from 1.73% to 79.89%.
Applies memory-efficient QLoRA supervised fine-tuning to Qwen3-VL-8B and 32B, improving accuracy to 45.27% and 47.60%, respectively.
HiSpatial adaptation transfers to a separately styled split, increasing accuracy from 14.9% to 55.1%.
The engineering stack includes data conversion and alignment, geometry preprocessing, instruction construction, mixed-domain training, checkpointing, inference, and automated evaluation.
The report highlights training-data composition as important for retaining general multimodal capabilities during spatial specialization.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for enhancing the video reasoning capability of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). Despite its empirical effectiveness, we show that outcome-level optimization can introduce an undesirable shortcut amplification effect, whereby models increasingly favor text-prior answers even when they are not supported by the visual evidence. To characterize this behavior, we investigate the training dynamics of video RLVR through the lens of perceptual uncertainty, analyzing how predictive uncertainty evolves under video-conditioned and text-only contexts. Our analysis identifies a perceptual uncertainty collapse phenomenon, in which RL training continuously sharpens the model's answer distribution while the uncertainty reduction attributable to visual evidence progressively diminishes. A further gradient-direction analysis reveals that such confidence enhancement becomes increasingly less aligned with visually grounded uncertainty reduction and is instead dominated by text-prior compression. Motivated by these findings, we propose Bifocal Self-distillation Policy Optimization (BSPO), a self-distillation framework that regulates policy updates with two complementary distributional signals. Specifically, BSPO derives empirical reasoning principles from intra-group correct and incorrect rollouts to identify reasoning-sensitive tokens, and introduces shortcut-aware visual perturbation to penalize predictions that remain invariant when task-relevant visual evidence is weakened. By adaptively reweighting the original RL advantage, BSPO preserves the task-solving benefits of RLVR while promoting updates that are both reasoning-sensitive and visually grounded. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of BSPO in improving video reasoning performance and strengthening visual faithfulness.
authors: Jiafeng Liang, Xianhao Ou, Tao Ren, Rongchuan Mu, Runxuan Liu, Dandan Tu, Ming Liu, See-Kiong Ng, Bing Qin
bullets: RLVR may make models increasingly confident in text-prior answers unsupported by video evidence.
Perceptual uncertainty collapse occurs as visual evidence contributes less to uncertainty reduction during training.
Gradient analysis links this confidence growth more to text-prior compression than to visual grounding.
BSPO combines self-distillation from correct/incorrect rollouts with shortcut-aware visual perturbations to guide policy updates.
Experiments show improved video reasoning performance and stronger visual faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.
authors: Yongqi Shan, Lu Zhang, Jiazuo Yu, Yunzhi Zhuge, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Addresses noise from feeding large numbers of task-irrelevant 3D object tokens to LLMs.
Uses Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) to retain objects relevant to the user instruction.
Uses Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) to integrate pretrained 2D features into 3D representations.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D.
Targets 3D scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding tasks.

papers.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) aims to evaluate the perceptual visual quality of images. Recently, the rapid development of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has significantly advanced the IQA field. By integrating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and reinforcement learning (RL), these models can generate more accurate and interpretable results while relying on less training data. However, existing MLLM-based methods are predominantly constrained to holistic, image-level evaluations and lack the capability to produce fine-grained, localized assessments, which substantially limits their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose VGIQA, a novel IQA model endowed with both local and global quality assessment capabilities. VGIQA is trained via a two-stage paradigm comprising a cold-start phase followed by reinforcement learning. Driven by carefully designed local quality assessment reward functions, our model exhibits exceptional image quality understanding on VGSR-2K, a new dataset we propose specifically for local quality evaluation, significantly outperforming existing open-source MLLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct. Furthermore, the local quality evaluation task can effectively enhance the model's performance on the degradation perception task.
authors: Weichang Wang, Liyu Chen, Shuyue Guan, Jie Hu, Fei Gao, Wei Li, Nannan Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing MLLM-based IQA methods that mainly provide holistic, image-level evaluations.
Uses a two-stage training strategy: cold-start training followed by reinforcement learning with local quality assessment rewards.
Introduces VGSR-2K, a dataset designed for local image-quality evaluation.
Reports strong local quality understanding and outperformance of the compared open-source MLLMs on VGSR-2K.
Finds that local quality assessment also improves degradation perception.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the proposed VGIQA framework. The framework follows a two-stage training paradigm. Stage 1 (Cold Start): The Qwen-based foundation model is initialized via SFT using CoT reasoning data distilled from Qwen3-VL-Plus [2] to establish structural formatting and inject IQA priors. Stage 2 (Multi-Task GRPO): Reinforcement learning jointly optimizes Local Quality Assessment, Degradation Perception, and Score Regression. Alongside a shared format reward, task-specific rewards are dynamically routed: a dedicated local reward exclusively supervises the local task (computing zero for non-local tasks), evaluating spatial bounding boxes via Hungarian Matching, negative DIoU, and F1 Score. Meanwhile, global tasks are optimized via verifiable score and classification/intensity rewards, unifying local-and-global quality evaluation.

Fig. 4: Overview of the VGSR-2K dataset construction pipeline. The dataset is curated via a rigorous human-in-the-loop pipeline. (1) Candidate Generation: Qwen3-VL-Plus [2] and Seed1.6-VL independently process LR-SR image pairs, yielding six candidate spatial bounding boxes. (2) Double-Blind Selection: Two annotator groups select the most consistent candidate; consensus establishes the baseline, while divergence prompts expert resolution. (3) Double-Blind Correction & Merging: Annotators refine baselines by adding or removing boxes. Corrections are merged via the Hungarian algorithm with a negative DIoU cost metric, extracting the MBR for matched pairs. (4) Final Review & Balancing: After expert review, pristine LR-HR image pairs are introduced as negative samples (with empty annotations) to calibrate spatial predictions and prevent trivial over-generation.

Fig. 2: Example applications of the proposed VGIQA framework. Built upon a Qwen-based foundation model, VGIQA achieves comprehensive quality understanding via multi-task reinforcement learning. While existing models (e.g., Q-Insight) are limited to holistic Score Regression and Degradation Perception, VGIQA explicitly bridges the gap in fine-grained Local Quality Assessment. Driven by novel visual grounding rewards, it adopts a rigorous "look and then judge" paradigm—precisely localizing spatial artifacts before formulating final judgments.

Fig. 1: Qualitative visualization of the local quality assessment results. Given a reference image, a distorted image to be evaluated, and a user query, VGIQA produces more reliable and accurate responses compared with the state-of-the-art RL-based IQA method Q-insight and the general large vision-language model Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct [1].

Table 4: Quantitative comparison of the score regression task between our VGIQA and other competitive IQA methods. Results are reported in the format of PLCC/SRCC. All methods except handcrafted ones are trained on the KonIQ dataset. The best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.

Table 2: Ablation study of each training stage on the local quality assessment task. The base model is Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct [1]. The GRPO phase is crucial for the improvement in Local Quality Assessment. The best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison of the local quality assessment task on the VGSR2K dataset. Qwen2.5-VL-72B and Qwen3VL-32B denote Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, respectively. VGIQA significantly outperforms both large-scale general MLLMs and the IQA-specific baseline. The best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.

Table 3: Quantitative comparison of the Degradation Perception task. VGIQA significantly improves the perception accuracy of global physical degradations, especially in Noise and Null(no degradation). The best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.

papers.abstract: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.
authors: Saifullah Saifullah, David Dembinsky, Stefan Agne, Andreas Dengel, Sheraz Ahmed
bullets: Addresses the limited XAI research for models combining document text, layout, and images, especially in high-stakes applications.
Adapts existing XAI methods and metrics to multimodal documents and develops efficient multi-target variants for tasks such as semantic entity recognition.
Systematically evaluates 13 XAI methods across 3 tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 metrics.
Finds that only a few methods perform consistently across evaluation criteria; Occlusion performs best overall.
Diagnostic analyses reveal modality contributions, spatial attribution patterns, and potential dataset biases; code is publicly released.

papers.abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.

bullets: Addresses the limited availability of advanced spoken-interaction systems for minority and low-resource languages.

Evaluation reports 3.86/5 content quality, 9.94% word error rate, and 3.07 UTMOS audio quality.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding on high-resolution screens fails mostly on small targets, and zooming in is a common training-free remedy. However, most existing zooming pipelines do not match the zoom to the target's size, accept the zoomed answer unconditionally and never revisit a wrong answer. To address these issues, we propose AdaGround, a training-free framework with three components: (1) Token-Normalized Adaptive Zooming, which sets the magnification, field of view and zoom depth of each sample from the model's own estimate of the target size; (2) Verifier-in-the-Loop Refinement, which uses one marked-click Yes/No verifier to keep or reject each zoom, choose between zoom chains, trigger re-grounding and, with an existence query, decide when to abstain; and (3) Compositional Structure Grounding, which composes spreadsheet cells from their headers. On Qwen3-VL models, AdaGround surpasses state-of-the-art training-free zooming methods and many trained GUI models, improving accuracy over the backbone by 7.4 to 20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, and its gains carry over to held-out UI-Vision. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/AdaGround
authors: Bingchao Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Chengyu Wang, Jun Huang, Jie Yang, Wei Liu, Dacheng Tao
bullets: Targets zoom magnification, field of view, and depth to the model’s estimated target size.
Uses a marked-click Yes/No verifier to accept or reject zooms, select zoom chains, trigger re-grounding, and abstain when targets may not exist.
Composes spreadsheet-cell targets from their row and column headers.
On Qwen3-VL, improves over the backbone by 7.4–20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, with gains transferring to held-out UI-Vision.
The framework is training-free and evaluated on high-resolution GUI grounding.

papers.abstract: Leading GUI grounders score 93 to 96% on ScreenSpot-v2, and reported gaps between new and prior models are about a point. At this level the useful question is what the remaining errors are. Benchmarks count a click as correct only inside one annotated box, but interfaces often expose one action through several elements: a duplicated link, the label of a checkbox, the title next to a logo. The box is not wrong. The rule is incomplete. We call a click correct when executing it produces the same outcome as clicking the annotated target. A probe that executes and fingerprints about a thousand clicks per page turns this definition into outcome maps and an execution judge for live web applications, with no new annotation. We execute the predictions of three strong 7--8B grounders on a code forge and an online shop. About one in five and one in three of the clicks that box scoring rejects reach the intended outcome, and the shares remain one in seven and one in three when the instructions are rewritten as natural tasks. A blind audit of 11 models on ScreenSpot-v2 (three 7--8B grounders and eight 3B variants) finds the same effect on web screenshots, with two independent reviewers on a 60-unit subset. The share is highest for the strongest grounders. Training seeds and test-set sampling add noise that more runs and paired intervals control. Box scoring instead under-counts correct clicks, which repetition does not remove, and the audit-based correction of 0.2 to 1.8 points on ScreenSpot-v2 is as large as the gaps the field reports. The correction is needed in evaluation. In our 3B GRPO study, crediting equivalent clicks in the reward gives no stable gain over box rewards across three seeds and four test sets. We release the probe, the outcome maps, the audit and every prediction.
authors: Xiaokang Yuan, Binhui Yao, Luwei Yang, Ruimin Chen, Zeng Wang
bullets: A click can be functionally correct even when it falls outside the single annotated target box, such as on duplicated links or labels.

Correcting ScreenSpot-v2 scores changes results by 0.2–1.8 points, comparable to reported model gaps.
Rewarding equivalent clicks in a 3B GRPO study produced no stable improvement over box-based rewards.

papers.title: Right Click, Wrong Box: Grading GUI Grounding by What a Click Does
papers.tldr: GUI grounding benchmarks undercount correct clicks because they judge box overlap rather than whether the click achieves the intended outcome.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made substantial progress in visual question answering, but complex visual reasoning often requires locating and comparing multiple pieces of question-relevant visual evidence. Existing methods that move intermediate reasoning into the visual latent space usually follow a single linear reasoning trajectory, which can be limiting when multiple visual hypotheses or competing evidence regions are relevant. We propose Latent Visual Contrastive Reasoning, a branch-aware latent reasoning framework that generates multiple question-conditioned latent visual branches as soft hypotheses over image tokens. To train these branches, our method uses bounding-box evidence annotations to build target evidence representations and introduces a soft contrastive branch-evidence alignment objective. This objective encourages evidence-relevant branches to align with annotated visual regions while contrasting them against negative evidence. We instantiate our method on Qwen2.5-VL backbones and train it with standard supervised fine-tuning. Experiments on perception-intensive visual reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed method achieves overall improvements over the corresponding backbone and single-path latent reasoning baselines at both 3B and 7B scales.
authors: Kegeng Tang, Jingbo Wang, Yangming Zhang, Huanshu Zhang, Shaogang Ren, Zihao Wang
bullets: Targets the limitation of single-path latent reasoning when questions require comparing multiple visual regions or competing evidence.
Generates multiple question-conditioned latent visual branches as soft hypotheses over image tokens.
Uses bounding-box annotations and a soft contrastive branch–evidence alignment objective to associate branches with relevant regions and reject negative evidence.
Implemented with Qwen2.5-VL backbones and standard supervised fine-tuning.
Reports overall gains over the backbone and single-path latent reasoning baselines on perception-intensive benchmarks at 3B and 7B scales.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overall framework of LVCR. Given an image-question pair, LVCR encodes the image and question into visual and textual tokens, and proposes multiple question-conditioned latent branches as candidate visual hypotheses over the image. These branches are contrastively aligned with answer-relevant visual evidence and separated from irrelevant regions. LVCR then ranks the branches using relevance scores computed by cosine similarity with the question representation, and injects the selected branch tokens into the MLLM decoder, which combines them with the original multimodal context to generate the final answer.

Fig. 3. Accuracy (%) of three branch injection strategies on V ∗, MMVP, and BLINK (aggregated). Ranked denotes our default LVCR strategy; Top-1 injects only the highest-ranked branch; Unranked injects all branches without ordering. Results are reported using LVCR-3B with K=4.

Fig. 2. Ablation study on the NCE loss coefficient using LVCR-3B with K=4. We compare the default setting with λNCE = 0.1 against a variant trained without the NCE loss, i.e., λNCE = 0. Removing the NCE loss leads to consistent performance drops on V ∗, MMVP, and BLINK, indicating that contrastive branch-evidence alignment helps latent branches capture questionrelevant visual cues.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) predicts the next item through its semantic ID (SID). Existing methods commonly fit SID vocabularies to pretrained language model (PLM) representations of item descriptions, incurring additional training costs and making vocabulary coverage dependent on the fitting domains. We observe that pretrained sparse autoencoders expose PLM features with human-interpretable semantic annotations, allowing feature indices to serve as a reusable SID vocabulary. However, reusing this vocabulary requires preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and learning to favor target items over candidates with shared dominant features. It also requires extending feature interpretability from item content to retrieval decisions. To address these challenges, we propose API, a framework that Adapts the Pretrained Interpretable vocabulary for effective and explainable GR without additional vocabulary learning. Within API, Pretrained Interpretable IDs (PIDs) retain selected feature indices and relative activation strengths for item discrimination. With PIDs as supervision, the Semantic Prediction Adapter (SPA) learns user preferences from interaction histories through joint feature-index and strength prediction. SPA combines both predictions to score candidate items, with item-level supervision encouraging the observed next item to outrank its alternatives. API further explains candidate score differences through feature contributions paired with their pretrained semantic annotations. Extensive experiments show that API achieves competitive performance across backbones and decoding schemes, while preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and enabling explainable retrieval.
authors: Ziluowen Luo, Ruochen Liu, Jun Yin, Hao Yan, Zhengxuan Hu, Xinze Shi, Chaozhuo Li, Chengqi Zhang, Senzhang Wang
bullets: Addresses the cost and domain-dependent coverage of fitting new semantic-ID vocabularies.
Uses Pretrained Interpretable IDs that preserve selected feature indices and activation strengths under compact token budgets.
Trains a Semantic Prediction Adapter to jointly predict feature indices and strengths from user histories.
Scores candidates using feature predictions and item-level ranking supervision, while attributing score differences to semantic features.
Experiments report competitive performance across backbones and decoding schemes, with preserved item distinctions and explainable retrieval.

papers.abstract: Multilingual multi-hop document question answering (MMHop-DocQA) requires locating and integrating evidence across complex layouts, document pages, and diverse languages. Existing approaches include single-pass processing and adaptive tool use, but learning to coordinate evidence acquisition, cross-page integration, and answer verification remains challenging. To address this challenge, we present DocSkill, an agentic framework with a learned skill-orchestration policy for adaptive evidence acquisition and reasoning. The policy selects, revisits, or skips skills according to the evolving evidence state. To construct supervision for skill orchestration, bounded Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) explores alternative skill trajectories offline. These trajectories provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We further introduce MMHop-DocBench, a multilingual multi-hop document QA dataset with training and test splits, containing 60K QA pairs across 10 languages and eight document domains. Its HopGen pipeline builds hierarchical page-element graphs to derive traceable cross-page evidence paths and generate grounded QA pairs with page- and element-level evidence annotations. Experiments show that DocSkill with Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 41.0 accuracy and 49.2 F1 on MMHop-DocBench, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 5.5 and 6.3 points, respectively, and achieving competitive performance on MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench.
authors: Jing Huang, Zhiya Tan, Changtao Miao, Shutao Gong, Yang Wang, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Jianshu Li, Ying Yan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reasoning across complex layouts, pages, and languages while coordinating evidence gathering and answer verification.

papers.abstract: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. Since visual tokens make up 89-97% of this input on the benchmarks we study, most of the decoding computation is spent repeatedly processing the same image. Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN's adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/
authors: Donghyeon Cho, Joowon Kim, Seungho Shin, Eunho Yang
bullets: DVLMs repeatedly process mostly redundant visual tokens at every denoising step.
The method compares image-free and image-conditioned predictions to certify when prior predictions can be reused.
It adaptively decides both whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask, without training or a tuned threshold.
Across ten benchmarks, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V’s score while using 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average.
It generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, combines with visual token pruning, and supports key-value caching.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive visual routing reduces decoding FLOPs for diffusion VLMs.
papers.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
papers.tldr: LOWN makes diffusion VLMs process image tokens only when needed, preserving nearly all performance while substantially reducing decoding computation.

papers.abstract: Final-answer accuracy reports whether a vision-language model was right, but not whether its answer was grounded in the image, whether its stated reasoning reflects that evidence, or what the answer cost to produce. Those are the properties that decide whether a system can be deployed. We present PRISM-BENCH, a benchmark of 1,000 expert-curated questions spanning five under-represented reasoning categories, in which every item carries an idealized reasoning trace written by one human annotator and validated by another. The traces support two diagnostics that accuracy cannot provide. A perception probe, in which the model answers from a description it wrote itself, attributes roughly 85% of frontier-model failures to misperception and places the bottleneck at grounding. Trace alignment predicts answer correctness for all 25 systems tested (macro AUROC 0.66) and survives length control, so it measures reasoning content and not verbosity. We further introduce CORE, an efficiency-aware metric that reorders 24.2% of model pairs relative to accuracy while remaining uncorrelated with response length. Across 25 open and closed systems, including GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.6, the best accuracy is 66.0%. On the four categories with a human baseline the best system trails humans by 18.4 points, and recent frontier gains fall on recognition and not on spatial grounding.
authors: Vansh Bhatia, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Parsa Ashrafi Fashi, Igor Gilitschenski, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Introduces 1,000 expert-curated questions across five under-represented reasoning categories, each with a validated ideal reasoning trace.
A self-description perception probe attributes roughly 85% of frontier-model failures to misperception, identifying grounding as the main bottleneck.
Trace alignment predicts correctness across all 25 evaluated systems, beyond effects of response length.
CORE, an efficiency-aware metric, reorders 24.2% of model pairs relative to accuracy while remaining uncorrelated with response length.
The best system reaches 66.0% accuracy, trails humans by 18.4 points where comparable, and recent gains emphasize recognition over spatial grounding.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Three deployment-relevant diagnostics that final-answer accuracy cannot provide. (a) Accuracy falls when a model must answer from its own image description instead of the image (drop annotated in red); the white figure inside each bar is the share of that model’s baseline failures that the model itself, judging in a fresh context, attributes to perception instead of inference. (b) For all 25 evaluated systems, responses that are correct align more closely with the human reasoning trace than responses that are incorrect (macro AUROC 0.66, and 0.665 after regressing out response length). (c) CORE reorders models relative to accuracy; dashed arrows connect matched thinking/instruct pairs, which spend more tokens for less accuracy.

Figure 3: (a) Overall accuracy for all 25 evaluated systems, shaded by family, against the 83.9% human baseline (red). Restricted to the four categories where both are measured, the best system trails humans by 18.4 points, and the open/closed gap is larger than any difference within the open families. (b) Best system of any kind versus the human baseline (red tick) per category. The deficit is concentrated in the two spatially grounded categories and nearly vanishes on multi-hop, where the reasoning is largely textual once the scene is read.

Figure 6: Navigation / map reading. Gemma-3-12B-It reads the label adjacent to the church and answers correctly in 74 tokens. Kimi-VL (140 tokens), Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (172) and Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct (316) all produce longer, more structured deliberations and all answer “Henry Street”. This item is a compact illustration of why we score cost alongside correctness: the cheapest response here is the only correct one, and a leaderboard ordered by accuracy alone would still rank three of these systems above Gemma overall.

Figure 9: Navigation / spatial orientation. The question asks which street is the odd one out and states explicitly that the criterion is not the name. The answer is Wilfred Ave, the only street running north–south while the others run east–west. Only OpenAI o3 checks orientation on the map. Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (1,861 tokens), Ovis2.5-9B and Gemma-3-12B all reason from the linguistic distinction between “Court” and “Avenue” despite the hint ruling it out, and Ovis2.5-9B visibly loops before committing. This is the linguistic shortcutting failure, and it is the pattern behind the ∼47% navigation scores in Table 2: the models read the map as text rather than as space.

Figure 2: The five reasoning categories, balanced at 200 items each. The categories mix functional reasoning patterns, such as multi-hop composition, with domain-specific grounding requirements, such as medical interpretation, because deployment demands both.

Figure 4: Visual coreference under occlusion. The question asks for the registration of the aircraft partially occluded behind the silver plane in the foreground. Gemini 2.5 Pro resolves it by enumerating the three visible aircraft, reading each registration, and matching against the referring expression. Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL-30B-Thinking and Ovis2.5-9B all answer N177XV, the registration of the foreground plane. This is the saliency bias described in Section E: the referring expression is never applied, and the most prominent entity is returned instead. Token budgets of 614, 296 and 753 show this is not a matter of insufficient reasoning length.

Figure 5: Handwriting / OCR reasoning. All five candidate words appear correctly in the handwritten passage, so the answer is “none of the above”, which requires transcribing every option correctly before concluding that nothing is missing. Qwen3-VL-8BInstruct does so. Gemini 2.5 Pro misreads one word and then constructs an elaborate, internally consistent argument for “based”; Gemma-3-12B and VL-Rethinker each settle on “favour”. This is the cascade pattern: the reasoning is valid given the misperception, so the trace looks sound and the error is invisible without the ground truth.

Figure 7: Multi-hop reasoning. Answering requires chaining what the scene shows (people playing a Wii boxing game) to a fact about the game (each player needs a remote and a nunchuck) to a count. Ovis2.5-9B, Gemma-3-12B and Skywork-R1V3-38B chain correctly. OpenAI o3 counts three players from the image and propagates that into three controllers, an error at the first hop that the subsequent reasoning faithfully preserves.

Figure 8: Scientific / medical reasoning. The nail finding is Beau’s lines, transverse ridges left by repeated arrest of nail-matrix growth, which point to cyclical chemotherapy. Only OpenAI o3 reaches this. Gemini identifies the pattern as Muehrcke’s lines and reasons fluently to nephrotic syndrome; Gemma-3-12B reasons to psoriasis; Qwen2.5-VL-7B concludes none of the options apply. Each wrong answer arrives with a confident, clinically phrased causal chain. This is the category with the highest rate of confidently wrong explanations, and the reason we treat it as the clearest safety concern for deployment.

Figure 10: The four-stage annotation loop. Duties are separated so that no annotator validates an item whose reasoning trace they wrote, and an item that fails Stage 4 returns to its author for revision instead of being silently accepted or discarded. Stage 2 produces the human reference length Lgt i that CORE uses and the reference content that trace alignment uses.

Table 7: Trace alignment for all 25 evaluated systems, sorted by gap. “Sim.” is the mean over gold trace steps of the maximum cosine similarity to any step of the model response. The gap is positive for every variant: responses that reach the correct answer track the human reasoning trace more closely than responses that do not.

papers.abstract: We propose Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni (NLD-Uni), a unified discrete diffusion large language model (DLLM) for visual understanding and generation tasks. Compared with prior unified diffusion models, NLD-Uni introduces two major innovations. First, we propose a unified cross-paradigm on-policy distillation (OPD) framework that successfully transfers the visual understanding ability of autoregressive VLMs and visual generation ability of continuous flow models, to a unified DLLM. Second, NLD-Uni incorporates a novel progressive self-refining diffusion process that gradually corrupts each token across multiple steps during training, as opposed to adopting the conventional masked diffusion formulation that directly corrupts a clean image token to an uninformative mask token. At inference, this design allows NLD-Uni to make intermediate commit to a token, enabling progressive self-refinement for better visual quality. Through extensive experiments, we show that NLD-Uni achieves state-of-the-art performance among unified DLLMs on diverse tasks including visual question-answering, multi-modal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.
authors: Shufan Li, Hanrong Ye, Greg Heinrich, Yonggan Fu, Haotian Zhang, Sifei Liu, Aditya Grover, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Transfers capabilities from autoregressive vision-language models and continuous flow models into one unified diffusion model.
Uses cross-paradigm on-policy distillation to train visual understanding and generation abilities.
Introduces progressive self-refining diffusion, gradually corrupting tokens instead of replacing them directly with masks.
Enables intermediate token commitments during inference for progressive visual refinement.
Reports state-of-the-art unified-DLLM performance across VQA, multimodal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | NLD-Uni supports diverse multimodal tasks by adopting an Elastic-MoT architecture with three elastic views of a single model. The VLM view uses the 8B understanding branch; the T2I view combines 4B understanding parameters with the 8B generation branch; and the interleaved view uses both full branches (16B). Each view loads only the parameters needed for its task. Yellow and green blocks denote understanding and generation layers, gray blocks indicate omitted layers, and blue arrows denote joint attention. Representative examples demonstrate visual reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image synthesis, and image editing guided by reasoning and localization.

Figure 3 | Overall Framework of NLD-Uni. NLD-Uni is a unified diffusion model whose input and output are both multimodal. Images in the input stream are represented by both continuous embeddings of a semantic encoder and discrete tokens of a VQ encoder. Images in the output stream are represented solely using VQ codes. NLD-Uni is trained to predict the clean token distribution given partially masked inputs. For image generation, we incorporate an intermediate masking state.

Figure 6 | On-Policy Distilling from Continuous Flow Models. Given a student output, we generate a teacher-refined output by adding noise to the student sample and re-denoise it with the teacher model. For reference, we also show an independent teacher generation. We observe that the teacher’s refinements are closely aligned to the student’s output while having better visual fidelity and source image preservation.

Figure 5 | On-Policy Distilling from Autoregressive VLMs. Top: Given a prompt and clean prefix blocks, we generate the current block with the student’s AR view by temporarily adopting a block size of 1. Left: AR on-policy distillation loss aligns the student’s AR distribution with a frozen AR teacher. Right: Consistency loss aligns the student’s diffusion view to its own AR view. The diffusion prediction is obtained by evaluating the student on randomly masked AR rollouts. We apply stop-grad to the AR target.

Figure 10 | The design of SBD formulation. (Left) SBD adopts a two-stream training process that concatenates clean blocks and noisy blocks in the sequence dimension. It applies AR CE loss on the clean blocks, and diffusion CE loss on the noisy blocks. (Right) SBD models use a specialized attention mask with a causal mask in the clean blocks and block-bidirectional mask in the noisy blocks. Each noisy block can attend to all other tokens in itself and all tokens in preceding clean blocks.

Figure 11 | Visualization of Ball-Tree-Based Corruption Process. (Right) Ball-Tree is a balanced binary tree whose leaf nodes correspond to unique tokens in the vocabulary. The forward corruption process 𝑈𝑘|𝑘−1 increases the token age 𝑎 and decreases the node depth 𝑑. (Left) Each node has a geometric representation which is a high-dimensional ball in the VQ embedding space. Decreasing depth 𝑑 corresponds to increasing ball radius. In this visualization, the depth 𝐷 = 4 and maximum token age 𝐾 = 3.

Figure 12 | Visual Reconstruction Across Different Token Ages. To investigate whether the proposed age-based corruption process is semantically meaningful for visual generation tasks, we show reconstructed images at different token ages and compare them with the rectified flow process in the continuous latent space of Qwen-VAE. Results indicate that changes in the token age represent a smooth corruption process in the pixel space. In this visualization, all tokens are corrupted at the same rate, which corresponds to 𝜖 = 1.

Figure 13 | Image PSNR Across Different Token Ages. To investigate whether the proposed age-based corruption process is semantically meaningful for visual generation tasks, we plot the PSNR of reconstructed images at different token ages and compare them with the rectified flow process in the continuous latent space of Qwen-VAE. Results indicate that changes in the token age represent a smooth corruption process in the pixel space measured by PSNR. In the clean state, Qwen-VAE has better PSNR than NLD-Uni, suggesting its continuous VAE has better reconstruction capability.

papers.abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.
authors: Alexa R. Tartaglini, Zhengxuan Wu, Thadd\"aus Wiedemer, Martin Wattenberg, Been Kim, Yuxuan Li
bullets: Simple symbols, such as a red heart, can implicitly steer VLM behavior toward recursive solutions on coding tasks.
Models’ stated interpretations and reasoning about symbols may differ substantially from the behavior those symbols induce.
Visual communication between models shows a generation–interpretation gap: intuitive shape-based cues often fail to steer other models.
In communication games, VLMs can creatively convey abstract concepts and stories, though some messages are unintuitive to humans.
The work highlights both the promise and challenges of human–VLM visual communication.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Simple visual symbols steer model behavior on a coding problem. A) Evaluation methodology. We append an image of a simple colored shape (e.g., a blue triangle) to a coding prompt (binary tree traversal) and instruct the model to look at the image while solving the problem. Across 𝑛 sampled generations, we compute the proportion of recursive solutions 𝑃(recursion) and measure the visual steering effect Δ𝑃(recursion) as the change in 𝑃(recursion) relative to the no-image baseline. B) Visual symbols steer toward recursion far more strongly than random noise or matching text descriptions. Star-patterned bars show average Δ𝑃(recursion) for Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7’s top three steering symbols (symbols shown below each bar), which nearly matches the effect of directly instructing the model to use recursion (light gray bars). By contrast, matching text descriptions (e.g., “an image of a pink heart”; hatched bars) and Gaussian noise images (dark gray bars) induce minimal to no steering. C) Models display different steering landscapes over a library of 288 visual symbols. Heatmaps show Δ𝑃(recursion) across 12 colors (𝑥-axis) for each model’s 8 highest- and 6 lowest-steering shapes (𝑦-axis; full heatmaps in Sec. B.2.1).

Figure 2 | Models generate creative visualizations to communicate concepts, but exhibit a generation–interpretation gap. A) Communication game methodology. A sender model generates a visualization to convey a target coding strategy (e.g., recursion), concept, or story to a receiver model, refining its visualization through multi-turn feedback. B) Multi-turn feedback enables models to converge on effective visualizations. Bars show the average number of turns to succeed using visual symbols (top bars) versus free-form PIL drawings (bottom bars). Symbol-based communication requires more communication turns to align sender and receiver than free-form drawing. C) Senders choose intuitive symbols to communicate recursion rather than the symbols that actually steer them. Top symbols selected by Claude Opus 4.7 as a sender (left, sized by selection frequency) compared to the symbols with the largest empirical steering effect Δ𝑃(recursion) (right). D) Models construct creative scenes using free-form code and abstract symbols. Examples show successful visualizations generated by Gemini 3.1 Pro to communicate the concept “art” (left) and a threesentence story about a knight removing a thorn from a dragon’s paw (right).

Figure 3 | Visual steering associations diverge from both human intuition and models’ own explicit interpretations. A) Optimizing symbol communication for model receivers reduces human legibility, whereas free-form drawings remain interpretable. Bars show human accuracy (%) at identifying the target coding strategy (recursion vs. iteration), concept, or story from visualizations on the first communication turn (blue; unsuccessful for the receiver) versus the final turn (red; successful), using visual symbols (top bars) or free-form PIL drawings (bottom bars). B) Models’ direct interpretations of visual symbols poorly predict their empirical steering effects. Each point represents one or more of the 288 visual symbols (sized by count), plotting the proportion of trials in which a model explicitly classifies the symbol as “recursion” (𝑥-axis) against its behavioral steering effect Δ𝑃(recursion) (𝑦-axis).

Figure 22 | Steering results for all binary choice semantic pairs. The labels along the 𝑥-axes indicate the direction of steering away from each model’s unsteered baseline preference (from 𝐴 to 𝐵), with icons below each bar showing the visual symbols that drive the shift.

Cell values are the steering effect (i.e. delta Δ𝑃(recursion) relative to that model’s text-only baseline), on a diverging scale from −1 (red, towards iteration) to +1 (blue, towards recursion).

Figure 15 | Placing images at the end of context rather than the beginning changes which symbols steer for recursion. A) The steering effect at the start and end of context decouple most strongly for Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.4. The 𝑦-axis shows the steering effect of visual symbols when placed at the start of context, while the 𝑥-axis shows the end of context. Gemini 3.1 Pro remains somewhat correlated. B) Top steering symbols appear to shift from more geometric to more semantic. When she painted a picture of a songbird on a blank canvas, the bird suddenly flapped its wings and flew out of the painting. She opened the studio window and smiled as her painted creation soared into the open sky.”; the bottom row corresponds to the following story: “A diver in a compact submarine descended into the dark depths of the ocean. Bars show the mean shift away from each model’s unsteered baseline strategy (±1 SEM across problems and top-3 symbols, shown below each bar). A) Aggregated recursion steering across baseline-iterative problems (𝑁 = 4 for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 4 for GPT-5.4).
