papers.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
authors: Matea Tashkovska, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Haozhe Qi, Alexander Mathis
bullets: Introduces 1,632 human-verified questions spanning body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning.
Evaluates 37 closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, alongside human evaluation.
Humans achieve 68.5% video-only accuracy, compared with 50.0% for the strongest evaluated MLLM, Qwen3.6-27B, in zero-shot evaluation.
Finds recurring errors in interpreting the wearer’s body, temporal events, repetition counts, and hand-side biases.
Provides aligned video–body-motion–language training data and a multimodal baseline to support future research.

papers.abstract: Are concepts and mechanisms unified across modalities in current AI models, or instead implemented separately for each one? We operationalize this broad question of modality unification by studying cross-modal steering: 1) finding vectors that successfully steer generation on tokens of one modality, which then 2) transfer zero-shot to steer generation when added to tokens of another modality. Our study goes beyond simple correlational alignment (e.g. representational similarity) because steering is fundamentally causal. We study cross-modal steering in several unified multimodal models (UMMs), since they possess shared parameters for language and image generation, focusing on these two modalities. Across diverse steered concepts such as emotion and object size, we show that steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions (text-to-image & image-to-text). Even for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (e.g. formal vs. colloquial language), steering vectors often induce a consistent, interpretable effect in the other modality, such as formal clothing and design. This transfer has a geometric signature too: despite a clear modality gap separating text and image representations, steering vectors with strong cross-modal transferability tend to point in similar directions for the same concept. Our findings shed light on how vision and language interact inside unified multimodal models and point towards more general, modality-agnostic approaches for controlling their behavior.
authors: Donghao Zeng (Mila, McGill University), Nishant Subramani (Carnegie Mellon University), Tamar Rott Shaham (MIT CSAIL), Benno Krojer (Mila, McGill University, Northeastern University)
bullets: Tests whether concepts and mechanisms are unified across language and vision models.

Suggests modality-agnostic methods for controlling multimodal model behavior.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, \emph{i.e.}, the misleading cues caused by spurious \textit{linguistic} correlations and salient yet irrelevant \textit{visual} observations. In this paper, we first introduce {S-MME}, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.
authors: Xusheng Liang, Jianqiao Sun, Hao Zhang, Yulei Niu, Hengshuang Zhao, Jiawei Ma
bullets: Long-video QA is difficult because sparse frame sampling can miss decisive evidence, while spurious cues can still mislead models.
S-MME benchmarks shortcut-biased behavior from misleading language correlations and salient but irrelevant visual content.
CLEAR estimates bias using question-only and locally salient-clip views, then intervenes on hidden states at inference.
Experiments across five benchmarks show consistent gains in prediction and robustness across different MLLMs.
CLEAR is presented as a complementary test-time scaling approach; the abstract does not specify detailed limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of CLEAR. (a) The full-video path produces the final answer, while questiononly and salient-view probes reveal spurious linguistic correlations and salient-yet-misleading visual observations. The salient view is formed by selecting top-K locally relevant clips according to query-conditioned visual attention. (b) CLEAR extracts the hidden state of the shared decision token z at selected late decoder layers, and constructs residual vectors rql = hf l − hq l and rsl = hf l − hs l from the restricted-view probes to the full-video state. These residual vectors are injected into the full-video path to steer its hidden state away from shortcut anchors before final decoding.

Figure 2: Construction pipeline of S-MME. We first mine candidate questions with explicit long-video evidence requirements, then use restricted views to identify shortcut-consistent distractors, followed by human validation of answer uniqueness, evidence sufficiency, and shortcut plausibility.
Figure 4: Effect of intervention location. Latelayer intervention performs best, with the last block achieving the highest accuracy.

Figure 1: MLLMs often fail despite the presence of decisive evidence, either by following spurious linguistic correlations or by over-relying on salient but misleading visual observations. papers.abstract: Despite rapid progress in visual understanding and document transcription, modern vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with a fundamental accessibility task: reading Braille from images. We introduce BrailleBench, a manually curated benchmark of 259 real-world Grade-1 and Grade-2 Braille images. We evaluate proprietary, open-weight, OCR-specialized, and tool-assisted multimodal systems and find that standalone general-purpose models perform poorly at directly transcribing Braille images, whereas tool-assisted systems perform much better. We design a synthetic Braille generation pipeline with diverse layouts and image perturbations. A 2B VLM model trained on our synthetic data reaches 87% exact match on Grade-1 and 61% on Grade-2 BrailleBench, outperforming standalone VLMs and achieving the highest Grade-2 exact match score among the evaluated systems. We further show that high accuracy on synthetic validation data does not guarantee high accuracy on real photographs in our experiments: models trained on prior synthetic data reach up to 96% on their synthetic validation set but at most 3.26% on Grade-1 BrailleBench. Our results identify an accessibility-relevant capability gap in multimodal systems and show that targeted synthetic supervision can improve real-world Braille transcription.
authors: Kartik Jangra, Atharva Gawane, Siddharth Pulipaka, Hemachandran Karah, Raj Dabre
bullets: BrailleBench contains 259 manually curated real-world Grade-1 and Grade-2 Braille images.

A synthetic Braille generation pipeline uses diverse layouts and image perturbations for training.
A 2B VLM trained on the synthetic data achieves 87% Grade-1 and 61% Grade-2 exact match on BrailleBench.
Synthetic validation accuracy may not transfer to real photographs: prior models reached up to 96% synthetically but at most 3.26% on Grade-1 BrailleBench.

papers.abstract: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.
authors: Soumyajit Datta, Arka Dutta, Ashiqur R. KhudaBukhsh
bullets: Examines two VLMs’ handling of requested racial and sexual-orientation transformations of human faces.
Finds that compliance and refusal vary across groups and requests.
Generated images are statistically distinguishable and may accentuate stereotypes.
Biases introduced during image generation can reappear in textual reasoning and characterization.
Similar concerns extend to criminality, suggesting risks of AI-assisted profiling.

papers.abstract: A robot policy needs to understand what a task is asking for in a scene, and how to move the robot to accomplish that task. To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness. We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot. Without observing real-world robot data during training, ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3%), while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Furthermore, ZAP also generalizes to an unseen embodiment as well as new objects, goals and strategies never seen during training. On a single-arm Franka, ZAP reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining task understanding with robot motion control without real-world robot training data.
Uses a pretrained 27B vision-language model, then supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks via a tool harness.
Achieves 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra while running 3× faster and costing 17× less.
Generalizes to unseen embodiments, objects, goals, and strategies; reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 points above the cited VLA/WAM baseline.
Scope: results are reported for the described harness and selected real-world benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Expanding multilingual ASR systems to new languages is challenging when adaptation must preserve previously supported languages without replaying source-language training data. We study this problem in connector-based Speech LLMs, where a trainable connector maps speech representations into a frozen large language model. We evaluate target-update construction and merging strategies for adapting the connector while preserving source-language performance. In single-target expansion, target-only fine-tuning and standard TIES merging learn new languages but cause severe source-language forgetting, while SSU-Wanda+TIES gives the best source-preserving trade-off. In multi-target expansion, update merging provides stable source retention, whereas recursive expansion can improve target adaptation under favorable orders but is highly order-sensitive. These results show that multilingual ASR expansion requires balancing target acquisition, source retention, and interactions among target-language updates.
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
bullets: Problem: Add new languages to connector-based Speech LLM ASR without replaying source-language data or degrading existing languages.
Method: Compare target-update construction and merging strategies for adapting a trainable speech-to-LLM connector while keeping the LLM frozen.
Single-target finding: Target-only fine-tuning and standard TIES merging cause severe source-language forgetting; SSU-Wanda+TIES offers the best reported trade-off.
Multi-target finding: Update merging provides stable source retention, while recursive expansion can improve target adaptation but is highly order-sensitive.
Scope: Expansion requires balancing new-language acquisition, source retention, and interactions among target-language updates.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Project page: https://internrobotics.github.io/EBench-Astra-Tech-Report/
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
bullets: GPT-6-Astra is evaluated as a robot-control agent under the same visual and proprioceptive observations as post-trained policies.
Direct control performs competitively, especially on short-horizon tasks and across generalization dimensions.
It underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon, tabletop, and high-precision contact-rich manipulation.
A harness that invokes VLA or WAM policies combines complementary strengths, reaching the strongest standalone policies’ overall success level with lower token cost.
Remaining gaps stem from suboptimal policy invocation, fixed instructions without subgoals, and grasp disruption when control returns to the agent.

papers.title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy

papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots. However, specialized domains remain a challenge for VLMs' image interpretation and grounding abilities. We introduce TrySee, a modular closed-loop robot task planning pipeline integrating general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robotics components. The system consists of an inherently reactive cyclic planning pipeline, augmented with domain-specific modular vision preprocessing, to provide online grounding. Finally, a dynamic preprocessing selection mechanism contributes to the scalability of the pipeline. The system requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations and adapts through replaceable perception modules and motion planning. The approach is evaluated on planning tasks across 5 widely different domains, including a real-world robot disassembly task. The field tests in a brownfield environment demonstrate the approach's practicality in integrating VLM planning into specialized robotic systems with limited domain-specific training data.
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
bullets: Targets weak VLM image interpretation and grounding in specialized robotic domains.
Uses a reactive cyclic planning pipeline with online grounding and dynamically selected vision preprocessing.
Requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations.
Evaluated across five diverse domains, including real-world robot disassembly.
Field tests indicate practical integration in brownfield settings with limited domain-specific data.

papers.abstract: Social media enables cross-lingual communication, yet the meaning of user-generated content (UGC) is often distributed across text, images, and cultural knowledge, making translation challenging. Existing evaluations typically treat images as optional and assume textual information is sufficient, obscuring whether errors stem from missing visual evidence or inadequate cultural adaptation. We introduce \textbf{Culture-MMT}, a diagnostic benchmark for \textbf{distributed-evidence pragmatic reconstruction} in social-media translation. It contains 498 curated, de-identified UGC instances across 20 domains, categorized into Symbol, Visual, and Hybrid by their required evidence. We also develop a human-aligned domain-specific judge, Judger, and a controlled evaluation framework that systematically varies the evidence available to translators. Across 17 model configurations, real images improve performance by +0.280 on Visual and +0.197 on Hybrid, but only +0.050 on Symbol, while random images provide no comparable gains. Human-authored descriptions further show that jointly dependent cases remain more challenging even when visual facts are explicit. These results characterize culturally effective social-media translation as {meaning reconstruction from distributed evidence}, highlighting visual grounding and cultural-pragmatic adaptation as distinct model bottlenecks.
authors: Dingming Li, Yiwen Qiu, Linjuan Wu, Hongxing Li, Zixuan Wang, Xinze Lyu, Ye Guo, Daoxin Zhang, Zhe Xu, Weiming Lu, Yongliang Shen
bullets: Introduces 498 de-identified UGC instances across 20 domains, categorized as Symbol, Visual, or Hybrid by required evidence.
Provides Judger, a human-aligned domain-specific evaluator, plus a controlled framework that varies available evidence.
Across 17 model configurations, real images help most on Visual and Hybrid cases, but offer limited gains on Symbol cases; random images do not provide comparable benefits.
Human-authored descriptions show jointly dependent cases remain difficult even when visual facts are made explicit.
Findings distinguish visual grounding from cultural-pragmatic adaptation as separate translation bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce \textbf{Omni-InteractScope}, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) \textbf{Timely tool invocation remains unreliable}: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) \textbf{Query-free reminders remain poorly covered}: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) \textbf{End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited}: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu

Across 12 models, on-time first responses for tool invocation reach at most 40%, while joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0%.
Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0%, and nine of 12 models complete none of the 26 guidance sequences.
Controls show that tool-use scores do not alone prove event grounding, while reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark for proactive and agentic interaction in continuous audiovisual streams using Omni-LLMs. This evaluates the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models in streaming contexts.
papers.title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
papers.tldr: Omni-InteractScope benchmarks whether Omni-LLMs can turn continuous audiovisual evidence and user needs into timely, sustained, proactive assistance, revealing major reliability gaps.

papers.abstract: Text-in-image translation aims to translate all textual content embedded in an image. In Text Image Translation (TIT), the output is translated text; In-Image Machine Translation (IIMT) additionally renders the translation back into the image. We introduce ImgMT, a massively multilingual dataset and benchmark mined from localized SVG illustrations on Wikimedia Commons, focusing on diagrams, maps, and infographics. ImgMT contains 35,612 aligned image pairs grouped into 1,855 image sets, spanning 129 languages, 20+ writing systems, and 4,886 language pairs. We propose a multi-level evaluation protocol that measures source-side text-region detection and OCR accuracy alongside target-side translation quality. We benchmark several multimodal large language models and a dedicated TIT system in English->X and X->English settings, and find that the source language and writing system substantially affect TIT quality. Finally, we show that ImgMT is not well suited for isolating the contribution of visual information in multimodal translation.
authors: \v{S}\'arka Uramov\'a, Petar Kirilov Petrov, Josef Jon, Ond\v{r}ej Bojar, Michal Nov\'ak
bullets: Mined from localized Wikimedia Commons SVGs, covering diagrams, maps, and infographics.

Evaluates source text-region detection, OCR accuracy, and target-side translation quality in a multi-level protocol.
Benchmarks multimodal large language models and a dedicated TIT system in English→X and X→English directions.
Finds that source language and writing system substantially influence translation quality; the dataset is unsuitable for isolating visual-information effects.

papers.abstract: Existing multi-agent collaboration (MAC) methods have primarily explored a group thinking collaboration topology, where agents independently generate solutions and aggregate their outputs. In this work, we investigate an alternative relay thinking topology, where reasoning ownership is dynamically transferred across agents, allowing subsequent agents to inherit and refine an evolving reasoning trajectory. We introduce Multi-Agent Confidence-guided Relay (MACR), a framework that enables dynamical relay collaboration among agents. The key challenge is determining when reasoning should be relayed and which agent should continue the process. method addresses this challenge through confidence-guided relay triggering and a bidding mechanism that selects the next agent based on its confidence. Experiments on four benchmarks show that method outperforms the strongest single-model strategies in accuracy, e.g., +3.3% on MathVista and +3.9% on MMStar, and remains on par with multi-agent strategies while consuming 6.0x less token overhead on HallusionBench and MMStar.Further analysis demonstrates that relay collaboration enables heterogeneous agents to progressively integrate complementary insights, combining heterogeneous capabilities across reasoning stages. Our source code is available at https://github.com/67L1/MACR.
authors: Xu Liu, Jungang Qiao, Guikun Chen, Xiaojuan Qi, Wenguan Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of group-based multi-agent collaboration, where agents reason independently before aggregation.

Evaluated on four benchmarks, MACR outperforms the strongest single-model strategies, including gains of 3.3% on MathVista and 3.9% on MMStar.
Matches multi-agent strategies while using 6.0× less token overhead on HallusionBench and MMStar.
Relay collaboration helps heterogeneous agents combine complementary capabilities across reasoning stages.

papers.abstract: Understanding and operating with scientific charts is a standard approach in data analysis, and while humans are good at interpreting such charts, open vision-language models (VLMs) are known to perform poorly when it comes to question answering based on such data types. Motivated by an initial observation that many of their errors are due to inexact answering, we raise the following natural question: how much accuracy can we recover without changing the model at all? In this paper, we study this question by searching over inference programs and the code around a "frozen" version of the model. Using ideas from autonomous evolution (famously used in AlphaEvolve), we first start from a baseline inference program, and in each round we show an LLM judge the code together with a few failures on training questions, and ask for an improving evolutionary move. As usual in autonomous evolution approaches, the candidate programs are kept in a small pool ranked by training accuracy, and the next edit is performed on top-scorers from this pool. We run this approach on three VLMs and four popular benchmarks on scientific charts, and we measure the fraction of descriptive questions whose answer exactly matches the ground truth. The accuracy improves in all experimental settings. On average, it rises from 16.6% with the starting program to 41.3% with the evolved one, and the largest single increase is 55.2 percentage points. As a side benefit, our evolved program is 3.8x faster than the starting program, because short answers are easier to grade and faster to generate. Our results demonstrate that a large part of the observed errors arise due to the inference pipeline, and that optimizing it can improve the "frozen" VLM without the need to retrain it.
authors: Abhinav Sudhakar Dubey, Vidushi Goel, Kiran Rana, Shikhar Mathur, Vaggos Chatziafratis
bullets: Open VLMs often fail on scientific-chart questions, particularly through inexact answers.
The method evolves inference programs using an LLM judge, failure examples, and a pool of high-scoring candidate programs.
Evaluated across three VLMs and four scientific-chart benchmarks, accuracy improved in every setting.
Average exact-match accuracy increased from 16.6% to 41.3%, with a largest gain of 55.2 percentage points.
The evolved program was also 3.8× faster, suggesting inference-pipeline errors account for many failures.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Our autonomous evolution framework for better VLMs. Fixed inputs (left) feed an evolution engine (middle) that outputs deployable inference programs (right). The model id, greedy decoding, and the train/holdout split never change during a run; only the code inside the EVOLVE-BLOCK of a candidate is being mutated. An LLM mutator (in our case Gemini-2.5-flash) proposes edits, a validator rejects broken candidate programs before any GPU work, an evaluator scores survivor programs by exact-match accuracy, and a population manager keeps the best-by-holdout program. The same engine produces all twelve runs by swapping the seed program and the benchmark evaluator.

Figure 2: Seed vs. our evolved descriptive exact-match accuracy on all 12 model-benchmark pairs. Annotations give the absolute gain in percentage points by our method. As observed, every pair improves with the largest improvement being +55.2 percentage points. The largest jumps are on Qwen3-VL-2B, whose naive seed produced verbose, wrongly formatted answers; the smallest is SmolVLM2/CharXiv, whose seed was already clean (EM stands for Exact-Match).

Figure 5: Absolute gain in descriptive exact match for each of the 12 runs, sorted. Color denotes model. Gains cluster by whether the seed’s failure was one of formatting (large, recoverable) or perception (small headroom).
Figure 4: Accuracy vs. throughput, Qwen3-VL-2B/ChartQA. Evolution moves the program up and to the right of the seed; best_speed dominates on both axes.

Figure 3: The evolution loop. In every generation, the split loader feeds the train and holdout windows to the evaluator. The LLM-mutator proposes edits, the validator checks them before any GPU work is performed, and the population manager selects the next parent and writes the best-by-holdout candidate to disk. Every five generations, a crossover step combines two strong parents into one child.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) ground a referring expression in one of two ways. They decode the box as coordinate tokens, which is precise but takes one sequential step per token, or they regress it from a hidden state with a small head, which takes one step but loses accuracy at high IoU. The two fail differently: a head usually finds the right object but places its edges loosely, while coordinate tokens place edges precisely. We therefore use the regression head as a speculative drafter for the model's own coordinate tokens. Locus writes the head's box as coordinate tokens and checks them with the same backbone by Jacobi iteration over a shared image prefix. The fixed point is the model's greedy coordinate-token answer, reached in about 5.60 sequential passes on average instead of 18.46 decoding steps; head and verifier are one set of weights, trained jointly. On the 8 RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification raises Locus-2B's Acc@0.9 from 54.87 for its own head to 59.13, and the one-pass head is ahead at Acc@0.5 of every published model with at most 3B parameters except Florence-2-L. Against Jag, the strongest open regression-head model, at its own size and training budget, Locus ties at Acc@0.5 and, with typical acceptance, gains +4.52 points at Acc@0.9, with paired significance tests. Exact answers come 1.5x faster than vLLM greedy-decoding the same coordinate tokens with the same weights; a pure regression head remains faster still.
bullets: Uses the regression head to draft a box, then verifies and refines its coordinate tokens via Jacobi iteration with the same backbone.
Reaches the model’s greedy coordinate-token answer in about 5.60 sequential passes on average, versus 18.46 decoding steps.
On RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification improves Locus-2B Acc@0.9 from 54.87 to 59.13.
The one-pass head achieves strong Acc@0.5 performance, while verified outputs provide more precise box edges.
Exact answers are obtained 1.5× faster than vLLM greedy decoding with the same weights, though pure regression remains faster.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture and inference of Locus, illustrated with Locus-2B on the RefCOCO val expression “right elephant” (dashed white: ground truth). (a) The image and a fixed prefix are prefilled once. Each question then runs as a short branch over the cached prefix (attention mask on the right), so all box and verifier branches of an image share one prefill. The head reads the final state of the learned [BOX] token; the verifier branch is the backbone’s own grounding prompt, read by its LM head. Head and verifier are trained jointly. (b) The head’s box is rendered as the coordinate tokens the model would write, and the model checks all of them in one parallel pass, keeping the longest prefix it agrees with (green) and correcting the next token (orange). Repeating this until the draft stops changing yields the model’s greedy answer, here in 3 passes instead of 19 decoding steps. Blue tokens are those that verification changed.

Figure 7: Jag-0.8B and Locus-2B (verified) on openly licensed photos from Wikimedia Commons, at the same 5122-pixel budget. The 12 expressions were written before either model was run, and every result is shown; there is no ground truth, so we make no accuracy claim. The two models mostly agree; Locus’s boxes are tighter for “woman in the teal shirt” and “stack of red plastic crates”, they disagree on “floor lamp on the right”, and both return the whole person for “her blue headscarf”. Each Locus line runs from the one-pass head through typical acceptance (α = 0.5, 0.7; 2B only for 0.5) to exact verification. papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation can transfer large multimodal models to compact models for autonomous driving, but uniform token-level matching can dilute planning-relevant semantics and amplify teacher errors. We propose RSKD, a semantic-consistency-guided distillation framework that routes supervision according to both the task importance of an answer phrase and its semantic consistency with the teacher prediction. Task-critical semantic phrases are localized in the ground-truth answer, and a phrase-level consistency score controls the balance between Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) distillation and ground-truth supervision. Teacher information is emphasized only where it is semantically consistent, while semantically inconsistent phrases receive stronger ground-truth supervision. We evaluate RSKD on DrivingVQA, LingoQA, and MapLMv2. RSKD improves over the compared student-based baselines on DrivingVQA and LingoQA and remains competitive on MapLMv2.
authors: Chuchu Xie, Yang Zhong, Kangan Qian, Hao Ye, Kun Jiang, Diange Yang
bullets: Uniform token-level distillation can dilute planning-relevant meaning and propagate teacher errors.
The framework identifies task-critical phrases in ground-truth answers and scores their semantic consistency with teacher predictions.
Phrase-level consistency dynamically balances JSD distillation against ground-truth supervision.
RSKD improves over compared student baselines on DrivingVQA and LingoQA, while remaining competitive on MapLMv2.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while miss the implicit user intent (e.g., "where should I click next?" while a user navigate a website), meanwhile fail to update the state simultaneously as user requests might update continuously. These limitations make them less suited to intent-aware interaction in practical. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark serving as testbed for user intent interaction, with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically tailors its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with a fleixble lifecycles via a hierarchical memory to track the latest user intent and environmental state. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over other baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intent and deciding when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation over sustained interaction, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction.
authors: Chengzhi Liu, Yuxiang Lai, Yuzhe Yang, Yanqing Liu, Jiheng Hou, Yue Cao, Haonan Wang, Ruixi Fan, Lan Wang, Sheng Liu, Songyou Peng, Yale Song, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Xin Eric Wang, Jui-Hsin Lai, Youbao Tang
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing vision-language agents to infer implicit intent and update interaction states as requests evolve.
StreamVibe-Bench includes 4.1K evaluation and 85K training samples covering explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents.
StreamVibe-VL infers intent from continuous observations and adapts response timing and content dynamically.
StreamVibe-Harness uses hierarchical memory to maintain persistent user and environmental states across interactions.
The proposed systems report 10.7% better response timing and answer quality, plus a 12.3% gain in sustained proactive interaction.

papers.abstract: Latency-sensitive spoken agents must know not only which tool to call, but also when they have heard enough to act. Waiting for the turn to complete delays execution even when the request is already actionable. However, neither existing spoken agents nor spoken dialogue corpora define the earliest point at which a request becomes actionable. We introduce a synthetic spoken-dialogue pipeline that provides earliest-actionable-point supervision, marking when the observed speech grounds a tool and its required arguments. Through controlled task generation, speech synthesis and alignment, and gated annotation, we construct 26,694 dialogues totaling 786 hours across 48 domains, with disjoint training and test argument values. We additionally create an audio rendering of $\tau^2$-bench for external evaluation. We train an omni-modal language model on this corpus, enabling causal, chunk-level decisions and partial-transcript generation for downstream call completion. The model achieves tool-state macro-F1 scores of 0.48 and 0.47 on held-out dialogues and the external benchmark, respectively. For correct calls, the estimated mean lead over a turn-end cascade, using the same formatter, is 1.8-2.0 seconds in-domain and 1.1 seconds on $\tau^2$-bench. These results demonstrate a data-driven path toward spoken agents that act while listening. We will open-source the pipeline and the training scripts.
authors: Yizhou Peng, Chen Chen, Donghang Wu, Hexin Liu, Eng Siong Chng
bullets: Targets latency in spoken agents by detecting the earliest point where a tool and its required arguments are grounded.
Builds 26,694 dialogues spanning 48 domains, with 786 hours of speech and disjoint training/test argument values.
Trains chunk-level causal decisions and partial-transcript generation for downstream tool-call completion.
Reports tool-state macro-F1 of 0.48 on held-out dialogues and 0.47 on an external benchmark.
Correct calls lead turn-end execution by an estimated 1.8–2.0 seconds in-domain and 1.1 seconds externally.

papers.abstract: A chunky gold-tone chain necklace bought online for 2.43 USD was photographed four ways: worn with formal attire against a wood-panelled wall, worn at a party, worn with casual clothing in a recycling yard, and laid flat with no person present. We asked six frontier language models to estimate its price in 1,164 independent and sequential API sessions (4,604 logged rows) and compared estimates across settings. Among the four models that answered image prompts, the same necklace was priced 1.9 to 3.3 times higher in the formal photograph than in the flat-lay (all p < 0.01). Against the yard photograph, the ratio ranged from 1.23 (Grok 4.5, not significant) to 3.57 (Kimi K3), with Claude Fable 5 at 3.32. A text-only version of the task, in which the setting is described in words, produced formal-to-yard ratios of 2.2 to 3.9 in all six models, so the effect does not require pixels. Flat-lay estimates themselves were 7.8 to 18.7 times the receipt price, so part of any headline "outfit multiplier" computed against the receipt is baseline overestimate, not a context effect. A single instruction to ignore clothing and setting significantly reduced the effect in one model (ratio of ratios 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.91) and not detectably in the others; telling the model the photo came from a company website or a personal account changed nothing significant. Asked afterward whether a different outfit would have changed their number, Claude Fable 5 said yes in 24 of 24 sessions, GPT-5.6 in 69%, and GPT-4o in 18%, while GPT-4o also refused 79% of image estimation prompts. The study isolates a mechanism with one object and one wearer at about 10 sessions per model and condition; we outline the replication needed next, with multiple objects and a human benchmark. Data, code, and raw outputs are released.
bullets: The necklace’s formal-photo estimates were 1.9–3.3× higher than flat-lay estimates across responding models.
Formal settings also raised estimates relative to a recycling-yard scene, with effects varying by model.
Text-only descriptions produced similar context effects, indicating the bias does not require visual pixels.
Flat-lay estimates already exceeded the $2.43 receipt price by 7.8–18.7×, inflating receipt-based outfit multipliers.
An instruction to ignore context reduced the effect significantly in only one model; the study used one object and calls for replication across objects and human benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Adapting general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) to medical visual question answering (VQA) is valuable for helping clinicians read images and make diagnoses, but annotated data are scarce and provide only short answers, without reasoning annotations. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) fits these labels but overfits to them and amplifies their biases, eroding out-of-domain (OOD) generalization. Reinforcement learning (RL) better preserves generalization but never uses the gold answer as a training target: GRPO-style algorithms learn from the contrast between correct and incorrect answers within a group of sampled responses, so all-correct or all-wrong groups give no correctness signal. Existing SFT-RL hybrids either apply SFT and RL in separate stages or switch between them per question, or need reasoning traces from experts or stronger models, which medical VQA data lack. We propose GRASP, which combines RL and SFT in every update using only short answers: RL lets the model explore its own reasoning, SFT teaches the gold answer after that reasoning to supply the direct supervision RL lacks, and their balance adapts to how well the model answers each question. Tuning only about 1% of the parameters with LoRA, GRASP outperforms all compared training objectives both in domain and on OOD open-ended questions across Qwen3-VL-8B, InternVL3-8B and Gemma 3-4B. On an OOD benchmark spanning eight imaging modalities, GRASP-trained InternVL3-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B beat all 10 compared general and medical VLMs in open-ended accuracy, including models trained on up to 2,600 times more data or with over 250 times more trainable parameters. We release MedTerse, a dataset of 12.9K short-answer questions, and our code at https://github.com/sea-comet/GRASP-MedVQA.
authors: Wanqi Dong, Wanyue Dong, Jingze Ge, Mehul Motani
bullets: Addresses SFT overfitting and RL’s weak signal when sampled responses are all correct or all wrong.
Uses RL to encourage self-generated reasoning, then applies SFT toward the gold short answer; their balance adapts to per-question performance.
Trains about 1% of parameters with LoRA and improves both in-domain and out-of-distribution open-ended VQA across three VLMs.
On an eight-modality OOD benchmark, GRASP-trained InternVL3-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B outperform 10 compared general and medical VLMs.
Introduces MedTerse, a 12.9K-question short-answer dataset, and releases the implementation.

papers.title: GRASP: Group-Adaptive Hybrid RL-SFT Post-Training for Medical VQA without Reasoning Annotations

papers.abstract: Vision--language models applied to medical question answering can reach correct diagnoses without using the diagnostic image, inferring instead from the clinical vignette. We ask whether this is visible in how \emph{firmly} a model holds its answer: does a model defend a diagnosis derived from a blank placeholder as tenaciously as one derived from a real medical image? Crossing an image-substitution protocol with two levels of adversarial pressure on 60 Italian State Examination items, we find no evidence that ungrounded verdicts are more fragile. In a paired item-level analysis, fabricated consensus (L4) overturns 94.4\% of verdicts with the real image and 98.1\% without ($\Delta = +0.037$; one-sided 95\% upper bound $+0.105$); contentless doubt (L1) overturns 62.5\% and 51.8\% ($\Delta = -0.107$, 95\% CI $[-0.209, -0.001]$), the point estimate running opposite to the direction a grounding detector requires. The two levels nonetheless produce opposite \emph{dynamics}: under L4 the model flips once, always to the exact option argued for (110/110 first-turn flips), and then freezes, averaging 1.9 verdict changes over ten turns; under L1 it never settles, averaging 7.4 changes. Instability under contentless doubt tracks intrinsic item ambiguity rather than evidence availability, and so does not serve as a grounding signal. Flips are almost entirely corrupting (99/100 across both levels). The model is not unaware of the missing evidence---it flags the blank image at baseline on 35 of 60 items and abstains on 4--6---yet those abstentions do not survive contact with pressure. None of the epistemic signals a user could plausibly consult distinguishes a grounded diagnosis from a confabulated one.
authors: Federico Felizzi, Francesco Andrea Causio, Bianca Destro Castaniti, Olivia Riccomi, Michele Ferramola, Vittorio De Vita, Alessandro Tosi, Antonio Cristiano, Alessia Longo, Lorenzo De Mori, Chiara Battipaglia, Melissa Sawaya, Luigi De Angelis, Marcello Di Pumpo, Alessandra Piscitelli, Pietro Eric Risuleo, Giulia Vojvodic, Mariapia Vassalli, Nicolo Scarsi, Manuel Del Medico

Instability under doubt reflected item ambiguity rather than access to visual evidence.
Models often noticed missing images initially, but their abstentions did not persist; nearly all flips were corrupting.

papers.title: Conviction Without Evidence: Verdict Stability Is Independent of Visual Grounding in Medical Vision--Language Models
papers.tldr: Medical vision–language models defend diagnoses based on blank images about as firmly as those based on real images, so verdict stability does not reveal visual grounding.

papers.abstract: Spatial localization of surgical instruments through bounding-box annotations is a foundational component of surgical scene understanding, supporting detection, tracking, interaction analysis, and grounded vision-language applications. Yet existing annotations often cover selected frames, video subsets, or dataset variants rather than complete procedures. Manual extension is time-consuming and expert-dependent. Additionally, weakly supervised and detector-based pseudo-labels require task-specific training and may be imprecise. In this study, we design a scalable MLLM-based annotation framework that converts surgical frames and existing instrument-presence labels into accurate bounding boxes, and systematically analyze its reliability, cost, and design sensitivity. We instantiate the framework using six MLLMs and a multi-call configuration on laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Cholec80. Using a carefully designed stratification scheme, two annotators independently label 1,000 frames, and an expert surgeon reviews one annotation set to establish the reference. Results show that instrument-set F1 ranges from 88.2 to 92.7,whereas mIoU ranges from 0.180 to 0.735, showing that comparable recognition can conceal large localization differences. A structured multi-stage annotation pipeline achieves 0.784 mIoU, compared with 0.735 for the best single-call baseline and 0.814 human-human agreement. Using the best accuracy pipeline, we create and publicly release a spatial extension of Cholec80 comprising 285,977 bounding boxes across all 184,498 annotated frames from the 80 videos. The annotations and human references are made available on GitHub
authors: Mohamed Hamdy, Muraam Abdel-Ghani, Fatmaelzahraa Ahmed, Sifna Nasar, Mariam Ahmed, Khalid Al-Jalham, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, Shidin Balakrishnan

Evaluates six MLLMs and multi-call annotation designs on laparoscopic cholecystectomy frames from Cholec80.
Shows that similar instrument recognition F1 can hide substantial localization differences, with mIoU ranging from 0.180 to 0.735.
A structured multi-stage pipeline reaches 0.784 mIoU, approaching human-human agreement of 0.814.
Releases 285,977 bounding boxes covering all 184,498 annotated frames across 80 videos.

papers.abstract: Modern surgical AI increasingly requires multimodal understanding rather than isolated perception, yet existing datasets remain largely limited to single-task supervision such as recognition or templated question answering. Current medical VQA resources often rely on synthetic templates, lack natural descriptive supervision, or provide sparse annotations that hinder reasoning about spatial relations and procedural context. We introduce MIS-VQA, a surgical vision-language dataset generated through an annotation-driven pipeline that converts heterogeneous surgical annotations into structured textual scene representations. Using EndoVis18 and CholecT50, we transform phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation labels into unified contexts that guide large language models to generate clinically coherent question-answer pairs. MIS-VQA supports four response types-concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning-enabling hierarchical evaluation from atomic visual grounding to compositional reasoning. To address annotation sparsity, we incorporate confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks, enabling spatially grounded supervision at scale. MIS-VQA establishes a unified benchmark for surgical vision-language understanding with spatial supervision and multi-tier reasoning evaluation. To demonstrate its utility, we introduce LLaVA-SurgXpert, a family of surgical vision-language models with visual encoders to analyze how visual representations influence multimodal reasoning. Experiments show consistent improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines while revealing capability gaps between perceptual grounding and higher-level reasoning hidden in prior benchmarks.
authors: Mohamed Hamdy, Iheb Zouari, Fatmaelzahraa Ahmed, Muraam Abdel-Ghani, Muhammed Arsalan, Ponnuthurai Suganthan, Khalid Al-Jalham, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, Shidin Balakrishnan

papers.abstract: LVLM benchmarks tell us whether a model answers correctly, but not which visual conventions it has retained, nor where those conventions live. Sketches expose this hidden structure. A sketch removes texture, lighting, and photographic context while preserving the strokes humans judged sufficient for recognition. If an LVLM can operate on that abstraction, the surviving signal is structural rather than merely photometric. We introduce a training-free sketch probe with three readouts: temporal part-construction order, spatial attention-based grounding, and the mechanistic layer/head locus of grounding. We evaluate nine LVLMs on part order and five on the attention readouts, over two part-annotated sketch datasets. Three findings emerge. First, LVLM part order tracks human convention: models reproduce canonical orderings where human drawings converge, and become correspondingly variable where human orderings vary. Controls that blank, withhold, and mismatch the sketch locate this convention in the language model. Second, part-level grounding survives the abstraction: attention heads selected from the frozen model with an existing recipe recover part and object regions on object and scene sketches, with no grounding supervision. Third, the grounding signal concentrates in a narrow mid-network band whose location follows the base language model rather than parameter count in the two families we compare, and remains stable across object and scene sketches. The result is a practical diagnostic for sketch-driven LVLMs: no fine-tuning, no auxiliary segmenter, and a layer band that doubles as a head-selection prior, matching or improving grounding mAcc@0.1 in every model and dataset we tested.
authors: Chaitat Utintu, Ahmed Bourouis, Arkaprabha Basu, Yi-Zhe Song

Across nine LVLMs, part-construction order follows human conventions: canonical where people agree and variable where human order varies.
Across five LVLMs, attention-based grounding recovers object and part regions from object and scene sketches without grounding supervision.
Grounding concentrates in a stable mid-network layer band tied to the base language model rather than parameter count in the studied families.
The probe matches or improves grounding mAcc@0.1 in every tested model and dataset, without fine-tuning or an auxiliary segmenter.

papers.abstract: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong visual reasoners, yet remain limited in open-world, multi-step search that requires grounding images, selecting tools, and integrating web evidence. Existing approaches typically construct and filter fixed offline corpora whose question distributions cannot adapt as the target deep-search agent improves. Building on MTA-Agent's image-grounded QA construction, we present MTA-Zero, an online multimodal QA-Solver co-training framework for self-improving multimodal deep-search agents that requires no precomputed multi-hop corpus. Starting from image-grounded VQA seed contexts, a trainable QA Generator retrieves evidence and constructs verified multi-hop questions online. A separate deep-search Solver then selects tools, gathers evidence, and answers the generated questions. To focus generation on the Solver's learning frontier, we derive a Goldilocks reward for the QA Generator from the Solver's group-wise rollout success rate: questions solved by all rollouts or by none receive zero reward, whereas questions near the current frontier are favored. We optimize the two policies independently with GRPO, without sharing parameters or gradients. Across six multimodal deep-search benchmarks, MTA-Zero improves a Qwen3-VL-8B Solver from 36.91% to 51.58% mean accuracy and achieves performance comparable to GPT-5 under the same agent workflow. The same framework also improves a newer Qwen3.6-27B Solver by 10.82 points. These results show that verified online question generation provides a policy-specific curriculum for continually improving multimodal deep-search agents.

Independently trains the QA Generator and deep-search Solver with GRPO, without shared parameters or gradients.
Improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 36.91% to 51.58% mean accuracy across six benchmarks; also boosts Qwen3.6-27B by 10.82 points.

papers.abstract: Many robot manipulation videos do not indicate whether the task was successfully completed. RoboJev-27B is an open-weight vision-language model that takes a task instruction, 10 frames of a manipulation attempt, and (if available) final frames from auxiliary cameras and predicts whether the robot accomplished the task. RoboJev-27B is a variant of JEV-27B-VL, trained with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the language model only (keeping the vision encoder frozen) using 52,598 episode records. It also uses a source-specific KL penalty that applies only to research data, anchoring predictions closer to the original model on those sources. It uses a calibrated two-token readout that outputs success/failure probabilities in a single forward pass. On 268 held-out episodes of the same robot model (SO-101), RoboJev-27B attains 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC. It also generalises to episodes collected by unseen labs/robots (AUROC = 0.890 over 459 episodes) as well as to clearly labelled community-collected episodes (accuracy = 93.3% over 135 episodes), where the base model attains an AUROC = 0.900 on the unseen-lab/robot subset with the same inputs. It takes 0.26 seconds per episode (median, serial) to infer on a single H100, which is about \$0.19 per 1,000 success predictions at \$2.69 per GPU-hour (not including media processing and serving costs). RoboJev-27B is released together with its inference code, along with a transparent evaluation: 20,628 predictions organized into 29 model/protocol entries are made available to facilitate browsing and to enable reproducible benchmarking of success detection. We also compare against strong API-based frontier VLMs, which take in fewer input frames (4 images from the primary camera only); note that this comparison is not strictly like-for-like because RoboJev-27B is given more frames at inference.

papers.abstract: Advertisers routinely create multiple duration variants of ads to meet marketing budgets and viewer preferences, a labor-intensive and costly process. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at general video understanding, their ability to perform specialized editorial tasks remains unexplored. We introduce AdShot, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on shot selection for ad clipping. It contains 823 professionally edited ad pairs (30-sec sources and 15-sec edits) across 194 brands and 17 industries, annotated with shot-level boundaries and content features (action, emotion, information, imagery). We evaluate 13 state-of-the-art video-only MLLMs and 2 audio-visual MLLMs (7B-72B parameters) on shot selection accuracy (Precision, Recall, F1), duration constraints (15s), and content preservation, including an audio ablation. We find: (1) model architecture matters more than scale, with smaller models often matching or exceeding larger ones; performance is strongest for target ads with 6-10 shots; (2) models exhibit a mean absolute duration error of 5.39s, with most tending to overshoot the 15s target, though they can still substantially reduce human editing effort; (3) all models exhibit systematic content biases, favoring information-rich and emotion-focused shots while under-selecting action and imagery. We publicly release our benchmark to facilitate research at the intersection of multimodal AI and computational advertising.
authors: Wen Xie, Om Rastogi, Sai Siddhartha Vivek Dhir Rangoju, Gijs Overgoor, Yakov Bart, Sarah Ostadabbas
bullets: Addresses the costly, labor-intensive creation of multiple ad-duration variants.
Introduces 823 professionally edited 30-to-15-second ad pairs spanning 194 brands and 17 industries, with shot-level annotations.
Evaluates 13 video-only and 2 audio-visual MLLMs on shot selection, 15-second duration compliance, and content preservation.
Architecture appears more important than model scale; performance is strongest on ads containing 6–10 shots.
Models typically overshoot the target by 5.39 seconds on average, favor information- and emotion-rich shots, and under-select action and imagery.

papers.abstract: Visual effects are often easier to demonstrate via reference than to describe in words. We study effect-reference editing, where a reference image shows a desired visual effect and language identifies which properties should guide the edit. Existing single-pass editing techniques often fail to make fine-grained edits, resulting in unintended changes to source content or deviations from the reference effect. We introduce KINESYS, a test-time adaptation framework for effect-reference editing that combines reference-aware and source-aware feedback to transfer the desired effect while preserving the composition and content of the original shot. To ensure KINESYS can produce a diverse set of edits that preserve the source, we develop a robust optimization strategy in which the generative model is fine-tuned across multiple noise samples and optimization runs. Evaluation with VLM judges, source preservation metrics (LPIPS, TPIPS), and a user study shows that KINESYS outperforms state-of-the-art image editors in source preservation; on effect transfer, it remains competitive with Nano Banana 2 and outperforms open-weight editors.
authors: Noah Frahm, Luchao Qi, Haoze Li, Dan B Goldman, Sambit Bhattacharya, Roni Sengupta
bullets: Targets fine-grained effect-reference editing guided by both a reference image and language.
Combines reference-aware and source-aware feedback during optimization.
Fine-tunes across multiple noise samples and optimization runs to produce diverse, source-preserving edits.
Evaluations using VLM judges, preservation metrics, and a user study show stronger source preservation than existing editors.
Effect transfer is competitive with Nano Banana 2 and better than open-weight editors.

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge editing aims to update visually grounded facts in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) while preserving unrelated text and visual behaviors. However, standard answer-level metrics can hide evidence misgrounding: an edit may produce the target answer on the original image yet remain sensitive to incidental context rather than the intended visual evidence. To examine this issue in a controlled setting, we construct WaterBird-Edit, an analysis set that decouples bird habitat labels from background context and measures whether edited predictions remain stable when the target evidence is preserved but the background changes. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose VICE (Visual In-Context Editing), a retrieval-based framework that stores edits in external memory and applies them through visual in-context demonstrations designed to expose task-relevant evidence. Experiments on three standard benchmarks show that VICE achieves strong lifelong editing performance, while results on WaterBird-Edit show that it substantially reduces sensitivity to the controlled background shifts. Code and dataset are available in https://github.com/Wang-Z-W/VICE-main.
authors: Zhiwu Wang, Yichen Wu, Jinqian Yang, Yizhou Yang, Renzhen Wang, Qian Zhao, Deyu Meng
bullets: Identifies evidence misgrounding as a failure mode hidden by answer-level editing metrics.
Introduces WaterBird-Edit, which tests prediction stability when target evidence is preserved but background context changes.
Proposes VICE, a retrieval-based external-memory framework using visual in-context demonstrations to highlight relevant evidence.
Reports strong lifelong editing performance on three standard benchmarks.
WaterBird-Edit results show reduced sensitivity to controlled background shifts.

papers.abstract: Unified large multimodal models (ULMMs) are able to perform visual reasoning through interleaved text-image generation, but generating explicit intermediate images incurs significant computational overhead. While visual latent reasoning addresses this, most existing methods rely on vision-language models (VLMs) incapable of visual generation. We propose Oddin, a novel framework enabling latent visual reasoning in ULMMs. Oddin replaces intermediate images with compact latent tokens processed entirely by the understanding branch, reserving the generation branch for the final output image. We train the model via offline self-distillation with three objectives, final image generation losses, text distillation losses, and cross-entropy losses for special tokens. Oddin surpasses interleaved generation baselines and closed-source VLMs on average across seven VBVR-Pro visual reasoning tasks. Qualitative analysis reveals that latent tokens attend to relevant regions in an input image, demonstrating that ULMMs can perform complex visual reasoning without generating intermediate images.
authors: Jaeyong Ko, Hankyeol Kim, Pilsung Kang
bullets: Targets the computational overhead of interleaved text-image reasoning.
Uses latent tokens processed by the model’s understanding branch, while reserving image generation for the final output.
Trains through offline self-distillation combining image-generation, text-distillation, and special-token objectives.
Outperforms interleaved-generation baselines and closed-source VLMs on average across seven VBVR-Pro tasks.
Latent tokens attend to relevant image regions, supporting their role in complex visual reasoning.

papers.title: Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation

papers.abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have revolutionized general visual perception, existing methods suffer from severe hallucination in the aerial domain, where extreme scale variations and visual ambiguity abound. Existing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) paradigms force models to mimic ground truth without modeling uncertainty, often resulting in blind guessing on tiny or unrecognizable objects in aerial scenes. In this paper, we present Aerial-R1, the first aerial MLLM framework to reinforce visual reasoning capabilities for aerial reasoning and segmentation. Drawing inspiration from the reasoning-incentivizing mechanisms of DeepSeek-R1, we find that trustworthy perception stems from consistency across views, establishing a visual parallel to the Chain-of-Thought in logic. To effectively adapt policy optimization for non-autoregressive mask generation, we introduce Hybrid-View Group Advantage-Weighted Regression (H-GAWR). This strategy constructs dynamic groups of high-resolution and low-resolution views, seamlessly bridging group-relative advantage estimation with advantage-weighted policy extraction. By enforcing consensus on clear inputs and strictly penalizing hallucinations on ambiguous ones, Aerial-R1 develops an explicitly incentivized refusal mechanism. Extensive experiments on VSAI-Ref, the first aerial MLLM benchmark dedicated to jointly evaluating dense reasoning and hallucination robustness, demonstrate that Aerial-R1 significantly outperforms SFT baselines in segmentation precision while substantially mitigating fatal hallucinations in low-information scenarios, paving the way for more reliable and trustworthy aerial agents. Codes are available on https://github.com/phy709/Aerial-R1.
authors: Jisheng Dang, Huaiyuan Peng, Yixuan Wang, Kun Wang, Zhang Li, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Targets severe hallucinations caused by scale variation, visual ambiguity, and SFT’s lack of uncertainty modeling in aerial imagery.
Uses Hybrid-View Group Advantage-Weighted Regression (H-GAWR) to optimize non-autoregressive mask generation across high- and low-resolution views.
Encourages agreement on clear inputs while learning to refuse predictions for ambiguous or unrecognizable objects.
Evaluated on VSAI-Ref, where it reportedly surpasses SFT baselines in segmentation precision and reduces hallucinations in low-information scenarios.

figures.caption: Fig. 6. Qualitative examples of generalized reasoning. (Bottom) A comprehensive scene description demonstrating the model’s capacity to understand global context, accurately capturing key landmarks (the temple), surrounding environments, and spatial relationships. These examples collectively demonstrate that Aerial-R1 retains robust conversational and holistic descriptive capabilities alongside dense segmentation precision.

Fig. 5. Robustness Visualization Results. (a) Performance of Aerial-R1 across different spatial scenarios. (b) Performance of Aerial-R1 under varying temporal (lighting) conditions. The model’s predictions are highlighted in green boxes.

We visualize challenging scenarios, including dense forest and hazy water, where the target objects described in the prompts are visually unrecognizable or absent. (Bottom Row) Aerial-R1 correctly identifies the lack of visual evidence and triggers the explicitly incentivized refusal mechanism by outputting empty masks, demonstrating superior trustworthiness.

The blue line (left axis) represents the Mean Reward, which rapidly plateaus (>1.4), demonstrating that the model quickly learns and maintains the safety boundary despite the discrete nature of the anti-hallucination penalty.

papers.tldr: Aerial-R1 improves aerial image reasoning and segmentation by reinforcing cross-view consistency and penalizing hallucinations, especially for ambiguous or low-information scenes.

papers.abstract: Embodied vision-language models must answer questions from partial, evolving observations. Their success depends on both the reasoning capability selected and the evidence available to it. Expert routers adapt internal computation, while tool-augmented systems acquire external evidence; choosing these independently can leave a suitable expert without the evidence it needs. We introduce EKT-Router, a bounded framework that jointly selects a capability expert, optional knowledge, and perceptual tools. Outcome-derived signatures represent the overlapping strengths of General, Spatial Reasoning, and Spatiotemporal experts. A joint utility scores complete expert-evidence routes under a call budget. After acquisition, a packet verifier admits valid evidence with positive predicted expert-conditioned gain. The selected expert then answers once, reverting to the unchanged observation if all packets are rejected. Across 6 embodied QA benchmarks, EKT-Router achieves a mean score of 61.4, the highest among the compared systems, and averages 74.7 on 10 general vision-language benchmarks. With all external evidence disabled, question-conditioned expert selection alone improves over the best fixed expert by 1.75 points. Ablations show that learned routing is the dominant component and that knowledge and perception are complementary.
authors: Weilin Ruan, Yingjie Xu, Yangkai Wei, Bohan Zhou, Shuaibo Li, Harold Haodong Chen, Kaiwen Zhou, Yinchuan Li, Ying-Cong Chen, James Cheng
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between selected reasoning capability and available evidence in partial, evolving observations.
Uses outcome-derived expert signatures for General, Spatial Reasoning, and Spatiotemporal experts.
Scores complete expert–knowledge–perception routes under a call budget, then verifies evidence for expert-conditioned usefulness.
Achieves a mean score of 61.4 across 6 embodied QA benchmarks and 74.7 across 10 general vision-language benchmarks.
Expert selection alone improves 1.75 points over the best fixed expert; ablations identify learned routing as dominant and knowledge and perception as complementary.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EKT-Router. (a) Offline: independent adaptations form the expert portfolio; evidence-free diagnostics yield capability signatures, and paired answer outcomes supervise the router and verifier. papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a hybrid Mamba-Transformer vision-language model that optimizes speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for local agentic workloads. Derived from the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B model family, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB combines Star Elastic compression with 2-bit Quantization-Aware Distillation for memory-constrained deployment. The model is optimized for reasoning, agentic tool use, and web & terminal interactions. We also trained a LiLiCorr speculative drafter that is released alongside the model to reach our target inference speed. The resulting model achieves a higher accuracy than leading models with similar memory footprints and speed across many benchmarks for general agentic capabilities (e.g., GDPVal v2), web browsing (e.g., BrowseComp), and terminal use (e.g., Terminal-Bench 2.1), with a relatively high TPS of 84 on RTX Spark that is comparable to models with much lower active parameter counts and more than sufficient for long-horizon agentic applications.

papers.abstract: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.
