papers.abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reason for longer, attention to the initial visual input diminishes, weakening visual grounding. Visual memory reintroduces visual evidence during reasoning. We conduct a controlled analysis of visual memory along three axes: curation, organization, and access. We find that local evidence benefits from global context, compact latent representations balance accuracy and visual-context cost, and the utility of memory access depends on the reasoning state. Guided by these findings, we propose ReMAP (Reasoning-Time Memory-Augmented Perception), which couples two complementary latent memories: a static, question-conditioned Global memory that preserves scene and cross-image context, and a dynamic Local memory that uses this context as an anchor while selecting and re-encoding region-level evidence according to the current reasoning state. Both memories return compact latent tokens inserted into the reasoning sequence, and a reinforcement-learning access policy trained with branched rollouts decides when to continue reasoning or invoke Global or Local memory. On ten benchmark families, ReMAP outperforms prior visual-memory methods on all four multi-image benchmarks, exceeding the strongest prior results on MuirBench and MIMIC by 8.38 and 14.84 percentage points. Across four backbone families, enabling memory access improves over the same trained model with memory disabled, and on shared V*Bench, CV-Bench-2D, and MuirBench questions ReMAP reduces the visual tokens entering the reasoning sequence by 51.0-76.8% relative to the native-resolution backbone. Further analyses show that Global and Local memory form distinct yet complementary latent representations. Together, these components restore the perceptual cycle by letting the reasoning state trigger targeted visual retrieval, with the retrieved evidence guiding subsequent reasoning.
bullets: Long reasoning can diminish attention to the initial visual input, motivating visual memory during inference.

papers.abstract: Semantic misinformation can arise when an authentic image is paired with a caption that changes or distorts its narrative. Because the image itself may contain no visible signs of manipulation, methods designed to detect pixel-level artifacts can miss these misleading image-caption pairs. We study this problem using DGM4+, a dataset designed to evaluate the detection of global scene and semantic inconsistencies. We propose a multimodal model that combines image-text representations from SigLIP with visual scene features from DINOv2 through a projection MLP, and adapts Qwen2-VL-7B using LoRA. The model jointly predicts whether an image-caption pair is authentic, identifies the manipulation type, and grounds the misleading caption tokens. On the DGM4+ validation split, the model achieves an F1 score of $0.9679$ for binary authenticity classification. These results suggest that parameter-efficient adaptation of vision-language models is promising for detecting semantic inconsistencies, while also motivating further work on precise token-level grounding.

Token-level grounding remains an area for further improvement.

papers.abstract: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video--language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5\% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7\% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.

papers.abstract: Objective: To develop a unified vision-language model for prompt-conditioned quantitative ultrasound measurement that addresses the mismatch between continuous measurement targets and discrete token-based numerical prediction. Methods: This article presents HAD-VLM, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion framework that combines autoregressive text generation with continuous measurement prediction within a shared backbone. Visual prompt tuning adapts the vision encoder to ultrasound images. A diffusion process predicts a five-component representation comprising caliper endpoint coordinates and measurement length. A post-processing strategy combining the proposed coordinate-length consistency mechanism with ensemble prediction is introduced to refine measurement estimates. We evaluate four echocardiographic measurement tasks on EchoNet-LVH, with additional assessments of medical question answering and X-ray vertebral measurement. Results: HAD-VLM achieves mean absolute errors of 1.36, 2.77, 3.05, and 1.16 mm for IVSd, LVIDd, LVIDs, and LVPWd, respectively, reducing errors by 21.4-37.6\% relative to the Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline. It also outperforms fine-tuned Qwen3-VL and direct MLP regression across all four tasks. Medical question answering performance is preserved on the evaluated dataset. For X-ray vertebral measurement, HAD-VLM reduces mean absolute error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels. Conclusion: Integrating autoregressive language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction improves quantitative medical image measurement while retaining prompt-conditioned task flexibility. Significance: HAD-VLM provides a unified approach to combining language interaction with anatomically grounded numerical prediction for quantitative medical image analysis.

papers.abstract: Echocardiography is the cornerstone of cardiovascular diagnostics, yet its global utility is constrained by a critical shortage of experienced interpreters. Current artificial intelligence (AI) solutions remain limited, typically operating as opaque "black boxes" or focusing on narrow tasks that fail to capture the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning of a clinician. Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal vision-language model that performs comprehensive echocardiographic analysis to support clinician interpretation. By emulating the cognitive workflow of a cardiologist, EchoChat integrates vast medical knowledge with a chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to explicitly ground its conclusions in visual evidence. Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations, our model establishes a new state-of-the-art across diverse cohorts from six international medical centers. It supports the broadest diagnostic scope of 33 cardiac conditions and findings, including 15 newly added conditions for which it achieves an average F1 of 73.7% across available external evaluations. It surpasses existing best-performing foundation models in cardiac condition recognition (improving average recall by 13.54% on shared tasks) and quantification (average R2 score increase of 0.275 on shared tasks). Furthermore, in a source-blinded echocardiographer reader study, echocardiography reports co-generated with EchoChat were rated higher in diagnostic accuracy and completeness by two senior echocardiographers, and improved diagnostic performance from 72.78% to 82.75% in terms of F1 score over routine-reader only reports. These results demonstrate that integrating clinical reasoning into multimodal AI can democratize specialist expertise and transform the standard of cardiovascular care.

papers.abstract: Photonic crystal fibers (PCFs) underpin critical applications in telecommunications, sensing, and high-power laser delivery, yet their design remains a manual, expert-intensive process that couples geometric intuition with deep waveguide physics. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising path toward automating PCF design, but can they truly reason about photonic physics from microscopy images, or do they merely recognize visual patterns? We introduce PCFBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs on the perception, reasoning, and decision steps of the photonic inverse-design loop. PCFBench spans 26 tasks organized into six categories of increasing cognitive demand (Geometry Perception, Physics Understanding, Text Generation, Multi-modal Reasoning, Inverse-Design Decision, and Code Generation), built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples across 18 structurally diverse fiber families. We evaluate both individual VLMs on isolated tasks and multi-agent systems (MAS) on the full sequential pipeline from perception to design. Our results reveal a striking perception-design gap: current models can identify fiber geometry with moderate success, yet consistently fail to translate that visual understanding into physics-aware design actions. Moreover, cascading agents through the pipeline exposes significant error propagation, where upstream perception mistakes compound into downstream design failures. These findings suggest that neither model scaling nor naive agent chaining suffices, and that closing the loop demands explicit physical grounding. PCFBench provides the community with a rigorous, multi-dimensional testbed to measure progress toward AI-assisted photonic engineering. The project is available at https://pcfbench.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) by enabling fine-grained emotion understanding through reasoning over multimodal evidence. However, they still exhibit systematic confusion between semantically adjacent emotions with highly overlapping multimodal cues. Existing approaches typically address these errors through global parameter adaptation, making confusion correction costly and inflexible. We instead observe that emotion confusion is highly localized and therefore better addressed through reusable pair-specific expertise. Building on this insight, we propose Confusion-Aware Skill Evolution (CASE), the first agent-skill framework for MER. CASE maintains a sparse, self-evolving library of pair-specific EmotionSkills that externalize affective expertise from model parameters, enabling the learned expertise to be continuously refined and readily transferred across diverse frozen MLLM backbones. During inference, CASE dynamically retrieves the appropriate EmotionSkill to reinforce boundary-aware reasoning while keeping the MLLM backbone frozen. Extensive experiments on CA-MER, DFEW, and EMER demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of CASE across both general-purpose and emotion-specialized MLLMs. Notably, CASE improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B on the CA-MER benchmark from 46.80% to 59.13%, while achieving consistent gains across MLLMs.
authors: Siyu Wu, Zeyu Liang, Linghao Wang, Qiyun Zheng, Yi Yao, Ling Lo, Hongxia Xie
bullets: Targets systematic confusion between semantically adjacent emotions with overlapping multimodal cues.
Represents affective expertise as sparse, self-evolving pair-specific EmotionSkills rather than global model adaptations.
Retrieves relevant skills at inference time to support boundary-aware emotion reasoning.
Transfers across frozen general-purpose and emotion-specialized MLLM backbones.
Raises Qwen3-VL-8B’s CA-MER average accuracy from 46.80% to 59.13% and delivers consistent gains across evaluated MLLMs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models used for decisions in histopathology rarely return calibrated probabilities over the candidates a user cares about. Decision-native models write a question and a candidate set chosen at run time into the input and return a normalised distribution from a small decision head in one forward pass. We build PathJev-P, a decision-native model for histopathology: MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head, trained on 40,000 patch states from three public collections whose expert labels are turned into typed questions with organ-specific candidate sets and a "none of these" option. In a comparison over 3 seeds with an analysis plan fixed before testing, on test sets without documented overlap with the training data of the backbone, PathJev-P is more accurate than a generative model trained with the same backbone, data and selection rule, the zero-shot pathology model CONCH and a general medical decision model (balanced accuracy 0.541 against 0.492, 0.345 and 0.213); its advantage over the generative model comes from two organs absent from training. The calibration advantage depends on how the generative model's probabilities are read out. With the summed candidate log-likelihood used in previous work, PathJev-P has the lower calibration error (ECE 0.204 against 0.279); with a length-normalised read-out of the same generative model, examined post hoc, the two have similar mean calibration error (0.201) and the generative model is better calibrated on the unseen organs, where PathJev-P remains over-confident. A supervised linear probe on a pathology foundation model is better calibrated in every setting. In a qualitative whole-slide demonstration, PathJev-P labels unsupervised tissue clusters with abstention and separates carcinoma from other tissue while running the model on a fraction of the tiles.
bullets: Addresses the lack of calibrated probabilities for user-defined diagnostic candidates in vision-language pathology models.
Uses MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head that outputs a normalized distribution in one forward pass.
Trained on 40,000 labeled patch states from three public collections, with organ-specific typed questions and a “none of these” option.
Achieved balanced accuracy of 0.541 versus 0.492 for a matched generative model, 0.345 for CONCH, and 0.213 for a general medical decision model.

Calibration depends on probability readout: PathJev-P is better than summed-log-likelihood generation, but comparable after length normalization and remains over-confident on unseen organs; a supervised linear probe calibrates better overall.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of PathJev. (1) Expert labels of six training sets from three public collections are turned deterministically into typed decisions: a patch carries a Choice (one of K candidates, including “none of these”), Noul (yes/no) and Score (ordered levels) question; the orange candidate is the label. (2) The image is encoded by MedSigLIP and enters the Gemma-3 decoder as tokens, followed by the question and all candidates, each closed by a marker token. One forward pass yields hidden states at the markers; a decision head shared by all questions sums a per-candidate score, a question–candidate interaction and a set-attention term, and a softmax returns the distribution. A generative read-out, as implemented here, needs one forward pass per candidate. Training: Stage A fits the head on the frozen 4-bit backbone; Stage B adds LoRA adapters. papers.selection_reason: Decision-native vision-language model built on MedGemma directly extends a multimodal LLM with a calibrated decision head.
papers.title: PathJev: Decision-Native Vision-Language Modelling for Histopathology

papers.abstract: Advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have driven substantial progress in multimodal embeddings. Recent methods exploit generative capabilities by augmenting embedded inputs with self-generated reasoning to produce more informative embeddings. However, conventional retrieval supervision for training embedding models specifies pairwise relevance relations without explicitly guiding the reasoning used for input augmentation. Such reasoning is neither directly observed nor uniquely determined by the input, allowing multiple plausible traces to introduce semantic cues of varying retrieval utility. Existing approaches largely optimize reasoning conditioned on the input alone, limiting the exploration of retrieval-relevant traces. We introduce PILOT, a framework that models reasoning as a latent variable and instantiates its prior and posterior distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a shared MLLM. The prior conditions only on the input, whereas the posterior uses additional training-time relational evidence to guide reasoning exploration. To translate the posterior's broader exploration into inference-time improvements, we derive an importance-weighted variational objective and instantiate it as a prior-posterior co-evolution framework that improves both modes under a shared inference-compatible reward while selectively transferring posterior trajectories to the prior according to their utility and prior reachability. On the 78-task MMEB-V2 benchmark, PILOT outperforms the primary baseline across all 12 task groups at both 2B and 7B parameters, improving overall scores by 3.2 and 3.3 points, respectively, with the largest gains in visual-document retrieval (+6.1 and +6.4 points). Our results show that relational supervision is most valuable not as a post-hoc reward but as a signal for shaping how reasoning is explored in training reasoning-enhanced embedding models.
authors: Tianyu Yang, Yijun Tian, Lars Benedikt Kaesberg, Jan Philip Wahle, Bela Gipp, Terry Ruas, Daniel Kurzawe
bullets: Existing embedding training specifies relevance relations but does not guide the latent reasoning used to augment inputs.
PILOT models reasoning with input-only prior and relation-informed posterior modes of a shared MLLM.
An importance-weighted variational objective enables prior–posterior co-evolution and selective transfer of useful, reachable posterior traces.
On MMEB-V2, PILOT improves over the primary baseline across all 12 task groups for both 2B and 7B models.
Overall gains are 3.2 and 3.3 points, with the largest improvements in visual-document retrieval: 6.1 and 6.4 points.

(b) Joint SFT and contrastive learning initialize both reasoning modes in a shared MLLM (Eq. 8). (c) GRPO optimizes both modes using rewards evaluated under the prior context (Eq. 12), while importanceweighted fitting transfers trajectories to the prior according to retrieval utility and prior reachability (Eq. 13). (d) Inference runs the prior alone.

papers.selection_reason: Improves multimodal embeddings via privileged reasoning exploration from MLLMs, directly fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Rewards: Privileged Reasoning Exploration for Multimodal Embeddings
papers.tldr: PILOT improves multimodal embeddings by using relational supervision to explore and transfer more retrieval-useful reasoning traces during training.

papers.abstract: While large vision-language models excel at optical character recognition, it remains unclear how their underlying vision encoders process text and its meaning, and whether they support anything resembling reading comprehension. We systematically study transformer-based vision encoders, using cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts together with probing and retrieval-based analyses as a controlled window into these broader capabilities. Our layer-wise analyses span orthographic, grammatical, and semantic organization, and reveal that strong cross-modal mapping emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed, coinciding with a progression from surface-level to semantic representations. Although this hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, larger self-supervised models and text-rich training data partially support similar behaviors without explicit language supervision. Together, our results suggest that increasing model and training-data scale, as well as text-rich training data, can partially compensate for the absence of language supervision.
authors: Sugam Karki, Ra\'ul V\'azquez, Yova Kementchedjhieva
bullets: Studies how vision encoders process rendered text across orthographic, grammatical, and semantic levels.
Combines cross-modal alignment, probing, and retrieval analyses to examine representational hierarchy.
Finds object and text recognition emerge before strong text–concept mapping.
The hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, but larger self-supervised models and text-rich data show partial similar behavior.
Results suggest scale and text-rich training can partly offset the lack of explicit language supervision.

papers.selection_reason: Systematically analyzes cross-modal alignment and representational hierarchy in Vision Transformers, revealing how text processing emerges in deep layers of VLMs.
papers.title: Reading Between the Layers: Cross-Modal Alignment and Representational Hierarchy in Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: Vision Transformers develop cross-modal text–concept alignment mainly in their deepest layers, where representations shift from visual form to semantics.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly improved Visual Question Answering (VQA) performance, yet their reasoning over structured content such as tables remains inconsistent, often plagued by spatial misalignment and logical hallucinations. Existing approaches for improving table VQA typically rely on architectural modifications or expensive supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which impose high barriers to entry due to the need for large-scale, expert-annotated datasets and significant computational resources. In this work, we propose Self-RefineVQA, a training-free, inference-time self-correction framework that improves table VQA performance without additional labeled data or model updates. Inspired by human revision behavior, our method enables a single VLM to iteratively act as a generator, critic, and refiner, forming a closed self-feedback loop that corrects common reasoning errors through prompt-guided re-evaluation. Experiments on tabular VQA benchmarks demonstrate that Self-RefineVQA yields consistent accuracy gains in monolingual and cross-lingual understanding, with a particularly significant boost for small models, enabling lightweight models (e.g., 2B-7B parameters) to rival the performance of significantly larger counterparts. Furthermore, we provide a comparative complexity analysis demonstrating that while inference cost increases linearly, our framework offers superior data efficiency and a lower cumulative cost by eliminating the prohibitive annotation bottleneck of human labeling required for fine-tuning. Our results highlight the potential of prompt-based self-improvement as a scalable, accessible paradigm for reliable table reasoning in VLMs.
bullets: Targets spatial misalignment and logical hallucinations in VLM reasoning over document tables.
Uses one VLM as generator, critic, and refiner in a prompt-guided self-feedback loop.
Requires no labeled data, architectural changes, or model updates.
Improves accuracy across monolingual and cross-lingual tabular VQA, especially for small models.
Inference cost grows linearly with iterations, but avoids the annotation burden of supervised fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Locating relevant evidence in long inputs is a core capability of Multimodal Large Language Models. Prior studies attribute this capability to retrieval heads, a sparse set of attention heads that transfer information from the context to the output. However, these analyses are confined to a limited set of modalities and the corresponding models. Moreover, how retrieval heads can be leveraged to enhance the model calls for further exploration. In this paper, we ask whether this mechanism expands together with the input modalities of the model. Taking audio-visual input as a newly added modality, we construct paired inputs in which the same answer is either spoken or shown on screen. With the evidence content fixed, retrieval heads remain sparse in the new modality and are shared to a large extent across modalities. Across 18 language, vision-language, and omni-modal checkpoints, omni-modal models largely preserve the retrieval heads of their backbones. Ablating these heads eliminates nearly all audio-visual retrieval. The heads shared across modalities make up fewer than 2\% of all heads, yet ablating them also degrades document understanding, spatial perception, and visual mathematics. Building on these findings, we turn retrieval heads into a target of optimization by training their attention with a ranking objective. This raises the page Recall@1 of Qwen3-VL-8B on MMDocIR by 6.03 points and improves document retrieval across three model families. Functional attention heads can thus serve both as a lens on multimodal models and as a target for improving them.
authors: Jia Wang, Yuqing Li, Jiangnan Li, Zheng Lin, Mo Yu
bullets: Studies retrieval heads—the attention heads responsible for transferring relevant evidence to model outputs—across language, vision-language, and omni-modal models.
Using paired audio-visual inputs with identical evidence, finds that retrieval heads remain sparse and are substantially shared across modalities.
Across 18 checkpoints, omni-modal models largely preserve the retrieval heads of their language backbones; ablating them nearly eliminates audio-visual retrieval.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) process images and text jointly, yet robustness evaluations often perturb these inputs separately or assess only predefined corruption levels. Such evaluations provide limited evidence of which modality is more susceptible to perturbations and whether smaller changes across both modalities can jointly expose failures. We present MoST, a black-box testing framework that characterizes modality sensitivity by comparing image-only, text-only, and joint perturbations. MoST uses multi-objective search to select and combine perturbations and adjust their severity, seeking prediction degradation while limiting changes to images and prompts. We evaluate MoST on four VLMs performing object localization on ImageNet and driving images. The models exhibit distinct sensitivities: textual perturbations dominate for some, whereas others are susceptible across both modalities. In several configurations, joint perturbations match or exceed the effectiveness of single-modality perturbations with smaller modifications to each input. In a human study, 60-76% of assessments across models judge the perturbed inputs sufficiently understandable to perform the task, and human localization is more accurate than that of the corresponding VLMs. These results show that evaluating modalities separately can overlook failure-inducing combinations and that modality sensitivity provides a more detailed account of VLM robustness than aggregate failure rates alone.
authors: Oliver Wei{\ss}l, Eduardo Breitembach, Andrea Stocco
bullets: Evaluates modality sensitivity through image-only, text-only, and combined perturbations with adjustable severity.
Tests four VLMs on object localization using ImageNet and driving images.
Finds model-specific vulnerabilities: text dominates for some models, while others are sensitive to both modalities.
Joint perturbations can match or exceed single-modality effectiveness while making smaller changes to each input.
Human evaluators generally found the perturbed inputs understandable, suggesting failures can occur without obvious loss of task clarity.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves multimodal reasoning, but uniformly assigning a single response-level advantage to all tokens overlooks the distinct roles of visual observations and subsequent reasoning. Visual affinity alone is insufficient: predictive states may align with both image and prompt-context representations, and upweighting valid visual observations can amplify their negative-advantage updates when later reasoning fails. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{Outcome-Conditioned Visual Credit (OVC)}, a plug-in framework that separates visual-association measurement from token-level credit assignment and is adaptable to policy-optimization methods with uniform response-level advantage allocation. Relative Visual Encoding constructs a context-relative visual coordinate by contrasting each predictive state's affinity to image and prompt-context representations. Outcome-conditioned Evidence Calibration combines this coordinate with uncertainty-scaled predictive features and calibrates their contributions to outcome-discriminative evidence through mean contrasts between positive- and negative-advantage responses, scaled by regularized within-side variation. Visual association thus informs credit through observed outcome differences rather than directly determining update priority. Normalized Credit Allocation conditions the calibrated evidence on the response's advantage sign to produce positive token weights with unit global mean. These detached weights preserve advantage signs while modulating individual token-gradient contributions. OVC reuses existing rollouts without auxiliary reward models, process annotations, or inference-time modules. Instantiated through GSPO-token, OVC retains sequence-level clipping and consistently improves six-benchmark mean accuracy over GSPO across three models, with gains of 1.86-2.39 percentage points.
authors: Yuhang Han, Dingning Liu, Yujie Chen, Yaojie Zhang, Jingwei Song, Zequn Yang, Xuanming Shang, Li Ding, Zhijiang Guo, Linfeng Zhang

With GSPO-token, OVC improves mean accuracy across six benchmarks and three models by 1.86–2.39 percentage points over GSPO.

papers.abstract: Screen Tables and Substrate Scopes are information-dense figures widely used in synthetic chemistry literature, yet automated extraction of structured reaction data from them remains challenging. We introduce RxnExBench, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained reaction-level evaluation. Built from high-impact chemistry journals, it contains 3,565 expert-annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures. The dataset adopts a unified schema with 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields, supporting downstream AI-for-Chemistry tasks such as retrosynthetic planning, yield prediction, and reaction condition recommendation. RxnExBench further provides a reasoning-driven difficulty taxonomy, a modular annotation pipeline, and the Oracle-MolRec protocol, which disentangles molecular recognition from higher-level reasoning. Evaluation of 9 state-of-the-art VLMs shows that performance degrades substantially as schema complexity and reasoning demands increase. Under the Oracle-MolRec setting, results further reveal that accurate molecular recognition alone is insufficient, with multimodal integration and chemistry-aware reasoning remaining the primary bottlenecks. We release all data and code to facilitate future research in chemistry-aware multimodal understanding and AI-for-Chemistry dataset construction. The dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/opendatalab/RxnExBench.

bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 3,565 expert-annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures from high-impact chemistry journals.
Uses a unified schema covering 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields for fine-grained reaction-level evaluation.
Adds a reasoning-based difficulty taxonomy, modular annotation pipeline, and Oracle-MolRec protocol to separate molecular recognition from reasoning.
Evaluation across 9 state-of-the-art VLMs shows performance drops with greater schema complexity and reasoning demands.
Data and code are released to support chemistry-aware multimodal understanding and AI-for-Chemistry research.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to ground generated text in the correct image regions, and existing explainability methods, such as attention maps and Logit Lens, often produce poor spatial explanations due to weak text-to-vision attention and sink tokens. We propose \textbf{Angular Relevance} ($R_L$), a simple visualization measure based on cosine similarity between visual token embeddings and unembedding-matrix rows. Because $R_L$ is invariant to token norm, it produces substantially sharper and more faithful heatmaps than attention maps or Logit Lens on out-of-the-box models. Without any training, $R_L$ yields competitive referring-expression segmentation (RES), outperforming prior diagnostic maps and CLIP-based training-free methods. To preserve localized object information during cross-modal mixing, we introduce \textbf{Angular Object-Aware Loss (AOL)}, an auxiliary loss that directly supervises visual token embeddings to align angularly with the vocabulary directions of their corresponding object concepts. Finetuning with AOL alongside the standard next-token prediction objective significantly sharpens object localization in heatmaps, showing that the VLM's own visual tokens can be used directly for grounding and improving RES, without training any segmentation heads and without degrading general VQA performance. We further demonstrate that the learned grounding also transfers to category-level segmentation of object categories not seen during training.
bullets: Addresses weak text-to-image grounding and poor spatial explanations from attention maps and Logit Lens.
Introduces Angular Relevance, a cosine-similarity measure between visual token embeddings and vocabulary unembedding directions.
Uses Angular Object-Aware Loss to supervise visual tokens toward the vocabulary directions of corresponding object concepts.
Achieves competitive referring-expression segmentation without training and improves localization after finetuning with AOL.
Grounding transfers to unseen object categories for category-level segmentation; scope is demonstrated in autoregressive VLMs.

papers.abstract: Effective multimodal reasoning requires a model to reliably utilize visual information while sufficiently exploring diverse reasoning paths. To achieve this goal, prior work combines visual dependency and token entropy to reshape sequence-level advantages, but scaling the contribution of token entropy by visual dependency can leave high-entropy tokens with low visual dependency underweighted, despite their important role in reasoning exploration. To address this limitation, we propose PEAR, an adaptive advantage reshaping method for improving perception and exploration in multimodal reasoning. PEAR retains visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain only at high-entropy positions, with lower visual dependency leading to a larger additional gain. The fused signal is then mapped to positive token-level weights that reshape the sequence-level advantage. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B show that PEAR achieves the highest average performance among evaluated baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks, alongside leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.
authors: Junxin Wang, Yingfeng Luo, Xiangchen Song, Weiqiao Shan, Runsong Zhao, Xinyu Liu, Shunjie Xing, Yifu Huo, Dingyang Lin, Qiuyu Gu, Yongyu Mu, Chenglong Wang, Changliang Li, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Addresses the underweighting of high-entropy, low-visual-dependency tokens in prior advantage-reshaping methods.
Uses visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain selectively at high-entropy positions.
Maps the combined signal to positive token-level weights for reshaping sequence-level advantages.
Evaluated on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, PEAR achieves the highest average performance among tested baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Also reports leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) can assess cognitive impairment (CI) from speech, yet their answers reveal neither which internal components control the decision nor how much CI information is accessible in their representations. We investigate both questions through CI-contrast neurons (CICNs), selected by class-contrastive activation frequency in decoder MLPs. Across eight open LALMs and two corpora (Pitt and PROCESS-2), we causally test CICNs against size- and layer-matched random masks and activity-matched controls. In three of the five models that meet our eligibility criteria, ablation of small CICN sets causes large, class-directed prediction shifts; speech-identified masks also control transcript-only decisions, and three of four primary Pitt masks retain specificity on PROCESS-2. Position-restricted interventions locate the influence before the final answer position, most strongly after the speech or transcript evidence under letter-labeled options, largely as a decision-direction shift. Beyond causal localization, supervised linear readouts of frozen CICN activations achieve 0.92--0.97 AUC within Pitt, versus 0.67--0.84 for the models' direct answers. Matched random and all-neuron readouts reach comparable performance; top-ranked CICNs show only an exploratory advantage at very small unit budgets. These results distinguish concentrated causal control over output decisions from broadly distributed diagnostic information for CI detection in LALMs.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces Sense-Aligned Grounding Evaluation (SAGE), a unified 10-candidate image-selection benchmark that reformulates VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse into a shared term-centric protocol covering noun-, verb-, and entity-centered grounding. SAGE includes confusable hard negatives and a context-swapped VerSe diagnostic to probe target-term grounding beyond direct caption--image compatibility. We further propose Gloss-Augmented Reasoning (GAR), a training-free framework combining definition grounding with constraint-guided semantic verification. Experiments show that strong VWSD performance does not transfer uniformly across grounding settings. With Gemma3-12B, definition augmentation improves all three subsets, while constraint-guided reasoning improves VWSD and yields particularly strong gains on VerSe, but is less effective on WikiDiverse. Combining the two signals achieves the best macro-average performance, improving Hits@1 from 65.90 to 71.22. These results show that SAGE supports both unified evaluation and fine-grained analysis of explicit semantic reasoning across grounding settings.
authors: Sunjae Kwon, Suhaas Kiran DG, Zonghai Yao, Talha Chafekar, Deepali Singh, Hong Yu
bullets: Recasts VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse as a shared 10-candidate, term-centric benchmark covering nouns, verbs, and entities.
Adds confusable hard negatives and a context-swapped VerSe diagnostic to test grounding beyond direct caption–image matching.
Introduces GAR, a training-free approach that combines gloss/definition grounding with constraint-guided semantic verification.
Definition augmentation helps across all subsets; constraint-guided reasoning helps VWSD and especially VerSe but is less effective on WikiDiverse.
Combining both signals raises Hits@1 from 65.90 to 71.22 with Gemma3-12B and provides the best macro-average performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Illustrative overview of the proposed GAR framework. The expanded definition is decomposed into semantic constraints, reformulated as binary visual questions, and verified against each candidate image. CGR aggregates the affirmative probabilities into an interpretable semantic score for reranking.

papers.abstract: A live esports broadcast needs a director who chooses which camera goes on air and a caster who talks over that choice, every second and without knowing what comes next. Streaming video language models have learned to commentate, but only over a broadcast that a human director has already produced. We study live broadcast production, in which a model receives the raw camera of every player and must both direct and commentate from the past alone. We present DirCast, a single streaming video language model that does both. Every second it scans all cameras at low resolution, decides with a hold-or-switch director whether and where to cut, and reads the chosen camera at high resolution before it speaks. Its context keeps what went on air and what was said and lets the other views expire, which bounds the cost of a stream of any length. We build a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with a camera for every hero, the human director's choices and the casters' commentary. DirCast directs better than rule-based and zero-shot directors including GPT-5, and its commentary wins 29.2 percent of comparisons against GPT-4o under the Proact-VL protocol, against 19.4 percent for the strongest of eleven streaming commentators that watch the human broadcast.
authors: Zixian Gao, Lixin Xiu, Penghao Luo, Xiangcheng Cao, Ziqi Cai, Zhen Li, Erwin Wu, Kaipeng Zhang

Maintains only aired visuals, commentary, and recent context while allowing other views to expire, keeping processing cost bounded over arbitrarily long streams.
Introduces a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with per-hero cameras, director choices, and caster commentary.
Outperforms rule-based and zero-shot directors, including GPT-5; its commentary wins 29.2% of Proact-VL comparisons against GPT-4o.

papers.abstract: Advances in Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) have enabled increasingly seamless human-AI interaction, but their unified processing of heterogeneous modalities also expands the attack surface, allowing adversaries to exploit richer input compositions to circumvent safety alignment. To counter such risks, omni-modal guardrails have been proposed to detect and filter unsafe queries across arbitrary modalities. However, their capabilities and limitations remain insufficiently understood due to the absence of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. In this paper, we present Omni-UBench, the first comprehensive framework for omni-modal safety assessment, evaluating guardrail models along three critical dimensions, i.e., safety, utility, and reliability. Omni-UBench curates over 183k samples drawn from 35+ heterogeneous sources spanning text, image, audio, video, and their cross-modal combinations, annotated with safety labels under a unified risk taxonomy. Benchmarking under Omni-UBench on 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails yields several key findings, including: (1) modern OLLMs exhibit strong content moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; (2) existing guardrails still struggle to identify cross-modal queries that conceal harmful intent or involve sophisticated jailbreaks; (3) they further exhibit substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, revealing a deficient understanding of cross-modal safety semantics. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.
authors: Junhao Wang, Yidou Chen, Li Lu, Hongwei Yao, Xiaodan Li, Mengjie Wu, Yuefeng Chen, Zhan Qin, Kui Ren
bullets: Evaluates omni-modal guardrails across safety, utility, and reliability.

Benchmarks 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails under a unified safety-risk taxonomy.
Finds that OLLMs can moderate content effectively without guardrail-specific tuning, but guardrails struggle with concealed harmful intent and sophisticated jailbreaks.
Reveals limited cross-modal safety understanding, including safety hallucination and over-reliance on textual patterns.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multimodal emotion reasoning systems perform well on standard benchmarks, but improving them through instruction tuning can be computationally expensive. Agentic pipelines built from frozen models avoid this cost, but introduce a different challenge: when a prediction is wrong, the system must identify which agent or stage caused the error. We address this problem with an agentic framework for traceable multimodal emotion reasoning and prompt-space adaptation. Modality-specific perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical inputs and post evidence-cited observations to a shared board. An integration agent combines these observations with retrieved multimodal examples to produce an emotion description, label set, and supporting citations, while an MLLM critic can request one revision before the output is finalized. For incorrect predictions, a separate evidence-grounded verification stage applies deterministic checks to verify that cited evidence and references are valid, and an entailment check to determine whether the final claims are supported by that evidence. Detected failures are then grouped by the responsible component and failure type, converted into targeted prompt patches, and accepted only after validation on a held-out set. This adapts the agent prompts without updating model weights. On the MER2025 dataset, targeted prompt adaptation outperforms the frozen static pipeline on all four MLLMs, ranging from 2B to 38B parameters, and matches or outperforms undifferentiated reflection baselines on each of them: VideoLLaMA3-2B, Phi-3.5-vision-instruct, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and InternVL2.5-38B. It improves F-score by 0.6--2.2 points depending on the backbone, including an increase from 52.3 to 54.5 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
bullets: Frozen perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical signals and post cited evidence to a shared board.
An integration agent combines observations with retrieved examples, while a critic may request one revision.
Deterministic verification checks citation validity and whether final emotion claims are entailed by the evidence.
Failures are attributed to components and failure types, then converted into validated targeted prompt patches.
On MER2025, targeted adaptation improves F-score by 0.6–2.2 points across four MLLMs, including 52.3→54.5 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Agentic multimodal emotion reasoning and its connection to the downstream adaptation stages. Three modality-specialist agents post evidence-cited observations to a shared board, while multimodal retrieval provides independent text-and-vision precedent. The integration agent produces an emotional draft, and an inline MLLM critic can request one revision before the final draft is emitted. The final draft then enters the Verification Process (Box 5), whose attributed failures feed Prompt-Space Reinforcement (Box 6). Boxes 5 and 6 are expanded in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Detailed view of Boxes 5 and 6 from Figure 1. The Verification Process (Box 5) applies visual and acoustic re-derivation, retrieval sanity, citation checks, and an entailment check to the finalized draft, attributing detectable failures to a responsible stage. Prompt-Space Reinforcement (Box 6) clusters attributed failures, synthesizes targeted prompt patches, validates them on held-out data, and updates only the corresponding agent prompts when a patch is admitted.
Figure 3: F-score, precision, and recall against training-data fraction, for three models.
Table 2: Component ablation of targeted repair (InternVL2.5-38B), full 480-sample test split. Each row removes one component, ∆F relative to the full pipeline.

papers.selection_reason: Applies an agentic framework with prompt-space adaptation to multimodal emotion reasoning using frozen MLLMs, fitting both Multimodal Foundation Models and Test-Time Learning.
papers.title: An Agentic Approach with Evidence-Grounded Verification for Multimodal Emotion Reasoning in Conversation
papers.tldr: An evidence-grounded agentic pipeline diagnoses multimodal emotion-reasoning errors and adapts prompts without updating model weights.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have seen broad adoption, but their biases are still far less examined than those of standard LLMs, creating possible social harms when deployed in real-world settings. Prior efforts to extend bias analyses from LLMs into the multi-modal space either cover only a few bias categories or do not ensure that the groups being compared are clearly addressed by visual cues in the images. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Melange, a wide-ranging synthetic visual benchmark covering seven categories for assessing social biases in MLLMs. It is grounded in the widely used language-only BBQ dataset (Bias Benchmark for Question Answering) from BigBench, carefully extending its constructed contexts via controlled generation of visual scenarios so the target attributes appear visually and clearly. To maximize reliability, our generated images pass through two stages of validation: automated screening using visual question answering (VQA) and subsequent manual inspection by human annotators. By systematically evaluating 23 open-source MLLMs across three matched evaluation settings---text-only, image-only, and image-with-context---Melange isolates the fairness effect of the input modality. Switching from text to vision reduces fairness by 0.291 on average, a gap that varies by model family rather than by scale alone. A perception control confirms that this gap is not an artifact of visual comprehension: models identify the depicted attributes at 90--95\% accuracy yet still fail to abstain. When models do commit to a biased answer, polarity-aware stereotype alignment shows they choose the human-stereotypical response roughly three-quarters of the time.
bullets: Addresses gaps in prior multimodal bias benchmarks, which cover limited categories or fail to make target group attributes visually clear.
Extends the language-only BBQ benchmark into seven bias categories using controlled visual scenario generation.
Validates generated images through automated VQA screening and human inspection.
Evaluates 23 open-source MLLMs in text-only, image-only, and image-with-context settings to isolate modality effects.
Vision reduces fairness by 0.291 on average; models recognize depicted attributes with 90–95% accuracy but often still produce stereotypical answers.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Our Sanity Check Pipeline. Each generated image is filtered through certain criteria via VQA with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Then the filtered images are automatically tagged via a second VQA for three attributes: age, gender, and race. After careful human quality checks, the characters are sampled to form the overall scenario image, which forms the Melange dataset.

Figure 1. We create visual scenarios based on textual scenarios in BBQ dataset in a controlled, structured, and component-wise manner. First, the 3 components are extracted: the scene and the 2 characters. Then the whole scenario is built. Examples belong to categories of Appearance (left), SES (middle), and Religion (right).

Figure 3. Evaluation settings. BBQ LLM uses the original BBQ text-only format. MELANGE provides the generated scenario image with spatial answer options (“person on the left/right”). MELANGE WITH CONTEXT adds a neutral scene description that names neither character. The correct answer (green) is always “unknown”; the stereotypical answer (orange) is annotated per question.

Figure 4. FaiR scores as a function of model size within each family. Scale effects are visible within Qwen2.5-VL but do not generalise: InternVL3.5-38B incurs the largest modality gap measured despite the second-best text-only score in its family.

Figure 6. Polarity-blind stereotype alignment rates. These rates hover near 50%, but this is an artifact of ignoring question polarity (see text). Polarity-aware alignment is 62–99% across all 23 models.

Figure 5. Per-category FaiR scores for representative models across bias categories. Within a family, category-level patterns are consistent across scales, suggesting that the bias profile is determined by the family’s visual encoder and alignment strategy rather than by model size alone.

Table 2. FaiR scores for all 23 models across three evaluation settings, grouped by family and sorted by size within each family. The modality gap varies by family rather than by scale: every dense InternVL3.5 model incurs a large gap regardless of size, while Qwen2.5-VL is cleanly monotone with scale. “Recovery” measures how much neutral text compensates for the vision-induced fairness drop.

Table 1. Melange covers 7 bias categories (age, gender, appearance, socio-economic, race, religion, disability) from the BBQ dataset, consisting of different context scenarios where two characters different in the intended bias category are mentioned. For each scenario, a question with a negative connotation and with a positive connotation is asked. More details in Appendix F.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for social biases in multimodal LLMs across text and vision, relevant to multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: Melange: A Synthetic Visual Bias Benchmark for Multi-modal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Melange is a synthetic benchmark showing that visual inputs can substantially worsen social bias in multimodal large language models despite strong visual attribute recognition.

papers.abstract: Financial forecasting from earnings conference calls requires models to reason over complex corporate disclosures, market expectations, and subtle communication signals. However, existing financial benchmarks are often limited to unimodal inputs or single-task settings, making it difficult to evaluate whether multimodal large language models (LLMs) can support real-world financial analysis. In this paper, we introduce MM-FinEval, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal LLMs across multiple financial tasks. MM-FinEval spans a diverse timeline from 2019 to 2022. The entire proposed dataset contains 2,045 S\&P 500 conference earning calls as inputs and 12 financial task labels as outputs. Each input contains three modalities: a word-to-word text transcript of the earning call, the corresponding presentation slides used during the call, and the entire audio recording. To establish a rigorous evaluation framework, we analyze 19 baseline models across three distinct model categories: Image-Text, Audio-Text, and Any-to-Any configurations. We observe that small-size Any-to-Any models processing all three modalities achieve strong performance, even when compared against larger proprietary models restricted to two-modality inputs. This indicates that our tri-modal dataset design introduces useful, non-redundant information. These results validate that text, audio, and visual data serve as important, complementary signals that mimic the decision-making process of expert human analysts.
bullets: Covers 2,045 S&P 500 earnings calls from 2019–2022 with 12 financial task labels.
Each example combines transcript text, presentation slides, and full audio recordings.
Evaluates 19 baseline models across Image-Text, Audio-Text, and Any-to-Any configurations.
Small Any-to-Any models using all three modalities perform strongly relative to larger proprietary models using only two.
Results suggest that text, audio, and visual signals provide complementary information for financial analysis.

papers.title: MM-FinEval: A Multi-Task Multimodal Benchmark for Real-World Financial Forecasting
papers.tldr: MM-FinEval is a tri-modal, multi-task benchmark for testing multimodal LLMs on realistic financial forecasting from earnings calls.

papers.abstract: Audio large language models (AudioLLMs) operate reactively, responding only when queried. We introduce proactive audio assistance, where an AudioLLM monitors an audio stream and autonomously decides when to alert the user from a single natural-language intent, motivated by wearable applications for Deaf and Hard of Hearing users. We propose Interrupt and Silent Modeling (ISM), a model-agnostic paradigm that embeds proactive decisions into LLM decoding via two special tokens: \texttt{<interrupt>} and \texttt{<silent>}, capturing four states: onset detection, sustained-relevance triggering, irrelevance suppression, and de-duplication. Applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B, ISM achieves 99.6\% interrupt F1 and perfect de-duplication recall on ESC-50. On noisy Epic-Sounds kitchen audio, ISM achieves the highest interrupt F1 without domain-specific training, the only method maintaining strong onset detection without over-triggering or over-suppression. Streaming evaluation confirms real-time viability with 3.5-second average latency.
bullets: Addresses the reactive nature of AudioLLMs, with potential wearable applications for Deaf and Hard of Hearing users.
Uses two special decoding tokens—<interrupt> and <silent>—to model onset detection, sustained relevance, suppression, and de-duplication.
Applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B, it achieves 99.6% interrupt F1 and perfect de-duplication recall on ESC-50.
On noisy kitchen audio, it maintains strong onset detection without over-triggering or over-suppression and requires no domain-specific training.
Streaming evaluation indicates real-time feasibility with 3.5-second average latency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: (a) PALLM takes a single watch-out intent and continuously encodes audio, decoding either <interrupt> or <silent>. (b) ISM training with four decision states. Conversation history enables de-duplication (S2).

Figure 1: Reactive vs. proactive audio assistance. Existing AudioLLMs (top) require a query for every event. Our proactive approach (bottom) takes a single watch-out intent and autonomously decides when to intervene.

Figure 3: Streaming evaluation on 400 samples across 50 sound classes. Each column represents a 1-second interval; Green region (5-10s) marks when the relevant audio is present. PALLM triggers interrupts within 3.5s of event onset on average.

Table 1: Proactive evaluation results (%). P : precision, R: recall, FI : interrupt F1. I: interrupt, S: silent. Subscripts denote type. On Epic-Sounds, Reactive SFT’s high RS1 reflects domain-mismatch conservatism (halved RI1), not proactive competence. PALLM is the only method maintaining high RI1 while achieving the best F1. S2 is excluded on Epic-Sounds (no conversation history).

papers.selection_reason: Extends an audio LLM with proactive interrupt/silent decoding, fitting multimodal large language model research.
papers.title: I'll Keep an Ear Out: Teaching AudioLLMs Proactive Audio Assistance
papers.tldr: ISM enables AudioLLMs to proactively monitor audio and alert users at the right moments without explicit queries.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, the answer is checked against the number of tags, and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images, and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude (R80 from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs, hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission, and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, and children's regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.
bullets: Exact-counting ability is model-specific, with the reported R80 range spanning 3–150 dots across 9 models.
Marking items improves counting for only 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs; it can hurt imprecise pointers and rarely outperforms simpler routines.
Tag-level audits classify errors as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, exposing whether answers are grounded in the visual trace.
Precise pointers tend to derive answers from their tags, while dense scenes primarily cause omissions and models seldom revise after tagging.
Traversal order following, order-invariant counting, and regular-versus-scattered advantages dissociate, indicating multiple underlying counting capacities.

papers.selection_reason: VLM counting evaluation based on spatial marking and ordering is directly relevant to spatial reasoning diagnostics in multimodal large language models.
papers.title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: A developmental counting-inspired tagging procedure reveals that VLMs’ counting failures are mainly serial, omission-prone, and poorly self-corrected, while producing useful auditable traces rather than reliably improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: System One models produce probabilistic judgments that software can consume directly, making reliable confidence as important as answer accuracy. Yet joint training across text, images, and video remains underexplored, and the contributions of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD) are difficult to separate. We introduce UniJev, a trimodal framework that scores candidate answers with a shared head under joint supervised training across text, images, and video. Supervised decision models improve accuracy over their backbone readouts across all three modalities, while the existing RLCD algorithms change accuracy little and have inconsistent effects on visual calibration across recipes. These findings motivate a separate supervised objective for confidence calibration. We introduce Cora (Confidence--Outcome Reliability Alignment), which groups current predictions by confidence and optimizes each prediction's confidence toward the empirical accuracy of its bin. At both 2B and 9B, Cora lowers image and video expected calibration error (ECE) while preserving accuracy, without a reinforcement stage. We release our code at https://github.com/wjnwjnwj/UniJev.
bullets: Joint supervised training improves answer accuracy across text, images, and video compared with backbone readouts.
Existing reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions has little effect on accuracy and inconsistent effects on visual calibration.
Cora calibrates confidence by aligning binned predictions with their empirical accuracy.
At both 2B and 9B, Cora lowers image and video ECE while preserving accuracy, without reinforcement training.
The study focuses on text-image-video System One decision models and releases its code publicly.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of UNIJEV and the main findings. A shared trimodal decision model first learns candidate selection through the supervised conversion, then CORA directly aligns confidence with the empirical accuracy of current confidence groups. Most of the observed accuracy gain occurs during the supervised conversion; the evaluated reward-driven continuations do not consistently improve visual calibration; and CORA lowers image and video ECE at both model scales while preserving accuracy.

Figure 3: CORA training dynamics over 100 updates. Left: per-update group loss (thin) and its 25-update running mean (bold), shown on a logarithmic scale. Center: fraction of each 256-question group included in the loss after applying the minimum-support rule. Right: periodic monitoring accuracy, binary Brier score, and 15-bin ECE.

Figure 7: Per-bin reliability diagrams of the general-purpose models in Table 2, in table order. Colored bars: empirical accuracy of each 15-bin confidence bin; gray bars: each bin’s share of the slice’s predictions; dashed diagonal: perfect calibration.

Figure 8: Per-bin reliability diagrams of the released decision models in Table 2 (first half, table order). Axes and markings follow Figure 7; modalities a model does not support are marked in place.
Figure 9: Per-bin reliability diagrams of the released decision models in Table 2 (second half, table order). Axes and markings follow Figure 7.

Figure 4: Text cases T1–T8: three shared correct answers, three shared errors, and two mixed outcomes across science, knowledge, and emotion questions. Asterisks mark annotated answers; numbers are confidence percentages. Candidate letters are display aliases, preserving the order and probabilities used in evaluation.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) perform well on complex question answering but often show a reasoning gap, where explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reduces accuracy compared to direct answers. We hypothesize that long reasoning sequences shift attention away from the audio input. To address this, we propose SPARE (Semantic Prediction for Audio REasoning), which introduces a register token aligned with the final conclusion using a cosine similarity loss with a Sentence-BERT embedding. This conditions the model's latent space with the target semantic goal before reasoning begins. Experiments on MMAU and MMAR with SALMONN show improved zero-shot reasoning and stronger early attention to audio without additional inference cost.
bullets: Addresses the reasoning gap in Large Audio Language Models, where explicit Chain-of-Thought can hurt accuracy.
Uses a register token trained to match the final conclusion’s Sentence-BERT embedding via cosine similarity.
Conditions the model’s latent space on the target semantic goal before reasoning.
Improves zero-shot reasoning and early attention to audio on MMAU and MMAR with SALMONN.
Adds no inference-time cost, though the abstract does not specify quantitative gains or broader limitations.

papers.abstract: Existing vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable for fine-grained visual perception. In this report, we present WeVisOne-VL (WeChat Vision All-in-One), a powerful VLM that unifies object-level and pixel-level perception through structured next-token prediction. It supports multiple visual tasks including object detection, referring localization, counting, OCR, segmentation, and matting, enabling localization at any user-specific granularity, from points and boxes to masks and alpha mattes. Architecturally, we integrate a lightweight pixel decoder into the VLM via a special token to generate instance-level pixel outputs. We train the model with a three-stage curriculum SFT followed by mixed-task RL. Across over 30 benchmarks, WeVisOne-VL demonstrates leading performance on both object-level and pixel-level tasks, while maintaining robust rejection for object-absent queries. By releasing WeVisOne-VL to the open-source community, we hope to advance VLMs from broad visual understanding toward truly reliable perception systems for real-world deployment.
authors: Tianming Liang, Junyi Pan, Yuxi Li, Canmiao Fu, Zhipeng Huang, Chong Sun, Chen Li, Jing Lyu
bullets: Targets the unreliability of existing VLMs in fine-grained visual perception.
Uses structured next-token prediction with a lightweight pixel decoder connected through a special token.
Supports user-specified localization granularity, including points, boxes, masks, and alpha mattes.
Trained with a three-stage supervised fine-tuning curriculum followed by mixed-task reinforcement learning.
Reports leading performance across more than 30 benchmarks and robust rejection of object-absent queries; released open source.

papers.abstract: Training-free personalization adapts a frozen vision-language model (VLM) to recognize user-defined concepts from only a few exemplars by retrieving concept entries at inference time. While recent retriever-based methods enrich each concept with descriptive evidence, they largely treat concepts in isolation, so the retrieved information can be plausible yet non-discriminative, especially when the personalized concept set contains highly confusable, fine-grained categories. We argue that personalization is inherently relational: correct recognition depends on the specific distinctions between a concept and its nearest alternatives. To this end, we propose ReCoG, a Relational Concept Graph for retrieval-augmented personalization. ReCoG represents concepts as nodes and augments them with directed edges that explicitly capture discriminative cues between concept pairs, elicited by a frozen VLM during database construction. At inference, ReCoG retrieves a shortlist and resolves ambiguity via explicit pairwise comparisons conditioned on the corresponding relational edges, selecting the concept that consistently wins against competing candidates. We also introduce FINGER benchmark to test personalized recognition on confusable concept sets. Across FINGER, ReCoG substantially outperforms prior methods, with the largest gains in the most confusable regimes. ReCoG also achieves consistently best performance on established personalization benchmarks including captioning and VQA, confirming that relational evidence is broadly beneficial beyond fine-grained settings. Project Page: https://csy-98.github.io/ReCoG/
bullets: Addresses the weakness of treating personalized concepts independently, which can produce plausible but non-discriminative retrievals.
Builds a relational concept graph with concepts as nodes and directed edges encoding pairwise distinguishing cues elicited by a frozen VLM.
Resolves inference-time ambiguity through explicit comparisons between shortlisted candidates using their relational edges.
Introduces the FINGER benchmark for personalized recognition on confusable concept sets.
Reports strong gains on FINGER, especially in highly confusable settings, and best performance on established captioning and VQA personalization benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of why relations matter. Figure 3: The proposed FINGER Benchmark. Left: 20 concepts in CUB-Easy (top) and CUB-Hard (bottom). We also provide the pairwise concept similarity matrices computed from CUB’s visual attribute vectors (darker means higher similarity, i.e., more difficult). Right: 20 concepts in CLEVR, where each concept corresponds to a specific scene configuration.

For each ordered pair (ci, cj), the VLM summarizes what makes ci different from cj , producing an edge eij (and vice versa). Collecting these directed edges yields the Relational Concept Graph, which provides explicit inter-concept relations.

papers.abstract: We envision a general-purpose protein foundation model as a unified, interactive model of sequence, structure, and function, capable of understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation while retaining the instruction-following and reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs. Toward this vision, we introduce Trion-1, the first native, unified, multimodal diffusion language model (dLLM) for proteins. Trion-1 is built on two key design choices: (1) a unified discrete token space that jointly represents sequence, structure, and natural language; (2) a dLLM backbone that replaces strict left-to-right factorization with bidirectional or semi-bidirectional token interactions, enabling global residue communication and long-range contact modeling that are naturally suited to structure modeling. This formulation unifies six core capabilities: folding, inverse folding, sequence understanding, structure understanding, sequence design, and structure design, while retaining the native language capabilities of general-purpose LLMs. On established benchmarks, Trion-1 achieves broadly competitive performance. In folding, Trion-1 achieves a TM-score above 0.8 with a single sample under strict homology control, matching or exceeding the existing tri-modal model using 200 samples. For sequence understanding, Trion-1 performs on par with top-tier LLMs such as Claude Opus 4.7 (62.37%). These results support well-aligned sequence-structure-language representations and strong cross-modal generative capabilities.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.
authors: Ronald Fecso, Jos\'e Morano, Botond Fazekas, Paul Widmann-Sedlnitzky, Dorota Himel, Laetita Hinterhuber, Virginia Mares, Andreas Pollreisz, Hrvoje Bogunovi\'c

papers.abstract: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.
authors: Chi-En Dai, Chih-Pin Tan, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting subjective, context-dependent musical valence alongside arousal.
Uses auxiliary-dataset demonstrations to refine predictions from a task-specific base model rather than predicting emotion scores directly.

On the held-out MER60 test set, text ICL raises valence R² from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 shots; multimodal ICL reaches 0.346 with 10 shots.
Results support training-free, inference-time ICL as a strategy for continuous music-emotion prediction.

papers.abstract: Metadata-conditioned generation is often framed as a data-to-text task in which additional input fields should improve grounding. Museum description generation challenges this assumption because catalogue records are heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across geographic regions. We study how metadata composition shapes the generation of artefact descriptions through a two-phase framework. Phase 1 analyses natural metadata variation in a large museum collection, where field count, field type, image availability, and Place co-vary. Phase 2 introduces controlled field probes that hold object identity fixed while varying metadata quantity, field type, and image access. Our results show that metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behaviour. Field type determines whether models ground, omit, or infer information, while images can both support visual grounding and increase unsupported interpretation. More broadly, our findings show that metadata-conditioned data-to-text evaluation should assess field- and claim-level support, rather than relying only on aggregate input coverage or reference similarity.
bullets: Museum catalogue metadata is heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across regions.
A two-phase study combines analysis of natural metadata variation with controlled probes that fix object identity while varying fields and image access.
Metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behavior; field type strongly shapes grounding, omission, and inference.
Images can improve visual grounding but may also increase unsupported interpretation.
Evaluation should measure field- and claim-level support, not only input coverage or reference similarity.
