papers.selection_reason: Probes field-level grounding in LLM-generated descriptions with varying metadata and image access, relevant to multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: When More Metadata Misleads: Probing Field-Level Grounding in LLM-Generated Museum Descriptions
papers.tldr: More metadata does not reliably improve museum descriptions: field type and image access determine whether LLMs ground, omit, or invent details.

papers.abstract: Text-to-music alignment is commonly evaluated by the global similarity between text and audio embeddings, which collapses all described attributes into a single score and obscures which ones are missing. We instead introduce MQAScore, which verifies each atomic musical concept along five clip-level dimensions (genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal, and usage) by the probability that a large audio language model (LALM) answers affirmatively to a binary question. To assess evaluator reliability, we construct verification labels from presence/absence annotations and LLM-guided concept substitutions, and propose the Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio, which measures how selectively an evaluator responds to meaning-changing substitutions. Experiments show that concept-level scoring improves both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators, and MQAScore can be a more reliable and interpretable fine-grained complement to global similarity for evaluating text-to-music alignment.
authors: Wei-Jaw Lee, Chun-Ping Wang, Xuanjun Chen, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of global text-audio similarity scores, which hide which attributes are missing.
Evaluates atomic concepts across genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal, and usage dimensions.
Uses a large audio language model to answer binary presence questions for each concept.
Introduces verification labels and a Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio to assess evaluator reliability.
Experiments indicate improved evaluation for both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators, complementing global similarity with more interpretable scores.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a large audio language model for fine-grained text-music alignment evaluation, relevant to multimodal LLMs beyond vision-language.
papers.title: MQAScore: Fine-Grained Text-Music Alignment Evaluation via Large Audio Language Model
papers.tldr: MQAScore provides fine-grained text-to-music alignment evaluation by checking whether each described musical concept is present in the audio.

papers.abstract: Long-text image-text alignment is essential for fine-grained scene understanding, yet existing methods mainly focus on extending context length or improving local alignment. We identify an overlooked failure mode, saliency collapse, where models over-rely on text that features visual prominence while underutilizing non-salient context. Consequently, retrieval performance degrades sharply when salient content is reduced, despite that the non-salient context remains informative. To address this, we propose RoSA, a saliency-aware finetuning framework that decomposes image-text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views, enabling joint learning of prominent and contextual semantics. We propose a modality-independent decomposition strategy to combine object-level visual saliency estimation with LLM-based text decomposition to bridge vision and language. We employ auxiliary objectives to explicitly align these views, ensuring robust representation with both salient and contextual features. RoSA greatly improves long-text retrieval and demonstrates strong robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks. Moreover, our auxiliary objectives are plug-and-play, bringing consistent gains to existing tuning methods. Code and checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/intelligolabs/RoSA
authors: Qiuyu Kong, Zanxi Ruan, Marco Cristani, Yiming Wang
bullets: Problem: Existing methods underuse informative non-salient text and context, causing retrieval degradation when salient content is reduced.
Method: Decomposes image–text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views using visual saliency estimation and LLM-based text decomposition.
Method: Uses auxiliary objectives to align salient and contextual views across modalities.
Contribution: Provides a modality-independent, plug-and-play saliency-aware finetuning framework.
Result: Improves long-text retrieval and robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks, with consistent gains for existing tuning methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of ROSA. ROSA consists of two stages: Stage 1: Saliency-guided view decomposition of vision and text, where we independently decompose the text and image. On the text side, an LLM is used to split the original long caption into salient text and contextual text. On the visual side, an off-the-shelf saliency method is applied to derive salient/contextual visual regions. Stage 2: Saliency-aware alignment. During fine-tuning of the image and text encoders, ROSA augments the original image-text contrastive loss Lori with three saliency-aware objectives: the saliency-focused contrastive loss Lsal, which explicitly aligns salient images with salient texts; the context-preserving contrastive loss Lctx, which aligns contextual images with contextual texts; and the visual anchoring loss Lanc, which enforces representation consistency between the original image and the salient image, thereby preserving stable salient semantics.

Figure 1: Saliency collapse in long-text alignment. a) Different users may describe the same image with long queries that cover different subsets of salient objects; b1) Existing long-text alignment methods suffer from saliency collapse: they degrade sharply when salient text is progressively reduced, at a faster pace than when random content of the matched-length is removed. b2) Under both mild salient text reduction (α = 75%) and complete salient text removal (α = 0%), our method significantly improves over prior methods in terms of R@1. The relative gain of ours over the best competitor StructXLIP [Ruan et al., 2026] is highlighted in a darker tone.

papers.abstract: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution report-generation benchmarks. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. The code for DLoss is available at https://github.com/gmum/DLoss.
authors: Ignacy Kolton, Wenxuan Li, Zongwei Zhou, Jaros{\l}aw B. \'Cwik{\l}a, Arkadiusz Sitek, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Szymon P{\l}otka
bullets: Addresses objective misalignment in token-level maximum likelihood training, which can miss key diagnoses or add incorrect ones.
Introduces an architecture-agnostic differentiable loss operating on decoder token probabilities.
Uses asymmetric pooling to reward sufficient probability for supported diagnoses while suppressing spurious probability for unsupported alternatives.
Evaluated across several 3D MedVLMs on abdominal CT report-generation benchmarks, including in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.
Improves diagnostic faithfulness while retaining competitive conventional language-generation performance and adds no inference-time computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of DLoss and its workflow. DLoss supervises how probability is distributed over diagnostic targets alongside standard token prediction. (1) Integration. DLoss operates directly on decoder probabilities without modifying the architecture or decoding procedure (only the LoRA parameters and the projector are trained). Reports are decomposed into organ-level findings and mapped offline, via LLM tagging, to supported (D+ i ) and unsupported (D− i ) diagnostic targets in a controlled target space G. (2) Asymmetric pooling. Target probability masses mi,d,t across valid decoder positions are aggregated using distinct operators: noisy-OR for supported targets (saturates when present at any position) and temperature-controlled log-sum-exp for unsupported targets (ensures probability stays low everywhere). (3) Objective. The supported and unsupported target losses are added to cross-entropy with independent coefficients λ+ and λ−, respectively, and scaled by sample weight si. The diagnostic target sets are discarded at inference, so DLoss adds no inference-time computation.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison of organ-level CT report generation. papers.selection_reason: Asymmetric diagnostic supervision for MedVLMs is a transferable objective for improving multimodal LLM faithfulness.
papers.title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
papers.tldr: Diagnostic Loss improves radiology report generation by emphasizing supported diagnoses and suppressing unsupported ones without changing model architecture or inference.

papers.abstract: Auxiliary patient data can improve chest X-ray report generation, but directly concatenating heterogeneous clinical information with visual tokens produces long, variable-length decoder prompts and may expose the model to redundant or image-irrelevant context. We propose ICGF-CXRMate, an image-conditioned clinical context compression and gated fusion framework. Learnable queries are first conditioned on the current chest X-ray representations and then attend to the patient-data sequence, compressing it into a fixed number of clinical context tokens. Gated cross-attention selectively integrates these tokens into the visual stream, while the compressed tokens are retained in the decoder prompt as a direct clinical pathway. Experiments on linked MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV-ED examinations show that ICGF-CXRMate improves report quality while reducing the average prompt length. In Stage~2, it improves RadGraph-F1 from 24.00 to 28.86, CXR-BERT similarity from 56.86 to 62.80, and BLEU-4 from 5.14 to 7.96 compared with CXRMate-ED, while reducing the average prompt length from 373.89 to 288.37 tokens, corresponding to a 22.9\% reduction. After self-critical sequence training, ICGF-CXRMate outperforms CXRMate-ED on six of eight report-quality metrics in Stage~3. Ablation studies confirm the complementary contributions of image-conditioned compression, gated fusion, and direct retention of the compressed clinical tokens.
authors: Vu Minh Tran, Thuc Huynh, Son Thanh Luu, Doanh C. Bui
bullets: Addresses redundant, image-irrelevant, and variable-length auxiliary clinical data in chest X-ray report generation.
Uses image-conditioned learnable queries to compress patient data into a fixed number of clinical context tokens.
Applies gated cross-attention to integrate compressed context into visual features while retaining a direct clinical pathway in the decoder prompt.
On linked MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV-ED examinations, Stage 2 improves RadGraph-F1, CXR-BERT similarity, and BLEU-4 over CXRMate-ED while reducing average prompt length by 22.9%.
Ablations support complementary benefits from compression, gated fusion, and direct token retention; after self-critical training, it leads on six of eight report-quality metrics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of ICGF-CXRMate. The model encodes CXR images and heterogeneous auxiliary patient data into visual and clinical representations. Image-conditioned clinical context compression (Sec. 3.2) uses image-adapted queries to summarize the variable-length patient sequence into a fixed set of clinical tokens Z. Gated cross-attention fusion (Sec. 3.3) selectively integrates the compressed context into the visual representations to obtain Ẽimg. The resulting multimodal prompt PICGF = [Z; Ẽimg] is passed to the Llama-based decoder for report generation.
Fig. 3: Case study comparing CXRMate-ED and ICGF-CXRMate (K = 16).

Fig. 2: Example of a linked MIMIC-CXR examination and MIMIC-IVED stay. The left panel shows the CXR images, radiologist report, and image metadata, while the right panel shows the associated ED stay, triage, vital-sign, and medication records. The Findings and Impression sections are used as the report-generation targets.

papers.selection_reason: Image-conditioned context compression and gated fusion for multimodal report generation is transferable to MLLM context efficiency.
papers.title: ICGF-CXRMate: Image-Conditioned Clinical Context Compression and Gated Fusion for Chest X-ray Report Generation
papers.tldr: ICGF-CXRMate compresses image-relevant clinical context and selectively fuses it with chest X-ray features, improving report quality while shortening decoder prompts.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with in context learning compared to their textual counterparts. Our preliminary study shows that VLMs rely on textual shortcuts and underutilize the visual demonstrations. We therefore hypothesize that VLMs are insufficiently trained to perform visual in-context learning (vICL). To this end, we construct MIME, a task-agnostic vICL training set without textual shortcuts. We ensure the instruction does not state the rule linking the demonstration images to their answers, so the model must infer it from the visual demonstrations. Fine-tuning on MIME improves vICL accuracy by 8.1 to 18.0 points across three VLMs, preserves single-image performance, and improves multi-image and text only in-context learning. In contrast, stating the rule in the training data sharply reduces this gain. We further propose DTAD (Demonstration Text Attention Dropout), which randomly withholds demonstration labels during training so that the VLM must infer the rule from the demonstration images. While achieving comparable vICL accuracy to fine-tuning on MIME, DTAD yields more consistent attention to the demonstration images. On TrueMICL, Qwen3-VL-8B trained on MIME matches frontier models such as Claude Opus 5, and surpasses them with DTAD. Finally, adding MIME to the instruction-tuning mix of LLaVA 1.5 13B more than doubles its vICL accuracy without hurting single-image abilities, whereas a same-size multi-image set improves it only slightly. These results suggest that vICL data should be a standard component of VLM training.
authors: Nimrod Shabtay, Asaf Yehudai, Avihu Dekel, Eli Schwartz, Raja Giryes
bullets: VLMs often underuse visual demonstrations because training enables textual shortcuts.
MIME is a task-agnostic training set whose instructions omit the rule connecting images and answers.
Fine-tuning on MIME improves vICL accuracy across three VLMs while also benefiting multi-image and text-only in-context learning.
DTAD randomly hides demonstration labels, producing comparable vICL gains and more consistent attention to images.
Adding MIME to LLaVA 1.5 13B more than doubles vICL accuracy; results support including vICL data in standard VLM training.

figures.caption: Figure 1: We fine-tune on MIME, synthetic in-context instances whose task is a hidden rule that must be inferred from the demonstrations. Despite being synthetic, MIME improves results on unseen real-world benchmarks. DTAD, which masks demonstration answers, produces more stable attention patterns that focus on the demonstration images.

Figure 3: t-SNE of SigLIP image embeddings. Training sources (squares) form tight clusters. Figure 2: Mean visual share per layer for 1-shot (left), 2-shot (center), and 4-shot (right); lines show the mean over the 5 TrueMICL tasks and shaded bands show ±1 SD across tasks. DTAD raises the visual share in the late layers above the base model at every shot count, with a narrow spread across tasks. Fine-tuning on the same data increases it mainly in the middle layers; in the late layers it varies widely across tasks. Training with the rule stated in the prompt lowers the visual share below the base model, indicating that the model relies mostly on the textual pathway.

papers.selection_reason: Training VLMs for visual in-context learning directly targets multimodal large language model capabilities.
papers.title: Watch and Learn: Teaching Visual In-Context Learning by Removing Textual Shortcuts
papers.tldr: Training VLMs to infer rules from visual demonstrations—rather than textual shortcuts—substantially improves visual in-context learning without harming single-image abilities.

papers.abstract: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Yidi Wang, Yile Li, Siqi Zeng, Yingjie He, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao hu
bullets: Introduces 327 hand-written text–image–audio queries across 86 scene groups and 18 ambiguity categories.
Each item has a unique answer only when all three modalities are available; removing one leaves multiple plausible answers.
Evaluations of 14 omni-modal systems show strong item-level results but substantially weaker scene-level disambiguation than humans.
Models rely insufficiently on audio, especially when text and images are present; removing answer options worsens performance sharply.
Provides an ambiguity taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocols for evaluating cross-modal disambiguation.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an omni-modal ambiguity-resolution benchmark and diagnostic protocol for multimodal LLMs across text, image, and audio.
papers.title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: TRIAD benchmarks whether multimodal large language models can resolve ambiguity that requires jointly using text, images, and audio.

papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves vision-language models (VLMs), but it also exposes a temporal grounding failure: as generation unfolds, models may drift from image evidence while reinforcement learning still provides only a final-answer reward. We study this gap through visual revisit, a temporally localized reactivation of image evidence during reasoning. Across three VLM backbones, revisit peaks are predictive of correctness and causally linked to performance: masking them degrades accuracy more than masking non-peaks, while injecting revisit-like peaks into failed rollouts partially restores correct answers. Control analyses show that this signal is not explained by raw attention strength, uncertainty, logit margin, or hidden-state norm. We propose RECAP, a GRPO-compatible training method that turns detached revisit traces into a credit-assignment signal. RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantage estimation, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction to propagate final rewards through visually important reasoning steps, without extra rewards, additional rollouts, or inference-time changes. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and LLaVA-OV-7B, RECAP consistently improves over GRPO and VPPO, yielding $+6.1$--$+6.5$ HallusionBench gains over the SFT base while preserving reasoning and text-only performance. Results on larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human evaluation further demonstrate robust improvements in image-grounded reasoning.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Chenxin Li, Yingjie He, Zhenyu Yu, Fengyu Zhou, Jiachen Qian, Lei Wei, Shuang Chen, Jiachen Li, Eric Hanchen Jiang, Rongchao Zhang, Zhengtao Yao, Hoi Leong Lee, Guansu Wang, Kaiyue Zhou
bullets: Long chain-of-thought can cause VLMs to drift from visual evidence because training often rewards only the final answer.
Visual revisit peaks predict correctness and are causally important: masking them hurts accuracy, while adding them can recover some failed answers.
RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantages, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction within GRPO, without extra rewards, rollouts, or inference-time changes.
Across three VLM backbones, RECAP improves over GRPO and VPPO, including +6.1–+6.5 HallusionBench points over the SFT base.
Additional evaluations support robustness across larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human judgments.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The RECAP framework. A detached revisit signal r̃t is extracted from cross-modal attention and injected into three parts of the surrogate estimator: the trace-augmented input, dynamic discount, and revisit-gated value predictor. The rollout policy, clipped ratio, and KL anchor remain unchanged.

Figure 3: Causal and mechanistic evidence. Top revisit positions are more decision-relevant than random positions, and revisit peaks align with annotated decision steps. The revisit signal further concentrates in a small set of heads, and zeroing those heads reproduces most of the accuracy drop from masking cross-modal attention.

Figure 1: Visual revisits are causal and localized. Correct rollouts show recurring CMA peaks, while incorrect rollouts lose visual grounding after the initial window. Masking revisit peaks hurts accuracy more than masking random non-peaks, and peak injection partially recovers failed rollouts. A small set of heads explains most of the causal effect.

Figure 6: RECAP training consolidates revisit responsibility onto fewer heads. The top-10 head share of the total revisit signal rises from 34% (SFT base) to 54% after RECAP training, while GRPO on identical data produces only a +4 pt shift (±3 bootstrap CI). Concentration is therefore specific to revisit-aware optimization rather than to RL post-training in general. Similar pattern on the other two backbones (section G.3).

Figure 5: RAP correlates with HallusionBench accuracy on checkpoints from every method, not just RECAP. Pearson ρ ≥ 0.38 on all four methods with 95% bootstrap CIs strictly above zero (≥ 48 checkpoints per method pooled over three backbones), establishing RAP as a method-agnostic diagnostic. The correlation is highest on RECAP (as expected, since RECAP explicitly optimizes revisit-aware return propagation), but substantial non-RECAP correlations confirm RAP is not a restatement of the training objective.

Figure 7: RECAP is consistently more robust to image-side perturbations on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Across four perturbation families, RECAP has smaller relative accuracy drops than VPPO and maintains a clear advantage over GRPO under stronger perturbations.
Figure 4: RAP rises early under RECAP training. RECAP reaches a higher RAP plateau than VPPO, GRPO, and the SFT reference, and the plateau appears before final accuracy convergence.

Table 8: Cross-method RAP–accuracy correlations. Pearson correlations between RAP and HallusionBench accuracy across checkpoints, reported per backbone and pooled across backbones.

Table 19: Where each method places its per-token visual signal, broken down by the five structural slots in the GRPO update. Only RECAP uses revisit at all three of post-hoc estimator context, discount, and value; every baseline touches exactly one slot (typically the advantage) and leaves the others at their GRPO defaults. This is the structural statement behind the expressiveness gap of Proposition 1: because dynamic discount acts multiplicatively across future tokens, no single-slot advantage reweighting (VPPO, λ-GRPO) can realize its effect, regardless of how wt is chosen. RECAP still forms the surrogate advantage AVR t in Eq. (11); “no local reweight” means that it does not multiply an otherwise fixed advantage by a same-step visual weight.

papers.selection_reason: Improves image-grounded reasoning in VLMs by leveraging visual revisit signals during long chain-of-thought, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: RECAP: Looking Once Is Not Enough for Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.tldr: RECAP improves vision-language reasoning by using moments when models revisit image evidence to better assign credit during reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Visual perception should be iterative and task-directed, with representations refined in response to the question and the need for further processing. While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly support extended reasoning, their visual tokens are still typically acquired in a single, task-agnostic encoder pass. This creates an evidence-acquisition bottleneck: models may reason longer without refining the visual evidence needed to answer the question. We propose LoopLook, a lightweight encoder-side recurrent perception framework that equips pretrained VLMs with adaptive visual depth. LoopLook recurrently revisits a middle-to-late window of the vision encoder, injecting question representations at each loop to guide visual refinement. A learned stopping mechanism adaptively determines the recurrent depth, while a token-wise Mixture-of-Looks (MoL) combines representations from different loops, allowing each visual token to selectively integrate information acquired across recurrent steps. Across four backbones and eight benchmarks, LoopLook consistently improves performance over the baseline, yielding gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench. Our analysis shows that LoopLook progressively refines visual attention and adaptively allocates depth according to task difficulty. It also better preserves task-relevant visual information under reduced input resolution, while increasing time to first token (TTFT) by only 5.1-6.5%. By bringing recurrence from reasoning back into perception, LoopLook transforms visual perception from a one-shot glimpse into an adaptive process of recurrent refinement.
authors: Wencheng Ye, Anning Hu, Hongye Fang, Tianyi Wang, Junchi Yan
bullets: Addresses the evidence-acquisition bottleneck caused by one-pass, task-agnostic visual encoding.
Recurrently revisits a middle-to-late vision-encoder window, injecting question representations to guide refinement.
Uses learned adaptive stopping and token-wise Mixture-of-Looks to select and combine information across loops.
Improves results across four backbones and eight benchmarks, with gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench.
Allocates more depth to difficult tasks, preserves relevant information at lower resolution, and increases TTFT by 5.1–6.5%.

papers.selection_reason: Adds recurrent question-guided visual refinement to pretrained VLMs, improving multimodal reasoning and perception.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly embedded in software systems. Testing them raises two problems. Mutating either input can change the expected answer, so an output change is not by itself a failure. Some failures appear only when both inputs are mutated; attributing them to the combination requires testing each mutation alone. We present VLTest, a black-box VLM testing approach. It generates image variants by editing VQGAN latent codes and text variants with a rewrite-expand-prune pipeline, filters variants likely to change the expected answer, and tests each variant alone before testing combinations, so every joint failure has four matched cells. A VLM judge confirms a failure only after checking that the input keeps the expected answer. On three tasks with eight VLMs, including two commercial API models, the oracle confirms 81.7% of the candidates, with 88.8% to 94.6% precision against human labels, and four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates. Under the same budget, VLTest's generators find 1.8 to 2.5 times as many confirmed failures as SINVAD and TextFooler, and its joint tests find 91 to 197 attributed joint failures per 1,000 joint calls, 1.3 times as many as the same pairing applied to the baselines' variants.
authors: Bin Duan, Jintao Lin, Guowei Yang
bullets: Generates image variants via VQGAN latent-code editing and text variants through rewrite, expansion, and pruning.
Filters variants likely to preserve the expected answer, then tests image-only, text-only, and combined mutations in four matched cells.
Uses a VLM judge to confirm failures while checking answer preservation; it confirms 81.7% of candidates with 88.8–94.6% precision against human labels.
Across three tasks and eight VLMs, VLTest finds 1.8–2.5× more confirmed failures than SINVAD and TextFooler under the same budget.
Four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates and enables attribution of failures specifically to image-text interactions.

papers.abstract: Mixing requires not only applying processing but also assessing the resulting mix. Audio-language models can provide conversa- tional mixing advice, but existing evaluations do not separately test whether they can judge specific mixing issues. Since professional supervision for such judgments is scarce, we construct a curriculum of 11 vocal-mix issues at multiple severity levels and use it to train MixJudge, a language-queryable audio critic. MixJudge shows its ability to retrieve mixing issues, distinguish opposite issues, and order the severity of an issue. Moreover, its judgments transfer to menu selection: given a set of processing candidates, MixJudge often favors versions acoustically closer to a held-out professional version, demonstrating how explicit mixing judgment can support comparison and downstream mixing decisions.
authors: Kuan-Hsun Ho, Yuan-Chiao Cheng, Yen-Tung Yeh, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the lack of separate evaluation and professional supervision for specific vocal-mixing judgments.
Uses a curriculum covering 11 vocal-mix issues across multiple severity levels.
Can retrieve requested issues, distinguish opposing issues, and order issue severity.
Its judgments transfer to processing-menu selection, often favoring candidates acoustically closer to a held-out professional mix.
Scope: focuses on vocal-mix issues and comparative downstream selection; the abstract does not quantify performance.

papers.abstract: LLMs have shown strong in-context learning (ICL) capability, but extending it to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains challenging. Prior multimodal ICL methods often rely on ICL-specific datasets for additional training or task vector extraction, which can improve performance on the same ICL benchmark used for adaptation. However, they do not generalize well to other benchmarks and often induce forgetting in previously well-solved tasks. For this reason, we identify 'visual grounding' as the key bottleneck in multimodal ICL; MLLMs often fail to attend to task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, instead over-relying on textual cues and producing hallucinated outputs. To address this, we propose ProCoRe to enhance visual grounding through contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data for improving multimodal ICL. ProCoRe generates captions for contrastive image pairs, decomposes them into propositions, and optimizes contrastive rewards that encourage alignment with corresponding images while discouraging mismatched ones. Despite never seeing ICL-formatted training examples, ProCoRe improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over the off-the-shelf Qwen-VL-3-8B model, outperforming ICL-data-dependent state of the arts across benchmarks. Finally, we introduce PICL, a personalized multimodal ICL captioning benchmark that tests whether MLLMs genuinely understand visual demonstrations rather than relying on pre-trained semantic priors.
authors: Minhyuk Seo, Minjae Lee, Chaeeun Lee, Wei Lin, Muhammad Jehanzeb Mirza, Tinne Tuytelaars, Jonghyun Choi
bullets: Problem: MLLMs often rely on textual cues instead of task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, causing hallucinations, poor cross-benchmark generalization, and forgetting.
Method: ProCoRe uses contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data, rewarding captions aligned with matching images and penalizing mismatches.
Results: It improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over Qwen-VL-3-8B.
Scope: The method is evaluated across benchmarks and compared with ICL-data-dependent approaches.
Contribution: The authors introduce PICL, a personalized captioning benchmark designed to test genuine understanding of visual demonstrations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of ProCoRe. (1) MLLM f predict captions t̂1, t̂2 for contrastive images. (2) Decompose them into propositions using ChatGPT: unique to I1 (i.e., P̂1), I2 (i.e., P̂2), or shared (i.e., P̂s). (3) Compute proposition-level contrastive reward: RI and RT encourage t̂1 to reflect discriminative visual details (i.e., fire hydrant vs. parking meter), while Rs preserves shared details.

Figure 2: ICL data-dependent methods show limited generalization. Blue-shaded bars denote ICL data-dependent baselines trained on TrueMICL ICL dataset, while red-shaded bars denote those based on ISEKAI. They often outperform the off-the-shelf model when evaluated on the same ICL dataset used for training (i.e., train: TrueMICL→ test: TrueMICL), but degrade significantly when their training and test ICL datasets differ (i.e., train: ISEKAI→ test: TrueMICL). In contrast, even without using any ICL data, ProCoRe outperforms them through strong visual grounding.
Figure 7: Comparison of hallucinations on MS COCO ICL captioning benchmark. ProCoRe consistently reduces hallucinations across varying numbers of demonstrations compared to baselines.

Figure 8: Accuracy heatmap over reward weights (λI , λT ) with λs = 4. If the text reward weight (λT ) outweighs the visual contrastive reward weight (λI ), the model over-focuses on textual demonstrations, weakening visual grounding and degrading performance. Conversely, if λI is too large compared to λT , the model underutilizes useful information from ground-truth captions, also leading to performance drops. Moderate ratios that emphasize visual rewards while retaining text signals (e.g., λI/λT = 2, red dotted box) consistently show strong performance across shots. We evaluate ICL performance on the MS COCO captioning benchmark, with InpaintCOCO used for contrastive RL training in ProCoRe.

Figure 5: Effect of ICL training on simple VQA tasks. ICL training-based methods, which perform additional instruction tuning on ICL datasets, degrade performance on previously well-solved simple VQA tasks (i.e., IconQA, TextVQA) due to forgetting. In contrast, ProCoRe improves these tasks by enhancing visual grounding, while also achieving strong multimodal ICL performance (Tab. 2).

Figure 6: Comparison of target attention score (TAS) on multimodal ICL captioning benchmarks. While hallucination-mitigation baselines sometimes enhance TAS compared to off-the-shelf model, our proposed ProCoRe significantly outperforms both off-the-shelf model and baselines.

Figure 11: Comparison across ICL-shot settings. Higher-shot settings require reasoning over increasingly complex relationships among demonstrations, rather than simply providing more context. For example, in the 3-shot case, the first demo lets the model infer that the dinosaur is “Henry”, while the second remains ambiguous since “Ava” and “Mason” perform the same action; only after the third demo (where the fox is identified as “Henry”) can the model resolve the ambiguity and infer that the pink character in the second demo is “Ava”. In contrast, lower-shot settings can be easier due to fewer required inferences (e.g., in 1-shot, the pink character can be directly identified as “Amella”).

Figure 4: Example of 2-shot PICL. (left) Query image alone cannot infer the personalized identity. (right) (1) Identifying the dinosaur as “Charlotte” in the first demo and (2) linking it to the dinosaur in the second enables (3) inferring that the pink beaver is “Emma” in the second, allowing correct prediction of the personalized identifier for the query. See Fig. 10 and Fig. 11 for more examples.

Figure 9: Examples of multimodal contrastive datasets. Each sample consists of two image-text pairs, (I1, t1) and (I2, t2), with captions t1 and t2 describe images I1 and I2, respectively. I1 and I2 are visually contrastive (e.g., differing in objects (left) or object attributes (right)).
Figure 12: Visual grounding in multimodal ICL with generic vs. personalized identifiers. Attention maps show visual-token attention when predicting the highlighted token using Qwen-VL-3-8B.

Figure 10: Examples comparing PICL and MS COCO. While PICL requires visual understanding all demonstrations to answer correctly (e.g., resolving “Mason” in the first demo is necessary to correctly identify “Isabella” for Pororo in the second, enabling the query prediction), MS COCO ICL task can often be solved using pre-trained priors without understanding demonstrations.

papers.tldr: ProCoRe improves multimodal in-context learning by strengthening visual grounding without training on ICL-formatted examples.

papers.abstract: LLM correctors of ASR output are judged by aggregate WER, which hides what they fix and what they break. We decompose every WER change exactly into repaired tokens, damaged tokens and insertions, and use this to ask what the source audio adds to a corrector. We compare correction with and without the audio, for the model's own draft and for the output of an independent recogniser, on three corpora. With Gemini 2.5 Flash, text-only correction of its own draft breaks 13-32% of already-correct transcripts; with the audio, 1-3%. Damage falls in both settings. Repair falls against the own draft and rises against the recogniser. On medical dictation, kept insertions cancel the gain in net WER. The open-weight Voxtral, which rarely edits, does not show this pattern. Prompts differ between the two arms, so the contrasts bound the effect of the audio and do not isolate it.
authors: Vasiliy Kudryavtsev, Kirill Borodin, Nikita Vasiliev, Mikhail Gorodnichev, Grach Mkrtchian
bullets: Aggregate WER is decomposed into repaired tokens, damaged tokens, and insertions to expose correction trade-offs.
Gemini 2.5 Flash text-only correction damages 13–32% of already-correct outputs from its own draft; adding audio reduces this to 1–3%.
Audio reduces damage in both settings, but repairs decrease on the model’s own draft and increase on an independent recognizer’s output.
On medical dictation, retained insertions offset the net WER improvement.
Voxtral rarely edits and does not exhibit the same damage pattern; differing prompts mean the audio effect is bounded rather than isolated.

papers.selection_reason: Audio-grounded LLM correction of ASR output is a multimodal LLM application, and the repair-damage decomposition is a transferable evaluation method for multimodal language models.
papers.title: Text-Only LLM Correctors Break Correct Transcripts: A Repair-Damage Analysis of Audio Grounding in ASR Error Correction
papers.tldr: Audio grounding substantially reduces the tendency of Gemini 2.5 Flash to damage already-correct ASR transcripts, but its net benefit depends on the recognizer, domain, and retained insertions.

papers.abstract: Visual mathematical reasoning can fail before reasoning begins: when a vision-language model (VLM) misreads a diagram, subsequent reasoning proceeds from false premises. This perceptual bottleneck is especially pronounced in smaller models, while accurate textual descriptions can substantially narrow the gap to larger models. Because obtaining such descriptions at inference requires additional annotation or model calls, we propose minimal-edit corrective on-policy distillation. Using reference figure descriptions and verified reference solutions as training-only information, a teacher scores incorrect student rollouts under a minimal-edit objective, and only teacher-disfavored tokens contribute to the corrective loss. Correct rollouts receive task-reward reinforcement learning. This preserves on-policy supervision while avoiding full-response imitation. Across model scales, the method requires no descriptions at test time and meets or exceeds the corresponding base model supplied with a reference figure description at inference. It also improves perception-oriented performance, particularly low-level geometric perception, and transfers to external mathematics and perception benchmarks. Because the minimal-edit teacher evaluates corrections rather than generating its own solution, the method remains effective with a frozen same-size teacher, although its gains are smaller than with a larger teacher on most metrics.
authors: Wen Ye, Ailin Deng, Zirui Wang, Shixing Yu, Han Zhang, Tian Yun, Nikhil Mehta, Tarun Kalluri, Xuefei Cao, Xuezhe Ma, Hengduo Li
bullets: Targets perceptual errors in visual mathematical reasoning, especially for smaller VLMs.
A teacher scores incorrect student rollouts using reference descriptions and solutions available only during training.
Only teacher-disfavored tokens receive corrective loss; correct rollouts use task-reward reinforcement learning.
Improves perception and transfers to external math and perception benchmarks across model scales.
Works with a frozen same-size teacher, though larger teachers generally provide greater gains.

Figure 4 Training dynamics for Qwen3-VL-2B component ablations: policy entropy (left), mean response length (center), and distillation loss (right). Only the full method remains stable.

papers.title: Edit, Don't Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: Minimal-edit on-policy distillation teaches VLMs to correct visual misreadings without requiring figure descriptions or extra model calls at test time.

papers.abstract: LLMs can act as scientific agents using tools to consult specialists and run experiments. Yet specialist information must enter their context, generally as text, images, audio or video: a bottleneck between models with rich, high-dimensional representations. We advocate direct representation exchange: a mindmeld conveying many properties, including information an LLM would not think to request. It should be extensible to new specialists, flexible across questions and tasks, and compositional across independently connected specialists without joint training. The Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP) learns connectors mapping specialist representations into LLM internal states. Training only connectors keeps this practical as LLMs grow and evolve. We connect three protein and three small molecule specialists to Gemma 3 (4B and 12B parameters) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active), freezing all pretrained models. Independently trained connectors provide useful information without changing the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to cross-domain tasks without joint training. Task performance and compositionality generally improve with LLM capability, with especially strong gains in zero-shot task transfer. Limitations remain: current LLMs were not trained for specialist representations as native inputs; access does not ensure reliable interpretation, integration or use in reasoning. We call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and, especially, on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine and reason with these inputs. These efforts could expand scientific agents' information while preserving conventional tools' flexibility. Data, pretrained connectors, and code for training, evaluation and interactive inference: https://github.com/PolymathicAI/AI-Mindmeld
authors: Siavash Golkar, Jake Kovalic, Shirley Ho
bullets: Addresses the bottleneck of passing specialist knowledge to LLMs only through text, images, audio, or video.
Trains lightweight connectors from protein and small-molecule specialists into the internal states of Gemma 3 and Kimi K2.6, while freezing all pretrained models.
Supports independently adding specialists without joint training or modifying existing connectors, including questions about unseen objects and new task types.
Demonstrates zero-shot cross-domain transfer; performance and compositionality generally improve with greater LLM capability.
Current LLMs may not reliably interpret, integrate, or reason over specialist representations because they were not trained to receive them natively.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Three stages of independent connector training. 1. Align. Layer-specific maps match specialist representations to text-derived reference states in the LLM. The schematic illustrates alignment to description states; the connectors evaluated here instead align to states obtained from object names. 2. Select. Injection layers are selected to span the LLM’s depth, guided by local peaks in single-layer AUROC on held-out scan objects. 3. Train. The selected maps write into the object’s slot and are refined by answer loss. Gradients pass through the frozen LLM to the connector; both pretrained models remain frozen throughout. Layer counts, bar lengths and example text are illustrative, not measured results or recorded model responses. Table 2 gives the actual schedules.

Figure 1: Latent Interconnect Protocol alongside tool calling. (a) The tool-output route returns selected properties as words or numbers; the latent route supplies specialist representations through learned connectors. The question and outputs are illustrative, and one agent can use both routes. (b) Connectors selected from the registry write the protein and compound representations into separate prompt slots at the marked layers. The ⊕ symbols denote the mixing operation defined in Section 2.1. The layer choices are schematic and may differ between specialists. Each representation occupies one token here; LIP also permits multiple-token slots. Registry entries are trained independently, and new connectors can be added without changing the shared language model or existing connectors. The displayed models and domains illustrate the registry’s organization.

Figure 4: Object, task and cross-domain evaluation design. (a) Training and held-out object pools, question types and data sources. Training counts give the pools used by the fitted connectors; held-out counts give the full validation and test splits, not evaluated sample sizes. The joint card reports evaluation groups from Rhea and BindingDB for reaction participation and protein–compound binding. Cross-domain evaluations include both familiar and held-out objects. (b) The progression from trained questions about held-out objects to held-out questions about heldout objects, then cross-domain questions using independently trained connectors. Solid slots denote training objects and dashed slots denote held-out objects. The example questions are illustrative. Within-domain composition of different connectors is an additional evaluation described in the text. Final task definitions, scored populations and controls are in Supplementary Section B.

Figure 7: Effects of connector training on trained and unseen tasks. Open and filled markers show AUROC after alignment and after connector training, respectively, averaged across the three specialists in each domain for each LLM. (a–b) Training improves performance on both trained and unseen protein tasks. (c) Training generally improves performance on trained molecule tasks. (d) Performance declines on most unseen molecule tasks; mass prediction improves only for Kimi K2.6. ∗Starred question types had exposure up to 0.32%, and in some cases related information may have been implied in the training examples’ free-text descriptions.

The first three columns compare LLMs using ESM-C 600M and ChemFM 1B with single-token linear connectors. The final column shows Kimi K2.6 using ESM-C 6B and ChemFM 3B with four-token MLP connectors (Section 4.5). Point estimates are higher for seen molecules. (b) Mean task AUROC for direct answers and answers after reasoning, averaged across protein connectors for each LLM. Vertical lines mark chosen layers, and dashed lines show the scores of the full chosen representations.

Retaining the embedding gives higher AUROC for all three LLMs. (b–c) Lineage and length discrimination among proteins sharing the same name, measured by within-name concordance; lineage uses four low-exposure questions, and length tests whether a protein exceeds 320 amino acids. Embeddings provide information beyond the shared name, with Kimi K2.6 showing the strongest performance in both tests. Supplied names score 0.5 by construction. Error bars show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 11: Effects of write location and token count. Gemma 3 12B with MIMIC (a) and ChemFM-1B (b). Mean of trained and unseen task performance; error bars show 95% bootstrap intervals. Six input tokens match the six-layer connector’s parameter count but require more inference compute; even so, performance is higher than single-token injection at the best layer but below the six-layer connector.
Figure 12: Connector extensions. ESM-C 6B with Kimi K2.6: mean AUROC across trained and unseen tasks after 2,000 training steps. Error bars show 95% bootstrap intervals.

Figure 19: Complementary specialists improve information merging. Mean task AUROC with Kimi K2.6 on 2,036 proteins for (a) five trained and (b) eight unseen questions, comparing three different specialists with the best single connector and the best triple repeating one specialist. Intervals are 95% paired protein-bootstrap intervals (2,000 draws).

papers.abstract: Fine-grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task-specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region-space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language-model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence-level Video-caption Evaluation), a human-verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3-VL initialization. These results establish region-text cycle consistency as a general self-evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized-CycleGRPO-Page/.
bullets: Addresses the need for models to describe designated regions and localize them from language using a shared objective rather than separate task-specific supervision.
Generates a description for a region, relocalizes that description, and uses reconstruction overlap plus localization rewards for self-verifiable training.
Extends a common region-space formulation to image masks/boxes, video intervals, and timestamped spatial evidence without reference captions or an external judge during RL.
Introduces DOVE, a human-verified benchmark for evaluating whether video descriptions distinguish a target event from similar recurrences.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models have achieved remarkable progress in multi-modal understanding, yet their capabilities in educational settings remain insufficiently evaluated. In AI-assisted language learning, models must interpret artistic imagery, understand its semantic, affective, and cultural content, and reason about visual context to support meaningful interaction. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on real-world images or domain-specific educational reasoning, providing limited coverage of artistic educational content. To address this gap, we introduce MUSE, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models on artistic image understanding in situated educational applications. MUSE decouples image annotation from question generation, enabling diverse tasks with controllable difficulty while reducing annotation effort. It comprises twelve tasks spanning visual perception, semantic and affective interpretation, culture understanding, and compositional reasoning, together with diverse artistic images deliberately curated to center Singaporean and Southeast Asian multicultural contexts alongside Western art traditions, covering multiple themes and difficulty levels. Evaluation of open-source and proprietary models reveals substantial disparities across capability dimensions, particularly in affective interpretation and compositional reasoning. Our analysis further identifies common failure modes and key challenges for developing trustworthy multi-modal models for education. We hope MUSE will serve as a standardized benchmark for advancing multi-modal understanding in situated educational applications.
bullets: Addresses limited evaluation of multimodal models on artistic content in education, especially language-learning contexts.
Separates image annotation from question generation to support diverse, controllable-difficulty tasks with lower annotation effort.
Covers 12 tasks spanning visual perception, semantic and affective interpretation, cultural understanding, and compositional reasoning.
Includes multicultural artistic imagery centered on Singaporean and Southeast Asian contexts alongside Western art traditions.
Finds substantial capability gaps, especially in affective interpretation and compositional reasoning, and analyzes common failure modes.

papers.abstract: Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438 staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects' falls (67% over all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at 160x120 with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the 9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt ("a person who goes out of view ... is not a fall") accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from 4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at 8x6 pixels (34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the model called a fall, its explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.
authors: Marcos Junca (Senecta Inc.), Mauro Junca (Senecta Inc.)
bullets: Evaluated Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.7 Flash as deployed decision stages using one request per short thermal clip, with audio when available.
On staged laboratory data, Gemini 3.8 Flash detected 69% of held-out-subject falls and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying down and rising.
In 76 hours of occupied-home footage, it produced no false calls and detected 4 of 9 visible staged falls; the reported upper bound was 1.2 false alarms per day.
Removing a prompt warning about people leaving view substantially increased sensitivity, but caused deliberate lie-downs to be labeled as falls.
Performance fell to 34% sensitivity at 8×6 pixels; identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows, while detected falls were temporally localized accurately.

papers.abstract: Pixel language models process text as rendered images instead of a finite vocabulary, which gives them strong cross-lingual transfer abilities. However, not much is known about how these abilities are influenced by larger-scale pretraining. In this paper, we train a family of MPIXEL models along three axes of variation: more languages, more scripts, and larger model capacity under fixed per-language compute. In evaluations on five tasks covering 83 languages, we find that scaling acts locally: each axis improves the added languages and scripts, while increased capacity mitigates the curse of multilinguality from pretraining on more languages. Transfer to unseen scripts improves with multilingual pretraining, but does not further improve with scaling. On typologically distant low-resource languages, our models outperform subword and character-level baselines across many writing systems. We also show that larger pixel models reserve more layers for visual processing, and that cross-lingual alignment weakens as more languages are added. Overall, our findings characterize how multilingual scaling improves pixel language models.
authors: Ilker Kesen, Jenny Kunz, Kasra Malihi, Desmond Elliott
bullets: Evaluates MPIXEL models across more languages, more scripts, and larger capacity under fixed per-language compute.

Pixel models outperform subword and character-level baselines on many typologically distant, low-resource languages.
Scaling increases visual-processing layers, while cross-lingual alignment weakens as more languages are added.

papers.abstract: Multimodal inputs may be missing or degraded, raising distinct questions of evidence availability and trust. We introduce a reliability-aware Gaussian Product-of-Experts (PoE) in which an input-dependent reliability weight tempers each modality's latent precision, while missing experts are omitted. We characterize how reliability and availability affect posterior information and expert influence. Across two clinical multimodal tasks, the full framework remains competitive with complete inputs and achieves its clearest mean-AUROC advantage under modality absence, particularly on HAIM-MIMIC-MM. Ablations show a substantial gain from missing-aware training and an additional HAIM improvement from reliability weighting under matched PoE, missing-aware, and consistency training. Unseen test-time corruptions are used diagnostically and reveal modality-dependent reliability-weight and latent-uncertainty responses, including failure under severe degradation. Thus, reliability weighting provides an explicit evidence-control mechanism, while learning dependable quality signals remains an open challenge.
authors: Patitapaban Palo, Abhisek Tiwari, Mattia Carletti, Anshul Thakur, Xiao Gu, David A. Clifton
bullets: Addresses both modality availability and trust in incomplete or corrupted multimodal evidence.
Uses input-dependent reliability weights to temper each modality’s latent precision and omits missing experts.
Analyzes how reliability and availability change posterior information and expert influence.

Unseen severe corruptions reveal modality-dependent uncertainty responses and failure modes.

papers.abstract: Biometric recognition often degrades under partial facial vis- ibility, where conventional facial cues are occluded. The forehead region remains consistently visible and contains distinctive crease patterns that can serve as a complementary biometric trait. We present a unified eval- uation of forehead-crease recognition across explainable zero-shot rea- soning, domain-adaptive learning, and trait-specific modeling. FIRE en- ables interpretable zero-shot verification using multimodal large language models, while pretrained face-recognition models are adapted to the fore- head domain through margin-based learning. Under open-set evaluation, the best zero-shot model GPT-4o+FIRE achieves 18.22% EER, while Edge-Forehead achieves 8.30% EER and 54.01% TMR@0.1% FMR. The results show that although MLLMs offer interpretable zero-shot verifi- cation, trait-specific learning remains more effective for robust forehead- crease biometric recognition.
authors: Geetanjali Sharma, Aryan Jain, Dev Nagaich, Aditya Nigam, Raghavendra Ramachandra
bullets: Forehead creases provide a complementary biometric cue when other facial regions are occluded.
FIRE supports interpretable zero-shot verification with multimodal large language models.
Pretrained face-recognition models are adapted to the forehead domain using margin-based learning.
Edge-Forehead achieves 8.30% EER and 54.01% TMR at 0.1% FMR, outperforming the best zero-shot result.
GPT-4o+FIRE reaches 18.22% EER, indicating weaker robustness despite interpretability.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are now routinely tested on theory of mind: whether they can work out what another person sees, knows, and means. A common design asks the model to report that perspective and then to act for the person, and reads a correct report beside a wrong action as a failure to use the perspective. That reading rests on a quiet assumption: that asking for the report leaves the action unchanged. We show that it does not. In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director who asks for "the largest block". Asking first which blocks the director can see raises the share of replies that choose this hidden block by 12 to 88 percentage points on six GPT models and by 17 on Qwen3.8-27B, even though the models mostly report correctly which blocks the director sees. Reasoning traces and prompt rewordings suggest why: the question shifts how the request is read, from the director's view toward the model's own. When the prompt states what the director knows and refers to, fewer than 1% of replies pair a correct report with a hidden-block choice. Any evaluation that elicits a perspective report before the action it scores needs a baseline without the question, and we deliver one: paired prompts that differ only in that question, a design any perspective-taking benchmark can adopt.
authors: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Kejia Zhang, Jingxin Yang, Youran Sun, Haizhao Yang
bullets: In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director requesting “the largest block.”
Asking models to report the director’s visual perspective first increased hidden-block choices by 12–88 percentage points across six GPT models and by 17 points on Qwen3.8-27B.
Models generally reported the director’s visibility correctly, suggesting the question changed how they interpreted the request rather than simply revealing a lack of perspective-taking.
Explicitly stating what the director knows and refers to reduced correct-report/hidden-choice pairings to below 1%.
The authors recommend paired prompts with and without the perspective question as a baseline for perspective-taking benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates perspective-taking behavior in vision-language models, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Asking What a Director Sees Can Change What Vision-Language Models Choose
papers.tldr: Asking vision-language models what a director can see can change their subsequent choice, making standard theory-of-mind evaluations confound perspective reporting with action.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) understand music, yet struggle to locate a described moment in time. We ask whether this reflects missing temporal information or a bottleneck in how the time span is extracted. Using a paired-query probe built from Slakh2100 stem activations, we attach a state query (e.g., ``only piano and bass are playing'') and a change query (e.g., ``the guitar drops out, leaving piano and bass'') to the same span and vary how much preceding audio the model is shown. Across frozen LALMs, three ways of extracting the span ask different questions: full-track prompting asking whether the model can say when; windowed yes/no scoring asking whether it verifies the moment when handed the segment, and whether it needs what came before; attention asking whether it can find the moment on its own. State queries score above baseline without context, while change queries improve with preceding context in most short-segment models; 30s padded encoders show no comparable recovery. Prompting and attention expose almost none of this. Prompting failures thus understate what LALMs can verify, though not what they can locate, by an amount set by query type and encoder.
bullets: LALMs struggle to identify when a described musical moment occurs, raising questions about missing temporal information versus extraction bottlenecks.
A paired-query probe compares state descriptions (what is playing) with change descriptions (what just stopped) over the same audio span and varying preceding context.
State queries perform above baseline without context, while change queries usually benefit from preceding audio in short-segment models.
Full-track prompting and attention reveal little of this contextual ability; windowed yes/no scoring exposes more verification capacity.
Thirty-second padded encoders do not show comparable recovery, indicating that effects depend on query type and encoder design.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of temporal information extraction in frozen audio-language models; meaningful for multimodal model understanding.
papers.title: Heard But Not Said: Prompting Understates Temporal Information of Musical Moments in Frozen Large Audio-Language Models
papers.tldr: Frozen large audio-language models can often verify musical states, but prompting and attention substantially understate their ability to use temporal context and locate musical changes.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
authors: Hong Ting Tsang, Boyi Zhang, Haoyu Huang, Jiaxin Bai, Yufei Li, Yisen Gao, Zhongwei Xie, Hongyu Luo, Jeff Z. Pan, Yangqiu Song
bullets: Evaluates 923 questions across persona-grounded histories spanning 11–24 sessions and four modalities.
Targets meaningful spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media.
Uses matched controls to isolate failures in representation, retrieval, delivery, and reading.
Finds modality-dependent representation loss, substantial residual reading errors even with gold evidence, and weak abstention.
Moves evaluation beyond a single leaderboard score toward component-level diagnosis.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MOSAIC. Top: what the benchmark tests—evidence scattered across months of text, image, video, and audio sessions must be chained across modalities. Bottom: where systems lose that signal—matched interventions on WRITE (representation compression), RETRIEVE (missed facts), DELIVER (retrieved but dropped under media caps), and READ (misread complete evidence).

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long-term memory and cross-modal reasoning in omni-modal conversational agents; directly relevant to LLM memory and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents
papers.tldr: MOSAIC is an omni-modal benchmark that diagnoses where conversational agents fail when remembering and reasoning over long-term text, image, video, and audio histories.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate why vision-language models (VLMs) produce errors by decomposing them into two sources: visual-representation failures, in which the visual evidence required for the correct answer is not encoded, and visual-utilization failures, in which this evidence is encoded but not successfully used. We propose to estimate the visual-utilization failure rate using lightweight probes and derive theoretical bounds on the true rate that account for probe imperfections. We introduce VELens (Visual Evidence Lens), a rank-based probe that traces visual evidence for both a target object and its ground-truth attribute, such as color, material, or shape, across VLM layers. We evaluate VELens on over 6,000 images using LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Our method achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.95 and 0.91, respectively, and outperforms alternative probes in both low-resource and unseen-attribute settings. Using it to diagnose errors, we estimate that visual-utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%, respectively. Overall, our study identifies visual utilization as the dominant bottleneck in VLMs and suggests that a central opportunity for improvement lies in developing better mechanisms to locate, route, and use the visual information they already encode.
authors: Anat Veikherman, Mor Ventura, Nitay Calderon, Lihi Zelnik-Manor, Roi Reichart
bullets: Decomposes VLM errors into visual-representation failures and visual-utilization failures.
Introduces VELens, a rank-based probe that traces object and attribute evidence across model layers.
Uses lightweight probes with theoretical bounds to estimate utilization-failure rates despite probe imperfections.
Evaluated on over 6,000 images with LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B; VELens achieves ROC-AUCs of 0.95 and 0.91 and outperforms alternative probes.
Estimated utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of VELens. Top: Visual-token representations from each LLM layer are projected through the output head WV to obtain vocabulary rankings. These rankings are converted into local evidence scores and aggregated into one score per layer. The layer-wise scores serve as input to a logistic-regression classifier. Bottom: For each visual token, the vocabulary ranks of target tokens (T +) and competing tokens (T −) are compared to produce a local evidence score.

Figure 4: Top: The object region is emphasized by blurring its surroundings (leftmost) or degraded by Gaussian noise, yielding the transformed image X ′ (§D.4). Lines report the LLaVA error rate (red) and joint visual-evidence detection among the original errors P(M(X ′, YX)= 1 |H(X)= 1) (yellow). Bottom: VELens estimates of visual-utilization (red) and visual-representation (gray) failures. The lines and bracketed values are the utilization-failure rate bounds.
Figure 1: Diagnosing the source of errors.

Figure 8: Question template, an example question, and the per-model chat formats. The template is filled with the attribute category a, the object name o, and the canonical option set Va in a randomly permuted order. The filled question, denoted {q}, is then wrapped in each model’s chat format.

Figure 6: Computing object and attribute attention ratios. Top: We identify the visual tokens inside the annotated object region and the tokens in query Q representing the target object (“car”, 1) and a candidate attribute (“yellow”, 2). Bottom: The highlighted rows show attention from these concept tokens to visual tokens at one layer l and head h. For each concept, attention inside the object region is summed and divided by total image attention to obtain the inside attention ratio αin l,h,j(c) (Eq. 9).

Figure 9: ROC curves for attribute-evidence detection. True-positive against false-positive rate for each method, shown for LLaVA (top) and Qwen (bottom) and separately for color, material, and shape, using the Separate pooling configuration. The areas under these curves are the attribute columns of Table 1. The dashed diagonal marks chance.

Figure 5: An example of evidence-positive error, where VELens detects both object and attribute evidence. Increasing attention to the target-object region changes the answer from wood to glass. More examples in Figure 12.

Figure 7: Logit-lens projection of visual tokens inside annotated object regions. Qualitative examples from VAW in LLaVA, for three target objects: a plate (green), a hat (orange), and a bowl (purple). Top: For each object, we randomly sample five visual tokens ki from its inside-region set Kin and show, at every layer l, the top-ranked vocabulary token, i.e. the v ∈ V with rankl(ki, v) = 1 (Eq. 14). Color intensity indicates the top-1 probability. Bottom: The corresponding images, each with the annotated bounding box b of its target object in the matching color. Semantics emerge at different depths across the three objects: the plate tokens are uninformative until the middle layers and then decode to plate, white and round, whereas hat and bowl are already top-ranked in the earliest layers, with red and glass following later.

Figure 10: Controlled transformations. Five images from the VAW dataset (rows) with each transformation applied (columns): the object emphasized by blurring its surroundings (ψ+), the clean image, and Gaussian noise within the bounding box b at λ = 0.1, 0.3, and 0.9 (ψ−).

Figure 3: Low-resource and unseen-value generalization. Left: ROC-AUC as the number of labeled examples per class varies, using Separate and averaging across color, material, and shape, with five independently sampled subsets for each size and category. Middle and right: Leaveone-value-out ROC-AUC, averaged over held-out values, using both pooling configurations. For Separate, individual probes are trained on each seen value, and their predictions are averaged for the held-out value. For All, one probe is trained jointly on all seen values and applied to the held-out value. Error bars are computed via 100 bootstraps.

Each panel shows attention from the last prompt token to image patches, averaged over the last four decoder layers (head-mean). Left: no intervention. Right: prompt→ inside-object visual-token attention increased at strength α=2, chosen as described in §D.6.

The complete trajectory captures evidence that becomes accessible at different depths across attributes and models.
