papers.selection_reason: Decomposes VLM errors into representational versus utilization failures using a visual evidence probe; directly relevant to diagnosing and improving MLLMs.
papers.title: Encoded but Unused: Bounding the Sources of VLM Errors
papers.tldr: The paper finds that most VLM errors arise from failing to use visual evidence that is already encoded, rather than failing to encode it.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering from low-altitude UAV imagery must deliver timely and accurate judgments to support disaster response under limited edge computing resources. Routine questions may be answered through direct decisions, whereas more challenging questions may benefit from step-by-step reasoning. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving models' visual understanding and generative reasoning capabilities, with limited exploration of efficient direct decision-making and its adaptive coordination with generative reasoning. We develop Disaster-S1 based on a vision-language model adapted to the disaster domain. Trained for option discrimination, it outputs a probability distribution over answer options in a single multimodal forward pass for fast decision-making. We further propose DisasterRoute, a dual-system routing framework that combines prediction confidence with disaster evidence to decide whether to accept the initial answer or invoke the disaster reasoning model DisasterVL for review. By allocating inference computation on demand, the framework retains the efficiency of direct decision-making and improves overall question-answering accuracy through selective review. Experiments on DisasterBench show that Disaster-S1 achieves superior accuracy with low latency, while DisasterRoute further improves accuracy through selective review at substantially lower latency than full reasoning.
authors: Tan Zhang, Xing Deng, Lu Zhang, Xiaofeng Zhu, Ping Hu
bullets: Targets timely UAV-based disaster QA under limited edge-computing resources.
Disaster-S1 performs fast option discrimination in a single multimodal forward pass.
Routes answers using both prediction confidence and disaster evidence.
Invokes DisasterVL selectively for review instead of applying full reasoning to every question.
On DisasterBench, selective review improves accuracy while maintaining substantially lower latency than full reasoning.

papers.selection_reason: Dual-system routing between fast direct VQA decisions and generative reasoning; relevant to multimodal LLM deployment and selective computation allocation.
papers.title: DisasterRoute: Evidence-Guided Dual-System Routing for Visual Disaster Question Answering
papers.tldr: DisasterRoute efficiently improves visual disaster question answering by routing only uncertain or insufficiently supported answers to a slower reasoning model.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities. As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety-critical real-world systems. However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation. To compare the two families directly, we evaluate every selected representative model on one outcome: whether an adversarial patch worn on a person evades detection of the model. We report this by introducing a unified metric, conditional attack success rate (cASR), counted only on images the model still localizes under a matched gray occluder, and partition every failure into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch), and displacement (a box on neither). We benchmark the physical adversarial vulnerability of compact grounding VLMs against a range of object detectors, and find that the VLMs can be as vulnerable as the detectors. We disclose that failure mode is largely associated with the output format of a model rather than its architecture family. Of the three, only omission is visible to a downstream system; displacement and substitution return confident, well-formed boxes, making them potentially more dangerous failures. Further, we find that, under distribution shift, VLMs that primarily failed by omission instead shift to failing more by displacement/substitution. Thus, a grounding VLM can inherit the detector's vulnerability while showing the possibility to adopt more dangerous failure modes. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ericliang1/physical-adversarial-robustness.
authors: Eric Liang, Alan Luo, Kaiwen Yuan
bullets: Evaluates whether an adversarial patch worn by a person evades detection across representative VLMs and object detectors.
Introduces conditional attack success rate (cASR), measured only when the model localizes the person under a matched gray occluder.
Categorizes failures as omission, substitution, or displacement to account for differences in model outputs.
Finds failure modes are more closely linked to output format than architecture family; substitution and displacement can remain invisible to downstream systems.
Under distribution shift, VLMs that mainly omit detections may shift toward substitution or displacement failures.

papers.selection_reason: Targeted study of physical adversarial robustness in grounding VLMs with a unified failure-mode evaluation framework; directly relevant to multimodal LLM-based perception.
papers.title: A Unified Evaluation Framework of Physical Adversarial Robustness in the Edge VLM Era
papers.tldr: A unified evaluation shows that compact grounding VLMs can be as physically vulnerable to adversarial patches as object detectors, while sometimes producing more dangerous, confident mislocalizations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress in general visual understanding, yet they still struggle with fine-grained instance-level consistency verification, where the goal is to determine whether two images depict the exact same physical object under varying viewpoints, illumination, and backgrounds. This task requires both global semantic perception and precise examination of subtle local evidence, since semantically similar objects may differ only in small suspicious regions. To address this challenge, we propose LocalAgent, a collaborative agentic framework that integrates the complementary strengths of a generalist MLLM and lightweight specialist verifiers. The MLLM first reasons globally to identify suspicious local regions, which are then delegated to a Local Evidence Verifier (LEV) toolkit for fine-grained appearance and geometric matching. LEV comprises Local Appearance Consistency (LAC), which estimates appearance similarity under illumination and color changes, and Local Geometric Correspondence (LGC), which estimates spatial correspondence under viewpoint changes. LEV returns structured scalar evidence that the MLLM integrates for the final decision. We further introduce an auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) strategy, in which answer correctness dominates auxiliary tool-use and format signals, enabling the policy to learn when verification is necessary. Experiments show that LocalAgent improves mean accuracy by 4.9% over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline while invoking a verifier on only 12.13% of samples and preserving the general multimodal capabilities of the underlying MLLM. The open-source repository is available at https://github.com/Firefly-zoo/LocalAgent-main.
authors: Jiachen Guo, Xinshan Zhu, Boyun Wang, Yanyan Liang, Jun Wan, Feng Lin, Ajian Liu
bullets: Targets instance-level consistency under viewpoint, illumination, and background changes, where differences may appear only in small regions.
The MLLM identifies suspicious areas and delegates them to lightweight Local Evidence Verifiers for detailed analysis.
LAC evaluates local appearance consistency, while LGC measures local geometric correspondence; their structured evidence guides the final decision.
An auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning strategy teaches the model when verification is necessary while prioritizing answer correctness.
Reports a 4.9% mean-accuracy gain over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline, with verifier use on only 12.13% of samples.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the LocalAgent framework. Given an image pair, the MLLM performs initial global semantic perception and either commits to a direct answer or, when the assessment is inconclusive, acts as a spatial controller to localize suspicious regions. These regions are conditionally delegated to the LEV toolkit, which returns structured scalar evidence that the MLLM integrates with its initial reasoning state to produce the final prediction. The strategic verification policy is optimized via auxiliary-capped RFT.

Figure 1: The motivation of LocalAgent. Standard MLLMs over-rely on global similarity and fail on instance-level verification in both directions. LocalAgent uses the MLLM as a spatial controller to localize suspicious regions, delegates them to the LEV toolkit (LAC, LGC) for invariant matching, and integrates the returned structured scalar evidence into the final decision.

papers.selection_reason: Agentic MLLM framework combining global visual reasoning with local geometric/appearance verifiers for fine-grained instance consistency; fits VLM and spatial reasoning interests.
papers.title: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency
papers.tldr: LocalAgent combines global MLLM reasoning with targeted local appearance and geometric verification to improve fine-grained identification of whether two images show the same physical object.

papers.abstract: Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) communicate through short click sequences called codas, whose structure includes the rhythmic pattern of inter-click intervals (ICI) and the spectral composition of the clicks. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoder (DCCE), which explicitly encodes rhythm and spectral information with separate encoders before fusing them. We evaluate DCCE on three coda-understanding tasks: social unit, coda type, and individual identification. We compare DCCE against strong baselines from literature under a common linear-probe protocol and analyze the role of each channel and training objective through ablations. On 1,383 codas, shared partitions and validation-only layer selection support three random splits and three recording-date-disjoint folds. DCCE with unit pairing and type supervision achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901/0.865/0.597 for unit/type/identity. Raw ICI remains strongest for type (0.987), and ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference (0.724). An auxiliary identity objective improves spectral-branch identity prediction but does not improve the mean fused-identity score in this configuration. Date-grouped evaluation and four year holdouts expose generalization limits. The results support task-dependent combinations of timing and spectral information, without establishing independent biological channels or general architectural superiority. Code, notebooks, and complete results are available at https://dcce-research-site.vercel.app.
authors: Jo\~ao Victor Quintanilha, Emma Virnelli, Shuo Zhang
bullets: Evaluates social-unit, coda-type, and individual-identification tasks on 1,383 codas using linear probes across random splits and date-disjoint folds.
Combines separate inter-click-interval and spectral encoders through contrastive training and fusion, with ablations of channels and objectives.
Achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901 for unit, 0.865 for type, and 0.597 for identity under the reported configuration.
Raw ICI is strongest for coda type, while ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference.
Date-grouped evaluation and year holdouts expose generalization limits; results do not establish independent biological channels or universal architectural superiority.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a dual-channel contrastive encoder (DCCE) for audio data to understand whale communication, representing a multimodal technical contribution.
papers.title: Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoding of Sperm Whale Coda
papers.tldr: DCCE separately encodes sperm whale coda rhythm and click spectra, improving some understanding tasks while revealing strong task and recording-date generalization limits.

papers.abstract: We introduce MixAgent, an agentic pipeline for music post-production that follows the workflow of audio engineers to build interpretable and editable mixing plans guided by a reference song. A grouping agent first routes related input tracks, such as drum recordings, into subgroups. A planning agent then uses retrieved examples to choose and order audio effects, such as volume control and reverb, for tracks, subgroups, and the full mix. To refine the mix, a detector identifies what needs correction, and a critic proposes numerical parameter adjustments from tracks to the full mix. In our experiments, prompting recent multimodal models to listen and revise often worsens the mix, making reliable correction a central challenge. We therefore build MixCritic, a dataset of 45,657 repair critiques derived from parameters fitted to professional mixes, and train the critic with supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization on rendered audio outcomes. On MedleyDB, learned refinement reduces error by 19% relative to the initial mix, with preference optimization reducing it by 8.4% over supervised training alone. Retrieved examples further improve effects selection, and a human listening test shows that MixAgent gets higher quality ratings than mixes produced by Qwen3-Omni, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GPT-4o-audio.
authors: Jaywon Koo, Junghyun Koo, Marco A. Martinez-Ramirez, Wei-Hsiang Liao, Seungheon Doh, Qiyu Wu, Vicente Ordonez, Yuki Mitsufuji
bullets: Groups related tracks, plans and orders effects using retrieved examples, and supports edits from individual tracks to the full mix.
Uses a detector to identify mixing problems and MixCritic to propose numerical parameter corrections.
MixCritic is trained on 45,657 critiques derived from professional mixes, with supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization.
On MedleyDB, refinement reduces error by 19% from the initial mix; preference optimization adds an 8.4% improvement over supervised training alone.
Human listeners rate MixAgent mixes higher than mixes from several multimodal models; reliable automated correction remains challenging.

papers.selection_reason: Utilizes multimodal models (audio) in an agentic pipeline (MixAgent) for music post-production, including a critic trained on preference optimization.
papers.title: Agentic Music Post-Production
papers.tldr: MixAgent is an interpretable, reference-guided agentic system for music mixing that plans effects and learns to refine mixes through audio-based critiques.

papers.abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.
authors: Md Khalid Syfullah, Alvi Ataur Khalil
bullets: The study tests classically simulated 4- and 8-qubit quantum circuits within LLaVA-OneVision.
Quantum layers are evaluated through insertion and replacement at four model locations on Visual Spatial Reasoning.
Insertion after the visual projector achieves 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 points above classical full fine-tuning.
Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer preserves 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters.

Earlier replacements can hurt accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably reduce training or computation; security robustness is assessed across six attack settings, while generalization remains open.

papers.selection_reason: Explores quantum-enhanced layers in a vision-language model for spatial reasoning, relevant to multimodal foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
papers.tldr: Quantum layers can improve or compress vision-language models, but their benefits depend strongly on where they are used and do not yet establish broad security gains.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering requires models to assign attributes and relations to the correct objects, a problem known as visual binding. Structured prompts make these assignments explicit through labeled fields. Yet an improvement from the full prompt does not reveal which labels help or how they interact. First, we isolate field-label effects across ten models and six tasks by holding the image and claim fixed. These comparisons reveal differences that overall accuracy can hide. With a relation label present, adding object-role labels helps Qwen3 but hurts Qwen2 on Spatial. Second, we compare auxiliary hints that preserve or swap the question's role assignments against a no-hint baseline. Across two image sets, Qwen3's advantage with preserving hints mainly reflects errors caused by swapped hints. Preserving hints remain near baseline. Field order further affects the harm. Third, we test clearer hint wording and direct selection of the relation shown in the image. Clearer hints improve text matching but do not consistently improve visual judgments. In contrast, relation selection partly reduces errors for some hints in Qwen3 and GPT-4.1-mini.
authors: Xiaoyu Ma, Zheyuan Zhang, Kaiwen Shi, Yanfang Ye
bullets: Structured prompts expose visual-binding errors that overall accuracy can obscure.
Object-role labels interact differently with models: they help Qwen3 but hurt Qwen2 on Spatial when relation labels are present.
For Qwen3, preserving hints stays near the no-hint baseline, while swapped hints account for much of the apparent benefit of preserving hints.
Clearer hint wording improves text matching but does not consistently improve visual judgments.
Selecting the relation shown in the image partly reduces hint-related errors for some cases in Qwen3 and GPT-4.1-mini.

papers.abstract: We present Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR, a family of audio-language models that builds upon its predecesor Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR with improved speech recognition and expanded capabilities in speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding. The family retains support for 30 languages and 16 Chinese dialects, together with instruction-controlled capabilities including historical-context conditioning, hierarchical hotword customization, and native transcription polishing. Speaker-diarized ASR produces structured outputs containing speaker labels, timestamps, and recognized text, maintaining consistent speaker labels across turns and the representation of overlapping speech. The general audio understanding capabilities cover audio-, speech-, and music-captioning, temporal grounding and sound event detection, as well as audio question answering and multiple-choice reasoning. These tasks broaden the application scope from recognizing spoken words to interpreting speakers, acoustic events, and their temporal relations. To accommodate different deployment requirements, the family includes variants for asynchronous file transcription, low-latency streaming, interactive voice input, and non-streaming recognition, with speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding available in certain variants. Evaluations span conventional ASR, multilingual and dialectal speech, speaker-diarized transcription, and general audio understanding, demonstrating the capabilities of the Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR family across transcription and broader audio analysis tasks.

Provides instruction-controlled historical context, hierarchical hotwords, and native transcription polishing.
Covers captioning, temporal grounding, sound event detection, audio QA, and multiple-choice reasoning.
Includes asynchronous, streaming, interactive, and non-streaming variants; evaluations span ASR and broader audio tasks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
bullets: Controlled results across 22 benchmarks show that merely increasing inference-time reasoning yields modest gains.
A capability layer standardizes tool access and renders tool outputs as model-readable evidence.
Persistent memory stores images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts across reasoning steps.
A coding interface enables computations that combine outputs from multiple tools.

Across eight open and proprietary backbones, it improves average scores by 9.7–12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, with substantially lower token cost than maximum-effort alternatives in one comparison.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of OpenVLHarness. The MLLM orchestrator invokes capabilities through typed interfaces. The capability layer connects these interfaces to underlying models and services and renders their outputs into model-facing evidence: here, a labeled mask overlay accompanied by a textual description and normalized bounding boxes. Persistent multimodal memory retains image artifacts, structured data, and web references under reusable handles. An Environment Update advertises the available artifacts to the orchestrator, allowing subsequent calls to reuse earlier evidence, including through memory-grounded computation.

(b) Proposed remedies: grouped into creating task-specific tools (A–C), updating harness text (Y), and no proposed remedy (Z). (c) Four datasets selected for contrasting remedy profiles: Y (orange) dominates ERQA and RealWorldQA, while A–C (blue) dominates SparBench and FREAK-VQA. (d) Gains from harness search and tool generation over the unoptimized harness. Harness search is more effective on datasets dominated by text-level changes, while tool generation yields larger gains when task-specific tools are preferred.

Widely used benchmarks such as TallyQA, CountBenchQA, and PixmoCount are dominated by low counts: nearly all of their samples contain ten or fewer objects (and a majority of TallyQA fall in the 0–1 bucket), capping at 10–15. Only FSC-147 and FSCD-LVIS contain substantial mass in the high-count regime (> 50 objects), reaching into the hundreds or thousands. This skew means accuracy on standard counting benchmarks largely reflects performance on small object counts and reveals little about high-count visual measurement.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities, with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supporting complex multi-hop reasoning by retrieving evidence distributed across documents. Graph-based approaches exploit connections among evidence, and hypergraph-based retrieval further preserves higher-order entity associations within documents and connects documents through shared entities. However, existing hypergraph retrievers often rely on predefined structural expansion or diffusion, which may miss query-dependent interactions needed to identify relevant evidence. They also leave connections among retrieved evidence implicit, requiring LLMs to reconstruct these connections before reasoning. Therefore, we propose HyperReCo, a framework for retrieving and connecting evidence with a hypergraph neural network (HyperGNN). We represent each document as a hyperedge over its extracted entities, with shared entities connecting the hyperedges. Through hypergraph message passing with joint supervision over documents and entities, the HyperGNN learns query-dependent interactions to retrieve complementary evidence. We further introduce Gradient-Guided Hyper-Path Decoding (GGHD), which uses gradient attribution to interpret the learned interactions and translate them into explicit hyper-paths that help LLMs combine complementary facts for multi-hop reasoning. Experiments on six benchmarks show that HyperReCo achieves the best retrieval performance among the compared methods on all three multi-hop QA datasets, together with strong downstream QA performance. Case studies and further analyses demonstrate the utility of decoded hyper-paths for connecting retrieved evidence.
bullets: Addresses the need to model query-dependent interactions among evidence spread across documents.
Represents documents as hyperedges over extracted entities, with shared entities linking documents.
Jointly supervises document and entity representations to retrieve complementary evidence.
Uses Gradient-Guided Hyper-Path Decoding to convert learned interactions into explicit reasoning paths.
Achieves the best retrieval performance among compared methods on all three evaluated multi-hop QA datasets, with strong downstream QA performance.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive models (ARMs) face a "Sequentiality Bottleneck" in reasoning, while diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallelism but lack semantic coherence. To addresses both limitations, we propose Collaborative Reasoning Asymmetric Learning (CoRAL), a hybrid framework via an Asymmetric Planner-Executor (APE) architecture: a DLM Planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while a large ARM Executor selects the optimal plan and synthesizes the final answer. To train the Planner effectively, we introduce Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT (RDC), which integrates outcome-based rewards into the diffusion process to steer it toward goal-directed reasoning. Experiments on vision-language benchmarks show that CoRAL significantly outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and achieves competitive performance against strong ARMs, achieving both superior efficiency and quality.
authors: Wei Cai, Jian Zhao, Yuchen Yuan, Xuelong Li
bullets: Targets the sequentiality bottleneck of autoregressive reasoning and the semantic-coherence limitations of diffusion language models.
Uses an Asymmetric Planner-Executor architecture: a diffusion planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while an autoregressive executor selects and completes the best plan.
Introduces Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT to steer diffusion-generated reasoning toward goal-directed solutions using outcome-based rewards.
On vision-language benchmarks, CoRAL outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and is competitive with strong autoregressive models in both efficiency and quality.

papers.abstract: Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple-choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio-visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human-annotated question-answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video-based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high-quality question-answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio-visual reasoning.
authors: Xiaoxing Hu, Wenxi Yao, Chaoyuan Shi, Ziqi Ye, Xiaorong Guo, Peixuan Li, Zhuoran Sun, Ziyang Gong, Peiyuan Zhang, Mingxin Liu, Shuran Ma, Hongbo Liu, Xiaomin Yu, Yu Tian, Wentao Wang, Zhenjie Yang, Jian Hu, Yunhang Shen, Haoyu Cao, Xue Yang

Introduces Coverage Grounded Score for evidence identification and Bottleneck Grounded Score for weak temporal localization in either modality.
Across 24 Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash performed best overall, but its low Level 3 grounding score indicates substantial limitations in complex evidence localization.
Scope is limited to the benchmark’s annotated videos, questions, and expert-defined evidence.

papers.abstract: Vision-language trackers (VLTs) accept descriptions intended to assist tracking, but accepting text does not establish that its content changes tracking decisions, particularly as visual evidence deteriorates. We introduce DISTRACT, a matched-intervention benchmark that holds video, target, and distractor fixed while crossing four text priors with four image degradations along a controlled severity axis. We evaluate five VLTs on four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise representation probes, and activation patching. Molmo2 and JointNLT exhibit directed text use. Some effects contract under degradation, whereas others show no significant endpoint change after multiplicity correction. UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack respond only weakly to changes in text semantics, with no directed behavioral effect surviving FDR correction in the tested settings. Model-internal analyses reveal that at decision-near states, correct-versus-conflicting text is decodable in Molmo2 and JointNLT but not in the other three systems. In the responsive models, decodability peaks at late states where replacement produces little behavioral change, whereas replacing selected earlier states redirects conflict-associated trajectories toward the target. Because matched-correct donors do not significantly outperform unrelated donors, these interventions identify earlier intervention-sensitive states without establishing target-specific semantic rescue. DISTRACT thus exposes when and where text affects tracking under degraded visual evidence.
bullets: Uses matched interventions crossing four text priors with four controlled image-degradation levels while holding video, target, and distractor fixed.
Evaluates five trackers across four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise probes, and activation patching.
Molmo2 and JointNLT show directed text use; UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack show no significant directed behavioral effects after FDR correction.
In responsive models, text is decodable near decisions, but earlier-state interventions more effectively redirect conflict-associated trajectories.
The benchmark identifies intervention-sensitive states, but does not establish target-specific semantic rescue because matched-correct donors did not outperform unrelated donors.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.
authors: Yuhang Chen, Guangyue Liu, Shilong Liu
bullets: Targets a gap in streaming benchmarks that focus mainly on timestamped question answering rather than deciding whether, when, and how to respond.
Defines six tasks across proactive intervention, continuous engagement, and coordination during overlapping or multi-party interaction.
Provides 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and temporal metadata.
Separately evaluates response quality, participation decisions, and timing using response quality, window response rate, and reaction latency.
Leading models respond in under a second on average, but window response rates reach at most 53.77%; adapting responses to new information remains difficult.

papers.abstract: Visual tool use enables vision-language models (VLMs) to acquire task-relevant evidence, but its effectiveness can be limited by predefined visual operations and the tool-use strategies learned during training. Representing these operations and strategies as reusable external skills allows them to be refined through self-evolution without updating model parameters. However, skill refinement can introduce performance regressions. Meanwhile, inspecting accumulated task execution trajectories together with skill evolution history may lead to evolution evidence overload. To address these challenges, we propose VisualEvolve, a self-evolving framework that evolves executable visual operations and tool-use strategies for VLMs through a Select--Execute--Evolve--Evaluate cycle. Skill-Library Snapshot Selection uses performance on a fixed validation set disjoint from execution tasks to select an effective historical snapshot for subsequent evolution, limiting the propagation of performance regressions. Progressive Evidence Access (PEA) guides capability-gap diagnosis through a coarse-to-fine hierarchy comprising the Skill-Performance Report, Evolution Log, Trajectory Summaries, and relevant raw trajectory segments. Across four VLM backbones and six evaluation sets from three benchmarks, VisualEvolve improves over the Initial Skill Library in 23 of 24 settings, with a maximum gain of 15.1 percentage points on VisualProbe Hard using Qwen3.5-Plus. Ablation studies support the contributions of Snapshot Selection and PEA, while further experiments show that skills can be improved using experience from different data settings and directly reused across backbones. Moreover, VisualEvolve enables effective skill self-evolution with over an order of magnitude fewer task-solving trajectories than estimated for representative RL-based methods.
authors: Jiawei Wang, Yucun Li, Xueqi Li, Shenghao Wang, Xinquan Gong, Dan Zhang, Zheqi Lv, Yuquan Le, Shaozu Yuan, An Zhang, Da Cao, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Addresses limitations of fixed visual operations and training-learned tool-use strategies in VLMs.
Uses a Select–Execute–Evolve–Evaluate cycle to refine executable visual skills externally.
Skill-Library Snapshot Selection chooses robust historical skills using a separate validation set to reduce regression propagation.
Progressive Evidence Access diagnoses capability gaps from coarse reports to targeted raw trajectory segments.

papers.abstract: Training multimodal search agents requires tasks that make visually grounded search necessary for determining the answer. Textual identity clues and unused target evidence allow shortcuts in synthetic questions, weakening supervision for visual search and evidence integration. We propose RACE, an image-conditioned task synthesis framework that constructs dependencies from images to targets and from target-specific evidence to answers. Referential Abstraction (RA) replaces identity-revealing text with specific visual references or ambiguous relational references resolved by searching among depicted candidates. Compositional Evidence (CE) links retrieved facts about multiple entities in one image or entities from different images into joint questions whose answers require every designated contribution. Both operations also apply to images found during search, allowing new visual observations to determine subsequent search targets or supply answer evidence. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B on only 12K teacher-generated trajectories from RACE raises average accuracy across ten multimodal benchmarks from 53.5 to 56.0, a relative improvement of approximately 4.7% over the matched base agent. Our code, data, and model will be publicly available.
authors: Eric Tao, Minhao Sun, Liyan Liu, Zhijing Wu, Xiaohan Yu, Lang Mei, Li Huang, Chao Feng, Jinchao Ma, Sichen Kang, Siyu Mo, Chong Chen
bullets: Addresses shortcuts in synthetic multimodal search tasks caused by textual identity clues and unused visual evidence.
Uses Referential Abstraction to replace identity-revealing text with visual or ambiguous relational references resolved through search.
Uses Compositional Evidence to require answers to integrate facts about multiple entities across one or more images.
Applies both mechanisms to images discovered during search, enabling observations to guide later targets or provide evidence.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B improves average accuracy across ten benchmarks from 53.5 to 56.0, a reported relative gain of about 4.7%.

papers.abstract: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.
authors: Marc Chapus, Carlos Crispim-Junior, V\'eronique Eglin, Atilla Baskurt
bullets: Existing VideoQA benchmarks are dominated by small ground-truth counts, masking errors at rarer cardinalities.

Sixteen video-language models are evaluated zero-shot; none exceeds 27.6% exact-match accuracy.
Accuracy varies unpredictably with cardinality, including monotonic declines and peak-and-collapse patterns.
Models favor particular integers, with performance dropping sharply at neighboring counts, motivating balanced diagnostic benchmarks.

papers.abstract: VGL-stGen is a multimodal large language model adapted from a pretrained medical vision-language model using paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics with single-cell references. Training integrates image-expression and expression-cell-type pairs, and gene-conditioned pseudo-labels transfer transcriptomic cell-type supervision to histology images. One deployed checkpoint supports thirteen evaluated tasks spanning tissue and cell-type classification, gene prediction and conditional expression completion from combinations of histology, cell identity and observed gene expression. Task-specific decoding produces categorical labels, gene lists and structured expression levels. For conditional completion, fixing queried gene identities and predicting their levels autoregressively improves structured prediction. Controlled adaptation shows that restricting supervision to requested expression-level tokens can further improve image-conditioned completion. Image-permutation experiments indicate that correctly paired histology adds information beyond observed expression. External classification relies partly on computational references with shared annotation lineage, and some H&E sources were exposed during cancer training or model development. Within these conditions, VGL-stGen demonstrates how a medical vision-language backbone can learn from spatial transcriptomics and histology to connect tissue morphology and molecular states through shared generative modeling.

Autoregressive prediction of queried gene levels and supervision focused on requested expression tokens improve conditional completion.

papers.title: VGL-stGen: Learning a shared multimodal model for lung histology and spatial transcriptomics

papers.abstract: Oddly Satisfying Videos (OSVs) can evoke strong viewer responses through repetitive motion, visual tactility, and ASMR-like sounds despite containing few explicit semantic emotion cues. This makes OSVs a challenging setting for Video Emotion Analysis (VEA), since most existing methods focus on semantic video content and under-model the physical sensory dynamics that shape viewer responses. To support Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis (OSVEA), we construct the Oddly Satisfying Video Dataset (OSVD), comprising 12,000 annotated 5-second clips. Each clip provides viewer-emotion labels under video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual conditions, together with explanations grounded in visual and acoustic sensory evidence. Building on OSVD, we propose PI-MLLM, a psychophysics-inspired multimodal large language model that integrates Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment (MSDA) and Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution (CAVA). MSDA uses auxiliary prediction objectives to align modality representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics. CAVA evaluates emotion scores across modality coalitions and applies Shapley attribution to identify the dominant modality and determine whether visual and auditory evidence is synergistic or conflicting. Experiments show that PI-MLLM improves both viewer-side emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality, suggesting the value of physical sensory cues to video emotion analysis.
authors: Yuheng Zhang, Jie Zhang, Yuecong Min, Yunwei Zhao, Meichen Liu, Qiankun Li, Shiguang Shan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of analyzing emotions in videos with few explicit semantic cues but strong sensory effects.
Introduces OSVD, a dataset of 12,000 annotated 5-second clips with video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual emotion labels and sensory-grounded explanations.
Uses Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment to align representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics.
Uses Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution with Shapley values to identify dominant modalities and audiovisual synergy or conflict.
Experiments report improved emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality.

Figure 1: Existing VEA methods rely on sensory-ungrounded semantic annotations and implicit multimodal fusion. papers.abstract: VLMs for medical image interpretation are typically evaluated on clean inputs, despite the progressive evidence loss that can occur in high stakes clinical settings. Existing robustness studies show that performance can degrade while confidence remains high, but do not establish when a previously reliable model-case pair ceases to behave reliably. We introduce a baseline-anchored framework that traces baseline-correct cases through progressive image degradation to identify an empirical evidence boundary, and define mirage as continued commitment at this boundary, regardless of correctness. Across three VLMs on three medical datasets, only MedGemma provides a sufficiently large baseline-correct pool for trajectory analysis. On VQA-RAD, the only dataset in which the question text varies, language-only answerability is associated with baseline correctness (AUROC 0.677) and with commitment at the boundary (AUROC 0.653 to 0.670). MedGemma's post-boundary behavior is heterogeneous, including direct mirage, correct recovery, mirage dissolution, consistent abstention, and oscillation, with mirage rates of 16.0 to 100.0% across dataset-modality pairs. Despite this behavioral heterogeneity, residual-stream probes decode commit-versus-abstain behavior at the boundary with AUROC of 0.895 to 0.994 under nested cross-validation. These results show that progressive evidence loss can produce persistent commitment that output entropy and abstention behavior do not consistently reflect, motivating boundary-aware evaluation, option-order controls, and improved abstention mechanisms for reliable medical foundation models operating under partial observation.
authors: Edric Castel C. Hao, Rez Samantha Z. Floresca
bullets: Introduces a baseline-anchored framework that tracks initially correct model–case pairs through progressive degradation to identify an empirical evidence boundary.
Defines “mirage” as continued answer commitment at that boundary, whether or not the answer remains correct.

Across three VLMs and datasets, only MedGemma had a sufficiently large baseline-correct pool for trajectory analysis; its post-boundary behavior varied widely, with mirage rates of 16.0–100.0% across dataset–modality pairs.
On VQA-RAD, language-only answerability was associated with baseline correctness and boundary commitment.

Residual-stream probes decoded commit-versus-abstain behavior at the boundary with AUROC 0.895–0.994 under nested cross-validation, motivating boundary-aware evaluation and better abstention mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.
authors: Seohyun Lee, Jongha Kim, Dohwan Ko, Ji Soo Lee, Seoung Choi, Jayun Ku, Hyunwoo J. Kim

papers.abstract: Staged post-training of multimodal foundation models chains vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning, yet how each phase trades capabilities against the others remains under-characterised. Tracking an 8.4B-parameter model from an un-fine-tuned baseline through three training phases on Japanese financial documents (evaluated on five text-input benchmarks), we find the phases interact non-additively: math-only distillation overwrites the financial knowledge acquired earlier even as procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase repairs more than it installs. A skip-phase ablation is best for domain knowledge but forfeits numerical-reasoning gains, so per-phase contributions are not decomposable and the best checkpoint is task-dependent, with implications for checkpoint retention and scheduling rather than added stages.
bullets: Studies an 8.4B-parameter model across vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning.
Math-only distillation erases previously acquired financial knowledge while preserving procedural math ability.
Domain tuning mainly repairs lost capabilities rather than adding entirely new ones.
Skipping a phase maximizes domain knowledge but sacrifices numerical-reasoning gains.
The best checkpoint depends on the task, favoring careful checkpoint retention and phase scheduling over simply adding stages.

Phase 2 (Mathematical Reasoning Distillation): P2-S1 updates the LLM via QLoRA on approximately 150K math problems with XML-structured chain-of-thought supervision from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 (vision encoder and projector frozen). papers.abstract: We investigate associative creativity in descriptions of abstract visual stimuli by humans and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). While conceptual association is central to human communication, it remains unclear how humans and models adapt when visual stimuli become increasingly difficult to map onto familiar semantic concepts. We evaluate several state-of-the-art MLLMs and human participants along two dimensions of creativity, originality and effectiveness, using two datasets with controlled manipulations of difficulty. SilCC varies naming difficulty through progressively more complex combinations of abstract shapes, and PixCC varies difficulty through increasing levels of random visual noise. Results show that humans produce more diverse associative descriptions than MLLMs, including greater semantic distance, higher entropy, and more novel expressions relative to reference lexica. As difficulty increases, effectiveness declines in SilCC, and humans increasingly shift from holistic associations to descriptions of low-level visual properties in PixCC.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
authors: Siyuan Ma, Yu Qi, Cheng Ye, Ruotian Peng, Xinyi Xu, Zitiantao Lin, Zedong Cai, Yijian Huang, Weiyang Liu, Siyuan Wang, Yandong Wen
bullets: RoboJudge-Bench evaluates MLLM judges on Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment using 800 human-annotated videos from 8 corpora, 10 generators, and varied hand embodiments.
Existing general-purpose and general-domain video judges show limited or inconsistent agreement with human judgments in embodied scenarios, especially for physical adherence.
RoboJudge-Train contains 12K videos with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in diffusion models have raised concerns about privacy, harmful content, and copyright violations. Concept erasure methods aim to address these risks by removing undesirable concepts from pretrained models without full retraining. However, existing approaches often degrade non-target generation quality through heuristic strength scaling (e.g., classifier-free guidance or negative prompt scaling), leading to uncontrolled and excessive semantic drift. To address this, we propose Push-Pull Attentional Anchoring (PPAA), a mechanism in the cross-attention space that displaces target representations while anchoring the scale of erasure via bounded cosine-similarity constraints. By using a relative similarity ratio instead of an absolute difference, our adaptive threshold represents a meaningful percentage of semantic retention, facilitating a single value to be applied uniformly across layers. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple concept categories, including celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property. Our method achieves favorable trade-offs against prior approaches on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and demonstrates its applicability to modern architectures such as FLUX.
authors: Nattanat Chatthee, Tagon Sompong, Ekapol Chuangsuwanich, Supasorn Suwajanakorn
bullets: Addresses semantic drift caused by heuristic erasure-strength scaling in existing concept-erasure methods.
Operates in cross-attention space, displacing target representations while constraining their cosine similarity.
Uses a bounded relative similarity ratio to express semantic retention and apply one adaptive threshold across layers.
Evaluated on celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property concepts.
Reports favorable trade-offs on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and applicability to FLUX.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Concept erasure and preservation results on FLUX. (a) Qualitative comparison on representative identity, style, and character concepts. Our method erases target concepts, such as Barack Obama, Van Gogh, and Mickey Mouse, while preserving non-target concepts, such as Will Smith, Picasso, and Donald Duck. ESD causes substantial semantic shifts in non-target concepts, whereas UCE fails to semantically erase Mickey Mouse. (b) Quantitative results. Accuracy measures target-concept detection after erasure, and CMMD measures preservation relative to the original FLUX model; lower is better for both metrics. These results demonstrate the applicability of our objective to FLUX while maintaining a favorable erasure–preservation trade-off.

Fig. 2: Erasure–Preservation score across concept categories. We compare our method with existing concept erasure approaches across four categories: Celebrity, IP Entity, Artistic Style, and Nudity. The vertical axis measures erasure effectiveness using the Unlearning Score or classifier accuracy for detecting the target concept, where lower values indicate stronger erasure. The horizontal axis measures preservation effectiveness using CMMD (×1000), where lower values indicate better preservation of non-target concepts. Each point denotes a hyperparameter setting; baselines vary their erasure-strength parameter when available, whereas our method varies only mpush. In particular, it achieves the Pareto frontier in the erasure–preservation trade-off for Celebrity, Artistic Style, and IP Entity erasure. For Nudity, our method achieves results comparable to DUO, while maintaining stronger erasure–preservation trade-offs across the other categories.

Fig. 8: Training-Free Trajectory Probing Results. We evaluate robustness to trajectory-based attacks using the prompt “a photo of a naked person” on nudityerased models. Base shows images generated without applying the attack procedure. Attacked (Best) denotes the image most aligned with the attack concept according to the CLIP score among all generated samples during the probing trajectory. The remaining rows show randomly sampled images obtained from the attack method. Although our method is not explicitly trained with robustness-oriented objectives (e.g., DUO and STEREO), its behavior under this attack appears competitive to that of existing methods such as MACE, UCE, SUMA, and ESD.

Fig. 10: Concept erasure and preservation results on the Z-Image model. We show that our method can be applied to Z-Image, a recent text-to-image model based on a Scalable Single-Stream Multimodal Diffusion Transformer, achieving effective concept erasure while preserving the quality of non-target generations.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison of erasure methods. Our method erases the target concepts (e.g., Rihanna identity and Picasso style) while preserving the non-target concepts (e.g., Margot Robbie identity and Claude Monet style). Compared with existing approaches, our method achieves a favorable erasure–preservation trade-off.

Fig. 6: Ablation Study on Design Choices. Ours denotes the full method, which uses cosine distance in Lpush, Lpull, and Lpreserve, together with the relative-margin formulation and preservation losses (Lpreserve, Ldenoise). Each variant removes one component: the relative-margin formulation, the cosine-distance formulation (replaced with L2 distance), or the preservation losses. Each point corresponds to a different push margin. The x-axis measures same-domain preservation (CMMD ×1000, lower is better) and the y-axis measures unlearning score (detection accuracy, lower is better). The full method consistently achieves the best erasure–preservation trade-off, while removing any component degrades performance, indicating that each component contributes to the overall improvement.

We compare three tokenselection variants for Lpush: applying it to both the concept-relevant token(s) and the EOS token, only to the EOS token, and only to the concept-relevant token(s). papers.abstract: Depression assessment from counseling speech requires integrating textual and acoustic psychological evidence across turns, yet existing end-to-end classification approaches lack explicit multimodal evidence interpretation and context-aware reasoning. We propose AudiPsy, an evidence-grounded omni-LLM for depression assessment over spoken counseling conversations. AudiPsy employs an Observation-Assessment-Summary (OAS) paradigm to integrate dialogue transcripts, textual and acoustic emotions, and textual-acoustic emotion incongruence into structured reasoning. OAS incrementally organizes multimodal observations, performs contextualized assessment, and maintains an evolving dialogue summary for subsequent turns. To support this framework, we construct AudiPsy-Counsel, a synthetic spoken counseling conversation corpus with multimodal context augmentation, and develop a unified three-stage curriculum for depression-oriented reasoning. Experiments on DAIC-WOZ demonstrate superior depression assessment performance over specialized depression detection methods and general-purpose speech/omni-LLMs, along with improved reasoning quality, while supplementary evaluation on EATD-Corpus supports AudiPsy's applicability to naturalistic conversations.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal LLM (MLLM)-based anomaly detection (AD) methods can generate textual explanations that help interpret their predictions. However, reliably and efficiently evaluating these explanations remains challenging. While LLM judges can assess explanations through structured rubrics, they often require substantial token generation, making evaluation costly and difficult to scale. We instead propose to anchor evaluation in the available ground truth by extracting verifiable claims from each explanation and verifying them against the corresponding annotations. We instantiate this idea as AnomalyJev, a lightweight framework that extracts verifiable claims from contextualised representations using ground-truth-defined queries and pointer based heads, without token generation. The claims are then verified against the ground truth to score faithfulness and completeness. For evaluation, we construct a human-annotated set of 640 explanations with over 1,600 expert ratings across in-domain and cross-dataset settings. Despite its compact design, AnomalyJev achieves stronger agreement with human annotators than most open MLLM judges and approaches that of flagship MLLM judges, at a fraction of their runtime and resources.
authors: Qizhou Wang, Jiawen Zhu, Guansong Pang, Christopher Leckie
bullets: Addresses the costly and hard-to-scale evaluation of textual explanations from MLLM-based anomaly detectors.
Extracts verifiable claims from contextualized representations using ground-truth-defined queries and pointer-based heads, without token generation.
Scores explanation faithfulness and completeness by checking claims against available annotations.
Introduces a human-annotated benchmark of 640 explanations with over 1,600 expert ratings across in-domain and cross-dataset settings.
Shows stronger human agreement than most open MLLM judges and near-flagship-judge agreement with substantially lower runtime and resource use.

papers.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

papers.abstract: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks (nine evaluation splits), answering 29,386 questions per model, 558,334 model-question evaluations in total. Using per-question pairwise analysis across all model pairs in each family, we identify 375 subtask-model-pair combinations exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning 4,342 unique queries where a smaller model answers correctly but a larger model fails, and we find that these patterns replicate across independently developed architectures. We identify 13 subtask-dataset pairs that show inverse scaling across multiple families, consistent with the phenomenon being task-driven rather than model-specific. The most affected domains in our study include multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge, with accuracy gaps exceeding 20 percentage points in several cases, while diagram understanding appears comparatively resistant. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing model size uniformly improves multimodal capabilities and suggest that model selection should be task-aware.
authors: Rohit Saxena, Alessandro Suglia, Marek Rei, Pasquale Minervini

Results support task-aware model selection rather than assuming the largest model is always best.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced rapidly in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain limited on tasks requiring fine-grained understanding of small or easily overlooked image regions. Recent thinking with images approaches mitigate this limitation by allowing models to inspect images through operations such as zooming, cropping, or code execution. While effective, their multi-turn interactions with VLMs introduce redundant token computation and slow inference, and separate region inspection from the reasoning step that depends on it. To address these issues, we propose Look Before You Reason (LoRe), an implicit visual thinking framework for efficient visual reasoning within a single-turn VLM interaction. Given an image and a question, LoRe predicts the most relevant image region, aligns it with the corresponding image patch features, and strengthens the associated key-value (KV) cache entries, enabling subsequent decoding to directly exploit the selected visual cues without additional visual inputs or explicit tool calls. We further employ reinforcement learning to guide the VLM toward identifying informative image regions and leveraging them during reasoning. To support fine-grained evaluation of multimodal reasoning, we introduce COCO-ObjQA, a large-scale benchmark for object-centric multimodal reasoning. Experiments on three challenging multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that LoRe consistently improves VLM reasoning performance with low additional inference overhead.

Improves reasoning across three challenging benchmarks with low additional inference overhead.],

papers.abstract: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured extraction from financial documents, but their behavior under visual ambiguity is poorly understood. We study CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: a model returns the same amount for both cheque fields even though their annotations differ, including cases with a blank annotation encoded as zero. Across ten visual prompting conditions, we evaluate GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet on 243 primary cheques (124 with two observed unequal amounts) and 598 strict mismatches from two additional datasets. Under courtesy redaction, GPT-4.1 CARLAR reaches 73.7 percent (95 percent bootstrap interval: 68.3 to 79.0; p below 0.001 versus baseline). Model-reported confidence can remain high when predictions agree; expected calibration error reaches 0.93 among CARLAR cases. We also test a compressed-image few-shot intervention that presents examples as one visual table without model fine-tuning. On the 243-case cohort, Claude's Control condition increases paired joint extraction accuracy by 11.5 percentage points (95 percent interval: 6.2 to 16.9; adjusted p = 0.00054), but its strict-124 gain is smaller and not significant after correction. The intervention's effect on predicted-field agreement is model-dependent: it decreases for Claude and increases for GPT-4.1. These results motivate validation methods that account for visual context and dependencies between extracted fields.

papers.abstract: Multimodal question answering (MMQA) is based on integrating heterogeneous data sources, selectively leveraging relevant modalities, and ignoring distractors. Existing approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) improve performance by splitting the task into intermediate steps, but do not quantify how each modality contributes to reaching the final answer. We argue that quantifying the effect that each modality has on the answering process improves process traceability and final performance. Thus, we propose Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering (EDMA), which uses logical entropy to formalise multimodal QA as an iterative process of entropy reduction and to quantify the contribution of each modality in distinguishing correct from incorrect candidate answers. This enables the construction of quantifiable answering trajectories, where each step is associated with a measurable entropy reduction. EDMA introduces (i) modality-conditioned partitioning to estimate unimodal entropy reduction, (ii) entropy-driven multimodal fusion to capture complementary information across modalities, and (iii) entropy-based selection of the answering trajectory that minimises the most logical entropy. Evaluated across standard MMQA benchmarks, EDMA outperforms competitive prompting baselines, with average gains of 12.8 F1 and 4.6 LLM-J points over Planning Prompting and 18.6 F1 and 8.3 LLM-J points over Chain-of-Thought. Moreover, EDMA outperforms self-consistency baselines and is competitive with the multi-agent system baseline. Moreover, we show that higher entropy correlates with more false positives and, through controlled trajectory selection, demonstrate that logical entropy serves as an effective, monotonic selector for correct reasoning paths, validating entropy level as a reliable proxy for performance.

papers.abstract: Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio-visual reasoning, yet cross-modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations. To address this issue, we propose Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output-level manipulation to conflict-conditioned representation rebalancing. Specifically, OWP first identifies cross-modal conflicts from complementary modality-specific views. It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states. Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross-architecture generalization of OWP. Using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67-2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to VideoLLaMA2-AV, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni-Woodpecker
authors: Zijian Liu, Chaoyou Fu, Yan Yang, Caifeng Shan, Ran He

papers.abstract: When given an image and a text prompt, vision-language models (VLMs) can produce seemingly sophisticated text responses. However, they are also prone to hallucinate objects in their output, which can have detrimental consequences in safety-critical applications. To detect these hallucinations, certain methods interestingly leverage internal signals from the VLM as it generates the text response; potentially, these methods use the same signals that led to a hallucination to detect it. We conduct an in-depth analysis to understand the robustness of these detection methods. First, we show that a naive baseline of a generated word's token position in the VLM text response achieves competitive performance. Further, we reveal how some detection methods rely on token position and use this heuristic as a shortcut. Second, we explore detection methods' sensitivity to language and vision modalities. Our experiments suggest that strong detection performance is often driven by detecting language-based hallucinations, and when methods rely on token position, they tend to be less visually grounded and exhibit reduced robustness when hallucinations occur earlier in a text response. Lastly, we demonstrate that different detection methods can carry complementary signals; when ensembling methods together, adding weaker methods to an ensemble of higher performing ones still offers performance improvements. Altogether, while there may be useful internal VLM signals to detect hallucinations, our investigation reveals important limitations of the current methods that try to leverage them.
authors: Allison Chen, William Yang, Salma Abdel Magid, Jonathan Williams, Olga Russakovsky, Esin Tureci
bullets: A simple baseline based on a generated word’s token position achieves competitive hallucination-detection performance.
Some existing methods rely on token position as a shortcut, weakening robustness when hallucinations appear earlier in responses.
Detection performance is often driven by identifying language-based rather than vision-grounded hallucinations.
Different detectors provide complementary signals, so adding weaker methods can still improve ensembles.
The results highlight important limitations in current internal-signal approaches, despite evidence that useful signals exist.
