papers.selection_reason: Analyzes internal signals of vision-language models for hallucination detection, directly relevant to MLLM robustness and understanding.
papers.title: Robustness of Internal Signals for Hallucination Detection in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: The study finds that internal-signal methods for detecting VLM hallucinations can perform well but often exploit token-position and language cues rather than robust visual grounding.

papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text-only settings, offering limited insight into multimodal reasoning capabilities, the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, and robustness against reasoning errors. To address these limitations, we introduce MAMath-Bench, a process-aware benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities of MASs. MAMath-Bench comprises 1,003 problems spanning 11 mathematical categories, multiple difficulty levels, and several modalities, including text, images, and audio. It features fine-grained milestone annotations to evaluate systems across three dimensions: problem-solving correctness, reasoning-process reliability, and robustness to adversarial reasoning-chain perturbations. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, multi-agent collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy. Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira-ai-lab/AgentMath.
authors: Xinping Wang, Jie Ma, Rui Xing, Wensong Guo, Xiayi Zhang, Jianhao Deng, Zihao Zhou, Boqian Yang, Feijuan He
bullets: Introduces a process-aware benchmark for evaluating multimodal mathematical reasoning in multi-agent systems.
Covers 1,003 problems across 11 categories, multiple difficulty levels, and text, image, and audio modalities.
Uses fine-grained milestone annotations to assess answer correctness, reasoning-process reliability, and robustness to perturbed reasoning chains.
Finds that collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs, though it can expand intermediate-reasoning coverage.
Reports increased reasoning redundancy and continued sensitivity to subtle adversarial reasoning errors.

papers.abstract: We empirically analyze two recently proposed encoder-free multimodal LLMs, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small. Unlike previous multimodal LLMs, these models do not use modality-specific encoders to extract tokenized embeddings representing audio and image input; instead, they directly feed windows of samples, pixels, or spectral features to the Transformer language model. We analyze whether the early layers of these models learn to function similarly to dedicated audio and visual encoders. We find that these early layers do in fact act as ``implicit encoders,'' encoding audio and visual inputs in a way that is largely invariant to their cross-modal context. Furthermore, when performing multimodal reasoning tasks, we show that independently encoding the modalities throughout these early model layers achieves the same accuracy as jointly encoding them from the first layer onwards. Finally, we use layer-wise probing to analyze the salient information captured by the implicit encoders and find their behavior to be similar to several popular encoder models.
authors: David Harwath, Desh Raj, Xavier Velez, Sandra Arcos-Holzinger, Willie Jeng, Karen Livescu, Leibny Paola Garcia-Perera, Sanjeev Khudanpur
bullets: Analyzes Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small, which process raw audio and image features without dedicated modality-specific encoders.
Finds that early layers encode audio and visual inputs in ways that are largely invariant to cross-modal context.
Shows that independently encoding modalities through early layers matches the accuracy of jointly encoding them from the first layer.
Layer-wise probing indicates that the learned representations capture salient information similarly to several established encoder models.

papers.tldr: Encoder-free multimodal LLMs appear to develop early Transformer layers that function as implicit, largely modality-independent audio and vision encoders.

papers.abstract: This paper studies dynamic model routing under uncertainty in multimodal settings, where a system must select and potentially compose multiple models to answer a query. Standard reinforcement learning approaches for routing often suffer from premature convergence to suboptimal models due to noisy rewards and insufficient exploration. We propose a unified vision-language framework (VL-Scout) for efficient multimodal and multi-step reasoning with turn-based reinforcement fusion. First, VL-Scout combines Bayesian priors, policy gradient optimization, and sequential decision-making to enable structured exploration and adaptive inference. A context-dependent Dirichlet belief model allows for epistemic uncertainty over model quality and is updated online based on observed rewards and context-specific evidence, enabling Thompson-style exploration while serving as a prior for regularization. Second, a routing policy is trained via a KL-regularized REINFORCE objective by maximizing a reward-weighted evidence lower bound, where the policy acts as an amortized posterior, and the Dirichlet belief serves as a prior. Third, we introduce a fusion policy trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) or Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which operates over intermediate model rationales and selects between two actions: CONTINUE or ANSWER, terminating with a generated output. We evaluate VL-Scout on four representative multi-modal benchmarks (MMMU, MMMU-Pro, OKVQA, and RealWorldQA), compared against 11 representative routing and policy optimization baselines. Our method provides consistent performance improvements while reducing premature policy collapse. These results highlight the importance of integrating uncertainty-aware priors with both amortized policy learning and sequential fusion for robust and efficient model selection in discrete action spaces
bullets: Targets dynamic selection and composition of models for uncertain multimodal queries.
Uses context-dependent Dirichlet beliefs, Bayesian/Thompson-style exploration, and KL-regularized REINFORCE for adaptive routing.
Adds a fusion policy trained with GRPO or RLVR to decide whether to CONTINUE reasoning or ANSWER.
Evaluated on MMMU, MMMU-Pro, OKVQA, and RealWorldQA against 11 baselines.
Reports consistent performance improvements and reduced premature policy collapse, without specifying numeric gains.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a vision-language routing and fusion framework for multimodal reasoning, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Alliance of Stochastic Routing and Reinforcement Fusion for Multi-Model Reasoning
papers.tldr: VL-Scout combines uncertainty-aware routing with reinforcement-based multi-model fusion to improve robust multimodal reasoning and reduce premature policy collapse.

papers.abstract: Humans perceive far more in a scene than what is explicitly depicted: a single glance captures past causes and future trajectories; a quick peek determines if a vehicle can fit between two parked cars; a few seconds of video reveals who holds authority in a room; and a fleeting clip highlights subtle abstract patterns like unwritten rules or hidden labels. This capacity reflects a form of humanity's sixth sense: an intuitive reasoning mechanism that recovers implicit information beyond raw sensory perception. Crucially, this rapid, zero-shot visual intuition underpins everyday navigation and social interaction, making it a vital capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) deployed alongside people. Existing visual benchmarks, however, target either deliberate expert-level analysis in academic and mathematical domains or low-level perception, leaving the intuitive reasoning that people perform largely untested. To bridge this gap, we introduce Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning. HSS spans diverse image and video inputs, organizes items under a structured taxonomy, and pairs each with human-written prompts probing the implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structure that people infer at a glance. Frontier MLLMs fall short of human performance: participants reach 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, reaches only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. Despite excelling in many complex tasks that require advanced perception and knowledge, current models still struggle significantly on these visual tasks that are intuitive for humans. We further explore agentic setup that apply dynamic visual manipulation to HSS, which narrows but does not close the gap. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and directs attention to a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has so far left behind.
bullets: Targets implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract information inferred at a glance.
Uses diverse visual inputs with a structured taxonomy and human-written prompts.
Humans achieve 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest reported model reaches 53.6%.
Agentic visual manipulation narrows the gap but does not eliminate it.
Highlights intuitive reasoning as an under-tested capability for multimodal models.

Figure 8: How an HSS task is built and reviewed, with the attrition at each stage. A task is authored in three steps, then faces three independent review rounds; each round may pass it on, return it to authoring for revision (after which it re-enters the pipeline from the start), or drop it outright. Counts are net survivors: a task returned for revision and later re-admitted is counted once, at the round it finally passes, so each dropped figure is the net loss at that round. Of 3,466 authored tasks, 522 survive all three rounds, a yield of 15.1%. The first gate is by far the steepest: it turns away 2,302 tasks, two in three of everything written, overwhelmingly because the answer was already depicted in the scene, or for want of unambiguous consensus on the ground truth (principles 1 and 3 of Section 2.3).

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) adapts frozen large multimodal models (LMMs) to new tasks from a few demonstrations (demos), but re-encodes them at every query, where each demo image adds up to hundreds of visual tokens. Demo-free methods remove this cost with a compact task state. However, they add it at locations searched per task or at every decoder layer, where task parameters grow with depth. Moreover, inserted tokens or keys cannot change how the original prompt divides its attention within a layer. To address these issues, we propose Structured Task Adaptation via Embeddings (STAVE), which replaces demos with two task-specific vectors added to existing input embeddings. Specifically, a readout vector updates the answer-producing tokens and a context vector updates the other structural token groups. Both are trained with answer labels on prompts with and without demos. We justify these design choices theoretically using a first-order analysis of the loss and a margin bound. Extensive experiments on six LMMs and five large language models show that STAVE matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multimodal tasks with far fewer task parameters and surpasses 15-shot ICL and prior task vectors on 18 text tasks, all at zero-shot inference cost.
bullets: Addresses ICL’s costly repeated demo encoding and the parameter growth of prior demo-free adaptation methods.
Adds a readout vector to answer-producing tokens and a context vector to other structural token groups.
Trains both vectors using answer labels on prompts with and without demonstrations.
Supported by a first-order loss analysis and a margin bound.
Experiments across six LMMs, five LLMs, multimodal tasks, and 18 text tasks show performance matching or exceeding prior methods, including 15-shot ICL, without demo-time inference cost.

papers.abstract: The traditional Batak Ulos weaving industry faces growing challenges in producing diverse, innovative motifs due to limitations in conventional, manually driven design methods. This study proposes a multimodal generative framework integrating a fine-tuned Latent Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion XL v1.0 via LoRA) with a Multimodal Large Language Model (LLaMA 1.5-7B) to enable controllable, culturally faithful Ulos motif generation. Four complementary conditioning mechanisms: text, image, representation, and semantic map (via ControlNet) jointly guide the generation process, each governing a distinct aspect from semantic intent to spatial layout. A five level ablation study across three scenarios (shape transformation, colour variation, and high-complexity input) shows that conditioning effectiveness is not proportional to the number of mechanisms combined: Text + Image + Semantic Map achieved the best FID (270) and CLIP Score (0.65 - 0.70) but the weakest SSIM (0.65), while Text + Image + Representation offered the best overall balance, with stable SSIM (0.84) and competitive FID (280). Combining all four mechanisms yielded the weakest FID (330), indicating conflicting optimization signals. Qualitative evaluation by nine weavers and thirty public participants confirmed statistically significant positive acceptance (Wilcoxon, p=0.007 and p<0.001, respectively). A web-based prototype supporting text-to-image and image-to-image generation was also developed, offering a practical digital design tool for cultural heritage preservation.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of manual Ulos motif design and supports cultural heritage preservation.
Combines LoRA fine-tuned Stable Diffusion XL with LLaMA-based multimodal conditioning.
Uses text, image, representation, and ControlNet semantic-map guidance for semantic and spatial control.
Text + Image + Semantic Map achieved the best FID and CLIP scores, while Text + Image + Representation provided the best overall balance with stronger SSIM.
Weavers and public participants showed significant positive acceptance, and a web prototype supports text-to-image and image-to-image generation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.
authors: Shiao Xie, Siyu Chen, Jianwei Lv, Xiandong Li, Yujin Wang
bullets: RL with verifiable rewards provides task-level supervision but limited guidance for localizing visual-reasoning errors.
Privileged on-policy self-distillation adds token-level corrections, but these can be contaminated by linguistic priors, response style, or privileged-view effects.
Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG) validates corrections by comparing teacher outputs with evidence-present and evidence-degraded views.
VAG uses verifier-derived advantages as anchors and admits only directionally visually supported corrections.
Across six visual reasoning benchmarks, VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD, achieving new state-of-the-art average performance.

papers.abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.
authors: Wenhao Zhang, Zhongliang Zhou, Yi Ping, Zirui Wang, Sheng Li
bullets: Adding a frozen embedding of a stage-redacted report improves survival prediction across 1,633 TCGA patients; restoring the stage statement adds no benefit.
With visual features and pooling fixed, zero-shot prompts perform no better than supervised linear probes for lung and renal cancer subtyping.
SlideChat answers 74.82% of VQA items with the slide versus 74.41% without it, indicating weak visual grounding; its language-only backbone reaches 43.52%.
Paraphrasing preserves accuracy but changes 8–23% of answers, revealing sensitivity to wording.
The authors recommend minimum controlled evaluations to distinguish genuine language contributions from self-reported gains.

papers.abstract: Recent embodied systems increasingly build on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for their pretrained understanding and reasoning capabilities, but their perception of the physical world remains largely limited to basic modalities such as vision and audio. However, broadening MLLMs to more diverse sensory modalities from the physical environment is challenging: their representations are often weakly connected to the MLLM and vary substantially in structure and statistics, while their interpretation still requires shared high-level understanding and reasoning. We therefore propose Unisense, a unified embodied MLLM framework that supports diverse physical sensory modalities within a shared multimodal architecture. Unisense follows a two-stage training process: (i) aligning sensory representations with language to establish a language-accessible interface; and (ii) tuning modality-specific experts within the shared LLM to provide specialized processing for different sensory modalities. To support broad sensory learning, we curate Unisense-1M, a large-scale embodied sensory training corpus comprising 1M samples across 8 sensory modalities. We further evaluate Unisense on 12 benchmarks spanning depth, point cloud, IMU, tactile, thermal, radar, motion, and smell understanding. Across these heterogeneous sensing tasks, Unisense achieves strong performance and outperforms both generalist and specialized models on most benchmarks, demonstrating the potential of pretrained MLLMs as unified models for embodied sensory understanding.
authors: Shiyun Xiong, Dongming Wu, Peiwen Sun, Bokang Yang, Jiaxu Wang, Xiaolou Sun, Mingxing Wen, Xiangyu Yue
bullets: Addresses the weak integration and structural diversity of non-visual, non-audio sensory representations in MLLMs.
Uses two-stage training: language-align sensory representations, then tune modality-specific experts within a shared LLM.
Introduces Unisense-1M, a corpus of 1M embodied sensory samples covering 8 modalities.
Evaluated across 12 benchmarks for depth, point cloud, IMU, tactile, thermal, radar, motion, and smell understanding.
Reports strong performance, outperforming generalist and specialized models on most benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Unified MLLM for diverse embodied sensory modalities; directly fits embodied sensory understanding and multimodal LLM foundation models.
papers.title: Beyond Omni: A Unified MLLM for Embodied Sensory Understanding
papers.tldr: Unisense extends MLLMs beyond vision and audio by unifying eight physical sensory modalities for embodied understanding and reasoning.

papers.abstract: Photo-based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated six models from two vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under-estimated intake for five of six models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before-only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal-level error by only 2.2 to 3.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near-zero intake bias only because they under-estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for five models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, three models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre-set 10% margin, but no model reached the pre-set 30% limits of agreement. Protein was under-estimated by every model, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model (4.2 points) and changed the others by less than 1 point. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.
bullets: Evaluated six LLMs on 802 controlled-feeding-trial meals with weighed intake using before-only, before/after subtraction, and joint-photo inputs.
After photos improved accuracy for five models, but reduced meal-level error by only 2.2–3.4 points beyond scaling before-only estimates by the average proportion eaten.
Subtraction often under-estimated intake because models still assigned substantial calories to nearly empty trays.
Low average bias sometimes reflected under-estimated served energy rather than accurate accounting of uneaten food; no model met the pre-set individual-level agreement limits.
All models under-estimated protein, especially in protein-dense meals; estimates should support rather than replace dietitian assessment.

papers.abstract: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) localizes the image region described by a natural language expression, underpinning applications such as autonomous navigation, human-robot interaction, and medical image analysis. Under weak supervision, REC is challenged by the visual-linguistic semantic gap and the difficulty of inferring region-text correspondences from coarse image-level signals alone. Moreover, no single visual encoder captures all complementary properties---semantic alignment, fine-grained texture, and boundary awareness---while naively fusing multiple pretrained encoders yields heterogeneous, hard-to-reconcile representations. We propose LaMER, a weakly supervised REC framework that dynamically aggregates four frozen expert encoders through a language-conditioned Cross-Modal Routing Fusion module, adapting expert selection to each referring expression without instance-level bounding-box supervision. A Cell-Text Matching Head with Negative Anchor Augmentation, trained with a multi-objective loss combining contrastive, reconstruction, alignment, and load-balancing terms, further stabilizes optimization. LaMER achieves 77.67\%, 62.81\%, and 69.49\% Acc@IoU\(\geq 0.5\) on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, surpassing DViN and WeakMCN by up to 16.49 and 14.49 points, with ablations validating each component.
authors: Yu Yu Chang, Tzu-Hsuan Weng, Youssef Mohamed Amin, Mohaned Ahmed Elsayed, Hung-Hsuan Chen, Min-Te Sun, Sherine Shawky
bullets: Addresses the visual-linguistic gap and difficulty of learning region-text correspondences from image-level supervision.
Uses language-conditioned Cross-Modal Routing Fusion to dynamically select and combine four frozen visual encoders.
Adds a Cell-Text Matching Head with Negative Anchor Augmentation and a multi-objective training loss.
Reports 77.67% on RefCOCO, 62.81% on RefCOCO+, and 69.49% on RefCOCOg at IoU ≥ 0.5.
Ablations support the contribution of the proposed components; evaluation is limited to the reported REC benchmarks and weak-supervision setting.

papers.abstract: Video-Language Models (VLMs) excel at visual recognition but struggle with causal reasoning. Current evaluations are flawed: multiple-choice QA allows shortcuts, and open-ended QA lacks robust automatic evaluation. We introduce Causal Chain Generation (CCG), a novel task where models have to generate the sequence of intermediate events connecting a cause and an effect. This structured setup demands genuine reasoning and enables reliable automatic scoring. We accompany this task with two complementary metrics: SODA-Embedding, which measures the semantic matching of a generated chain against a reference, and Causal-QA, which probes the chain's causal coherence by asking whether it contains the specific causal facts needed to reconstruct the narrative. We provide two test sets: SF20K-CC, a manually annotated diagnostic on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, a movie clip benchmark derived from audio descriptions. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with narrative causality understanding, frequently hallucinating or omitting key events. To address this, we fine-tune VLMs with GRPO using a composite reward that combines a format reward, SODA-Embedding, and Causal-QA accuracy, demonstrating substantial improvements over strong baselines.
authors: Ridouane Ghermi, Vicky Kalogeiton, Ivan Laptev
bullets: Existing multiple-choice and open-ended evaluations can enable shortcuts or lack reliable automatic scoring for causal reasoning.
Causal Chain Generation (CCG) requires models to produce intermediate events connecting a video’s cause and effect.
SODA-Embedding evaluates semantic similarity to reference chains, while Causal-QA tests whether generated chains contain essential causal facts.
Two benchmarks are presented: SF20K-CC, based on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, derived from movie audio descriptions.
State-of-the-art VLMs often hallucinate or omit key events; GRPO fine-tuning with a composite reward substantially improves performance over strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.
bullets: Targets the high cost of processing dense, long-form audio token sequences in Large Audio Language Models.
Scores tokens conditioned on the user’s question rather than relying on attention, similarity, or temporal-sampling heuristics.
Distills token rankings from a frozen LALM’s answer-gradient saliency and uses downstream answer supervision.
At 10% token retention, achieves the best or tied-best performance on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks.
Evaluated across speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification, among other tasks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has improved video reasoning in multimodal large language models. However, standard video GRPO varies only linguistic trajectories while conditioning every rollout in a group on the same sampled frames, which can produce homogeneous rewards and weaken group-relative learning when the shared visual evidence is insufficient or distracting. We propose \textbf{FrameGRPO}, a simple and effective reinforcement-learning framework that requires neither auxiliary networks nor changes to the model architecture. Specifically, FrameGRPO combines two lightweight components: (1) \textbf{Multi-Frame Rollouts}, which use only uniform temporal subsampling of a single maximal-frame decode to construct aligned views that diversify visual evidence and reasoning trajectories; and (2) \textbf{Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit}, which selectively reinforces a correct lower-ratio trajectory when all rollouts in a fixed full-ratio reference subset fail, without imposing an unconditional preference for fewer frames. Extensive experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate robust overall improvements over standard GRPO, highlighting temporal-view diversification as an effective mechanism for exploration and credit assignment in video MLLMs.
authors: Jiaxuan Sun, Biao Wang, Shuai Li
bullets: Standard video GRPO gives every rollout the same frames, which can cause homogeneous rewards and weak group-relative learning.
Multi-Frame Rollouts create aligned, temporally subsampled views from one maximal-frame decode to diversify visual evidence without architectural changes.
Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit rewards a correct lower-frame-ratio trajectory only when all full-ratio reference rollouts fail.
Experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks show robust improvements over standard GRPO.
The method uses no auxiliary networks or model-architecture modifications.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FrameGRPO. Given a video–question pair, we assign the full-ratio input to a fixed subset of rollout slots and independently sample ρi ∼ U [0, 1] for the remaining slots to construct temporally aligned views Vρi . A shared policy generates {oi}Gi=1, and a verifier assigns rewards {ri}Gi=1. The outcomes of the fixed full-ratio subset jointly determine the gate for Temporal Efficiency Credit, which produces the modified advantages {Ãi}Gi=1. Policy optimization is conditioned only on the full-ratio input.

Figure 3: Complementarity across frame sampling ratios. Left: the lower-ratio 16-frame view captures the relevant condiment-spreading action, whereas the full-ratio 32-frame view is distracted by a subsequent event. Right: the higher-ratio view preserves the evidence required to associate the girl’s motion with the kite, whereas the lower-ratio view misses this critical evidence.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) for complex tasks, yet often overthink easy inputs, increasing token cost and latency, and sometimes degrading accuracy. Existing methods optimize reasoning length during training or impose external control at inference, but leave the underlying reasoning mechanism a black box. We find that fast and slow thinking exhibit distinct expert-routing patterns: holding the input fixed and varying only the prompted reasoning tempo produces stable routing shifts. Suppressing slow-thinking experts shortens the reasoning chain, whereas suppressing fast-thinking experts lengthens it, providing causal evidence that these experts influence reasoning depth. Based on this finding, we propose TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework. It identifies fast- and slow-thinking experts via tempo-contrastive routing analysis and redistributes routing weights within the original top-k set according to sample difficulty. It amplifies fast-thinking experts and suppresses slow-thinking experts on easy inputs and reverses this adjustment on hard ones, enabling difficulty-adaptive control over reasoning depth. We evaluate TempoMoE on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE consistently improves accuracy while reducing output tokens, with accuracy gains of up to 2.6 points and token reductions of up to 35.4%.
authors: Xiyue Zhang, Keru Zhou, Ziyi Wang, Bing Hu, Li Wang
bullets: Identifies distinct expert-routing patterns associated with fast versus slow reasoning and shows they causally affect chain-of-thought depth.
Uses a training-free, two-stage tempo-contrastive analysis to identify these experts.
Redistributes routing weights within the original top-k experts based on input difficulty: favoring fast experts for easy inputs and slow experts for hard ones.
Evaluated on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks, improving accuracy by up to 2.6 points and reducing output tokens by up to 35.4%.
Scope: controls reasoning depth through expert routing without changing model training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TempoMoE. (A) Fast-slow experts are identified offline by contrasting routing patterns under paired prompts. (B) Prefill routing entropy determines fast-slow gates that reweight the original top-k experts during decoding, preserving the selected expert set, total routing mass, and all model parameters.
Figure 3: Visual localization case with Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking-2506. TempoMoE gives the same correct answer with 35 reasoning tokens instead of 113 (69% fewer).
Figure 1: Average accuracy and output tokens over six benchmarks. Tokens are relative to Vanilla; bottom values show maximum gains.

Table 2: Main results comparing accuracy and output token usage across three multimodal MoE reasoning models and six benchmarks. Acc denotes answer accuracy (%), and Tok denotes the average number of tokens generated per sample, including all tokens in the reasoning process and the final answer.
Table 3: Ablation results on Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking2506, aggregated across six benchmarks. Easy and Hard use the difficulty split defined in Section 5.1.

Table 1: Identified fast/slow experts and held-out validation. F/S denote fast/slow experts; each pair denotes (layer, expert); ∆M is averaged over the two experts; Stab./Cons. are percentages; ∆Tok is the mean token change after joint masking.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free expert routing steering for efficient multimodal reasoning; reduces token cost and latency in MLLMs.
papers.title: TempoMoE: Identifying and Steering Fast-Slow Thinking Experts for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: TempoMoE adaptively steers fast- and slow-thinking experts to reduce unnecessary multimodal reasoning while improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: We set out to reproduce a recent hallucination-mitigation result on the POPE benchmark. The LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline we measured, 82.21 F1 on the adversarial split, sat 1.21 to 8.67 points above the adversarial baselines we planned to compare against (81.00, 79.30, and 73.54). We looked at the evaluation code and found a readout choice that moves F1 on its own. A two-token logit readout decides yes versus no by comparing two vocabulary IDs, 3582 ("yes") and 1217 ("no"). Across 9,000 greedy-decode questions spanning all three splits, neither ID is generated even once. The model emits " Yes" (token 3869) and " No" (token 1939), because SentencePiece prepends a space byte after the prompt suffix "ASSISTANT:". Read with an eight-token lookup that covers the space-prefixed surface forms, LLaVA-1.5-7B scores F1 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on the adversarial, popular, and random splits. That 6.13-point adversarial shift exceeds the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed. None of them states its readout, and our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, so we cannot say how much of any reported gain a matched evaluation would keep. That comparison stays unresolved until readout and precision are matched. On the fixed baseline we run nine inference-time corrections of our own (none beat it) and dissect why the adversarial split resists logit-level intervention. In a 3,000-question probe, wrong predictions draw more image attention than correct ones (Cohen's $d=-0.46$, $p=1.4\times10^{-24}$), the opposite of what grounding-based corrections assume. A four-readout audit across four further VLMs from three tokenizer families confirms the confound is protocol-level, not model-specific: porting the LLaVA-1.5 IDs verbatim drops F1 to 0.00 on the two disjoint-vocabulary models, whereas a tokenizer-derived readout holds between 0.80 and 0.92.
bullets: A two-token readout using unspaced “yes”/“no” IDs never matches LLaVA-1.5-7B’s generated space-prefixed tokens, distorting evaluation.
A tokenizer-derived eight-token readout yields LLaVA-1.5-7B F1 scores of 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on adversarial, popular, and random splits.
The adversarial readout shift is larger than gains reported by five of six surveyed papers, but comparisons remain unresolved because precision and readout settings differ.
Across four additional VLMs, copying LLaVA’s IDs causes F1 to fall to 0.00 for two models, while tokenizer-specific readouts produce 0.80–0.92.
Nine tested inference-time corrections did not improve the fixed baseline; attention analysis also challenges assumptions behind grounding-based interventions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Decision path at the POPE answer position for LLaVA-1.5-7B. The model always emits a space-prefixed surface form (‘ Yes’ or ‘ No’). The two-token check inspects two IDs the model never produces in this context, so every comparison is between two candidates the decoder excluded. On the adversarial split that comparison reads 924 of the model’s 1,644 ‘ No’ answers (56%) as yes, pushing the yes-rate to 0.760 on a 50% positive split.

Figure 3: Running yes-rate over the 3,000-question POPE adversarial stream. The eight-token protocol (blue) stabilises near the ground-truth yes-rate (dashed). The two-token protocol (red) stabilises around 0.760 because it reads 924 of the model’s 1,644 ‘ No’ emissions (56%) as yes.

Figure 2: Confusion matrices for POPE adversarial (3,000 questions) under each protocol. Under two-token evaluation, 660 of the 1,318 true-No predictions migrate to the FP cell, leaving precision at 0.6307. Under eight-token evaluation only 182 stay there, and precision is 0.8658. The model’s behaviour is identical across both matrices; only the readout changes.

Figure 7: Nine inference-time corrections on POPE adversarial, two views. (a) F1 against the corrected baseline at 0.8221. (b) The same methods on the precision-recall plane with F1 iso-curves. Every yes-suppression variant moves north and west of the baseline; no path crosses the F1=0.8221 iso-curve.

Figure 10: Yes/no surface forms map to different token IDs under each model. Blue rows are the forms the model actually generates first after ASSISTANT:; grey rows are valid single-token IDs that never appear; orange multi-token rows are space-prefixed forms the Mistral tokenizer splits into two tokens, so they cannot enter a first-token comparison.

Figure 4: Running yes-rate across all three POPE splits under both protocols. The two-token protocol (left) holds a yes-bias on every split, settling at 0.760, 0.707 and 0.644 on adversarial, popular and random; the eight-token protocol (right) tracks the underlying ground-truth mix.

Figure 6: Eight POPE adversarial samples from our run (question IDs 1, 7, 26, 72 on top; 14, 20, 35, 39 on the bottom), two per confusion-matrix outcome under eight-token evaluation. Blue borders mark predictions that match the label; red borders mark errors. The split queries objects that co-occur with present ones, which is what makes the FP and FN cases hard to fix with a generic visual-uncertainty signal.

Figure 9: Absolute logit gap |ℓyes − ℓno| at the answer position on the 3,000-question adversarial run. Left: per-category mean with one-standard-deviation error bars (TP n=1173, TN n=1317, FP n=183, FN n=327; means 2.07, 1.48, 0.70, 0.96). Right: kernel-density estimates. The order TP > TN > FN > FP at the mean separates confidence from correctness, which is why uncertainty-keyed corrections trade TPs for FNs at about the same rate as FPs for TNs.

Figure 5: First-token frequency at the answer position for all eight yes/no surface forms across the three POPE splits (log scale on y). The four right-side forms, including yes (3582) and no (1217), receive zero first-token mass in any split. The two-token protocol reads only 3582 and 1217.

Figure 8: Distribution of mean attention from the final text token to image positions, layers 14–20, on the 3,000-question adversarial run. Blue bars are correct (n=2490); red bars are wrong (n=510). Higher image attention associates with wrong predictions, so suppressing yes-logits when attention is low removes signal from the wrong side of the distribution.

papers.selection_reason: Systematic audit of VLM hallucination evaluation (POPE) revealing tokenization confounds. Directly relevant to Multimodal Large Language Models.
papers.title: Token-Set Choice Confounds POPE: A Systematic Audit of Yes/No Extraction in VLM Hallucination Evaluation
papers.tldr: POPE hallucination scores can be substantially confounded by using the wrong tokenizer-specific yes/no token IDs, making readout protocol matching essential.

papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed paradigm for Internet of Things (IoT) edge networks. However, deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) over wireless edge networks presents distinct challenges: large model parameters increase uplink transmission latency over bandwidth-constrained fading channels, and non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data exacerbates client drift. Existing feature alignment solutions often introduce auxiliary computations that consume time slots allocated for wireless parameter transmission, increasing the likelihood of straggler dropouts under system delay constraints. To address these issues, we propose DPGR-GCAM, a communication-efficient federated domain generalization framework. By employing a dual-parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) architecture, we design a channel-aware tiered transmission mechanism that adaptively truncates payloads to maximize node survival rates under fading conditions. To mitigate client drift, we introduce the Gradient-Conflict Aware Modulation (GCAM) mechanism. GCAM operates within the low-dimensional feature manifold to dynamically resolve multi-objective optimization conflicts with minimal edge computation latency, thereby reducing computation-induced network outages. Experiments demonstrate that DPGR-GCAM improves cross-domain generalization and sustains convergence under network fading scenarios with a 10\% client participation rate.
authors: Yuankun Xia, Hui Wang, Ling Yuan, Ziyu Hong, Di Yin, Yufeng Zhou
bullets: Targets high uplink latency, fading-induced dropouts, and client drift from Non-IID edge data.
Uses dual parameter-efficient fine-tuning and channel-aware tiered transmission to adaptively truncate payloads.
Introduces Gradient-Conflict Aware Modulation to resolve optimization conflicts in a low-dimensional feature space with low computation overhead.
Experiments show improved cross-domain generalization and sustained convergence under fading with 10% client participation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The overall workflow of the proposed DPGR-GCAM framework for federated domain generalization over wireless edge networks. The system comprises three stages: (1) Global broadcast of lightweight tunable parameters and class prototypes; (2) Local training, where the GCAM mechanism dynamically resolves feature-level optimization conflicts to regulate the visual adapter update; and (3) Channel-aware aggregation, which adaptively truncates the uplink payload based on real-time Shannon capacity to maximize node survival rates under fading channels.
Fig. 2: Robustness evaluation under intermittent connectivity on different datasets. (a) Moderate-scale Office-Caltech10. (b) Large-scale DomainNet.

TABLE II: Communication and Computation Overhead on Edge Nodes

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a communication-efficient federated learning framework for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to address domain generalization and client drift.
papers.title: Communication-Efficient Federated Domain Generalization in Edge Networks via Dynamic Prototype Regulation
papers.tldr: DPGR-GCAM enables communication-efficient federated domain generalization for VLMs in fading edge networks by adapting transmissions and reducing client drift with lightweight feature modulation.

papers.abstract: Negation-aware image generation remains challenging for text-to-image diffusion models, which often struggle with negation due to implicit linguistic biases that are deeply entangled within text representations. As a result, bias-aligned semantics frequently dominate over intended negative constraints. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple training-free method of Decompose and Recompose text embedding (Dero), which constructs a semantic-preserving subspace and a bias subspace using auxiliary prompts and performs semantic disentanglement based on bidirectional SVD. By decomposing entangled representations and selectively recomposing disentangled semantic components, Dero realigns text representations toward intended negation semantics while restoring residual stylistic features to preserve semantic fidelity and image quality. As a model-agnostic inference-time framework operating solely on text representations, Dero can be seamlessly applied to diverse diffusion architectures, including both U-Net and DiT based models. Extensive experiments on both object- and concept-level negation demonstrate consistent improvements in negation-aware image generation, achieving stronger text-image alignment, better semantic fidelity, and higher human preference scores.
authors: Sooyeon Park, Hemraj Singh, Kyunghyun Min, Youngjae Yu, Sung-Bae Cho
bullets: Negation is difficult for text-to-image diffusion models because implicit biases in text representations can override negative constraints.
Dero uses auxiliary prompts to construct semantic-preserving and bias subspaces, then disentangles them with bidirectional SVD.
It selectively recomposes semantic components while restoring stylistic features to maintain image quality and fidelity.
The inference-time method operates only on text representations and supports both U-Net- and DiT-based diffusion models.
Experiments on object- and concept-level negation show improved text-image alignment, semantic fidelity, and human preference.

papers.abstract: Extended reasoning has substantially improved multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on tasks requiring compositional and relational inference. However, multimodal grounding imposes a distinct requirement: reasoning must ultimately converge on a target-specific compact representation that supports precise localization. As reasoning trajectories grow longer, they often expand into broad scene narratives and peripheral relational details, which can dilute grounded perceptual evidence and lead to ambiguous or incorrect predictions. Motivated by the information bottleneck principle, we propose Think-Compress-Answer (TCA), a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes multimodal grounding into three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation conditioned on the compressed context. TCA is optimized through a multi-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with progressive rewards that establish the structured output protocol, minimize reasoning-specific information while preserving target-relevant content, and directly improve localization accuracy. This staged design enables MLLMs to retain the benefits of extended reasoning while distilling it into the minimal context required for grounding. Experiments across six multimodal grounding benchmarks show that TCA attains substantial zero-shot performance gains, demonstrating the effectiveness of reasoning compression.
authors: Jinbae Seo, Hyeongjun Kwon, Jiyoung Lee, Hyunsung Jang, Namkoo Ha, Jungin Park, Kwanghoon Sohn
bullets: Addresses the problem that lengthy reasoning can dilute relevant visual evidence with broad scene descriptions and peripheral details.
Uses three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation from the compressed context.
Trains the framework with multi-stage GRPO and progressive rewards for structured outputs, information reduction, relevance preservation, and localization accuracy.
Evaluated on six multimodal grounding benchmarks, where it achieves substantial zero-shot performance gains.
Scope: focuses on retaining useful extended reasoning while distilling it for precise grounding.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Think-Compress-Answer. The model generates N grouped responses [T, c,a] per input. Stage 1 establishes the required output protocol, Stage 2 encourages reasoning compression, Stage 3 uses a judge MLLM to promote compression fidelity and target relevance, and Stage 4 improves grounding accuracy. The stage-specific rewards are converted into group-relative advantages to progressively update the model.

(d) Our Think-Compress-Answer distills reasoning into a concise, faithful cue, yielding accurate grounding. papers.abstract: Audio LLMs deployed in settings such as crisis hotlines and customer support are only useful beyond speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues rather than the transcript alone. We test whether they prioritise transcript content over paralinguistic cues (emotion, speaker identity, sarcasm) and trace the mechanism when they do. Across six audio LLMs under LISTEN-style conflict conditions, the mean text-dominance rate on mismatched text+audio items is 0.78 (0.86 excluding sarcasm). In the most text-dominant screened model, probing shows speaker identity remains linearly decodable at ceiling at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Back-patching, reported to repair lexical text dominance, has no measurable effect here; but it also fails on its own source task in our replication (n=300), so we treat its null as uninformative rather than as evidence of non-transfer. Attention knockout partially restores audio-grounded output by blocking the claim from propagating through intermediate tokens during open-ended generation, whereas blocking the answer position's direct connection to the conflicting claim has no effect. The claim's influence therefore travels through an intermediate relay rather than a single severable edge. The effect appears only in free-form generation and not in closed-set multiple choice, suggesting that benchmarks relying on that format may be systematically blind to interventions of this kind. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp.
authors: Ankur Banerjee, Vishnu Guntakala, Danity Pike, Advay Roongta, Kevin Yang, Ruizhe Li
bullets: Across six models, text dominated mismatched text–audio inputs in most cases, especially when sarcasm was involved.
Speaker identity remained decodable at the language-model input, indicating that acoustic information was perceived but suppressed downstream.
Attention knockout partially restored audio-grounded outputs by disrupting an intermediate relay during open-ended generation.
Back-patching showed no measurable repair, but its null result was inconclusive because replication failed on its original task.
The effect was absent in multiple-choice evaluation, suggesting closed-set benchmarks can miss this failure mode and related interventions.

papers.abstract: Video Question Grounding (VideoQG) requires both accurate question answering and precise temporal localization. Existing supervised methods rely on costly temporal annotations, while existing zero-shot approaches are primarily designed for Video Question Answering (VQA) and are not optimized for temporal grounding. We propose DiffGround, an action-driven zero-shot framework built upon frozen Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Our framework first predicts an answer-relevant action cue that transforms the input question into an explicit semantic target for grounding. Action Cue converts a reasoningoriented question into an action-centric retrieval query. Guided by the action cue, a Vision-Language Model (VLM) efficiently selects informative keyframes for reasoning. Finally, we introduce Semantic Diff Refinement, a training-free temporal refinement method that exploits semantic differences between neighboring SigLIP2 embeddings to recover complete action segments from sparse predictions. Extensive experiments on NExT-GQA and STAR show that DiffGround consistently outperforms existing zero-shot and supervised methods, establishing a new state of the art for Video Question Grounding.
authors: Cheng-Han Lee, Amir Salimi, Hsiang-Wei Huang, Che-Chun Su, Min Sun, Cheng-Hao Kuo
bullets: Targets Video Question Grounding without costly temporal annotations.
Uses frozen multimodal models to predict answer-relevant action cues and select informative keyframes.
Applies training-free Semantic Diff Refinement to recover complete action segments from neighboring SigLIP2 embeddings.
Evaluated on NExT-GQA and STAR, where it outperforms existing zero-shot and supervised methods.
Scope: relies on frozen MLLMs/VLMs and is designed for action-centric temporal grounding.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed DiffGround framework. Given a video and a question, DiffGround first performs offline, question-agnostic action segment preprocessing to partition the video into semantically coherent action segments. A frozen MLLM then predicts an action cue describing the target action with a single MLLM call. Guided by the question and predicted action cue, a Vision-Language Model (VLM) ranks video frames to select the most informative keyframes for Video Question Answering (VQA). Finally, Semantic Diff Refinement expands the initial grounding prediction by leveraging SigLIP2 semantic differences to align temporal boundaries with the complete action segment, producing more accurate Video Question Grounding (VideoQG) results.

Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed DiffGround framework. DiffGround consists of three stages. First, a frozen MLLM predicts an Action Cue from the input question and uniformly sampled video frames, converting a reasoning-oriented question into an action-centric retrieval query. Second, a frozen VLM (SigLIP2) jointly matches the question and Action Cue to retrieve the Top-K most informative keyframes. Meanwhile, an offline Semantic Diff Segmentation module partitions the video into semantically coherent action segments. Finally, the retrieved keyframes are used for Video Question Answering, and the predicted timestamps are refined by the precomputed semantic segments to recover complete temporal boundaries for Video Question Grounding.
Fig. 4: Prompt Template Design. The prompt for our final VQG prediction, which is adapted from TStar [18].

Fig. 3: Visualization of the proposed Semantic Diff segmentation. By measuring semantic transitions between neighboring clips, our offline preprocessing partitions the video into semantically coherent action segments. Besides separating distinct scenes (e.g., piano playing versus woman and child), it further identifies fine-grained action boundaries, isolating the brief “touch child” interaction (38.8–40.9 s) from surrounding activities. During online inference, Semantic Diff Refinement aligns the retrieved keyframe with the corresponding action segment, producing accurate temporal grounding.
Fig. 5: Prompt Template Design for Object Cue. The prompt for generating object cues, which is adapted from TStar [18].

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are asked to report what they see: to count objects, box them, parse a screen or pick a click target (GUI grounding). We argue that reporting is part of the visual task, not merely its formatting. In a dense scene with 173 shapes, GPT-6.1 lists 173 records that match every shape, yet the counts it states in the same response sum to 188. From Seeing to Reporting (FSR) is a theory of visual reporting and a set of inference-time procedures that improve the reports of frozen VLMs. It models reporting as a chain from responses to decoded records, constructed sets and task answers, linked by task-compatible matching. The chain gives exact relations for deleting records, averaging their coordinates and switching readouts, and it splits the error of one answer chosen among several calls into missing candidates, lost representatives and wrong choices. These relations guide procedures for counting, detection, document layout, screen parsing and GUI grounding that use the task specification and a shipped configuration, without requiring labels from the target task. On 50 dense synthetic scenes, a one-call reporting-and-decoding protocol cuts per-type count error by 85.2% for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5. On 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items, a GUI-grounding tier that combines three models lowers the miss rate from 13.67% for GPT-6.1's two-stage zoom to 9.33%, against 12.67% for three such zooms combined by a cluster vote at about the same cost. A plain vote over the same three models misses 12.33%: the other models supply the candidates, and selecting among them turns those candidates into fewer misses. We release the protocols, the stored responses and the analysis code.
authors: Junzhe Shi, Yuan Gan, Shida Jiang
bullets: Frames reporting as a chain from model responses to decoded records, sets, and final task answers.
Uses task-compatible matching to identify missing candidates, lost representatives, and wrong selections.
Requires no target-task labels, relying on the task specification and a shipped configuration.
Reduces per-type count error by 85.2% for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 on 50 dense synthetic scenes.
On 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items, a three-model grounding tier lowers miss rate to 9.33%, outperforming the reported comparison protocols at similar cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2: FSR for visual reporting with vision-language models. Top lane: the reporting chain of the default pipeline (Algorithm 1), from the image, task and budget to the answer, with the repair at each step (blue cards) and the result that governs it. Bottom lane: the same four steps for GUI grounding with three models (Algorithm 2), and where each kind of miss arises: F , no correct candidate after the calls; L, a correct candidate but no correct representative after construction; W , a correct representative that readout does not choose. The miss rate is F + L+W (Proposition 8). Calls determine coverage, what the responses contain; decoding, construction and readout determine what is delivered from it. F , L and W locate a miss; an operation can change more than one of them. Judge: choosing between configurations, for which the shipped defaults need no target labels. Detect: errors flagged without labels; in GUI grounding the alarm triggers the comparison. Every item is scored, and an item with no point counts as a miss.

Figure 1: Three repairs that change what a model delivers. (a) One response of GPT-6.1 to a dense synthetic scene (image 28 of SCP-dense, our dense synthetic counting scenes; 173 shapes of five classes): the list count, the records of each class in the model’s list counted by code, matches the truth, while the stated count the model wrote in the same response sums to 188; each of the 173 records matches a different shape of the same class (Section 7.2). (b) For the instruction “only allow values from a list” in an Excel menu, a single click by Gemini 3.8 lands on “Time”; a second call on a zoomed crop (ReGround, Li et al., 2025b) lands inside the target “List” (green box). On 200 ScreenSpot-Pro items, two-stage zoom cuts Gemini 3.8’s miss rate by 65% (Section 7.5). (c) Miss rate against cost per item at list prices on 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items: GPT-6.1’s two-stage zoom, three such zooms with a cluster vote, a crop-first baseline in the style of GUI-Lens (Fu et al., 2026), a cluster vote over three models’ zoomed points, and FSR’s GUI-grounding tier (Algorithm 2), which selects among the same points with a scorer and a comparison; every item is in the denominator. Paired differences with intervals are in Section 7.7: the tier’s difference from the crop-first baseline has an interval that reaches 0, and its differences from the other flows exclude 0.

Figure 6: Risk-coverage of click alarms (260 items; point estimates). An alarm sets an item aside when the acted-on point and a second point for the same item are farther apart than δ of the longer image side; the system acts on the other items. Acceptance coverage is the share of items acted on, and the miss rate when acting the share of those items whose point is outside the target; lower and further right is better. Each curve traces δ ∈ {0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 8}%, and a smaller δ sets more items aside. Grey: the second point comes from a second call of the same model; blue: from the partner, the cheapest other model (Gemini 3.8 for GPT-6.1 and Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 for Gemini 3.8). papers.selection_reason: Inference-time procedures for reliable visual set generation in VLMs; relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial/GUI grounding.
papers.title: From Seeing to Reporting: A Theory of Reliable Visual Set Generation in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: FSR treats visual reporting as part of VLM reasoning and improves counting, detection, parsing, and GUI grounding through task-aware inference-time procedures for frozen models.

papers.abstract: Video large multimodal models have improved at identifying cross-frame visual evidence and conducting open-web retrieval, as reflected in recent video deep research (VDR) benchmarks. However, existing VDR benchmarks primarily evaluate tool-use trajectories and final responses without verifying whether a model actually uses the temporal video information or the retrieved web evidence. To fill this gap, we introduce \method{}, an evidence-grounded benchmark with three features. First, it combines human review with restricted-access probing across multiple models to exclude questions answerable from parametric knowledge or a single information source. Second, each question carries structured video-to-web evidence annotations that link the relevant video segments to their supporting web evidence. Third, its evaluation protocol separately scores video grounding, web evidence grounding, and final-answer correctness. Across eight multimodal agent systems, the best reaches 76.0\% answer accuracy, yet none recovers the complete required web evidence for more than 8\% of questions. Our benchmark is publicly available at \url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hh721/vdr_temp}.
authors: Xiyuan Liang, Yu Wang, Zuhao Yang, Ziting Wang, Duo Li, Sudong Wang, Zhongyu Yang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Targets a gap in existing VDR benchmarks, which assess trajectories and answers without verifying evidence use.
Filters questions through human review and restricted-access probing to require both video and web information.
Provides structured annotations linking relevant video segments to their supporting web evidence.
Separately evaluates video grounding, web-evidence grounding, and final-answer correctness.
Across eight multimodal agents, the best answer accuracy is 76.0%, while no system recovers complete web evidence for over 8% of questions.

papers.title: GroundedVDR: Grounding Video-to-Web Evidence Dependencies in Video Deep Research

papers.abstract: Vision-language (VL) models are typically built by fine-tuning a language model to attend to visual features in service of a Visual Question-Answering objective. We ask whether this alignment changes how language models represent text---especially on tasks where visualization would help, like geometry questions posed in words. We distinguish weak multimodality (the model can answer questions about an input image) from strong multimodality (the model's text representations themselves become vision-aligned, improving performance on text-only tasks with latent visual structure). To test for strong multimodality, we construct a task of shape-counting problems with paired equivalent text and image specifications. This task is trivial when the image is provided, but requires visualization when specified in text as line coordinates. We compare instruction-tuned Qwen-2.5 and Mistral models against their vision-aligned counterparts on the text variant of the task. We find that the multimodal models do no better in this setting, despite strong performance on the image version of the task. Probing experiments corroborate this: vision-aligned decoder embeddings carry no more visual structure than their text-only counterparts. Finally, we provide an optimization objective that distills in-context visual embeddings into text embeddings. This alignment induces gains on the text variant of the task without explicit task supervision, even on samples more complex than seen during alignment. This suggests that VQA-style alignment leaves available cross-modal transfer untapped.
authors: Shashwat Singh, He He, Tal Linzen
bullets: The paper distinguishes weak multimodality—answering questions about images—from strong multimodality, where text representations become vision-aligned.
On paired shape-counting tasks, multimodal models perform no better than text-only models when given coordinate-based text, despite performing well with images.
Probing shows that vision-aligned decoder embeddings contain no more visual structure than embeddings from text-only models.
A self-distillation objective aligns in-context visual and text embeddings without explicit task supervision.
This alignment improves text-based shape counting, including examples more complex than those used during alignment.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Given paired text-image data our alignment method trains the model to predict from text (code) the embeddings it would’ve had given the image. During alignment (left) we provide no task context or answer labels. During evaluation (right) the model performs the shape counting task.

Figure 3: Vision-alignment does not add more visual structure to the embeddings of the multimodal model, compared to the text-only model. While probes trained on the embeddings from both classes of models show above-chance accuracy, the performance for the two classes of models is very similar.

Figure 2: When the problem is provided in text, for all the settings tested—with and without in-context examples (ICL), and with and without chain of thought (CoT)—the performance of the multimodal models is similar to their text-only counterparts, and far below the image ceiling. This indicates that vision alignment did not transfer visualization capabilities to the text decoder. Error bars are based on the 95% confidence interval on accuracy estimates using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution.

Figure 4: The trends on learnt retrieval corroborate that the multimodal decoder does not have better visual representations of textual inputs than the text-only model. However, the VL embeddings closely track text embeddings.

papers.selection_reason: Examines vision-language models' cross-modal transfer and spatial/geometric reasoning, fitting multimodal LLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help
papers.tldr: VQA-style vision-language alignment does not make text representations visually grounded, but self-distilling visual embeddings into text representations improves reasoning over text with latent visual structure.

papers.abstract: The assessment of surgical skills in robotic surgery training has traditionally relied on subjective evaluations by human experts, creating bottlenecks in surgical education and limiting scalability. We present a novel foundation model that automatically analyzes robotic surgical videos to provide comprehensive skill assessment and gesture understanding. Combining a visual encoder with a transformer architecture, the model performs three key tasks simultaneously: 1) surgical task classification (knot tying, needle passing, suturing), 2) skill level assessment on a standardized scale, and 3) natural language generation of surgical gesture descriptions. The model processes video sequences from the da Vinci surgical robot and generates human-readable text descriptions of surgical actions, similar to how language models generate text from prompts, using a multi-task learning framework with adaptive uncertainty weighting to optimize performance across all objectives. Our transformer-based architecture incorporates positional encoding for temporal understanding and attention mechanisms for spatiotemporal feature integration. Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, the proposed framework demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in surgical task recognition and provides interpretable skill assessments that correlate with expert evaluations, with the model's ability to generate natural language descriptions of surgical gestures opening new possibilities for automated surgical education, real-time feedback systems, and objective skill assessment in surgical training and certification programs.
authors: Parham M. Kebria, Saeid Nahavandi, Mehrdad Saif, Fernando Bello
bullets: Addresses subjective, expert-dependent surgical skill assessment and its scalability limitations.
Combines a visual encoder with a transformer to model spatial and temporal information in da Vinci surgical videos.
Jointly performs task classification, standardized skill assessment, and gesture-description generation using adaptive uncertainty weighting.
Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, it reports state-of-the-art task recognition and skill assessments correlated with expert evaluations.
Its scope includes automated surgical education, real-time feedback, and objective training or certification support.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.
authors: Jaehong Myung, Seunghun Oh, Unsang Park
bullets: Full-video speech-vision decisions can fail despite useful evidence being available in nearby visual windows.
Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED) is a training-free diagnostic that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation.
TED uses ASR transcripts and utterance intervals to query audio-free windows for temporal forecasting, alignment, or cross-modal binding.
Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, temporal forecasting accuracy improves from 29.3–33.7% to 79.3–82.2% with TED.
Controls indicate that the observed temporal anchor—not merely query replacement or region availability—drives recovery.

papers.title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) fail at some tasks that are simple for humans---but why? We hypothesize that many such failures stem from VLMs' difficulties translating between vision and language representations, a misalignment the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts should disappear with scale. This paper is composed of two parts: in the first, we show that existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable. This misalignment is an inherent property of the data and hence expected to persist regardless of either scale or the alignment's complexity. In the second, we demonstrate how this misalignment both leads to a predictably induced generalization failure and correlates with existing failure modes, where more representationally aligned VLM backbones accordingly exhibit fewer failures. Overall, these results imply representations will not become aligned simply given sufficient scale, providing evidence against a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
authors: Yonatan Gideoni, Yoav Gelberg, Tim G. J. Rudner, Yarin Gal
bullets: Existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable.
Because the misalignment is inherent to the data, increasing model scale or alignment complexity is unlikely to eliminate it.
The misalignment induces predictable generalization failures and correlates with known VLM failure modes.
VLM backbones with better representational alignment exhibit fewer failures.
The findings challenge the strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

papers.abstract: The success of chain-of-thought (CoT) in complex reasoning can be attributed to a textual scaffolding effect: explicit intermediate results can be examined, reused, and composed to support subsequent reasoning, much as scaffolding supports a building under construction. However, mainstream multimodal LLMs lack an equivalent scaffold for visual distinctions that are difficult to express in concise verbal descriptions. We therefore ask: Can native visual representations become first-class citizens alongside language, providing a visual scaffold for reasoning? We define native multimodal reasoning as reasoning in which native visual representations and language jointly carry reusable intermediate states. As a concrete implementation, the visual scaffolding mechanism we proposed lets the MLLM autonomously initiate a retrieval action at any reasoning step. A lightweight retriever selects native visual features, which are then incorporated directly into the evolving CoT and remain available to subsequent steps. To evaluate this mechanism under controlled visual demands, we introduce NMR-Bench, comprising Burden Counting and Path Tracing. With 88M added parameters (approximately 2%) on Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking, our model achieves 66.43% and 72.50% accuracy, respectively, surpassing the evaluated GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro baselines. Controlled interventions show that changing selected visual content affects task accuracy and can redirect subsequent visual selection even when intervening text is held fixed. These findings show that native visual states can function as intermediate reasoning material and point toward reusable scaffolds for additional modalities.

With 88M added parameters, the model achieves 66.43% and 72.50% accuracy and surpasses the evaluated GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro baselines.
Interventions show that selected visual content influences accuracy and later visual selection, supporting native visual states as reasoning material.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models often exhibit hidden stratification, where high overall performance masks failures on subtle visual findings and overlapping clinical conditions. We trace this failure mode to modality imbalance during fine-tuning, where strong linguistic priors can suppress visually grounded learning and induce plausible but weakly grounded rationales. Existing data selection methods usually score image-text pairs as holistic units, without separating visually necessary samples from shortcut-solvable ones. To address this problem, we propose ViCoR, a counterfactual-residual-based data selection method for Med-VLM fine-tuning. ViCoR estimates visual necessity through image-dependent optimization residuals, calibrates the resulting scores with medical supervision compatibility, and constructs a diversity-aware fine-tuning subset. Across two backbones, four external generalization benchmarks, and one multi-disease robustness benchmark, ViCoR-selected 20\% subsets achieve the strongest average performance compared with full-data fine-tuning and selection baselines. Gradient-level analysis and perturbation audits further show that ViCoR enriches image-dependent training signals and strengthens image-level and evidence-region dependence. The code will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/ViCoR.
