papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) commonly suffer from hallucinations, which appear as fabricating non-existent objects or outputting incorrect attributes and spatial relationships in images. Previous works empirically indicate that CLIP-style vision encoders tend to focus on primary objects while ignoring image details, which is one of the causes of hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose plug-and-play fine-grained visual experts (PLANE) comprising two components: LoRA visual experts operating on CLIP for multi-aspect image encoding, and an instruction-aware gate network for adaptive image feature fusion. During training, we construct a fine-grained image-caption pairs dataset, where images are described from three aspects: objects, attributes, and relations between objects. Image-caption pairs from different aspects are used to train the three fine-grained LoRA experts respectively. Aiming at comprehensively evaluate our method's capabilities, we manually annotate a fine-grained hallucination evaluation benchmark for LVLMs which is GPT4-independent during evaluation phase (GIFT). We conduct experiments both on popular hallucination evaluation benchmarks and GIFT. The results show that our method effectively reduces hallucinations across models of different types and sizes while introducing minimal inference latency. Compared to advanced baselines, our model also demonstrates superior performance.

papers.abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a \emph{video reference gap} between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce \textbf{Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP)}, a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query-relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP-SFT-15k and TCoVP-RL-13k to learn this representation through supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: \url{https://victor-wjw.github.io/TCoVP/}
authors: Junwei Wen, Deshui Miao, Guangming Lu, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Xin Li, Wenjie Pei
bullets: Addresses the video reference gap between language-based reasoning and visual evidence across frames.

Trains the representation with supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) encode images into dense visual token sequences, creating substantial attention and KV-cache overhead. Existing visual token compression methods reduce this cost by pruning low-saliency tokens in shallow layers, but this practice couples temporary computational deactivation with irreversible information deletion. We show that this coupling breaks an intrinsic inference pattern in MLLMs. Through layer-wise attention analysis, we identify \textbf{Visual Backtracking}: visual pivots remain spatially stable, yet in middle layers they actively retrieve context from tokens that appeared unimportant earlier. Thus, early low-saliency tokens can be inactive for computation while still being useful for later reasoning. Motivated by this finding, we propose \textbf{ReTrace}, a backtracking-aware compression framework that introduces a dormant token state. ReTrace caches non-pivot tokens outside expensive layer-wise computation, restores them during the backtracking window, and prunes only after their information has been absorbed. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 demonstrate nearly 90\% reductions in FLOPs and KV cache, a 2.83$\times$ prefilling speedup, and strong performance retention across complex vision-language benchmarks.
authors: Guangzong Si, Dong Wang, Yifan Yu, Miao Liu, Panwang Pan, Wentao Zhu
bullets: Visual token compression can harm reasoning by permanently deleting tokens that appear unimportant in early layers.
Layer-wise analysis reveals visual backtracking: stable visual pivots later retrieve context from previously low-saliency tokens.
ReTrace adds a dormant token state, caching non-pivot tokens outside expensive computation and restoring them during a backtracking window.
Tokens are pruned only after their information has been absorbed, preserving more visual context for reasoning.
Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 report nearly 90% lower FLOPs and KV-cache usage, a 2.83× prefilling speedup, and strong benchmark performance retention.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Overall architecture of ReTrace. ReTrace follows a cache–inject–prune schedule. papers.abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

papers.abstract: Enabling humanoid robots to participate effectively in social interactions is important for their integration into human-centered environments. Existing methods, however, typically map pre-generated speech directly to continuous motion trajectories but have limited awareness of complex social environments and lack explicit high-level semantic action planning. We introduce SocialCoAct, a unified agent-centered framework for VLM-based egocentric social co-action. We formulate egocentric social co-action as an end-to-end agent task and develop SocialCoAct-Agent, which transforms egocentric observations and dialogue history into verbal responses and atomic action sequences, aligns each action with its corresponding utterance span, and executes the resulting behaviors in MuJoCo and on a physical humanoid robot. To evaluate the VLM capabilities required by this task, we construct SocialCoAct-Bench from continuous egocentric recordings of natural multi-party interactions. The benchmark comprises 423 human-verified multiple-choice questions across three subtasks: Long Episode Understanding (LEU), Speaker Intention Understanding (SIU), and Coordinated Action Planning (CAP). Across a diverse set of closed-source and open-weight VLMs, including general and egocentric models, the highest overall accuracy is 77.54%, while accuracy on the hard subset reaches only 46.51%. Extended reasoning improves Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B by 19.62 and 17.02 percentage points, respectively, but reduces inference throughput by 53.6$\times$ and 20.2$\times$. Visual-input ablations further show that the benefits of visual context vary across models. SocialCoAct provides a foundation for developing and evaluating VLM-based humanoid agents that coordinate context-aware speech and action in complex social interactions. The codebase and benchmark will be made publicly available upon publication.

papers.abstract: Best-of-N methods improve text-only LLM reasoning by sampling multiple trajectories before selecting an answer. For Vision-Language Models (VLMs), answer frequency and model confidence alone can be insufficient, as sampled generations also vary in their engagement with the visual input. We find that distributional confidence and visual attention are complementary indicators of rollout quality. Each is limited on its own, while trajectories that show strong signals in both are more likely to be correct. Motivated by this, we introduce VisConf, a rollout-quality score that multiplicatively combines visual engagement with candidate-calibrated Self-Certainty, penalizing rollouts that are weak in either signal. We incorporate Rank-Weighted Consensus (RWC), a tuning-free aggregation rule that converts within-question VisConf ranks into answer-level vote weights. Across three VLMs on MathVista, MMMU-Pro, and MMStar, VisConf with RWC consistently outperforms strong BoN baselines. Our analysis shows particularly large gains when correct trajectories are present but underrepresented in the candidate pool.
authors: Muhammad Usman, Muhammad Qasim Ayub, Usman Ahad, Muhammad Tahir
bullets: VLM rollout quality depends on complementary signals: attention to visual input and distributional confidence.
VisConf multiplicatively combines visual engagement with candidate-calibrated Self-Certainty, penalizing weakness in either signal.
Rank-Weighted Consensus converts within-question VisConf rankings into tuning-free answer vote weights.
Across three VLMs and three multimodal benchmarks, VisConf with RWC consistently outperforms strong Best-of-N baselines.
Gains are especially large when correct trajectories exist but are underrepresented among sampled candidates.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate strong performance on multiple-choice question answering (MCQA), yet their reliability under biased conditions remains underexplored. We investigate length bias, the systematic preference for longer answer options, through controlled benchmarks spanning fine-grained visual domains. LVLMs consistently favor longer options even when visually inconsistent, with accuracy dropping 2--38\% when correct answers are shorter and increasing 1--70\% when longer. This bias persists across model scales. Through layer-wise mechanistic analysis, we reveal that length bias emerges from late-layer suppression of visual evidence in favor of language-side length priors. Blurry-image experiments show that bias intensifies when visual evidence weakens, while abstention tests reveal that LVLMs struggle to refuse incorrect predictions. We propose and evaluate multiple inference-time mitigation strategies; while these provide partial improvements, none achieves deployable bias mitigation without relying on oracle information unavailable at inference time. These results underscore that inference-time interventions are insufficient, pointing to the need for architectural solutions and bias-aware training.
authors: Md. Atabuzzaman, Hani Alomari, Chris Thomas
bullets: Controlled benchmarks show LVLMs prefer longer answer options, even when those options conflict with visual evidence.
Accuracy changes substantially depending on whether the correct option is shorter or longer, and the bias persists across model scales.
Layer-wise analysis links the bias to late-layer suppression of visual evidence in favor of language-based length priors.
The bias becomes stronger with blurry images, while models also struggle to abstain from incorrect predictions.
Inference-time mitigation methods offer only partial improvements and require unavailable oracle information for reliable deployment.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our framework for investigating length bias in LVLMs. We create length-controlled MCQA variants to systematically expose length bias, conduct layer-wise analysis revealing late-layer suppression of visual evidence, perform diagnostic experiments using abstention and blurry images to localize bias sources, and evaluate mitigation strategies like ELED, caption-guided MCQA and Yes/No QA.

Figure 7: Example multiple-choice questions from the Dogs dataset illustrating four length-controlled variants: Equal Long, Equal Short, Shorter Correct, and Longer Correct. The correct answer (D: German Shepherd) remains constant while option lengths vary systematically to isolate the effect of textual length on model predictions.

Figure 4: Vision–language conflict resolution in late layers. Layer-wise probabilities for the short correct answer (green) versus average probability of each long distractor (red), both starting at unbiased baseline 0.25 (dotted line). (a) In length-biased errors (N=144, 72%), late layers (20–28, shaded) amplify long distractors to 0.31 while suppressing the correct answer to 0.10—each long option becomes 3.1× more likely than correct. (b) When predictions align with ground truth (visual wins) (N=56, 28%), the correct answer amplifies to 0.73 while each long distractor suppresses to 0.06 (8.0× preference ratio). Shaded regions: 95% confidence intervals. Despite stronger amplification capacity for correct answers (+0.48 vs +0.06), the model utilizes this in only 28% of cases.

Early layers show near-zero systematic preference for long options; mid layers exhibit a positive shift, indicating emergence of length bias in internal representations prior to decoding. Dashed line: stable inversion layer (L = 14), the first layer at which the mean ∆ℓ exceeds zero for three consecutive layers. Dotted line: median commitment layer (L = 24), beyond which the predicted answer remains unchanged.

Figure 2: Accuracy (%) of LVLMs across five datasets under different option-length conditions, with and without class names. The vertical line at "Equal Long" indicates baseline performance for each LVLM-dataset pair.

Dashed lines mark the median override layer under each condition. Clear images exhibit greater dispersion in probability trajectories due to heterogeneity in visual evidence strength across examples, while blurring homogenizes visual inputs and produces earlier, more uniform dominance of length bias. Figure 10: Prompt template used for caption-guided MCQA.

Late layers (20–28, shaded region) show statistically significant positive correlation (mean r = 0.063, p < 0.001), indicating that longer options query vision more than shorter options. Despite this increased visual grounding, long incorrect options are preferentially selected, demonstrating that length bias operates through override of visual evidence in the language decoder rather than insufficient visual information retrieval.

papers.abstract: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.
authors: unsu Kim, Naeun Kim, Dongyoon Han, Seungryul Baek
bullets: Targets ambiguous references to adjacent body parts, garments, and visually similar motions.
Uses per-avatar semantic and motion memories to connect language with persistent Gaussian regions and joint trajectories.
An MLLM selects regions by appearance, relation, or function, while composable operators identify matching motion intervals.
Selections are traceable and extensible through category choices and operator programs.
On three human-annotated benchmarks, it outperforms baselines in part, 3D, and 4D referring segmentation, with minutes of per-avatar setup.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HumanSkill-4D overview. (Offline) We build a semantic memory for each avatar, a motion memory for its driving pose sequence, and an operator registry shared across avatars. (Online) The frozen MLLM selects target categories from their names and descriptions, and their stored scores determine the spatial mask. For a 4D query, it also reads the registry’s text cards and composes operators into a motion program, and running the program on the joint trajectories gives the temporal mask. The two masks give the spatiotemporal selection. In this example, the program identifies intervals when both upper arms move outward, and StateAtEnd retains each movement interval whose last frame has both arms horizontal (orange band).

papers.abstract: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. In this work, we introduce UNICORNS, a benchmark for evaluating the reliability of 3D-LLM responses across four evidence conditions. UNICORNS contains 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans, covering eight challenge categories alongside answerable controls. A response passes only if it satisfies the required response behavior and contains no scene claim unsupported by the available evidence. Evaluation of six open-sourced 3D-LLMs reveals a pronounced performance gap: even the strongest zero-shot model achieves 61.22% accuracy on answerable controls, but only 40.94% across the eight challenge categories. To address this gap, we further propose HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method combining group-relative task rewards, leaf-conditioned obligation rewards, and supervised control replay. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HORN reaches $75.1 \pm 1.0\%$ across the challenge categories and $77.2 \pm 0.8\%$ overall, outperforming all baselines without degrading answerable-control accuracy. Our findings enable a systematic evaluation and improvement of evidence-grounded 3D reasoning for 3D-LLMs (code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/unicorns-6B38/).

papers.abstract: We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post-training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio-language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post-training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. Through a four-stage pipeline, LLT (1) builds multi-aspect dense audio descriptions spanning semantic, acoustic, and temporal information, (2) generates more challenging questions, (3) synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and (4) extends short reasoning traces into long ones via a thought-continuation strategy that elicits cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. Using LLT, we synthesize 1.6M reasoning traces and train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with a two-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). This improves accuracy on MMAU Test-mini (71.5 to 78.2), MMAR (56.7 to 63.7), and MMSU (60.6 to 66.0).

papers.abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.
authors: Savitha Sam Abraham, Marjan Alirezaie, Hossein Rahnama
bullets: Reframes T2I evaluation as constraint satisfaction over objects, attributes, and relations.
Tests nine constraint classes, including logical operators such as ∀, ∃, counting, and implication, across four T2I models.

Compositional generalization declines from 84% for single constraints to 20% for multiple constraints; unsatisfiable prompts are recognized correctly only 23% of the time by the best model.
On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.88–0.98 against human judgments.

papers.abstract: Generative AI is becoming an important medium for artistic creation, yet existing interactions often assume that creators can specify intentions in advance and accurately communicate them through text prompts. Artistic intentions, however, may be vague, latent, or recognizable only after seeing concrete visual possibilities. We propose a human-AI co-creation paradigm beyond explicit intent expression. By expanding model exploration, we expose artists to diverse visual possibilities, allowing them to identify previously unarticulated preferences through observation, comparison, and selection. We then integrate artists' curatorial judgments into reinforcement learning, assigning different learning strengths based on preferences over generation trajectories, so recognized directions are more strongly reinforced and the model gradually adapts to individual aesthetics. This creates a continuous "explore-identify-shape-re-explore" loop in which artistic intent is progressively discovered, externalized, and shaped. Through three user studies, we examine latent-preference discovery, personalized preference alignment, and the externalization of vague, difficult-to-express creative intentions.

papers.abstract: Native multimodal large language models (native MLLMs) jointly encode visual and linguistic sequences within a unified autoregressive Transformer, emerging as a promising paradigm for multimodal understanding. Unlike conventional ViT-based MLLMs relying on external vision encoders, ViT-free native MLLMs tokenize pixel patches directly, potentially suffering severe visual token redundancy. A pilot study confirms this: unlike ViT-based models that degrade under compression, ViT-free MLLMs tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance. Yet existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native MLLMs, which stand to gain the most, unexplored. To close this gap, we introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy, revealing that (i) redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and (ii) early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. Guided by these findings, we propose PACE (Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs), the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE. Leveraging dimensional decoupling of positional encoding, PACE decomposes attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. Experiments show PACE maintains near-lossless performance at only 25%-50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.
authors: Lei Tian, Chunzheng Zhu, Kai Wu, Yifan Zhang, Haihua Yang
bullets: Native MLLMs tokenize image patches directly, creating substantial visual-token redundancy that existing ViT-oriented compression methods do not address.
Analysis finds redundancy is heterogeneous and independently distributed across height and width, while early-layer tokens are broadly indiscriminable.
PACE estimates direction-aware spatial importance by decoupling Multimodal-RoPE attention along height and width with negligible overhead.
It allocates token budgets through Pareto optimization across performance, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage.
Experiments report near-lossless performance at 25–50% visual-token retention, with improvements on several benchmarks and over 2× FLOPs reduction.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer binary clinical questions with a yes or no token, leaving the decision threshold implicit and fixed. We derive a continuous score from a single forward pass by renormalizing the probabilities of the yes and no tokens, allowing the threshold to be adapted to clinical needs without retraining. We evaluated this approach with MedGemma and Gemma-3 (4B and 27B) on six medical imaging datasets. The default threshold was frequently misaligned with the task: for identifying normal chest radiographs, MedGemma-27B labeled every image as abnormal, whereas a validation-selected threshold yielded a sensitivity of 0.945 and a specificity of 0.696. Normalization achieved the highest AUROC on four of six datasets (CheXpert: 0.819 vs. 0.777 for raw and 0.743 for text-elicited probabilities), and a single decision required 53-79 ms on one GPU. This simple post-hoc method turns medical MLLMs into fast classifiers with adjustable operating points. Code: https://github.com/TruhnLab/llm-threshold-calibration
authors: Patrick Wienholt, Frederik Hauke, Christiane Kuhl, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Sven Nebelung, Daniel Truhn
bullets: Medical MLLMs’ default yes/no threshold can be poorly calibrated for binary clinical tasks.
The method renormalizes yes and no token probabilities from one forward pass to produce a continuous decision score.
Validation-selected thresholds can substantially improve task-specific operating points; for normal chest radiographs, sensitivity was 0.945 and specificity 0.696.
Normalization achieved the best AUROC on 4 of 6 medical imaging datasets, including 0.819 on CheXpert.
Inference took 53–79 ms per decision on one GPU; evaluation covered MedGemma and Gemma-3 models.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the experimental setup. We evaluated the threshold-shifting method on six medical imaging datasets spanning chest radiography, dermatology, ophthalmology, and histopathology. Notably, CheXpert was explicitly excluded from the training data of the MedGemma models [18], making it well suited for external validation. Each dataset was split into a validation set, used exclusively to select the decision threshold, and a test set, used only for the final performance evaluation. We compared four models, namely Gemma-3 and MedGemma each in a 4B and a 27B variant, using three scoring methods: the normalized yes/no token probability, the raw yes token probability, and a text-elicited probability generated directly as output. The threshold optimized on the validation set was compared against the model’s implicit default threshold of 0.5 on the test set.

Fig. 3: Class-specific AUROC values for the CheXpert dataset using MedGemma27B. (b) From the first decoding step, the model assigns probabilities to all vocabulary tokens, including the verbalizers yes and no. (d) Sweeping the threshold yields different operating points on the ROC curve, trading true positive rate (TPR) against false positive rate (FPR). papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires distinguishing subtle differences in local attributes and spatial relations, yet remains challenging for existing vision-language models. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) offer a new opportunity through generation pathways that preserve rich visual information complementary to understanding. However, existing generation-assisted understanding methods mainly rely on generative supervision or explicit generation and have not systematically explored direct use of native generation-side representations. To address this gap, we systematically analyze what generation-side representations offer for fine-grained understanding, finding that they are more sensitive to fine-grained semantic changes, capture task-relevant changes missed by understanding-side representations, and depend on correct spatial organization for this advantage. Guided by these findings, we design GAFU, a post-training framework that unlocks native generation-side information for fine-grained understanding. It compresses generation-side visual representations into compact \(G\) tokens that preserve fine-grained visual details, enabling task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway. Experiments show that GAFU consistently outperforms SFT baselines trained on the same data across diverse visual understanding tasks and UMM architectures, with maximum relative improvements of 20.00\%, 17.94\%, and 8.62\% on VStar-Bench, OmniSpatial, and VSR-Bench, respectively. Overall, GAFU converts complementary information from the generation pathway into gains in fine-grained visual understanding, providing an effective path toward synergy between generation and understanding in UMMs.
authors: Tengju Ru, Weitong Lian, Zecong Tang, Zhiheng Liu, Lingyi Meng, Haoran Li, Kaixuan Wang, Bohao Li, Xihui Liu
bullets: Fine-grained understanding of subtle attributes and spatial relations remains difficult for vision-language models.
Generation-side representations are more sensitive to fine-grained semantic changes, but their benefit depends on correct spatial organization.
GAFU compresses these representations into compact G tokens that preserve visual detail and support task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway.
Across multiple tasks and UMM architectures, GAFU outperforms same-data SFT baselines, with reported maximum relative gains of 20.00%, 17.94%, and 8.62%.
The approach is evaluated within unified multimodal models and focuses on improving fine-grained visual understanding through generation-understanding synergy.

papers.abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) effectively trains Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents, the mechanisms behind these capability gains are poorly understood. Across four diverse agent environments, we investigate whether the task-success gains from multi-turn RL are accompanied by improved grounded visual question answering about the environment. To assess this, we design environment-specific grounded VQA tasks that reveal improvements in grounded visual understanding. Representational probing shows that vision-encoder probe accuracy remains relatively stable, while LLM-layer probe accuracy improves. Attention analysis further reveals that LLM layers pay more attention to visual tokens during RL training. To test whether increased attention to visual tokens contributes to VQA gains, we introduce a lightweight plug-and-play intervention using a fixed attention bias. Without updating model parameters or computing gradients, this intervention partially restores VQA gains on the untrained model. These results reveal better utilization of visual information as a key mechanism behind the gains from RL.
authors: Ziqian Zhang, Junjie Liao, Zhining Zhang, Wentao Zhu
bullets: Across four agent environments, multi-turn RL gains are evaluated through environment-specific grounded visual question answering.
Vision-encoder probe accuracy stays relatively stable, while probe accuracy in LLM layers improves after RL.
Attention analysis shows that LLM layers attend more to visual tokens during RL training.
A fixed attention-bias intervention partially recovers VQA gains without parameter updates or gradients.
The findings suggest RL teaches VLMs where to attend, but not how to perceive visual content.

papers.abstract: In certain real-world scenarios, obtaining labeled data is excessively expensive, motivating increasing interest in adapting models without annotations. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide pseudo-labels for unlabeled images through image-text similarity, enabling adaptation without manual labeling. The previous unsupervised vision-language model adaption methods assume access to an adaptation vocabulary containing all class names. However, a complete vocabulary is difficult to construct in real-world scenarios, as unlabeled data may contain classes that are overlooked or fall outside the current task scope. Thus, we propose Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-language model Adaptation (VI-UVA), where only a subset of class names are available during adaptation. The vocabulary incompleteness induces an adaptation bias toward provided classes, which degrades omitted-class recognition. To address this issue, we propose Label Space Reconstruction (LSR), which reconstructs a latent label space from the unlabeled data and incorporates it into prompt tuning, thereby extending adaptation beyond the incomplete vocabulary and mitigating the adaptation bias. Furthermore, we derive an omitted-class semantic discrepancy bound for LSR and identify the key factors affecting the bound. Extensive experiments across eight benchmarks demonstrate that LSR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Si Qin, Jiawei Tang, Yaxin Hou, Yan Chen, Yutong Xie, Chen Li, Yuheng Jia
bullets: Existing unsupervised VLM adaptation assumes all relevant class names are available, which can bias adaptation toward known classes.
The proposed VI-UVA setting uses only a subset of class names during adaptation.
Label Space Reconstruction (LSR) infers a latent label space from unlabeled images and integrates it into prompt tuning.
The method derives a bound on omitted-class semantic discrepancy and analyzes factors influencing it.
Experiments on eight benchmarks show LSR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

Third, for each retained anchor, we retrieve the corresponding pseudo-token sequence and textual representation to construct a pseudovocabulary and a pseudo-labeled dataset, respectively. Then, we perform prompt tuning with the pseudo-vocabulary and pseudo-labeled dataset to preserve omitted-class recognition.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models answer questions about images and also generate images with one shared set of weights. This creates a post-training risk that single-purpose models do not have: fine-tuning one capability can damage another that works in a different modality. We measure this cross-modal forgetting for LoRA post-training of Janus-Pro-7B. Every target is chosen by how poorly the base model already handles it, from a poetic register to a language it barely speaks, so that retention is tested against a real intervention; we then evaluate the capabilities we never trained, first after a single run and then after chaining three. A single run looks entirely safe: nothing we did not train degrades on four public benchmarks or in free-form English, even when the adapter cuts held-out Welsh perplexity by 76% with a relative weight change under 2%. That safety belongs to the run, not to the recipe. Chaining three runs destroys the capability learned one run earlier and raises general-text perplexity by one to two orders of magnitude above the never-adapted model, on the very measures that stayed flat before. The cause is in the objective, which constrains only the modality being trained and leaves the other head unconstrained: cutting the learning rate to one fifth does not prevent the collapse, while anchoring the other head removes the damage to the capabilities we never trained, at no cost to what is learned. What is learned also stays inside its own modality, with Welsh acquired from text closing only 3% of the English-Welsh gap in image generation.
authors: Francesco Colasurdo, Ivan Slobozhan, Joaquin Vanschoren, Anna Vettoruzzo
bullets: The study measures whether adapting one modality harms capabilities in another for Janus-Pro-7B.
A single LoRA run caused no observed degradation on four benchmarks or free-form English, despite substantially improving held-out Welsh perplexity.
Chaining three runs erased a capability learned earlier and increased general-text perplexity by one to two orders of magnitude.
Reducing the learning rate did not prevent collapse; anchoring the other modality’s head did, without sacrificing the trained capability.
Knowledge transfer across modalities was weak: text-based Welsh learning closed only 3% of the English–Welsh gap in image generation.

papers.selection_reason: Studies cross-modal forgetting in unified multimodal post-training and proposes anchoring to prevent collapse, relevant to multimodal foundation models and continual learning.
papers.title: Cross-Modal Forgetting and Transfer in Unified Multimodal Post-Training
papers.tldr: LoRA post-training of unified multimodal models appears safe after one run but can cause severe cross-modal forgetting when three runs are chained, which is prevented by anchoring the untrained head.

papers.abstract: Characters, locations, and actions recur throughout a movie, so many of its moments differ only in fine-grained details. Grounding such a moment in a full-length movie requires resolving that detail rather than matching the attributes it shares with other moments, yet existing temporal movie grounding benchmarks rarely test this. We introduce CoM$^2$-Bench, a benchmark of confusable query pairs, where the two queries in each pair share most attributes but differ in a single distinguishing detail within a full movie, posing a challenge for recent temporal grounding approaches. To locate where grounding breaks down, we analyze a retrieve-then-localize pipeline, in which a retriever first selects a short candidate chunk and a localizer then performs temporal grounding within it. Separating the two stages lets us attribute each failure to either retrieval or localization. We find that retrieval is the major bottleneck: state-of-the-art retrievers often select a moment's confusable counterpart, because their choices follow the content the two moments share rather than the detail that tells them apart. To address these failures, we propose a simple, training-free remedy, Agentic Window Search (AWS): an MLLM agent $\textit{Decomposes}$ the query into attribute-level sub-queries, then $\textit{Inspects}$ each candidate window against them and $\textit{Expands}$ the window when evidence is cut off at its edge. AWS works with existing retrievers and localizers without additional training, raising mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8.
authors: Dong-Hee Kim, Seonwoo Choi, Changbeen Kim, Juyeon Ko, Youngju Choi, Il Hyeon Mun, Hyunwoo J. Kim, Donghyun Kim
bullets: Introduces paired queries that share most attributes but differ in one distinguishing detail.
Evaluates retrieve-then-localize pipelines on full-length movies and separates retrieval from localization failures.
Finds retrieval is the main bottleneck: systems often select a confusable counterpart based on shared content.
Proposes training-free Agentic Window Search, which decomposes queries, inspects candidate windows, and expands truncated windows.
Improves mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8 when used with existing retrievers and localizers.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as general-purpose multimodal assistants, making multimodal safety alignment an important challenge. Safety depends on the interplay between textual and visual content, with visual context often playing a critical role. However, VLMs may fail to use visual information appropriately, either overlooking safety-relevant visual content or over-interpreting sensitive visual content, leading to unsafe responses or over-refusal. Existing multimodal safety alignment datasets largely follow the response-preference paradigm, which teaches models how to respond but provides limited supervision on how visual context should inform the safety judgment, making it difficult to balance safety and over-refusal. To address this limitation, we introduce ContraSafe-VL, a Contrastive Safety preference dataset for Vision-Language Models. For each fixed textual query, ContraSafe-VL constructs paired visual contexts that result in multimodal queries with different safety labels, providing direct supervision for how visual context should inform multimodal safety judgments. It further provides response preference pairs based on harmlessness and helpfulness to encourage models to generate responses that are both safe and helpful. Experiments across three VLM architectures and multiple benchmarks demonstrate that training with ContraSafe-VL improves cross-modal safety recognition and achieves a better safety--over-refusal trade-off while preserving general multimodal capabilities. The dataset will be publicly released.
authors: Di Wu, Yanyan Zhao, Xin Lu, Hao Yang, Taotao Zhang, Yunzhen Zhao
bullets: Addresses VLM failures to notice safety-relevant visual content or overreact to benign sensitive content.
Pairs the same textual query with different visual contexts that receive different safety labels.
Adds harmlessness- and helpfulness-based response preference pairs.
Experiments across three VLM architectures and multiple benchmarks show improved cross-modal safety recognition and a better safety–over-refusal trade-off.
The dataset is intended for public release and aims to preserve general multimodal capabilities.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, making it better aligned with human-AI collaborative creation than single-turn editing. However, constructing high-quality multi-turn training data remains challenging, as conventional sequential rollout accumulates errors and introduces visual-quality drift across editing turns. To address this challenge, we introduce MTEdit, a multi-turn image editing dataset built through a pipeline centered on packed trajectory canvas (PTC) generation. By jointly generating multiple editing states within a unified visual context, this pipeline reduces visual-quality drift across turns. Covering both step-wise and context-aware editing scenarios, MTEdit comprises 500K multi-turn image editing trajectories, with up to 8 turns and an average of 5.38 turns per trajectory, making it one of the most extensive datasets for multi-turn image editing. We further introduce MTEdit-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate both scenarios by assessing models' ability to follow editing instructions, maintain content consistency, resist visual-quality drift, and effectively use historical context across turns. Using MTEdit, we fine-tune Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal to obtain Qwen-Image-MTEdit. On MTEdit-Bench, we evaluate a broad range of closed-source and open-source image editing models, including Qwen-Image-MTEdit. Experimental results show that Qwen-Image-MTEdit achieves the best performance among the evaluated open-source models, demonstrating the effectiveness of MTEdit in improving models' multi-turn image editing capabilities.
bullets: Targets visual-quality drift and error accumulation in sequential multi-turn editing data generation.
Introduces packed trajectory canvas generation, which jointly creates multiple editing states in one visual context.
Provides 500K trajectories covering step-wise and context-aware editing, with up to 8 turns.
Introduces MTEdit-Bench for instruction following, content consistency, drift resistance, and historical-context use.
Fine-tuned Qwen-Image-MTEdit performs best among the evaluated open-source models on MTEdit-Bench.

papers.abstract: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs' ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.
bullets: Existing benchmarks conflate acoustic perception with semantic reasoning, obscuring the source of model failures.
VocalGrad evaluates temporal change direction through binary classification, minimizing reliance on language understanding.
State-of-the-art LALMs show a substantial human–model gap and perform near chance on the benchmark.
Linear probing identifies two failure modes: relevant information is either unused by the language-model head or becomes less linearly decodable across layers.
The benchmark exposes acoustic-representation limitations not visible from text outputs.

papers.abstract: End-to-end visual generation with pixel-space loss has recently achieved competitive performance without the need for learned image tokenizers. In this work, we study whether language-informed supervision can provide a richer training signal than pixel loss for visual generation. We introduce LILIE (pronounced "lily"), a Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder. LILIE is an invertible image transform trained such that a vision-language model can recover captions from noised features. The encoder uses a normalizing flow transformer trained jointly with a vision-language model via next token prediction. We then use the encoder to extract a simple language-informed loss for text-to-image generation. We train JiT models with LILIE loss, reducing gFD by 14 points (66.84 $\to$ 53.01) against a pixel-only baseline on the GPIC dataset. Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at https://suchiragarwal.com/lilie.
authors: Suchir Agarwal, Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Ziyu Chen, Kyle Sargent, Juan Carlos Niebles, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Motivation: Pixel loss may provide a poorer training signal than supervision aligned with image semantics and language.
Method: Train an invertible normalizing-flow image encoder jointly with a vision-language model to recover captions from noised features.
Application: Use the encoder to define a language-informed loss for JiT text-to-image models.
Result: On GPIC, LILIE loss reduces gFD from 66.84 to 53.01 versus a pixel-only baseline.
Scope: The approach is evaluated on the GPIC dataset; broader applicability is not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Object hallucination in vision-language models (VLMs) is usually measured by checking each object a caption names against the image. Most benchmarks and detectors alike treat every object mention as a claim that the object is present. This assumption fails when a caption names an object without asserting it, as in "a bench for people to sit on", which mentions people without claiming that any are in the image. We call such mentions non-assertive. Treating them as hallucinations inflates the error rates attributed to models that use such language. To separate them from real hallucinations, we introduce NAME-Bench (Non-Assertive Mention Evaluation Benchmark), 25,497 object mentions from captions that five VLMs generate for COCO images. Each mention is labelled concrete (asserted and present), hallucinated (asserted and absent), or non-assertive, and non-assertive mentions are further divided into four subtypes: depictive, purpose, negation and hedged. All the hallucination detectors that we evaluate flag non-assertive mentions as hallucinations, at rates between 14% and 80%. Adding non-assertive mentions to detector training as negatives largely corrects this on LLaVA-1.5. On the four newer VLMs, a comparable correction takes five to ten times more data, and the detectors then catch fewer real hallucinations. These findings show that current detectors conflate mentioning an object with asserting it, and that this conflation is harder to undo on the four newer VLMs than on LLaVA-1.5. Hallucination evaluation should therefore separate what a caption asserts from what it merely mentions.
authors: Hsin-Ling Hsu, Neeraja Kirtane, Kuan-Hao Huang
bullets: Introduces NAME-Bench, containing 25,497 object mentions from VLM captions on COCO images.
Labels mentions as concrete, hallucinated, or non-assertive; non-assertive cases include depictive, purpose, negation, and hedged mentions.
All evaluated detectors incorrectly flag non-assertive mentions as hallucinations at rates of 14%–80%.
Training with non-assertive examples improves correction on LLaVA-1.5, but newer VLMs require 5–10× more data and then detect fewer real hallucinations.
The findings expose a persistent mismatch between object mentioning and object assertion in hallucination evaluation.

papers.abstract: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) have shown strong performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA), yet they may still produce factually inconsistent responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can mitigate this issue by incorporating external clinical evidence; however, retrieval is often guided by a single modality, potentially overlooking the joint semantics of medical images and clinical questions. We introduce a multimodal RAG framework that learns a joint query representation through a Gated Multimodal Unit, enabling evidence retrieval to leverage information from both modalities while keeping the underlying Med-LVLM frozen. We evaluate the proposed approach on benchmark datasets. Results show that the multimodal query representation consistently outperforms a reference Med-LVLM and remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate the potential of multimodal query representations for more effective evidence retrieval in Medical VQA.
authors: Daniela Jimenez-Pano, Hugo Jair Escalante, Delia Iraz\'u Hern\'andez-Far\'ias
bullets: Medical VQA models can generate factually inconsistent answers.
Single-modality retrieval may miss the joint meaning of medical images and questions.
The proposed RAG framework uses a Gated Multimodal Unit to combine both modalities into a query representation.
Evaluations on benchmark datasets show consistent gains over a reference Med-LVLM and competitiveness with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.abstract: Compact medical vision-language models (VLMs) can answer clinical questions correctly without reliably using the image, relying instead on question wording or learned priors. Standard knowledge distillation copies a teacher's answer preference on the original image, but it leaves unchecked whether that preference is conditional on the visual evidence required by the question. We study this missing target as medical visual evidence dependency: support for the correct answer should decrease when the matched evidence is absent. We introduce Evidence-Conditioned Dependency Distillation (ECDD), which pairs each training image with a control matched to the evidence level and distills the teacher's drop in answer margin across the pair. A lower bound objective transfers positive dependency by penalizing only shortfalls, while original-image supervision preserves task accuracy. The same formulation applies when the evidence is a queried clinical region, a surgical instrument, or whole-image visual content. Across three medical VQA settings, ECDD keeps original-image accuracy competitive with distillation and alignment baselines while making answer support more sensitive to evidence removal. Under the DME headline objective, for example, the positive-case margin response to target rather than random masking rises from 0.786 with KD to 2.023 with ECDD, while original-image accuracy differs by 0.11 points. These results suggest that medical VLM distillation should transfer both the teacher's answer preference and its dependence on visual evidence.
authors: Qizhen Lan, Yiling Ma, Ruiqi Chen, Mengchen Fan, Xi Xiao, Lin Zhao, Liang He, Baocheng Geng, Pulin Che, Tianyang Wang, Xiaoqian Jiang
bullets: Targets a failure mode where compact medical VLMs answer correctly from question wording or priors without using the image.
Pairs each image with an evidence-matched control and distills the teacher’s answer-margin drop when relevant evidence is removed.
Uses a shortfall-only lower-bound objective to encourage positive visual dependency while preserving original-image task accuracy.
Supports evidence at the level of clinical regions, surgical instruments, or whole-image content.

Across three medical VQA settings, ECDD increased sensitivity to evidence removal while maintaining competitive accuracy; under the reported DME objective, the margin response rose from 0.786 with KD to 2.023 with ECDD, with a 0.11-point accuracy difference.

papers.abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.
authors: Oscar Kemme, Janek Haberer, Ali Hojjat, Olaf Landsiedel
bullets: Uses the number of active attention heads to jointly control embedding, attention, feed-forward, and output widths.

Adds an elastic multimodal projection whose width matches the active text-model width.
Reports higher TriviaQA accuracy than a larger-parameter nested baseline at 75% active heads, comparable CLIPScore to a much larger Gemma 3 4B model at 50%, and 75.3% higher token throughput at 25%.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced instruction-driven perception through the "Embedding-as-Mask" paradigm. However, extending this capability to Remote Sensing (RS) reasoning segmentation remains exceptionally challenging under cluttered geographical contexts and extreme scale variations, often leading to Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification. We identify a critical yet underexplored bottleneck: the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within the autoregressive generation paradigm. Produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, [SEG] relies on visual evidence that has been progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. This information decay is particularly catastrophic for RS targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. To address these bottlenecks, we propose GeoReason, a novel framework designed to fortify logical deduction and preserve spatial integrity. First, we introduce an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This paradigm shift transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor, preventing information decay during long-form linguistic inference. Second, we enhance visual reasoning via a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought (CoT) that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes, coupled with a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment (PTA) Loss that explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical RS textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanc0126/GeoReason.
authors: Cheng Fan, Han Wu, Tingzhang Luo, Minjing Dong, Yehui Tang, Jianyuan Guo
bullets: Addresses spatial fidelity degradation and target misidentification in cluttered, scale-variable remote-sensing scenes.
Introduces an Anticipatory Prior that places the [SEG] token in the initial query as a persistent spatial anchor.
Uses Location-aware Chain-of-Thought for coarse-to-fine localization with bounding boxes.
Adds a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment loss to align segmentation representations with physical image textures.
Reports consistent improvements over existing methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks.

(Right) The Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment (PTA) loss aligns the hidden states of both prompt-side and answer-side [SEG] tokens with the visual patch embeddings corresponding to the GT target.

papers.abstract: As climate change intensifies, floods are becoming more frequent and destructive, making accurate flood understanding an urgent priority. However, existing vision-language models perform poorly on flood-related tasks, suffering from attentional bias and inaccurate descriptions of flood magnitude. To bridge this gap, we construct the first large-scale remote sensing flood multi-modal benchmark that supports language-level flood understanding and pixel-level flood segmentation. The benchmark contains 131,200 flood image patches and corresponding 443,100 textual descriptions for flood severity and evolution. Based on this benchmark, we propose FloodVLM-Pix, a language-guided pixel-level flood understanding model that includes a flood prior module and a multi-temporal flood pixel decoder to achieve accurate flood understanding. The flood prior module automatically distills sub-region flood spatial priors and inputs priors into FloodVLM-Pix, solving the attentional bias problem in flood language understanding. The flood pixel decoder introduces a novel general-specific feature fusion mechanism to address performance degradation caused by interference (e.g., clouds or mountain shadows) during flood segmentation. Experiments on FloodVL-Pix demonstrate that FloodVLM-Pix improves both flood description quality and pixel-level flood segmentation performance compared with state-of-the-art VLMs and flood segmentation models. Our code and data will be released at https://github.com/Haomiaoyanmeng/FloodPix.
authors: Chengyang Zhang, Zhihao Wang, Zhiyu Long, Xueqian Wang, Quanming Yao, Wei Wu, Gang Li

Reports improved flood description quality and pixel-level segmentation performance over existing vision-language and flood-segmentation models.
Scope is remote-sensing flood understanding, covering both language-level descriptions and pixel-level masks.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) repeatedly process hundreds of visual tokens across decoder layers, incurring substantial computation and memory costs. Existing inference-time visual token pruning methods often irreversibly remove low-ranked tokens, although the set of visual tokens receiving high query-conditioned attention can change across decoder depth. Recoverable routing preserves skipped tokens for later reconsideration, but re-admits them with stale representations after bypassing intermediate transformations. We further find that replacing stale re-admitted states with their current-depth oracle states from a full-token reference trajectory substantially improves grounding performance. We therefore propose CatchUp, a training-free framework for depth-aware visual-token re-admission. CatchUp repeatedly re-evaluates query-conditioned visual relevance, processes only selected visual tokens through each decoder interval, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission. Upon re-admission, CatchUp approximates missed representation evolution using reference-to-current transition signals from semantically and spatially related visual tokens. Across three referring-expression grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention in both benchmark groups at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets. At a 64-token budget with 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, CatchUp retains 92.17% of the full model's performance on average across six multimodal benchmarks while reducing end-to-end latency by 8.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/pej0918/CatchUp
bullets: Problem: Irreversible visual-token pruning can discard tokens that become relevant later, while recoverable routing may re-admit them with stale representations.

Key idea: Uses transition signals from semantically and spatially related tokens to approximate the representation evolution missed by skipped tokens.
Results: Across three grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets.
At 64 tokens, it uses 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, retains 92.17% of full-model performance on average, and reduces end-to-end latency by 8.0%.

papers.tldr: CatchUp is a training-free method that efficiently prunes and later re-admits visual tokens across decoder depth while approximating their updated representations, preserving LVLM performance with lower latency.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer questions about whole images well, yet they still struggle with fine-grained region understanding. A key reason is that text-only supervision never specifies which regions support an answer. To close this gap, we present Xiaomi-Lens-0, a 4B MLLM built on Qwen3.5 that predicts masks from its own visual representations. Specifically, a lightweight decoder combines vision-encoder patch features with visual latents, the language model's mask-token states, so mask supervision reaches the shared backbone without an additional segmentation encoder. Because each latent decodes to a mask, the model can interleave reasoning with region-specific latents and thus think with visual latents, while grounded reasoning traces supervise the regions it visits during chain-of-thought. As a result, across all eight RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg splits, Xiaomi-Lens-0 gains 5.6 points on average over Qwen3.5 in referring comprehension and achieves the highest segmentation cIoU among compared models. Moreover, it surpasses Qwen3.5 across all perception benchmarks. Homepage: \href{https://seerray-lab.github.io/Xiaomi-Lens-0}{this https URL}
authors: Pei Fu, Yike Liu, Yue Sun, Hanmo Wang, Xiuwen Xi, Ruoceng Zhang, Shaojie Zhang, Chao Jiang, Hang Li, Bingrui Liu, Zhenbo Luo, Heng Qu, Changjian Xu, Ming Xu, Jian Luan
bullets: Addresses the gap between strong whole-image question answering and weak region-level understanding caused by insufficient region-grounded supervision.
Uses a lightweight decoder that combines vision patch features, visual latents, and mask-token states to predict region masks without a separate segmentation encoder.
Supports region-specific visual latents and grounded reasoning traces, allowing reasoning to reference and supervise the regions it visits.
Improves referring comprehension by an average of 5.6 points over Qwen3.5 across eight RefCOCO-family splits and achieves the highest reported segmentation cIoU among compared models.
Surpasses Qwen3.5 across all reported perception benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Making a conference poster is visual coding in miniature: an entire paper must be compressed onto a single page, which exercises summarization, visual design, and code implementation at once, using nothing beyond the paper itself. Yet benchmarks for this task in the context of visual coding remain scarce: existing resources are small and annotated only with layout boxes, so evaluation must fall back on VLM-as-judge or human checklists rather than objective render-and-compare, and the generation methods they support design layouts from scratch, leaving human-crafted posters unusable as either a retrievable design library or as verified supervision. We introduce RAP (Reconstruct A Poster), a dataset and benchmark for paper-to-poster generation as a visual coding task. RAP contains 25K+ verified paper-poster pairs from various machine learning conferences held between 2022 and 2026, annotated with a three-level content taxonomy, plus a held-out benchmark of 150 test papers each paired with its human poster. A fully automated derendering pipeline turns each poster into styled HTML/CSS of typed, refillable slots, so every sample is a paper-poster-markup triplet verifiable by rendering against the source poster. The corpus serves both inference and training: PosterRAG, a training-free multi-agent pipeline, retrieves an exemplar and refills its slots without touching layout or styling, while an SFT+RL recipe trains a dedicated model from the same triplets. An online demo is available at https://reconstruct-a-poster.github.io/.
authors: Haonan Han, Yukang Lin, Minliang Lin, Haoxian Tan, Jun-Yan He, Rui Yang, Zhi-Qi Cheng, Jie Hu, Guanglu Wan, Xiu Li

Uses automated derendering to convert posters into styled HTML/CSS with typed, refillable slots, enabling render-and-compare verification.
Supports both retrieval-based inference through PosterRAG and model training with an SFT+RL recipe.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the overview of the runs related to the Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS) and Video Question Answering (VQA) tracks of TRECVID 2025 on behalf of the CERTH-ITI team. For the AVS track, we introduce a two-stage framework built on foundation models. In the first stage, multiple vision-language models (VLMs) encode both the input query, augmented through LLM-generated rephrasings, and the candidate video shots, producing weighted similarity scores for initial retrieval. In the second stage, we utilize a Multimodal-LLM(MLLM)-based reranking module that evaluates the semantic alignment between each shot among the top-N highest-ranked ones and the original query, generating updated relevance scores for reordering these shots. This MLLM-driven reranking significantly improves contextual matching and produces more accurate final rankings without requiring any model training. Regarding the VQA track, we fine-tune an audio-visual MLLM model on the provided TRECVID training dataset and we implement an inference-time scaling technique to enhance the multimodal understanding capabilities of the MLLM. For the open-ended Answer Generation (AG) task, we aggregate multiple model responses per question via a majority vote. The responses are generated with greedy sampling from different random frame subsets of the video and they are ranked based on the number of votes. For the Multiple-Choice (MC) task, instead of voting, we use mean pooling on the logits assigned by the fine-tuned model to each candidate response. Through the combination of fine-tuning and frame subset ensembling we achieve the highest score across 3 metrics in the VQA AG task and the second highest in the VQA MC task.
authors: Andreas Goulas, Damianos Galanopoulos, Ioannis Patras, Vasileios Mezaris
bullets: AVS uses LLM-generated query rephrasings and multiple VLMs for initial video-shot retrieval, followed by MLLM-based reranking of the top-N shots.

The approach achieves the highest score on three VQA answer-generation metrics and the second-highest score on the multiple-choice task.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) aims to detect anomalies in previously unseen classes using auxiliary images, with applications such as industrial visual inspection and medical imaging. Recent vision-language-model-based approaches improve ZSAD by aligning textual and visual representations, while distributional prompting further models prompt variability for unseen categories. However, existing methods do not explicitly combine normality-referenced distributional modeling with hierarchy-specific prompt specialization, limiting their ability to model anomalous semantics relative to normality while addressing both image-level detection and fine-grained localization. We propose Hierarchical Knowledge-Guided Distributional Prompt Learning (HiDist), a normality-referenced hierarchical distributional prompt framework for ZSAD. HiDist models each prompt token with a diagonal Gaussian distribution and generates stochastic prompt variations through Monte Carlo sampling. Rather than learning normal and anomalous distributions independently, anomalous prompt distributions are parameterized as deviations from learned normal references, explicitly encoding their dependency. The resulting distributions are specialized into global and local representations for image-level detection and pixel-level localization, respectively, while an adapted global visual representation guides hierarchical alignment. Experiments on seven industrial and medical datasets demonstrate strong cross-dataset performance across anomaly detection and localization tasks. Extensive ablation and representation analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed distributional modeling and hierarchy-specific representation learning.

papers.abstract: Generating complete, coherent, and usable 3D indoor scenes from natural language requires strong \textbf{design intelligence}: the ability to design high-quality scenes and critique their quality. However, existing approaches either rely on general-purpose models lacking domain-specific design experience or learn from static scenes. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Scene-Designer}, an agentic framework that learns design intelligence through complementary design and critique experiences. We construct two datasets: \textbf{Scene-OTA-35K}, which provides Observation--Thought--Action supervision for learning scene design and efficient error correction, and \textbf{Scene-OTC-15K}, which provides Observation--Thought--Critic supervision for learning scene quality critique across physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence. Based on these experiences, we propose \textbf{Scene-GRPO}, a Critic-guided GRPO framework that improves design decisions and reduces unnecessary trial-and-error corrections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Scene-Designer achieves superior performance in physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, while the learned Scene-Critic significantly outperforms general-purpose models in scene critique. Moreover, test-time Critic guidance further improves scene generation, showing that the Critic can provide useful guidance beyond training. Additional analysis suggests a trend of mutual enhancement between scene design and critique abilities.
authors: Xuanyu Liu, Hongyan Feng, Miao Pan, Sunlai Chen, Lizhou Liang, Bing Sun, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly serve as judges in training and evaluation pipelines, often assessing answers together with explanations. Although AI judges are sensitive to textual factors, it remains unclear whether ordinary plausible explanations can sway judgments requiring visual verification. We introduce JUPE, a visual-question-answering (VQA)-style benchmark that fixes answers while varying explanations. Across 14 MLLM judges, ordinary explanations that sound plausible mislead judges, with effects comparable on average to deliberately persuasive arguments. Plain justifications and chain-of-thought rationales reduce rejection of incorrect answers by 12.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively. We call this failure plausibility capture. Using signal detection theory, we find a significant mean shift in decision criterion toward acceptance, without a clear change in mean discriminability. Explanations sway judgments across domains, explanation generators, and judging protocols, while tested mitigations offer limited, model-dependent protection. Such shifts can inflate performance estimates when judges evaluate answers with explanations.

Plain justifications and chain-of-thought rationales reduced rejection of incorrect answers by 12.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively.
The effect reflects a shift toward accepting answers rather than improved ability to distinguish correct from incorrect answers.
The vulnerability persisted across domains, explanation generators, and judging protocols; mitigations were limited and model-dependent.

papers.title: A Plausible Explanation Is Enough to Mislead Multimodal Judges
papers.tldr: Plausible explanations can make multimodal LLM judges accept incorrect answers even when visual verification is required.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are usually chosen from leaderboards, which give one ranking for every application. On questions about objects that a scene suggests but does not contain, however, the model with the lowest error on the POPE hallucination benchmark is not the one with the lowest error on such questions. For yes/no questions about object presence, we show that the best model for a target domain can be predicted without running any candidate on that domain, given 650 to 1,200 labeled target items that calibrate a detector. We measure each model's reliance on a cue, a feature such as scene context or text in the image, by editing 100 labeled source images so that the cue suggests the wrong answer, and comparing with a matched control edit. Reliance predicts which VLMs are misled by physical sticker attacks (Spearman .93 on nine models not used to design the score) and which hallucinate on unedited COCO photographs, beyond what their tendency to answer yes explains. Shift-Reliance Alignment (SRA) scores a model by its source error on the labeled source questions plus its reliance multiplied by the shift. The shift is the proportion of target questions on which the cue misleads, and a detector estimates it on the unlabeled target images. SRA selects the model with the lowest score. In pre-registered tests on new images where most questions mislead, it lowered the error of the selected model from 30.4% under selection by source error to 18.8% on Objects365 and OpenImages but, against its prediction, not on COCO. On CueDial, a benchmark we release that varies how often a cue misleads, selection by model confidence falls more than 40 percentage points behind the best model when overlaid text denies a visible object, and SRA stays within 3 points.
bullets: Leaderboard rankings can fail when target questions rely on misleading scene context or image text.
SRA measures each model’s cue reliance using edited labeled source images and estimates how often that cue misleads in unlabeled target images.
With 650–1,200 labeled target items for detector calibration, SRA predicts target model errors without evaluating every candidate on the target domain.
Cue reliance strongly predicted vulnerability to sticker attacks and hallucinations on COCO images beyond models’ general tendency to answer yes.

In preregistered tests, SRA reduced selected-model error from 30.4% to 18.8% on Objects365 and OpenImages; it did not improve selection on COCO and stayed within 3 points of the best model on CueDial.
