papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) that segment from language must pass the location of the referent to a pixel decoder. The dominant interface compresses it into the hidden state of a single [SEG] token, a d-dimensional vector with no spatial index, and leaves the decoder, which never sees the expression, to recover the referent's extent. We show that the VLM already computes a better signal: the [SEG] token's attention over the image tokens, which is defined on the patch grid by construction. Probing a frozen segmentation VLM, we find that this attention yields 18 to 22 more gIoU than the [SEG] hidden state when read by the same probe, that it gains nothing from the image where the hidden state does, and that it is concentrated in the late layers. Building on these findings, we introduce AttnSeg, which replaces the [SEG] embedding with this attention as the decoder's prompt. A learned, signed combination of the attention heads forms a dense spatial prompt, and an attention-guidance objective supervises it directly. A two-stage recipe first trains the VLM to localize without the decoder, then trains the decoder to refine, within the budget of standard fine-tuning. Applied to Sa2VA, AttnSeg improves ReasonSeg by 6.4 gIoU and GS-Eval by 10.2 at 4B (4.2 and 9.6 over the same model fine-tuned on the same data), and by 8.8 and 11.3 at 14B. The gains reach 13 to 18 gIoU on object parts, multiple objects, and single objects, where the referent must be singled out, and are negligible on stuff regions, which the decoder already recovers unaided. Code and models are available at https://eslambakr.github.io/attseg_project_page/
authors: Eslam Abdelrahman, Hamza Omar Alkaf, Yuheng Li, Siddharth Srinivasan Iyer, Nanxuan Zhao, Eli Shechtman, Krishna Kumar Singh, Mohamed Elhoseiny
bullets: The standard [SEG] embedding discards spatial information, forcing the pixel decoder to infer the referent’s extent.
[SEG]-token attention over image patches is a stronger localization signal, yielding 18–22 higher gIoU with the same probe and concentrating in late layers.
AttnSeg learns a signed combination of attention heads as a dense spatial prompt and directly supervises it with attention guidance.
A two-stage training recipe separates VLM localization from decoder refinement within standard fine-tuning.
On Sa2VA, AttnSeg improves ReasonSeg and GS-Eval, especially for single objects, multiple objects, and object parts; gains are negligible for stuff regions.

papers.abstract: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.
authors: Yuhan Zhu, Xiangyu Zeng, Qingyi Si, Chenxu Yang, Yifei Li, Luozheng Qin, Junhao Zhou, Dingyu Yao, Jun Zhang, Chuanyu Qin, Zhiqiu Zhang, Yuandong Yang, Yuqi Xu, Tianyu Zhang, Hongcheng Guo, Jiaqi Wang, Nan Duan, Limin Wang
bullets: Frames video understanding and interaction as structured decisions over temporal intervals or textual answer choices.
Adapts pretrained multimodal language models with a shared scoring head instead of autoregressive answer generation.
Supports cached inference for sequential queries and joint inference for multiple queries over the same video history.
Improves temporal-grounding mean mIoU over backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, with 2.8–3.1× inference speedups.
Matches backbone performance on four video-QA benchmarks in Thinking mode while exceeding 100× inference speedups.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) have significantly promoted using text-to-image (T2I) models to generate images with specific affective intentions. However, the emotional effects conveyed by generated images frequently deviate from target expectations, and it remains unclear whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reliably interpret the emotion of AI-generated visual content. Existing affective benchmarks are predominantly built on natural images, while affective studies of generated images have largely focused on emotions expressed in portraits, lacking a unified benchmark for studying the emotions expressed and evoked by generated images. We therefore introduce EmoGenie, a benchmark of emotion for AI-generated images that evaluates capabilities in T2I generation and MLLM understanding across expressed and evoked emotions. It comprises 6,400 images generated by eight T2I models using 800 emotion-targeted prompts, annotated with question-answer (QA) pairs, termed EmoGenie-QA, and continuous human ratings, termed EmoGenie-Assess. EmoGenie-QA contains 90,000 closed-set questions in single-image and image-pair settings, as well as 1,057 open-ended questions for emotion description. EmoGenie-Assess benchmarks continuous affective and aesthetic prediction using 13,175 mean opinion scores (MOSs) aggregated from human ratings in terms of valence, arousal, dominance, and aesthetic quality. We further develop EmoProbe, which combines emotion question answering with response-aligned, dimension-specific regression heads for continuous score prediction. Experimental results show that EmoProbe achieves superior results on emotion-related QA tasks, while its affective and aesthetic predictions correlate better with human ratings, demonstrating its state-of-the-art capabilities of unified coarse-to-fine affective understanding for AI-generated images.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appears highly effective, with existing methods retaining over 95% of unpruned performance on common VQA benchmarks using a quarter of the visual tokens or fewer. However, our extensive evaluation of ten methods across three MLLM families and five ability groups reveals a critical gap: strong general performance often comes at the cost of severe degradation on fine-grained tasks such as OCR and visual grounding. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest-ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage pruning method built on a mixed-granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query-focused and image-intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm-debiased image saliency, while selecting image-intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density-adjusted text-to-image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model-budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Bifocal
authors: Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Fengyu Zhou, Yijuan Liang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen

Using roughly one-quarter of the visual tokens, it retained over 90% of unpruned performance in every evaluated ability group across three MLLM families.
The method was evaluated across ten pruning methods, five ability groups, and nine model-budget settings; code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for remote sensing understanding, yet reliable reasoning remains challenging when tasks require fine-grained visual grounding and multi-step inference. Existing approaches typically rely on either costly pre-constructed reasoning trajectories or self-generated signals such as response consistency, which can reinforce shared errors and provide unreliable supervision. We introduce \textbf{Reasoning--Diagnosis Self-Evolution (ReDiS)}, a framework that separates reasoning exploration from candidate evaluation while allowing the two processes to evolve jointly. ReDiS instantiates two role-specific experts from a shared multimodal backbone: a \textbf{Reasoner} that explores diverse visual evidence--answer candidates and a \textbf{Diagnoser} that jointly evaluates the complete candidate set and provides credibility-aware feedback. As the Reasoner evolves, it exposes new candidate distributions and failure modes; the Diagnoser adapts to these changes and, in turn, reshapes the learning signal for subsequent exploration. To handle groups in which all sampled answers are incorrect and group-relative advantages vanish, we further introduce \textbf{Failure-Triggered Recovery (FTR)}, which provides minimal outcome-level correction without prescribing intermediate reasoning trajectories. Experiments on LHRS-Bench, MME-RS, and CHOICE show consistent improvements over Qwen3.5 backbones at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B scales. ReDiS improves category-averaged accuracy by 6.47 percentage points at 0.8B, while ReDiS-4B achieves the highest average performance among the compared remote sensing MLLMs.
authors: Yi Liu, Wentao Jiang, Shuo Ni, Zhiming Luo, Di Wang, Zengmao Wang, Jing Zhang, Bo Du

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for remote sensing reasoning, yet they frequently generate visually unsupported reasoning that contradicts the visual evidence. Existing post-training methods optimize primarily for final-answer correctness, providing limited supervision for identifying and correcting hallucinations that arise during the reasoning process. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{FaithRS}, a hallucination-aware self-reflection framework for faithful reasoning in remote sensing. We first construct \textbf{SFHD-43K}, a dataset of 43K structured, fine-grained hallucination annotations, and train a detector to identify hallucination types, underlying causes, and supporting visual evidence. FaithRS then incorporates this diagnostic feedback into a Safe Detector-Guided Corrective Rollout framework, where a safety-aware gate selectively determines whether and how to revise the response. Training is driven by a composite reward that jointly optimizes answer accuracy, reasoning faithfulness, hallucination reduction, format compliance, and revision safety. Experiments with Qwen3.5 backbones (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) show consistent improvements across four remote sensing benchmarks, with gains of up to 11.64 points.

Experiments across four remote-sensing benchmarks and three Qwen3.5 backbones report improvements of up to 11.64 points.

papers.abstract: Practical remote sensing applications often require both understanding and generation capabilities for the same geographic scene. However, most existing methods address either understanding or generation in isolation, while existing unified remote sensing models' generative ability is limited to text-to-image. To bridge this gap, we propose Omni-RS, a unified framework supporting four remote sensing understanding tasks and five generation tasks. Specifically, we introduce the "Scene-Guided Two-Stage Training" strategy, which first adapts a multimodal large language model to remote sensing understanding and then uses its hidden states to guide a diffusion transformer for image generation. To enable joint learning across diverse generation tasks, we construct UniGen, a unified multi-task generation dataset, by organizing heterogeneous remote sensing data into a unified format. Furthermore, we introduce "Detailed Visual Conditioning", which uses visual conditions encoded by a VAE to guide the generation process, thereby supporting additional generation tasks that require reference images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Omni-RS performs exceptionally well in understanding tasks and has achieved outstanding results in a variety of generative tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have been widely adopted for document parsing and optical character recognition (OCR), as they can accurately extract page-level elements. However, downstream applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) also require coherent document-level structure. Although these models indicate heading levels using different numbers of preceding ``\#'' symbols, page-by-page prediction often lacks document-level consistency. In practice, input-resolution and context-length constraints make it infeasible for a VLM to jointly process all page images in documents containing tens or hundreds of pages. To address this limitation, we propose a VLM-based framework that incrementally reconstructs heading hierarchies with a \emph{level-wise multimodal memory}. The memory retains a compact subset of all previously processed pages, selected by anchors. Our framework supports flexible anchor selection, and in this work we select the most recent node at each level, allowing the VLM to observe the visual, textual, and layout patterns of headings at every level. For comprehensive evaluation, we also introduce the Complex and Long Document Heading Hierarchy Reconstruction Benchmark (CLDoc-HHRBench), comprising 250 documents and 11,212 pages with expert-verified annotations. Experiments on CLDoc-HHRBench and three existing benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question-answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose CaRe (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time method for identifying and correcting modality misrouting. CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to identify a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, and flags potential misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the original joint prediction. For such cases, CaRe computes a residual direction from the discrepancy between the counterfactual and fused representations and uses it to steer the original multimodal state toward the relevant modality evidence, while retaining both modalities in the original audio-visual inference path. The intervention strength is adapted based on the confidence of the counterfactual branch. Experiments on CMM and AVHBench across two OLLMs show that CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.

bullets: Audio-visual interference can cause incorrect joint predictions even when the question-relevant unimodal branch predicts correctly.

papers.abstract: A medical vision-language model may analyze a given CT scan and correctly detect both kidneys in view. Continuing this conversation, if a user provides a prescription with an opposite direction, medical VLMs often sycophantically choose to realign their diagnosis. In this work, we study regressive sycophancy under fabricated evidence, where a model abandons a correct answer when pushback comes with a fake document. We test four open VLMs on 400 VQA-RAD yes/no questions in 19,200 multi-turn conversations, with and without a fabricated prescription. Without a disclosure that documents are synthetic, the models abandon 80.1% of 6,488 correct answers. Notably, under one script each, the same prescription raises the flip rate of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 45.9% to 89.6% and lowers that of Qwen3-VL-8B from 77.7% to 50.9%. A model rejected the prescription while still preserving the correct answer in 915 of 3,232 conversations with the prescription (28.3%), and 40% of these flipped in later turns. System-prompt sentences that disclose the documents as synthetic lower one model's flip rate from 77.8% to 47.3%. Thus, we conclude that awareness about a forgery does not prevent a model from adopting its answer.

papers.abstract: Table reasoning with language models typically assumes access to clean textual tables. In practice, tables are often serialized into text, which can corrupt cell contents, distort structural relationships, and discard visual cues, leaving the model to reason over incomplete evidence. In contrast, table images retain this information, but using it requires both accurate perception and reasoning grounded in the relevant cells. To address this, we propose MERIT (Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over Image Tables), a three-stage framework for learning to reason over table images, with serialized tables serving as optional auxiliary inputs (if provided). Our analysis identifies visual evidence acquisition as a bottleneck, motivating table-specific encoder adaptation through reconstruction, localization, and color-conditioned supervision. Building on the adapted representations, supervised fine-tuning teaches explicit evidence selection and reasoning using verified trajectories. Finally, reinforcement learning refines the policy with separate rewards for evidence correctness, calculation, final answers, and output format. By providing feedback on intermediate steps, the framework targets retrieval and computational errors that final-answer supervision alone does not distinguish. We evaluate the approach on table question answering and fact verification, analyze the contributions of visual inputs and training components, and assess generalization to additional datasets with different table structures and visual presentations.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering models often produce plausible responses even when the available visual evidence is insufficient to support a valid answer. Although prior work has introduced benchmarks and abstention mechanisms for unanswerable visual questions, it remains unclear which signals derived from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen image-question pairs. We systematically evaluate answerability signals on a stratified 10K subset of UNK-VQA using frozen InstructBLIP, covering predictive uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, visual grounding, visual dependence, internal representations, and learned probes. Answerability discrimination remains weak, with test AUROC largely confined to 0.50-0.54. CLIP alignment yields the highest point estimate but does not significantly outperform generation confidence under paired bootstrap analysis. Targeted removal of question-relevant visual evidence causes substantially larger changes in answer confidence than same-size random masking, yet intervention sensitivity provides essentially no answerability discrimination. Increasing probe capacity, combining multiple signals, and adding reason-aware supervision do not provide robust improvements, while post-freeze cross-validation yields similarly weak discrimination. Selective-answering analysis shows limited usable coverage under low-risk operating criteria. Failure-mode analysis shows that the relative utility of individual signals varies across perturbation mechanisms. Taken together, these results show that, on our UNK-VQA subset with frozen InstructBLIP, visual dependence, uncertainty, semantic alignment, and static representations are not robust standalone proxies for answerability. Our findings emphasize the need to distinguish a model's reliance on visual evidence from whether that evidence is sufficient to support an answer.
authors: Minjun Kim, Hyunmin Song, Changwon Lim
bullets: Evaluates answerability signals across uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, grounding, visual dependence, representations, and learned probes.
Discrimination is weak, with test AUROC generally around 0.50–0.54.

Removing question-relevant visual evidence changes confidence more than random masking, yet intervention sensitivity remains uninformative for answerability.
More powerful probes, signal combinations, reason-aware supervision, and post-freeze cross-validation yield no robust gains; useful selective-answering coverage is limited.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes answerability signals in a frozen vision-language model, relevant to multimodal LLM behavior and reliability.
papers.title: Visual Dependence Does Not Imply Answerability: A Systematic Analysis of Answerability Signals in Frozen InstructBLIP

papers.abstract: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- robotics, autonomous driving, human action, manufacturing, AR assistance, healthcare, recommendation, finance, and climate -- under video+TS and image+TS layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split covering classification and forecasting. The benchmark standardizes heterogeneous real-world sources into a shared schema with domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs reveals a shared bottleneck: representing time series as text creates very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence, especially in long-video settings. We then introduce TimeOmni-v, a multimodal LLM extension with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head. TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, showing that MMTA not only exposes representation and grounding failures but also motivates targeted model design.
authors: Ziyang Zhang, Shenyi Li, Yilin Wang, Ziyun Cui, Bowen Zhou, Wen Wu, Chao Zhang
bullets: Introduces tri-modal classification and forecasting tasks across nine domains using video+time-series and image+time-series layouts.
Standardizes heterogeneous sources with shared schemas, domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics.
Evaluates eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs, finding that text-based time-series representations produce long token sequences and weak visual alignment, especially for long videos.
Proposes TimeOmni-v with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and forecasting head.
TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, though the abstract does not report quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today's multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations, especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM, a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds the key temporal moments (When), the facial regions (Where), and verifies its causal necessity (Why) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87% (+13.39), with gains of +4.38 on actions, +6.77 on temporal emotion, and +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use.
authors: Anubhav Kataria, Shreya Ghosh, Jingwen Ye, Abhinav Dhall
bullets: Targets faithful explanations for small, evolving facial movements that existing MLLMs often describe without causal grounding.
Introduces ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video–text corpus built from CelebV-HQ and validated by humans and a two-model audit with at most 2.3% contradictions.
Uses H-TCC to identify key moments, relevant facial regions, and causal necessity through targeted occlusion.
Fine-tuning improves appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87%, with additional gains for actions, temporal emotion, and deepfake detection.
Evaluates explanation quality using pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, a sanity check, and a necessity test.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models often exhibit object hallucination, generating claims that are not supported by the input image. To mitigate this issue, we propose Evidence-Guided Visual Claim Admission (EGVCA), a training-free framework that admits a semantic claim only when it receives sufficient image-dependent support. EGVCA measures this support by comparing the claim likelihood under the observed image and a visual-null input. For captioning, it controls semantic expansion without altering token generation. For binary visual question answering, it combines atomic visual support with the image-induced change in the model's native Yes--No margin. Experiments on CHAIR, POPE, and MME across three LVLM backbones show that EGVCA substantially reduces object hallucination while preserving caption quality. It achieves the highest POPE F1 in eight of nine backbone--sampling settings and improves the native MME total score on all three backbones. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of claim-level admission as a simple alternative to token-level distribution correction.
authors: Hyeonggeun Han, Taehyun Cho, Sangwoo Hong
bullets: Targets object hallucination: models generate claims unsupported by the input image.
Compares claim likelihood with the observed image against a visual-null input to measure image-dependent support.
Controls semantic expansion for captioning and combines atomic support with image-induced Yes–No margin changes for binary VQA.
Across CHAIR, POPE, and MME on three backbones, it reduces hallucination while preserving caption quality.
Achieves the highest POPE F1 in eight of nine backbone–sampling settings and improves native MME total scores on all backbones.

papers.abstract: Although chain-of-thought prompting has improved multimodal reasoning, it is still difficult to produce correct final answers, as the reasoning can drift away from the image. Besides, the trace is already fixed when the answer is generated, leaving no room for self-correction. Considering the image is still available at the final-answer step, we think it is reasonable to fix the answer there without rewriting the reasoning. As such, the problem becomes to correct the final answer using the image under fixed reasoning. Unlike methods that improve trace generation through training, resampling, or decoding-time grounding, we repair the final-answer readout while keeping the reasoning trace fixed. The motivation is based on our finding that a wrong option can become prematurely committed in the reasoning while the correct option still has stronger image support in middle-to-deep layers. Thus, we propose Text-to-Visual Evidence Reallocation (TVER), a training-free method for final-answer repair. Specifically, TVER selects answer-related text and question-matched image patches, and moves bounded attention from text to patches. Furthermore, the patches are chosen in a middle-to-deep layer window based on question relevance. Our method improves answers across benchmarks and backbones, with gains in both multiple-choice and open-answer evaluations.
authors: Yulan Pan, Xiaoyu Xu, Zhihong Shen
bullets: Addresses answer errors caused when reasoning drifts from the image or prematurely commits to a wrong option.
Uses a training-free final-answer repair step rather than retraining, resampling, or modifying the reasoning trace.
Selects answer-related text and question-relevant image patches, then reallocates bounded attention from text to patches.
Chooses patches from a middle-to-deep layer window based on question relevance.
Improves performance across benchmarks and backbones in both multiple-choice and open-answer settings.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of TVER. The image, question, options, and CoT prefix are fixed. TVER selects a text-side source and a visual evidence target from the unmodified readout, then reruns only the final-answer line with capped attention reallocation.

Figure 1: The problem and our main idea. Prior training or decoding-time methods change the reasoning trace before the final answer is read. TVER keeps the trace fixed and changes only the final-answer readout by reallocating attention from answer-related text in the fixed context to selected visual evidence.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free final-answer repair for multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning directly fits multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: The Image Still Has a Say: Final-Answer Repair for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
papers.tldr: TVER repairs multimodal chain-of-thought answers by redirecting final-answer attention toward image evidence while leaving the reasoning trace unchanged.

papers.abstract: Reliable video reasoning requires models to produce correct answers and expose supporting visual evidence. Open-o3-Video enables verifiable reasoning by embedding timestamps and object-level bounding boxes into reasoning traces, but is restricted to frames from an initial sparse sampler. We introduce Open-o3-Video-v2, which formulates video reasoning as a unified agentic evidencegrounded process. The model identifies missing information, acquires additional observations, grounds the moments and objects supporting its reasoning, and writes this evidence into the trajectory before continuing or answering. To support this behavior, we construct STGR-v2-CoT135K, including 52K multi-turn agentic grounded reasoning trajectories, and STGR-v2-RL-13K for reinforcement learning. We further propose Clue-Seek GRPO (CS-GRPO), which tracks how tool calls change accumulated evidence, rewards clue coverage and step-wise gains, and penalizes excessive, repetitive, or uninformative retrieval. On V-STaR, Open-o3-Video-v2-4B achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM, outperforming its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone by 8.5% and 12.6%, respectively. It also delivers consistent gains across general video understanding, long-video reasoning, and temporal grounding benchmarks. These results show that active evidence acquisition and verifiable object-level grounding are complementary for reliable video reasoning. The code and models are released at https://msalab-pku.github.io/projects/Open-o3-Video-v2.
authors: Jiahao Meng, Zhongyuan Bao, Yue Tan, Haiquan Wen, Renrui Zhang, Anna Wang, Jason Li, Yanwei Fu, Yunhai Tong, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Frames video reasoning as an agentic process: identify gaps, retrieve additional observations, ground relevant moments and objects, then answer.
Introduces STGR-v2-CoT135K and STGR-v2-RL-13K datasets for multi-turn grounded reasoning and reinforcement learning.
Proposes Clue-Seek GRPO, rewarding evidence coverage and useful retrieval while penalizing repetitive or uninformative tool calls.
The 4B model achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM on V-STaR, with gains over its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone and across multiple video benchmarks.
Code and models are publicly released.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of the data construction pipelines and STGR-v2 data statistics. (a) Open-o3-Video constructs single-turn spatio-temporal grounded reasoning data through initial annotation, bounding-box filtering, and selfconsistency checking. (b) Open-o3-Video-v2 extends this pipeline to agentic multi-turn reasoning through strict data filtering, spatio-temporal evidence annotation, CoT (chain-of-thought) rewriting with tool observations, and quality checking. (c) STGR-v2-CoT-135K contains 135K SFT samples across seven task groups, including 59K spatio-temporal grounded reasoning samples, while STGR-v2-RL-13K contains 13K RL samples selected through strict filtering.

Figure 3 Overview of the reinforcement learning designs in Open-o3-Video and Open-o3-Video-v2. (a) Open-o3-Video produces a single-turn spatio-temporal grounded reasoning trace and optimizes it with format, answer-accuracy, and grounded thinking rewards; the thinking reward jointly evaluates temporal proximity and spatial overlap with the target evidence. (b) Open-o3-Video-v2 extends this formulation to multi-turn agentic reasoning with CS-GRPO. The model iteratively calls crop_video to acquire denser observations, while CS-GRPO tracks how the accumulated evidence evolves across calls and assigns credit according to whether each interaction contributes useful new evidence.

Figure 1 From single-pass spatio-temporal grounded reasoning to agentic evidence seeking and grounded reasoning. Left: Open-o3-Video-v1 reasons over fixed sampled frames and grounds visible evidence, yielding verifiable spatio-temporal support on short videos. Center: Open-o3-Video-v2 performs adaptive temporal zoom-in through iterative crop_video calls, following a seek–ground–reason process to find evidence beyond the initial frames for long video understanding. Right: Comparison of five models on V-STaR and six general video understanding and reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly used to identify and describe places, yet their recognition and knowledge of specific cultures remain poorly understood, particularly in underrepresented regions such as the Philippines. This study introduces the Tanawpamana Dataset, a repository of Philippine heritage site images with metadata based on the Talapamana registry of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts of the Philippines. We also introduce the Tanawpamana Benchmark, comprising 4,046 tasks designed to evaluate models' recognition and knowledge of heritage sites. Evaluating seven vision-language models, we find that they struggle more with fine-grained visual discrimination among similar heritage sites than with coarse recognition, and that their geographic knowledge is weaker when inferred from image inputs than from text.

papers.abstract: Sampling multiple reports creates an inference problem: how should sampled evidence be converted into a final decision, and does a better structured decision yield a better report? We study these questions through a framework that separates the decision signal, scoring objective, and feasible decision set, followed by text realization. On MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, controlled comparisons across 13 generator configurations per benchmark under grouped development/test evaluation reveal three findings. First, changing the objective under fixed evidence and rule capacity changes predictions and their held-out metric trade-offs. Second, relaxing candidate constraints has objective-dependent effects under shared signals and frozen scores. Diagnostics connect the IU macro-oriented assertion increase to near-zero label thresholds and show that limited candidate coverage coexists with selection headroom. Third, a controlled realization study with SFT-Qwen3-VL-8B shows that decision-level gains can be attenuated, amplified, or reversed. Change decomposition reveals that realization can remove incorrect assertions while losing correct findings, so target fidelity and reference accuracy need not improve together. Finding gains also do not consistently improve reference-based report quality. These results motivate separate evaluation of decision rules, candidate constraints, and realized reports.
authors: Kun Zhao, Haoteng Tang, Chenghua Lin, Liang Zhan
bullets: Studies how sampled report evidence is converted into structured decisions and then realized as text.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) support simultaneous listening and speaking, but often lag behind half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capabilities. We propose Dialogue-to-Duplex (D2), a framework that converts pretrained HD-SLMs into high-capability FD-SLMs at fine temporal granularity. D2 adapts the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and learns full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning. We systematically study the effects of chunk size on full-duplex interaction, general capabilities, and inference computation. We apply D2 to two distinct HD-SLM architectures, Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2. At a 12.5Hz update rate, Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves 99.2% turn-taking success with 521-ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art VoiceBench score of 70.1.
authors: Cheng-Kuang Chang, Alexander H. Liu, Brian Kingsbury, Hilde Kuehne, Rogerio Feris, Samuel Thomas, James Glass, Kai-Wei Chang

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) provide an interface for interleaved text-image generation, where generated visual states can directly inform subsequent reasoning and synthesis. However, existing systems are still primarily demonstrated on short trajectories or simplified visual content. We develop a large UMM natively trained on interleaved multimodal data, with strong capabilities in image synthesis, text rendering, complex composition, and multimodal planning, and study how to extend these native capabilities to substantially longer autoregressive trajectories. The main challenge is that generated images continuously accumulate in context: irrelevant or imperfect visual states interfere with future synthesis, while previously established characters and scenes must still be recovered after long intervals. We introduce a visual-memory framework that maintains persistent visual references, selectively retrieves scene-relevant historical states while preserving the complete semantic history, and uses few-step self-rollout to adapt the model to imperfect generated histories. We further introduce LongMIG-Bench for evaluating long-horizon text-to-multi-image and image-to-multi-image generation. Our model achieves high-fidelity long-horizon interleaved generation with strong character and scene consistency, demonstrating how visual memory can scale native interleaved generation to substantially longer trajectories.

papers.abstract: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (VQA) requires reasoning that extends beyond visible image content, demanding external commonsense and factual knowledge. While recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) as knowledge sources, the question of how deeply such guidance should be integrated into a vision language architecture remains underexplored. In this work, we generate structured reasoning guidance, visual focus concepts, distractor elements and external knowledge using Llama~3.3~70B and systematically compare two integration strategies within a unified frozen ViT + FLAN-T5 framework on the OK-VQA benchmark: decision level late fusion and attention-matrix injection. Contrary to the prevailing assumption that deeper integration is superior, we find that shallow late fusion achieves the strongest results (39.4% exact match, +10.0 over the no guidance baseline), outperforming deep attention modification (31.8%) under data scarce fine-tuning. We further contribute an LLM based augmentation pipeline that expands training data more than tenfold via question paraphrasing. Our findings indicate that integration depth must be matched to the data regime.
authors: Aneerban Saha, Vijay Kumar, Sameer Madhav D., Priyam Srivastava, Dhruv Bansal
bullets: Studies how deeply LLM-generated knowledge should be integrated into vision-language models for knowledge-based VQA.
Uses Llama 3.3 70B to generate reasoning guidance, visual focus concepts, distractors, and external knowledge.
Compares late decision-level fusion with attention-matrix injection in a frozen ViT + FLAN-T5 framework on OK-VQA.
Late fusion achieves 39.4% exact match, 10.0 points above the no-guidance baseline, versus 31.8% for deep attention modification.
Introduces an LLM-based question-paraphrasing pipeline that expands training data more than tenfold; results suggest integration depth should match the data regime.

papers.abstract: Visual in-context learning (ICL) enables vision-language models (VLMs) to adapt at test time via demonstration examples, but its effectiveness depends critically on the examples selected. Recent counterfactual selection methods improve ICL by constructing demonstrations that expose how individual attribute changes affect the answer. However, they require multi-stage pipelines involving attribute extraction, caption engineering, and composed image matching. We propose a simpler alternative grounded in a key observation: a model's own prediction errors are natural counterfactual demonstrations that directly encode its failure modes. Our method, SMILE (Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors), builds a model-specific pool of hard negatives offline by recording the target VLM's own mistakes. At test time, the prediction serves as a direction signal that surfaces, in the semantic embedding space, the past mistakes most likely to recur for the current query. This prediction-conditioned identification provides a unified mechanism for both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design. Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE delivers an average task-score gain of +3.09 points over the SOTA baseline at 5x lower latency. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/SMILE/
bullets: Visual ICL depends heavily on selecting effective demonstrations, while prior counterfactual methods require complex multi-stage pipelines.
SMILE offline-mines hard negatives from the target VLM’s own prediction errors to capture model-specific failure modes.
At test time, the model’s prediction guides semantic retrieval of likely recurring mistakes for the current query.
The same mechanism supports both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design.
Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE gains an average of 3.09 task-score points over the SOTA baseline with 5× lower latency.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
authors: Zhe Sun, Liang An, Jiayu Yao, Ronglai Qian, Jianing Cai, Ziwei Huang, Qing Fan, Zhiyuan Yang, Yujun Cai, Hongli Cao, Yiwei Wang, Xiaoyan Wang
bullets: Targets underwater signal recognition for vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing.

Includes a silent-audio control, gated coarse-to-fine evaluation, and a released training partition for future adaptation.

papers.abstract: Recent work has investigated Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs), models which can take multiple modalities and their combinations as input, as a way forward to have systems really capable of interacting with their environment. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for OLLMs, however, remains an open problem: existing methods largely target at most two modalities at a time, require access to model internals, or re-invocation of the evaluated model. We propose a model-agnostic UQ framework that scores a Chain-of-Thought response entirely through external omni-modal embeddings, measuring the grounding of the reasoning in the multimodal input and its internal coherence. Our contribution is the family of signals and an empirical characterisation of when it is reliable, rather than any single estimator: we find the geometric scores to be largely redundant with one another (mean within-split rank correlation 0.91-0.94) but strongly complementary to answer-dispersion baselines, and their reliability to depend on the generator and the modality. The resulting confidence estimates require no access to logits, hidden states or gradients of the evaluated model and no additional inference from it; they do require segmenting the reasoning trace with an auxiliary model and, for the aggregated score, a labelled calibration set that we show can be as small as 25 examples (although we also show that such a set buys little over fixing one signal a priori). On UNO-Bench, with both a closed and an open model, our scores yield small gains over self-consistency (systematic with the closed generator, mixed with the open one) and are competitive with self-verbalisation and internal-state baselines, especially in open-ended, omni-modal questions where previous state-of-the-art baselines struggle.
authors: Iacopo Ghinassi, Hy Nguyen Gia La, Luke Ong
bullets: Targets uncertainty quantification for inputs combining multiple modalities, beyond methods limited to two modalities.
Scores Chain-of-Thought grounding in multimodal inputs and internal coherence using external omni-modal embeddings.
Geometric signals are highly redundant with each other but complementary to answer-dispersion baselines; reliability varies by generator and modality.
On UNO-Bench, results provide small, systematic gains over self-consistency for a closed model and mixed gains for an open model, while remaining competitive with other baselines.
Requires an auxiliary model to segment reasoning traces; aggregated scoring may use a small labelled calibration set, though its benefit is limited.

papers.abstract: The rapid spread of face forgeries on the Web challenges the credibility of visual content. In practical Web environments, manipulated media originate from evolving generation pipelines and undergo diverse processing during dissemination, making reliable authenticity assessment under unseen manipulations and visual changes a critical challenge. We observe that a standard LoRA-adapted CLIP detector exhibits uneven patch-level decision dependence, concen trating a disproportionate share of class-specific relevance on a small fraction of visual patches. To improve robustness to variations in such highly dependent evidence, we propose EviStress, a two-stage framework for generalizable face forgery detection with textual explanations. In the first stage, Evidence-Targeted Patch Perturbation (ETPP) estimates patch dependence from global, relational, and semantic cues and assigns positively correlated perturbation probabilities, explicitly stress-testing highly dependent visual evidence during training. We further introduce Discriminative Variation Preservation (DVP), which constrains the residual between clean and perturbed representations to retain authenticity discriminative information. In the second stage, Intrinsic Evidence Instruction Tuning (IEIT) transfers the adapted CLIP encoder into LLaVA as its vision tower and performs parameter-efficient multimodal instruction tuning, enabling authenticity prediction and textual explanation directly from the learned forgery-sensitive representation without an external detector. Experiments demonstrate improved cross-dataset and cross-method generalization and corruption robustness, with the multimodal model providing authenticity predictions and human-readable explanations.
authors: Jiuyao Jing, Xuanyu Yi, Yu Zheng, Chunlei Peng
bullets: Targets the brittleness of CLIP-based detectors that rely disproportionately on a small number of image patches.
Uses Evidence-Targeted Patch Perturbation to identify and perturb highly dependent evidence during training.
Applies Discriminative Variation Preservation to retain authenticity-related information in perturbed representations.
Transfers the adapted CLIP encoder into LLaVA with parameter-efficient instruction tuning for prediction and explanation.
Reports improved cross-dataset, cross-method generalization and corruption robustness, with human-readable authenticity explanations.

papers.abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires integrating visual findings with task-specific evidence rather than relying on direct visual recognition alone. While tool-augmented medical agents can supply such evidence via external modules, they often lack explicit mechanisms for learning when auxiliary evidence is needed and for preventing inapplicable quantitative evidence from entering diagnostic reasoning. To address this, we propose X-Ragent, a post-training framework for tool-augmented reinforcement learning that decouples learned auxiliary-evidence seeking from validity-gated quantitative measurement acquisition for evidence-grounded CXR reasoning. We construct Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus combining causally ordered tool-augmented trajectories with report-style diagnostic reasoning, and use it to initialize Qwen3-VL-8B via agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We then optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using an accuracy-gated reward that applies process-level terms for measurement consistency and auxiliary-tool cost only to correct trajectories, preventing plausible process behavior from compensating for an incorrect diagnosis. Across three CXR benchmarks, X-Ragent achieves the strongest results, including an 8.6-point improvement on the fully held-out ChestAgentBench. By seeking evidence selectively and admitting only valid measurements, X-Ragent supports more faithful and evidence-grounded CXR reasoning.
authors: Yi Wang, Zhenlong Yuan, Yuchan Guo, Maolei Huang, Zijian Song, Dapeng Zhang, Rongbin Tan, Jiyuan Wang, Zhiyuan Wang, Fangfang Lin, Shuhan Song, Huawei Cao
bullets: Addresses tool-augmented CXR agents that lack selective evidence-seeking and safeguards against inapplicable measurements.
Uses reinforcement learning to decouple auxiliary-evidence acquisition from validity-gated quantitative measurement use.
Builds Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus, and initializes Qwen3-VL-8B with agentic supervised fine-tuning.
Optimizes with GRPO using accuracy-gated process rewards for measurement consistency and tool cost.
Achieves the strongest results across three CXR benchmarks, including an 8.6-point gain on held-out ChestAgentBench.

(iii) GRPO optimizes the policy with accuracy and format supervision, while tool-use cost and radiographic evidence consistency are gated by answer correctness. (iv) At inference, the policy selectively routes auxiliary tools, while an independent validity gate decides whether quantitative measurements are exposed; both are integrated in the second turn.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards commonly assigns one sequence advantage to an entire response. This outcome-level signal distinguishes overall response quality but leaves changes in visual-evidence use across generated tokens implicit. We introduce VAttnPO (Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization), which uses answer-conditioned visual attention to refine token-level credit while preserving the verifier-derived trajectory-mean advantage. A frozen old policy constructs a visual reference by teacher forcing the known correct answer and produces a visual distribution for each rollout token. VAttnPO measures their agreement in visual-attention space using Jensen--Shannon divergence, rather than reading guidance from teacher output-token distributions or introducing an attention-matching objective. Trajectory centering, relative-position weighting, and credit balancing turn this agreement into a zero-mean, position-aware correction to the GRPO sequence advantage. Token intervention, visual-index permutation, and trajectory analysis provide diagnostic evidence linking this signal to model behavior, visual correspondence, and generation position. On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, VAttnPO raises six-task image AVE from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50 and scores higher on every reported structured, video, and MME metric. Gains over GRPO also hold on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL3-8B-Instruct.
authors: Lihao Zheng, Zhenwei Shao, Zhou Yu, Yan Yang, Haoyi Sun, Qian Wang, Ning Mao, Pan Zhou
bullets: Problem: Sequence-level advantages do not reveal how visual evidence contributes across individual generated tokens.
Method: A frozen old policy compares rollout-token visual attention with attention from teacher-forced correct answers using Jensen–Shannon divergence.
The resulting signal is trajectory-centered, position-aware, and balanced before correcting the GRPO sequence advantage.
Diagnostics examine token interventions, visual-index permutations, and generation-position effects.
On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, image AVE improves from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50; gains also hold across other reported models and metrics.

papers.abstract: Visual contrastive decoding corrects answers using the prediction difference between the original image and a reference condition, yet the same contrast also turns supported abstentions into incorrect answers. We find that abstentions are lost at two stages: contrastive decoding with candidate filtering can exclude the abstention token before any comparison takes place, and the reference branch's response to the abstention instruction is removed when the reference prediction is subtracted. We therefore propose instruction-preserving decoding, which keeps the effect of the abstention instruction on the original-image prediction intact while leaving the contrast strength freely adjustable. Using a perturbed image and an image-free prediction as references, we obtain IP-VCD and IP-M3ID. On decision utility (DU), which credits both correct answers and supported abstentions, both methods outperform all compared non-IP baselines on every one of nine models on VizWiz, and IP-VCD also leads on eight of nine models on Food-101. Candidate measurements and paired per-question comparisons show that computing the instruction effect and the visual contrast term separately lets contrastive decoding support both correct answers and supported abstentions.
authors: Haonan Zhang, Ting Jin, Wenzhong Tang, Shuai Wang
bullets: Visual contrastive decoding can wrongly eliminate supported abstentions during candidate filtering or reference subtraction.
The proposed method preserves the abstention instruction’s effect on the original-image prediction while keeping contrast strength adjustable.
Two variants use perturbed-image and image-free references: IP-VCD and IP-M3ID.
Both outperform non-instruction-preserving baselines on decision utility across nine models on VizWiz; IP-VCD leads on eight of nine models on Food-101.
Separate measurement of instruction effects and visual contrast supports both correct answers and supported abstentions.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
authors: Yihang Huang, Peisong Wen, Chenhao Zhou, Difu Feng, Qianqian Xu
bullets: Fixed relevance–diversity weights vary substantially across tasks and even among samples within the same benchmark.
SAVER infers a sample-specific weight from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens using a Geometric Intent Prior.
It combines Weighted Text Centroid relevance scoring with Visual Marginal Coverage Gain diversity selection.
The training-free method retains 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B while using 11.1% of the original visual tokens.
It also generalizes to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models answer questions about images they were never shown, a failure called mirage. Such an answer can be correct without being justified by the evidence, and the difference matters wherever a model's output is checked by someone who did not see its input. We locate the failure in the training objective: cross-entropy separates a model that reads the image from one that ignores it by only the conditional mutual information between answer and image, and no training example rewards declining. We formalise support completion, TIDE, which also shows each training question with a blank image, a same-domain wrong image and an out-of-domain image, with targets that decline, and prove that under TIDE every image-blind predictor is suboptimal by at least 1.04 nats per example, that the optimum declines exactly on the counterfactual kinds while keeping its behaviour on valid images, and that for any finite model the error of its answer-or-decline decision, declining on valid input plus answering on invalid input, is bounded below by how well its representation separates valid from invalid evidence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B under a frozen held-out protocol with two judges, the three-condition predecessor of TIDE reduced the invalid-evidence mirage rate from 0.759 to 0.097 and the blank-image rate from 0.700 to 0.003 at a false-abstention cost of 0.126; label-free grounding raised the rate to 0.859, a likelihood-advantage contrast moved it only to 0.718 because its empty-image term carries no gradient, and grounding applied after support completion re-opened the mirage. The four-condition protocol on three base models, with seeds and component ablations, is in progress and not reported here.
authors: Alfaj Uddin Ahmed, Md. Shaown Miah, Md Arid Hasan, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury
bullets: Mirage occurs when models answer questions about unseen or irrelevant images, even if the answer happens to be correct.
The proposed support-completion objective presents valid, blank, same-domain wrong, and out-of-domain image conditions, with decline targets for invalid evidence.
Theory shows image-blind predictors are suboptimal under TIDE and links decision errors to how well representations separate valid from invalid evidence.
On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, a three-condition predecessor reduced invalid-evidence mirages from 0.759 to 0.097 and blank-image responses from 0.700 to 0.003, with a false-abstention cost of 0.126.
The full four-condition evaluation across three base models is still in progress; reported results use a predecessor protocol and two judges.

papers.abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.
authors: Yike Wu, Keyan Chen, Qixiong Wang, Xi Xiang, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses redundant, noisy, or disruptive computation in MLLMs during video spatial reasoning.
Uses a training-free multiagent framework that plans steps to gather missing spatial evidence and combines it with native evidence.
Applies stage-aligned verification to identify whether failures arise from planning, perception, or reasoning.
Uses dependency-based recovery to recompute affected states while preserving valid intermediate results.
Achieves the highest overall score among compared methods across three MLLMs and two benchmarks, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Current ASR models perform well on general benchmarks but still struggle with acoustically ambiguous words. Visual context can aid recognition in screen-based scenarios, yet existing benchmarks provide limited insight into the benefits of different types of visual evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ScreenASR-Bench , a tiered benchmark with three progressively challenging levels: Explicit Textual Evidence (ETE), based on direct on-screen text; Explicit Visual Evidence (EVE), using visible content rather than on-screen text; and Implicit Semantic Evidence (ISE), requiring scene-level inference. Extensive experiments on ASR models, Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) and Omni models show that incorporating visual context substantially improves recall over the audio-only setting across all three model families. The gains are largest for ETE and smallest for ISE, indicating that models leverage direct visual evidence more effectively than indirect semantic cues. To facilitate future research on visually grounded speech recognition, we publicly release ScreenASR-Bench.
authors: Mingwei Fu, Zheshu Song, Zhikai Zhou, Shen Huang, Shidong Shang, Mengxiao Zhu
bullets: Targets acoustically ambiguous words in screen-based ASR scenarios.
Introduces three tiers: Explicit Textual Evidence, Explicit Visual Evidence, and Implicit Semantic Evidence.
Tests ASR, Large Audio-Language, and Omni models with visual context.
Visual input improves recall across all model families, with the largest gains for direct on-screen text and the smallest for scene-level inference.
The benchmark is publicly released to support research on visually grounded speech recognition.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image models have made remarkable progress in visual fidelity and instruction following, yet complex compositional generation remains challenging. Existing agentic approaches address this limitation through iterative generation and editing, adapting their actions based on interaction history. However, they typically fix the continuation state (i.e., the image from which refinement proceeds) to the latest image. Since iterative editing is not necessarily monotonic, the agent may continue refining from the latest image even when it has already degraded. In this work, we introduce GenRevisit, an agentic framework that extends action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection. The agent can not only use interaction history to adjust editing instructions but also select an image candidate to edit, jointly deciding where to continue from and how to refine. We train GenRevisit with SFT followed by agentic reinforcement learning. To address the coarse credit assignment of final outcome reward in GRPO, which assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, we further propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to redistribute positive advantage according to each action's contribution to reducing the remaining objective. On GenEval2, GenRevisit achieves GM scores of 84.3 and 74.4 with Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo, surpassing the strongest baselines using the same generators by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively. GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2 among baselines.
authors: Zixu Wang, Xiaoran Zhao, Yahui Liu, Feng-ao Wang, Junhao Xiao, You Shu, Bing Liu, Yiting Liu, Songlei Jian, Zhiliang Tian, Dongsheng Li
bullets: Addresses degradation caused by always refining the latest image in iterative editing.
Jointly selects a continuation image from interaction history and the next editing action.
Uses supervised fine-tuning followed by agentic reinforcement learning.
Introduces Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to assign credit based on each action’s contribution.
Achieves state-of-the-art results among baselines on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2; on GenEval2, it improves GM scores by 12.7 and 10.9 points with two generators.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) extend LLMs to process heterogeneous modalities (e.g., vision, audio, and IMU signals) alongside language, enabling a broader range of multimodal tasks. Yet we find that these models often fail to express information from non-textual modalities even when they perceive it correctly. We term this disconnect knows-but-cannot-say. To investigate this phenomenon, we introduce Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA), which measures the alignment between individual modality representations and response representations. Our analysis shows that non-textual representations are less aligned with response tokens and receive less attention than textual representations, suggesting a potential explanation for uneven modality preferences. Motivated by these findings, we propose OmniCatalyst, a simple perceive $\rightarrow$ infer strategy that complements the original modality inputs with self-generated text, making non-textual knowledge more accessible. Across seven Omni-LLMs, OmniCatalyst consistently improves performance (+7.29%) and yields more balanced modality preferences, with further gains from diverse training strategies. Further analysis demonstrates that the knowledge extraction phases increase TMA, suggesting that improved alignment makes non-textual information more accessible during response generation. In summary, our findings uncover how Omni-LLMs can better express modality knowledge through language. Our code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/OmniLLM.
authors: Na Min An, Taekyung Kim, Jaemyung Yu, Hyunjung Shim, Dongyoon Han
bullets: Identifies a “knows-but-cannot-say” gap between multimodal perception and language responses.
Introduces Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA) to measure alignment between modality representations and response tokens.

OmniCatalyst uses a perceive → infer strategy to supplement original inputs with generated textual knowledge.
Across seven Omni-LLMs, it consistently improves performance by 7.29% and balances modality preferences; gains are linked to increased TMA.

(b) Across samples, text representations systematically exhibit higher TMA and attention than non-textual representations, revealing their greater accessibility to language-centric generation. papers.abstract: Reusable skills improve multimodal agents without updating model weights, but their effectiveness depends on both the evidence presented and the procedure used to read it. We introduce ViewCraft, which jointly evolves an executable evidence interface and its reading procedure. The interface selects, transforms, and organizes observations; the reader interprets the resulting views. Failure traces guide revisions, replay and paired evaluation retain useful changes, and interface projection recovers visual edits from eligible rejected joint proposals. Across eight benchmarks, ViewCraft improves over direct execution by an average of $6.1$ points in task score, with gains on every benchmark. The advantage persists at a matched input-token budget. On all five multi-source tasks, the learned interface uses 8%-15% fewer input tokens than Initial skill. The learned skills also transfer across executors and outperform direct execution in every evaluated transfer, supporting evidence construction and reading as a coupled, reusable skill.
authors: Binxiao Xu, Ruichuan An, Bocheng Zou, Weihua Du, Xinyu Wei, Hangyu Guo, YiFan Zhang, Renye Yan, Chengqi Duan, Hang Hua
bullets: Addresses the limitation that reusable multimodal-agent skills depend on both evidence presentation and reading procedures.

Maintains its advantage under matched input-token budgets and uses 8%–15% fewer input tokens on five multi-source tasks.
Learned skills transfer across executors, supporting coupled evidence construction and reading as reusable capabilities.

papers.abstract: We study how to detect and mitigate visual attention sinks in vision-language models (VLMs). Visual attention sinks are image tokens that absorb a large share of attention over the image regardless of the query or task, and they mislead methods that treat attention maps as a record of where the model ``looked.'' Prior work has detected sinks through massive activation dimensions and proposed redistributing their attention, but none have addressed what makes a token become a sink. Comparing six candidate detectors on ten VLMs from four families, we find that only the centered cosine similarity between an image token's key and the key of the language model's text-sink detects visual sinks. Thus, a visual sink is an image token whose key aligns with the text-sink's key. Moving a sink's key component along this direction to the median of the image keys sends its attention back to the text-sink (\textbf{Are Borrowed}) while leaving model answers unchanged~(\textbf{Not Seen}). Building on this, we propose a training-free, entropy-triggered re-look that first cleans the attention map, then crops the most-attended region of the cleaned map and inserts it into the reasoning trace. Cleaning adds negligible computation to the forward pass, and the re-look improves accuracy with a mean gain of $+4.3$ points on fine-detail VQA benchmarks across model families.

bullets: Only centered cosine similarity between an image token’s key and the language model’s text-sink key reliably detects visual sinks across six detectors and ten VLMs.

papers.title: Attention Sinks in VLMs Are Borrowed, Not Seen
papers.tldr: Visual attention sinks in VLMs are borrowed from the text-sink key direction, and removing them enables a training-free re-look that improves fine-detail VQA accuracy.

papers.abstract: The introduction of long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and external tools has substantially improved the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on general and reasoning tasks. However, existing fast-slow reasoning paradigms mainly regulate textual reasoning length, while visual computation introduced by external tools or visual tokens is often treated as an auxiliary component. This separation prevents MLLMs from jointly optimizing visual perception and textual reasoning. To address this issue, we propose L2T (adaptive Look, flexible Thought), a unified reasoning framework that jointly optimizes the form and depth of computation. L2T first discretizes tool-produced visual states into visual tokens, bringing visual perception and textual reasoning into a shared autoregressive space. Based on this unified representation, L2T introduces a modality-aware routing reward to select appropriate reasoning modes and a difficulty-aware fast-slow strategy to adapt reasoning depth according to task complexity. Experiments on general perception and reasoning-intensive tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of L2T. Compared with explicit tool-calling approaches, L2T maintains competitive performance while achieving 1.7--3.6 times higher throughput.
authors: Quanlin Chen, Xiuwei Chen, Kun Xiang, Zehua Ma, Chunjin Ye, Boqiang Guo, Xianming Liu, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Addresses the separation between visual computation and textual fast-slow reasoning in multimodal large language models.

Uses modality-aware routing to select reasoning modes and a difficulty-aware strategy to adapt reasoning depth.
Performs effectively on general perception and reasoning-intensive tasks.
Achieves 1.7–3.6× higher throughput than explicit tool-calling approaches while maintaining competitive performance.
