papers.abstract: Scene classification of remote sensing imagery with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is formulated as a single-forward-pass decision problem: candidate class names are lettered options in the prompt, a registered answer slot is conditioned on the prompt, and classification is read out by scoring letter tokens with the language-modeling head. We show that although this letter binding is highly effective within its training vocabulary (97.71% OA on UCM), it behaves erratically out of vocabulary: zero-adaptation accuracy across four cross-dataset directions fluctuates between 7.35% and 96.40%, and under out-of-vocabulary weights its confidence fails inversely on open-set evaluation, assigning higher confidence to unseen than to seen classes (AUROC 0.38), a failure we term silent hallucination. We retain the slot representation and replace the readout with RSAJEV, a training-free abstaining prototype memory that performs retrieval-based prototype matching: K reference images per class are cached as prototypes via their slot representations under the same prompt, and classification becomes nearest-neighbor retrieval over the prototypes, refined by a shrinkage-Mahalanobis geometric correction. This readout is mechanistically isomorphic to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) but operates on discriminative decisions; it is the first retrieval-based readout for MLLM slot representations. The retrieval readout reaches 89.43% on the UCM cross-dataset gate with 16 references per class and zero gradient updates, and 96.90% on AID. Its ID-ness scores attain 0.91-0.99 AUROC on open-set evaluation over two datasets, exceeding symbolic confidence (0.38-0.96) in all four open-set settings, restoring a calibratable abstention channel and supporting class addition/removal at zero extra inference cost via offline rescoring of the cached matrix.
authors: Man Chen, Antai Chen, Shuai Xu, Chengjie Gu, Huaping Zhou, Kelei Sun, Tao Wu, Yongjie Huang
bullets: Problem: MLLM letter binding is unreliable out of vocabulary, with unstable cross-dataset accuracy and higher confidence on unseen classes.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are good at video understanding and code generation, but it remains unclear whether they can recover the physical laws underlying videos, a capability essential for converting videos into executable simulations and for providing structured physical supervision in robotics. Captioning motion video does not imply that a model has inferred its governing dynamics, estimated quantitative parameters, or can regenerate the observed scene from code. Existing video-physics benchmarks evaluate plausibility, property estimation, or future-state prediction, but offer limited insight into whether models can translate visual dynamics into runnable simulation code. We introduce PhySimCode, a benchmark for physics video-to-code generation: given only a raw video, a model must infer the relevant physics, recover parameter values, and generate runnable Python that reproduces the input video. The dataset contains 160.6K procedurally generated samples spanning 162 physics phenomena across analytic SciPy simulations and PyBullet-rendered rigid-body, articulated, fluid, and contact-rich scenes; each sample bundles the simulation code, physical parameters, rendered video, and a structured chain-of-thought covering observations, laws, ODEs, numerical methods, and validation checks. We evaluate ten state-of-the-art closed- and open-source MLLMs along physical-law correctness, simulation equivalence, code executability, and parameter recovery. Models reliably state physics laws (4.27-4.93/5) yet score only 1.51-2.47/5 on inferring them from video, and the best system (Claude Sonnet 4.6) recovers just 7.7% of ground-truth parameters within $\pm 20\%$, exposing a substantial video-to-simulation gap. The 2,430-video evaluation set is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SourajaKundu123/PhySimCode and the evaluation code at https://github.com/SourajaKundu/PhySimCode
authors: Souraja Kundu, Aditya Gupta, Joel Julin, Yizhou Zhao, Liuyue Xie, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Targets video-to-code generation requiring physical-law inference, parameter recovery, and runnable simulation reproduction.

Evaluates law correctness, simulation equivalence, code executability, and parameter recovery across 10 MLLMs.
Models state physics laws well (4.27–4.93/5) but infer them from video poorly (1.51–2.47/5).
The best system recovers only 7.7% of ground-truth parameters within ±20%, highlighting the benchmark’s challenging scope.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) substantially enhances the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by explicitly modeling intermediate reasoning processes. However, most learning-based MCoT methods follow a stage-centric paradigm, where different reasoning behaviors are assigned to predefined stages and optimized separately. This results in fragmented reasoning and a training-inference reasoning-state gap. To address these limitations, we propose ReState, a unified iterative reasoning framework that reformulates multimodal reasoning from a stage-driven pipeline into a state-driven dynamic process. It comprises two complementary components: Unified Reasoning State Modeling (URSM) and Closed-Loop Reasoning-State Learning (CRSL). URSM unifies reasoning construction, correct reasoning preservation, and erroneous reasoning correction as reasoning-state transitions within a shared state space, enabling these heterogeneous reasoning behaviors to be learned jointly. CRSL further incorporates self-generated historical reasoning states during training and recursively updates the current state during inference, thereby mitigating the reasoning-state gap and enabling iterative self-refinement without requiring an additional reflection module, critic, or independent correction stage. Furthermore, we construct VersaCoT-10K, a high-quality CoT dataset spanning eight visual reasoning domains, which provides diverse supervision for multi-domain reasoning and reasoning-state refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReState exhibits strong adaptability across different MLLM backbones and achieves strong performance on multiple public reasoning benchmarks, supporting the shift from stage-centric reasoning toward state-centric reasoning. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/YuChuang1205/ReState
authors: Chuang Yu, Xuefei Ma, Yuanhao Feng, Wuxiong Zeng, Bo Wang, Minghong Cai, Dongming Wu, Fei Zhou, Chen Tang, Wenwen Tong, Lewei Lu, Xiangyu Yue
bullets: Stage-centric MCoT can fragment reasoning and create a gap between training and inference reasoning states.
Unified Reasoning State Modeling jointly represents reasoning construction, preservation, and correction in one state space.
Closed-Loop Reasoning-State Learning uses historical self-generated states during training and recursive updates during inference.
VersaCoT-10K provides supervision across eight visual reasoning domains for multi-domain reasoning and state refinement.
Experiments show strong adaptability across MLLM backbones and performance across multiple public reasoning benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the ReState framework. During training, URSM learns a shared state-update operator from empty, correct, and erroneous reasoning states, while CRSL feeds model-generated historical states back into training to reduce the training-inference reasoning-state mismatch. At inference, the same model recursively updates the current reasoning state and answer, enabling iterative self-refinement without additional critics, reflection modules, or separate correction stages.
Figure 3: Construction pipeline of VersaCoT-10K dataset. It consists of three stages: Data Collection and Standardization, CoT Annotation and Quality Control, and Reasoning-State Augmentation.

Figure 1: Comparison of reasoning paradigms and performance. The stage-centric paradigm assigns different reasoning behaviors to predefined stages, leading to fragmented modeling and a traininginference reasoning-state gap. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified state-driven iterative reasoning framework for MLLMs, directly relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs
papers.tldr: ReState reframes multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning as iterative state transitions, enabling unified learning and self-refinement across reasoning behaviors and domains.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models achieve promising results on visual reasoning tasks, approaching human-level performance on existing STEM benchmarks. However, these capabilities degrade under complex real-world scenes. We identify that chain-of-thought reasoning remains largely confined to the linguistic space, rarely anchoring each step in visual evidence. The main cause is the absence of such data during training. In this work, we introduce a training data augmentation pipeline, \textbf{Visual Augmentation Primitives} (VAP), which leverages state-of-the-art vision generative models to synthesize diverse photorealistic training samples and corresponding reasoning text. VAP introduces some basic operators and applies them to a seed image and gets a variant. It also constructs coherent multimodal reasoning chains throughout the generation process. Such training data force models to perceive visual content and perform logical reasoning according to them at every step. We further introduce multimodal chain-of-thought rubric-based reinforcement learning to enhance this. It rewards not only text reasoning but also visual reasoning by scoring intermediate reasoning steps for logical validity, completeness, and consistency. Moreover, we construct the UNREAL benchmark to systematically evaluate visual reasoning on hyperrealistic scenes across controllable difficulty levels. Experiments show that a 4B model built on this framework surpasses 8B baselines, with performance improving consistently as the model scales to 32B, validating the scaling law for visual reasoning.
authors: Fan Yang, Lifeng Chen, Yipu Wang, Han Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Zhiyang Chen, Chaoyang Zhao, Lingxiang Wu, Hanqi Jiang, Yibo Chen, Xu Tang, Yao Hu, Ming Tang, Xiaojie Jin, Xiaolong Zheng, Jinqiao Wang
bullets: Addresses the weak visual grounding of chain-of-thought reasoning in complex real-world scenes.
Introduces Visual Augmentation Primitives (VAP), which generate photorealistic image variants and coherent multimodal reasoning chains.
Uses rubric-based reinforcement learning to reward logical validity, completeness, and consistency in both textual and visual reasoning.
Introduces UNREAL, a benchmark for visual reasoning on hyperrealistic scenes with controllable difficulty.
A 4B model surpasses 8B baselines, with performance improving through 32B scale, supporting a visual-reasoning scaling law.

papers.abstract: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.

papers.abstract: Image-computable low-level image saliency has shaped perceptual psychology and computer science, but is limited by its inability to capture human high-level cognitive factors that influence attention and eye movements. Here, we propose a new fully automated method to compute semantic saliency by quantifying each object's contribution to scene comprehension without fitting any parameters to human data: the Automated Scene Understanding Map (AUTO-SUM). AUTO-SUM automatically segments and removes individual objects from a scene, uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to describe the original and modified scenes, and measures the semantic similarity between these descriptions using text embeddings. We show that AUTO-SUM can predict which object is most important in a human-measured scene understanding map (H-SUM) estimated using human scene descriptions. We also show that AUTO-SUM can predict the object most fixated by human observers during free viewing and scene description tasks better than a low-level saliency model (GBVS, Itti-Koch), a saliency model trained based on human meaning ratings (Meaning Map), and comparable to DeepGaze, which is trained on human fixation data. We contend that AUTO-SUM can be used as a semantic saliency model that complements lower-level saliency models. Code are available at https://github.com/starsky77/AUTO-SUM-Source-Code .
authors: Ziqi Wen, Shravan Murlidaran, Jonathan Skaza, William Wang, Miguel P. Eckstein
bullets: Addresses the limits of low-level saliency models, which do not capture high-level semantic factors influencing attention.
Removes objects from scenes, compares MLLM descriptions of the original and altered scenes, and uses text-embedding similarity to quantify object importance.
Predicts the most important object in human scene-understanding maps without fitting parameters to human data.
Predicts human fixations in free viewing and scene-description tasks better than several baseline saliency models and comparably to DeepGaze.
Designed to complement, rather than replace, low-level saliency models; code is publicly available.

Figure 1: Generation of human and automated scene understanding maps. (a) The original Human scene understanding map (H-SUM) procedure from Murlidaran and Eckstein [36]. In the Object Removal (OR) stage, objects are digitally removed from the scene one at a time. In the Scene Description (SD) stage, human participants describe the original scene (gold standard description, GS) and each object-removed version (D1, . . . , Dn). In the Similarity Rating (SR) stage, human raters judge the similarity between the GS and each description of a manipulated scene; the lower the similarity, the larger the contribution of the removed object to scene understanding, and the object’s region is weighted accordingly to produce the scene understanding map. The fixation heatmap from an eye-tracking study of the same scene is shown for comparison. In the present study, the H-SUM uses human descriptions (SD stage) but the same automated OR and SR stages as AUTO-SUM. (b) AUTO-SUM. OR stage: an MLLM is prompted to list all objects in the scene; each object name is passed to a text-prompted detection and segmentation model to obtain the object’s mask, and an image inpainting model removes the masked object. This is repeated for every listed object. SD stage: an MLLM describes the original image and each object-removed image. SR stage: the descriptions are encoded by a language-embedding model, and the cosine similarity between the embeddings of the original and the manipulated scene descriptions replaces the human similarity rating. Each object’s mask is weighted by its similarity-based score to produce the AUTO-SUM.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison of scene understanding maps, low-level saliency (GBVS), and human fixations. Each row shows the original image, AUTO-SUM-C, H-SUM, the GBVS saliency map, and the human fixation map; all maps are normalized to [0, 1]. (a) Scenes in which AUTO-SUM-C and H-SUM identify the same most critical object. (b) Scenes in which the two maps assign the highest importance to different objects. In both cases, GBVS often peaks on high-contrast regions that humans rarely fixate, such as the volleyball net pole and the washing machine in (a) or the countertop edge in (b). In contrast, AUTO-SUM-C and H-SUM more often assign high importance to the objects that attract the most fixations, such as the volleyball, the cat and its food, and the small bird next to the bottle.

papers.abstract: With the rapid proliferation of social media, harmful memes have become a growing threat to online ecosystems. Their harmfulness is often implicitly conveyed through complex interactions among visual, textual, and contextual cues, making accurate detection challenging. Recent studies have introduced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and external knowledge into harmful meme detection. However, existing methods mainly retrieve similar instances or auxiliary information, limiting their ability to capture reusable harmfulness knowledge and underlying reasoning mechanisms, and thus constraining both detection performance and interpretability. To address these challenges, we propose MemeLogos, a knowledge-driven retrieval-augmented reasoning framework for harmful meme detection. MemeLogos abstracts recurring harmfulness patterns and reasoning structures from diverse harmful cases into reusable knowledge units and organizes them into a dedicated star-shaped knowledge graph. By combining structured knowledge retrieval with an explicit multi-stage reasoning process inspired by cognitive mechanisms, MemeLogos leverages retrieved knowledge to guide harmfulness reasoning, improving both detection reliability and interpretability. Extensive experiments show that MemeLogos consistently outperforms existing harmful meme detection methods while generating more coherent and interpretable reasoning, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured harmfulness knowledge for multimodal content understanding.
authors: Hexiang Gu, Saihui Hou, Changlan Liu, Min Ren, Huijia Wu, Hongxun Gu, Zhaofeng He
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of detecting implicitly harmful content expressed through visual, textual, and contextual interactions.

papers.abstract: Despite significant advances in language understanding, Large Language Models (LLMs) can still miss meaning hidden in plain sight, failing to identify harmful intent in expressions readily understood by humans. Malicious users exploit this gap by strategically disguising harmful content to evade automated moderation, posing a serious threat to online platform safety. The vulnerability reflects a fundamental cognitive asymmetry between human readers, who integrate contextual, phonetic, and visual cues to decipher the intent behind deliberate obfuscation, and text-based LLMs, which rely primarily on token sequences and have limited exposure to evolving evasions. To bridge this asymmetry, we propose PASP (Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play), which combines multi-perceptual views with adversarial self-play to improve understanding of harmful intent as evasions evolve. Specifically, PASP constructs textual, phonetic, and visual views of each input, preserving its original context while exposing pronunciation and glyph cues obscured in token space. During adversarial self-play, an attacker uses defender feedback to generate intent-preserving evasions, while the defender is trained using an intent-invariance reward to understand harmful intent across changing surface forms. Extensive experiments show that PASP reduces adaptive attack success rates by up to 73.71% and 74.49% on ChineseHarm-Bench and EvoHarmBench, respectively, preserves model capabilities with minimal degradation, and effectively interprets real-world evasive expressions in e-commerce.

papers.abstract: Most benchmarks for large language models in medicine are built from licensing examinations and theoretical questions. The few that draw on real clinical data do so only in part, and rarely require a model to read a patient's own imaging. ClinEdge addresses this gap with 32 real, de-identified patient cases from active clinical practice, each evaluated across seven frontier systems for a total of 224 expert-graded evaluations. Each case pairs primary imaging with a short vignette, contains a feature known to defeat pattern-matched reasoning, and is scored against the patient's documented clinical course. The suite is built for depth rather than volume. Grading followed a two-stage expert process. First, a senior orthopaedic surgeon graded all 224 responses on a weighted rubric and a pass-or-fail verdict. Second, a panel of nineteen physicians, largely senior specialists at teaching medical colleges, independently reviewed every case and every one of the 224 grades. All seven production systems were evaluated through their public interfaces, and all 224 conversations are preserved as replayable links. Performance was poor across all systems, and the failures were shared: different vendors missed the same findings and converged on the same wrong plans. From the experts' notes we catalogue 18 recurring failure modes in five families. The models stop reading an image at the first finding. They give generic plans and lean toward over-treatment. They trust a misleading history over correct imaging. Their answers vary across systems and runs, and change with question format. Failing answers were delivered fluently and without any expressed uncertainty. Four cases are released in full; the remaining 28 are held out, and we invite frontier AI labs and healthcare AI companies to evaluate their models against them (research@futrbridge.com)

papers.abstract: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) perform both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one shared Transformer backbone, yet how the backbone processes the condition in either direction remains poorly understood. We study this question from the perspective of conditional guidance: we probe every attention head to show the activation difference between two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) with different conditional guidance. On two unified VLMs of autoregressive and masked-diffusion paradigms, the probing reveals a subset of heads that are more sensitive to the change of condition while others are agnostic to it. This characteristic pattern holds in both T2I and I2T generation and is largely stable across data samples, demonstrating the internal mechanism of unified VLMs. Motivated by this, we propose a new inference-time intervention approach for unified multimodal generation, named \textit{HeadTuned-CFG}, which uses the probed condition-change awareness to select and tune the conditional guidance at the attention-head level. Experiments show consistent benefits in both multimodal generation directions of unified VLMs without additional training, and in particular substantial improvements over strong baselines in T2I generation. These results further support the key finding of our probing analysis: the observed pattern of functional specialization is an intrinsic property of unified VLMs.
authors: Zhengyang Luo, Xiaoyu Qiu, Zhiheng Tan, Yuchen Liang, Yingbin Liang, Liyue Shen

Experiments report consistent gains in T2I and I2T generation, with particularly substantial T2I improvements over strong baselines.
The findings suggest functional specialization is an intrinsic property of unified VLMs.

papers.abstract: Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. Drawing on interactionally embedded Gestalt principles of multimodal human communication, we introduce GesBench: a human-grounded benchmark for cue-level social perception in multimodal LLMs. GesBench uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models form stable interpretations of speaker intention and social affordance, and human gaze-guided corruption to evaluate whether regions attended by humans are functionally important for model judgments. Built from more than 6000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversational datasets, GesBench includes human annotations of unfolding judgments and gaze on a representative subset. Across open and closed multimodal models, we find a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models often hedge or repeat across different clips. GesBench shifts social evaluation from whether models eventually recognize meaning to when and where that meaning is formed. Our codes are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/GesBench-share-212C.
authors: Zonghuan Li, Hayley Hung, Chirag Raman
bullets: Addresses the gap between final-answer benchmarks and humans’ incremental, cue-sensitive social perception.
Uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models stabilize interpretations of speaker intent and social affordance.
Applies human gaze-guided corruption to test whether human-attended regions influence model judgments.
Covers more than 6,000 scripted and unscripted conversational clips, with human annotations on a representative subset.
Finds that humans interpret earlier and revise more, while models often hedge or repeat across clips.

papers.abstract: Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation have posed a promising direction for multimodal tasks. However, learning effective tool invocation usually relies on curated question-answer pairs or expert demonstrations at scale, which are expensive to acquire. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple-yet-effective self-evolution approach that enables learning tool invocation from unlabeled images. Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning. To encourage effective tool invocation, a good training question should be difficult enough to warrant tool use, yet remain within the solver's capabilities. To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver's performance difference with and without access to tools. With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation. Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1\% --- demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision.

Scope: training relies on unlabeled images, while the approach targets adaptive question complexity without human supervision.

papers.abstract: As text-to-speech (TTS) systems continue to advance, provenance tracking and security verification of synthesized speech have become increasingly important. Audio watermarking provides active provenance by embedding imperceptible, machine-recoverable information into speech. However, existing post-hoc methods typically modify the waveform after synthesis, leaving the watermark vulnerable to compound perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose GAMW, a watermark injection framework integrated into the TTS generation process. Before waveform synthesis, GAMW embeds a content-adaptive multi-bit watermark residual into the generated representation, and its decoding objective combines focal modulation with dynamic per-bit weighting. We train and evaluate GAMW separately on two TTS backbones. With a 16-bit payload, GAMW improves decoding accuracy over the strongest baseline by 9.2 and 23.5 percentage points under individual and compound perturbations, respectively, while maintaining competitive speech quality. Reliable clean-speech decoding is also retained at higher payloads. Code is available at https://github.com/ZConJugaTe/GAMW.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have excelled in joint visual and language understanding, particularly in image captioning. However, LVLMs remain prone to object hallucination, describing non-existent entities in the given image. Previous remedies, including dataset-enhanced supervised training and reinforcement learning from human feedback, show promise but rely heavily on costly human involvement, limiting scalability. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning framework to mitigate object hallucination in LVLM-based image captioning, driven entirely by natural language processing (NLP) metrics. While optimizing reinforcement learning solely on NLP metrics offers scalability, it also introduces pitfalls: reward hacking, sparse feedback, and costly training. Our framework sidesteps these by introducing an Object Consistency Score (OCS) capturing both correctness and coverage of objects, incorporating KL-regularization for denser token-level guidance, and designing a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters atop a frozen LVLM backbone, achieving efficiency and stability. Extensive experiments on the InstructBLIP baseline demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our framework, achieving a substantial hallucination reduction of up to 41\% on the COCO dataset and 29\% on the Visual Genome. Furthermore, the framework can enhance caption quality by incorporating complementary evaluation metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR. These results reveal a broader insight in multimodal learning: LVLMs can effectively self-correct hallucinations using metric feedback, motivating deeper exploration into scalable reinforcement frameworks that significantly reduce human effort.
authors: Thanh Nguyen, Hee Suk Yoon, Tung Minh Luu, Eunseop Yoon, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Targets hallucinated objects—entities described in captions but absent from images—without human supervision.
Uses an Object Consistency Score to measure object correctness and coverage, plus KL regularization for denser guidance.
Introduces a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters while keeping the LVLM backbone frozen.
Reports hallucination reductions of up to 41% on COCO and 29% on Visual Genome with InstructBLIP.
Can also improve caption quality using complementary metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR.

papers.abstract: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has advanced vision-language reasoning, but its sequence-level rewards provide limited credit assignment for individual reasoning tokens. On-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this issue by providing dense supervision on student-generated trajectories, yet standard OPD assigns similar importance to all teacher-preferred tokens, including template phrases and visually irrelevant continuations. We introduce Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation (VC-OPD), a grounding-aware distillation method that prioritizes tokens whose correctness depends on image-specific evidence. After a teacher-supervised warm start that stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts, VC-OPD performs on-policy distillation with two teacher evaluations for each student trajectory: one under the original image and one under a counterfactual image with corrupted instance-specific evidence. The original-image teacher distribution determines the distillation target, while the original--counterfactual teacher gap estimates token-level visual dependence and softly reweights the loss. To avoid unstable response-level update scales, VC-OPD further applies mass-preserving normalization to the token weights. This design preserves the dense supervision of OPD while shifting learning capacity toward visually grounded reasoning tokens. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that VC-OPD improves visual reasoning performance and produces more effective token-level distillation.
bullets: Addresses weak token-level credit assignment in sequence-level GRPO rewards and uniform weighting in standard OPD.
Uses teacher distributions from the original and counterfactual images to estimate each token’s visual dependence.
Applies mass-preserving normalization to stabilize token-weighted distillation updates.
A teacher-supervised warm start stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts.
Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improved visual reasoning and more effective token-level distillation.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of multimodal tasks. However, object hallucination remains a persistent challenge, undermining model reliability in applications such as visual question answering, embodied agents, and human-AI decision support systems. In this paper, inspired by cognitive science studies on perceptual bias, we investigate a new failure mode termed Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination (PVFH). Specifically, PVFH refers to a premise-induced reasoning error in which models become anchored to visually confusable evidence, accept a false textual premise, and subsequently generate responses about an absent yet visually plausible object. To systematically study this phenomenon, we introduce PVFH-Bench, a benchmark that automatically constructs visually confusable but absent targets and pairs the core hallucination setting with diagnostic subsets to trace how models move from object recognition to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Experimental results on 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs demonstrate that all evaluated models are highly vulnerable to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Moreover, we find that explicit chain-of-thought reasoning can further exacerbate this failure mode by encouraging models to overinterpret weak visual cues as supporting evidence for hallucinated objects.
authors: Xinhao Wang, Junbo Cui, Zhenghao Liu, Yuan Yao, Xiaohua Li, Yu Gu, Ge Yu
bullets: Introduces Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination (PVFH), a failure mode combining false textual premises with visually confusable evidence.
Provides PVFH-Bench, which automatically constructs absent but visually plausible target objects and diagnostic subsets.
Evaluates 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs and finds all are highly vulnerable to PVFH.
Reports that explicit chain-of-thought reasoning can worsen the problem by amplifying weak visual cues.
Targets reliability concerns in visual question answering, embodied agents, and human-AI decision support.

papers.abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.

bullets: Addresses confabulation and hidden knowledge that surface-level refusal evaluations can miss.

Experiments show reduced target-information leakage, effective unlearning, and preserved performance on retained data.
Scope: targets honest ignorance rather than refusal behavior alone; code and data are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to understand how entities move and interact as a scene develops. This requires following the same entities over time and relating their observed motion to subsequent changes. We formulate Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), a task for predicting and interpreting this change. Given observed video, a model estimates entity histories and predicts one scene continuation through future trajectories and Events, accompanied by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. We construct SceneForesee, a benchmark for evaluating entity continuity and scene evolution reasoning through paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities. It contains 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events paired with observed evidence. We propose a spatiotemporal reasoning framework, EvoSee, that learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment. It selects one continuation per entity from observation and uses the selected changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. On SceneForesee, EvoSee outperforms Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1. On the 4D reasoning benchmark Dyn-Bench, it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over their respective base systems. These results support scene evolution as both a prediction target and a dynamic representation that brings predicted entity changes into spatiotemporal reasoning.The project is available at https://github.com/mikubaka88/SceneForesee-Spatiotemporal-Reasoning.

papers.abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.
authors: Aditi Khandelwal, Ayush K. Tarun, Yixuan Xu, Imanol Schlag, Golnoosh Farnadi, Siva Reddy, Luke Zettlemoyer, Antoine Bosselut
bullets: Audio benefits more from increasing model size than from adding tokens, while text and vision favor balanced scaling.
Repeating vision or audio data beyond 2× provides negligible additional benefit.
Vision substantially interferes with audio learning, but audio has negligible interference with text and vision.
The findings offer practical guidance for selecting multimodal pretraining mixtures.

papers.abstract: Learning reusable skills can improve visual reasoning agents, yet applying a skill still requires the agent to implement or invoke a procedure and produce the final answer. Errors and hallucinations at these steps can prevent acquired experience from translating into reliable single-run performance. We propose VisualCoding, which combines execution-guided acquisition of reusable visual programs with direct adoption of their answers on applicable inputs. Execution-Guided Program Acquisition composes visual primitives and additional code into family-level solvers, then iteratively tests and revises them on labeled training instances. Scope-Aware Direct Execution runs a retained solver and returns its valid in-scope answer. We evaluate VisualCoding on four models across four benchmarks spanning 69 task families. VisualCoding exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline in mean accuracy by 4.45 percentage points with Gemini-3.1-Pro and by 14.78 points when reusing the frozen Pro-acquired artifacts with Flash-Lite. Ablations support execution-guided acquisition and show that direct execution outperforms textual or callable reuse of the same programs. Code is available at https://github.com/jiaq-liu/VisualCoding.

Evaluated across four models, four benchmarks, and 69 task families; it improves mean accuracy over the strongest baseline by 4.45 points with Gemini-3.1-Pro and 14.78 points when transferring frozen artifacts to Flash-Lite.
Ablations support execution-guided acquisition and show direct execution is more effective than textual or callable reuse.

papers.abstract: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.

bullets: Benchmarks documentation and view acceptability across 11 Blender environments modeling unconstrained tasks such as solar installation and vehicle repair.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating VLMs on documenting physical work, testing spatial relations and scene understanding.
papers.title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
papers.tldr: RealityBench uses simulated physical-work environments to show that vision-language models struggle with visual proof-of-work quality, measurements, fine details, and spatial relations despite handling text-in-frame documentation well.

papers.abstract: We present CoPlanVLM, which uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to translate a single natural-language instruction and image into coordinated paths for a team of two robots. While VLMs offer a flexible, natural-language interface for commanding robot teams, their weak spatial reasoning has greatly limited VLM-based path planning. CoPlanVLM improves the VLM's spatial reasoning and path planning abilities through three components: (1) an image overlay marking both free space and obstacles, (2) task classification that selects the most appropriate low-level planner and reasoning prompt for each instruction, and (3) task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning that prompts the VLM to identify key objects, allocate roles, and verify routes are collision-free before committing to a plan. Together, these components enable the team to complete complex coordinated maneuvers requiring both robots and divide large tasks between robots to increase efficiency. CoPlanVLM also supports detailed maneuvers involving specific routes, loops, and coverage of large areas, as well as tasks requiring directional reasoning such as north/south or left/right. We validate CoPlanVLM in both Gazebo simulation and on physical Turtlebot 4 hardware. CoPlanVLM attains an average success rate of 84.4% compared to 50.0% for the closest baseline. On trials where both methods succeed, CoPlanVLM's paths are 27% shorter on average. Project code is available at https://github.com/AICPS/CoPlanVLM.
authors: David R. Martin, Jared Paquet, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque, Pramod Khargonekar, Kyle Volle, J. Humberto Ramos, Scott Nivison
bullets: Addresses weak VLM spatial reasoning for multi-robot path planning.
Uses free-space/obstacle overlays, task classification, and task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning.
Supports role allocation, collision-free route verification, coordinated maneuvers, task division, and directional or coverage-based instructions.
Validated in Gazebo and on Turtlebot 4 hardware, achieving 84.4% average success versus 50.0% for the closest baseline.
When both methods succeed, its paths are 27% shorter on average.

The executive VLM selects marked regions on the image which are used as inputs to the low-level path planning algorithms. These paths are then processed by low level controllers to send commands to the robots.

papers.selection_reason: VLM-based coordinated path planning for robot teams with spatial reasoning enhancements from language and image input.
papers.title: CoPlanVLM: Coordinated Path Planning for a Robot Team using Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: CoPlanVLM combines visual overlays, task-specific planning, and structured VLM reasoning to generate coordinated paths for two robots from a single instruction and image.

papers.abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) are often built using pretrained acoustic encoders as an audio interface to an LLM decoder. However, LLMs scale poorly with input sequence length, while acoustic encoders tend to produce substantially longer sequences than typical textual inputs. This motivates learning to compress encoder outputs while preserving task-oriented information. To this end, we introduce ASSET, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that learns to adaptively compress encoder outputs by first partitioning them into variable-duration segments and then pooling each segment into a continuous audio token. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to train a segmenter with task performance feedback and a token-rate penalty. In automatic speech recognition (ASR) experiments, ASSET achieves performance comparable to a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with approximately 25% fewer audio tokens on English LibriSpeech, while improving on a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL. Exploratory experiments on non-ASR tasks further illustrate how learned segmentation changes when the framework is adapted to tasks beyond transcription.
authors: Cihan Xiao, Yuan Tseng, Matthew Wiesner, Desh Raj, Leibny Paola Garcia Perera, Sanjeev Khudanpur, David Harwath
bullets: Addresses the sequence-length mismatch between long acoustic-encoder outputs and speech LLM inputs.
Learns variable-duration segments and pools each into a continuous audio token.
Trains the segmenter with GRPO using task-performance feedback and a token-rate penalty.
Matches a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with about 25% fewer tokens on English LibriSpeech.
Outperforms a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL; non-ASR behavior is explored but not fully characterized.

(b) Task losses score sampled boundary sequences; cross-entropy updates the pooler and decoder, while GRPO updates the segmenter.

papers.selection_reason: RL-based adaptive compression of speech encoder outputs into fewer audio tokens for speech LLMs; relevant to token efficiency and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: ASSET: Adaptive Speech Segmentation via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ASSET uses reinforcement learning to adaptively segment and compress speech encoder outputs into fewer task-relevant audio tokens while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multi-modal large language models have shifted toward the "thinking with images" paradigm to improve reasoning faithfulness, yet existing methods rely heavily on explicit coordinate- based grounding. We identify two fundamental limitations in this approach, i.e., a semantic gap where sparse regressions miss high-dimensional latent structures, and a resolution gap due to the granularity mismatch between patch-level tokens and pixel-level coordinates. To address these, we propose TiCO (Thinking with images without COordinates). It reformulates visual reasoning as a semantic evidence discovery process within the latent space, and evidence is injected as token-level regions without pixel coordinates. Specifically, TiCO utilizes a dedicated probe token to estimate similarity distributions and performs importance sampling over spatially connected components to generate diverse, semantically dominant evidence rollouts. Extensive experiments across multiple high-resolution and general visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our TiCO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art coordinate-based methods with significantly improved inference efficiency.
authors: Meng Cao, Haoze Zhao, Yi Wang, Ian Reid, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Coordinate-based visual reasoning suffers from semantic gaps in sparse regressions and resolution gaps between patch tokens and pixels.
TiCO reformulates reasoning as semantic evidence discovery in the model’s latent space.
A dedicated probe token estimates similarity distributions, while importance sampling over connected spatial components produces diverse evidence rollouts.
Evidence is injected as token-level regions rather than coordinate-based locations.
Experiments on high-resolution and general visual reasoning benchmarks show improved performance and inference efficiency over coordinate-based methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of TiCO. Given an image–text query pair, the policy model first produces a semantic probe token (<GROUND>) whose embedding interacts with visual patch tokens to generate a similarity map. After thresholding the similarity distribution, spatially connected components are extracted as candidate evidence regions. These components are treated as evidence rollouts and are subsequently fed back into the policy model to generate answer rollouts.

Figure 1 Comparison between coordinate-based methods and TiCO. Traditional model Mini-o3 [19] relies on explicit coordinate regression (<box>), which is sensitive to localization errors and prone to error propagation. In contrast, our TiCO replaces coordinate prediction with latent semantic region indexing, directly attending to informative regions in the token space.

Figure 10 Qualitative examples of failure cases in the "thinking" mode of coordinate-based methods. (a) Repeated Thinking: The model falls into an infinite loop during the multi-turn reasoning process, repeatedly generating the same crop coordinates and thoughts without progressing toward a final answer. (b) Inconsistent Logic: Although the model correctly identifies the target object (a yellow bicycle) in the final observation, it produces an incorrect final answer (Option B: red) that contradicts its own internal reasoning and visual evidence.

Figure 2 Conceptual comparison and performance trade-offs. (a) Coordinate-based methods [19, 56] localize evidence via explicit bounding-box prediction, reducing reasoning to geometric regression in image space; (b) Coordinate-free methods instead operate directly in visual token space, inducing a similarity distribution over patches and extracting semantically coherent evidence without explicit coordinates; (c) Performance–efficiency comparison on HR-Bench 8K [41]. Our TiCO achieves superior accuracy with substantially lower inference latency and fewer tokens compared to coordinate-based approaches such as Mini-o3 [19] and DeepEyes [56].

papers.abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.
authors: Laura Yao, Shixing Yu, Jie Peng, Promit Ghosal, Kyra Gan, Tianlong Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of spatially and multimodally grounded training-sample attribution for vision-language models.
Learns a shared sparse image–text latent space with localized, phrase-aligned, and approximately decorrelated concepts.
Uses EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these latent concepts.
Evaluated on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering.
Influence-ranked latent ablations alter outputs more than activation- or frequency-ranked ablations, while preserving task behavior.

papers.abstract: Digital libraries increasingly host scientific publications whose figures encode primary research findings, yet making this visual content searchable, accessible, and reusable remains an open challenge. Large language and multimodal models (LLMs/LMMs) provide the possibility to automate many figure parsing tasks such as determining data trends or extracting data from plots. In this work, we consider if these models can reliably support task-oriented visual data analysis when presented with synthetic, but realistic, scientific figures that contain multiple charts. Our Visual Question Answering (VQA) process scaffolds our tasks along a four-level description model from basic conceptual answers to interpretive and analytical understanding. Additionally, we outline our process for synthetically generating our single and multi-panel (charts in which there are multiple panels present) plots and testing the data with various LMMs using quantitative analysis. In general, we find LMMs become less accurate with increasing figure complexity as the number of panels, number of plot elements, and difficulty of questions increase. Finally, because LMM accuracy is expected to change rapidly, our analysis also considers cost relative to performance as a metric to inform future user decisions. We provide the detailed question-answer pairs used in this analysis, along with the code used to generate random plots, question-answer pairs and detailed bounding-box metadata for chart elements. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ReadingTimeMachine/LLM_VQA_MultiPanel and https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/visual\_qa\_multipanel
authors: Daniel J. Evans, J. P. Naiman, JooYoung Seo, J. Stephen Downie
bullets: Introduces a multi-panel chart VQA benchmark organized into four levels, from basic descriptions to interpretive and analytical questions.

papers.abstract: Existing jailbreak attacks have exposed serious safety weaknesses in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Most prior attacks rely on specially constructed visual inputs to carry or support harmful intent. In this paper, we uncover a different vulnerability: task-relevant scene semantics alone can shift an MLLM from refusal to compliance, even when the visual input introduces no additional attack instructions and the original task intent remains unchanged. We formalize this failure as a scene-grounded visual safety vulnerability and introduce SceneSafetyBench to investigate it across eight risk categories and nine white- and black-box MLLMs. Our analysis reveals that this failure is associated with how task-relevant visual evidence influences downstream safety representations, suggesting that visual grounding alone cannot fully explain the observed safety shift. Building on this finding, we propose Scene-Grounded Attacks (SGA), which preserve the original task while constructing validated scene-grounded queries and combining their independent responses. Across nine target MLLMs, SGA achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of 86.17%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.55 percentage points and achieving the highest ASR on eight models. Our results identify scene semantics as an overlooked attack surface in MLLMs and highlight a growing tension between stronger visual grounding and robust multimodal safety alignment.
authors: Tongxi Wu, Yuyang Cheng, Jiacheng Xian, Hu Huang, Zhihao Wu, Menglin Yang, Jian Zhang, Yang Gao

papers.abstract: Dense visual text requires image generators to reproduce long strings across multiple regions with correct placement and legibility. As short-string rendering improves, evaluation must test sustained performance across more demanding scenes. We introduce UltraText Bench, a bilingual benchmark for prompt-only generation of dense visual text. It contains 432 prompts spanning 24 real-world scene categories and three difficulty levels, split equally between English and Chinese. Each human-reviewed prompt supplies exact strings for four to twelve text regions, paired with structured references for their content, placement, and visual attributes. We use the Q-Judger vision-language model to assess each image against the complete reference, reporting text fidelity, text clarity, spatial quality, and scene quality. Across 24 model configurations, these dimensions reveal different strengths: Z-Image-Turbo gains 3.81 clarity points over Z-Image-Base while losing 14.76 fidelity points under the reported settings. Performance also varies with workload; Qwen-Image-2512's English composite falls from 86.50 at L1 to 42.86 at L3. Ten participants took part in human evaluation of the automatic scores. Repository: https://github.com/LINs-lab/UltraText_Bench.

papers.abstract: Existing attacks on unlearned diffusion models assume that the erased concepts are known in advance and focus on recovering them. In practice, however, model providers may not disclose which concepts have been removed, and even with access to the original base model, an adversary may still lack a clear target to attack. In this paper, we aim to answer the following critical but overlooked questions: which concepts have been erased from the model, and how many have been erased in total? To this end, we present Tracer, a framework that rapidly and accurately identifies erased concepts and estimates their number. Tracer efficiently identifies erased concepts without generating and classifying images. By combining lightweight spectral analysis of weight footprints, it enables efficient search over large candidate vocabularies. To distinguish multiple erased concepts, we introduce a footprint coverage objective that guides sequential discovery. Tracer estimates the number of erased concepts by detecting a sharp decline in candidate confidence as the selected concepts account for the erasure footprint, without requiring labeled examples for calibration. The framework requires only lightweight linear algebra and limited forward probes, with no prior knowledge of the unlearning algorithm. Experiments across text-to-image and text-to-video backbones and diverse unlearning methods demonstrate that Tracer identifies erased concepts and estimates their number in seconds, achieving 150 to 137,000 times and 133 to 20,000 times speedups over MIA and brute-force search on image and video models, respectively, with substantially higher identification accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the overlooked problem of identifying erased concepts when the provider does not disclose them.
Uses lightweight spectral analysis of model-weight footprints to search large candidate vocabularies efficiently.
Introduces footprint coverage for sequentially distinguishing multiple erased concepts.
Estimates the total number of erased concepts from a confidence drop, without labeled calibration data.
Works across text-to-image and text-to-video models, substantially outperforming MIA and brute-force search in speed and identification accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TRACER. (a) Erasure footprint assembly. Erasure imprints are grouped by their probed input representations. Spectrally reshaped and reweighted Gram matrices are fused within compatible groups into footprints Gg. (b) Candidate encoding. Candidates are encoded in each group’s input space, whitened to suppress shared structure, and normalized. (c) Unlearned concept disclosure. TRACER iteratively selects concepts explaining the remaining footprint energy. selection combines standardized gains across groups with confidence-based weights. Label-free self-calibration fixes parameters and group weights. Confidence drops determine set size without image generation or algorithm knowledge.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs report strong performance on scientific reasoning benchmarks, yet most treat perception and reasoning as a single measurable process. We introduce a five-task diagnostic experiment across physics and geometry benchmarks that isolates failures to perception, reasoning, or both. Incorrect diagram interpretation degrades performance even on problems models solve correctly from text alone, and accuracy generally rises from raw images to human-authored captions. Recovery under corrected captions is high for some models, separating perception-blocked failures from genuine reasoning bottlenecks. Which reasoning error follows a perception failure depends on domain: physics failures resolve into calculation errors, geometry into conceptual misapplication. As a discussion beyond our core experiments, InternS1-mini, despite heavy scientific pretraining and thinking capabilities, falls below the weakest model from experiments on every task, with reasoning traces frequently truncating before completion.
bullets: Incorrect diagram interpretation harms performance even when models solve the same problems from text alone.
Human-authored captions generally improve accuracy over raw images.
Corrected captions reveal which failures are perception-blocked versus genuine reasoning failures.
Perception failures tend to become calculation errors in physics and conceptual misapplication in geometry.
InternS1-mini underperforms all evaluated models across tasks, often truncating its reasoning traces.↩

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses perception vs reasoning failures in multimodal physics and geometry reasoning, directly relevant to MLLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Lost in Perception: Isolating Perceptual and Reasoning Failures in Multimodal Physics and Geometry Reasoning
papers.tldr: A five-task diagnostic shows that multimodal physics and geometry errors often stem from diagram perception, while remaining failures reflect domain-specific reasoning bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: Compositional Zero Shot Learning aims to recognize unseen compositions by recombining learned primitives. Recent methods rely on vision language models and attempt to explicitly model contextual variations of primitives through multiple representations. However, such approaches are limited by fixed variant capacity and competition between abstract and concrete semantics. In this work, we present a new perspective that views primitive variations as the context-driven activation of concrete visual cues rather than independent entities. Based on it, we propose CLEAR, a CLoze-style rEAsoning-based Re-ranking framework inspired by human perceptual processes. CLEAR extracts conditional variants from the primitive candidate set in a coarse-to-fine manner, performs cloze-style reasoning to infer high-level semantics, and re-ranks predictions to correct biases toward salient concrete primitives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CLEAR consistently improves the Base Model and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the challenging C-GQA and MIT-States datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/buptLwz/CLEAR.
bullets: Addresses limitations of fixed primitive-variant capacity and conflicts between concrete and abstract semantics.
Models primitive variations as context-driven activation of concrete visual cues rather than independent representations.
Uses coarse-to-fine variant extraction, cloze-style reasoning, and prediction re-ranking.
Reportedly improves its base model and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on C-GQA and MIT-States.,

figures.caption: Fig. 2. (a) Overview of CLEAR. The Base Model adopts a three-branch architecture to jointly fine-tune the CLIP visual encoder with adapters and learn CLIP-based textual primitive prompts θa, θo and θc. Based on the predictions of the Base Model, CLEAR uses learnable masked tokens Ma and Mo to decode high-level semantics from primitive candidates and visual patch features fP v . Finally, the re-ranking scores are computed by matching the highlevel semantics and the primitive features in the textual space. (b) The Reasoner consists of a set of lightweight Transformer decoders, which take masked representations as queries and the candidate set with visual patch features fP v to serve as keys and values.

Fig. 1. (a) Prior methods enumerate and model conditional variants for each primitive, but the number of variants is limited, and abstract and concrete semantics compete with each other; (b) Our method first constructs a primitive candidate set and then reasons over it to infer high-level semantics. Built from primitive combinations, the candidate set not only has a higher information capacity but also avoids competition between semantics. (c) The proposed CLEAR performs cloze-style reasoning over the candidate set derived from base predictions, and then re-ranks the base predictions to correct errors.

Fig. 4. Re-ranking effects of CLEAR. (a) Representative cases comparing the Base Model outputs before re-ranking with the final predictions. (b) Quantitative AUC gains of re-ranking across three datasets.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have intensified the need to understand how different modalities share, preserve, and complement information. Mutual Information (MI), the Information Bottleneck (IB), and Partial Information Decomposition (PID) provide complementary perspectives, yet existing studies often treat them as isolated tools. This survey presents an information-theoretic perspective connecting these principles as progressively refined views of multimodal information processing: MI characterizes inter-modal dependency, IB explains task-oriented information preservation under compression, and PID decomposes preserved information into redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy. We review 170 recent studies (2018--2026) and 12 foundational works, organizing multimodal learning around four challenges: cross-modal alignment, information-efficient fusion, interaction-type characterization, and scaling to multimodal foundation models. Rather than using application domains as primary taxonomy axes, we interpret healthcare, robotics, recommendation systems, affective computing, and wireless communications as empirical validations of these information principles. Beyond taxonomy, we organize existing multimodal paradigms within a single information-theoretic coordinate system -- the Generalized Multimodal Information Lagrangian -- in which they occupy exact or approximate parameter corners, and whose unoccupied regions name candidate method families the literature has not yet built. We further discuss how emerging multimodal foundation models instantiate these principles at scale and identify open challenges including scalable information estimation in high-dimensional settings, standardized evaluation across information-theoretic methods, combinatorial complexity of multimodal PID, and the transition from post-hoc information analysis toward information-aware multimodal learning.
authors: Liangjian Wen, Linjie Li, Jiang Duan, Yong Dai, Jianzhuang Liu, Zhao Kang
bullets: Reviews 170 recent studies and 12 foundational works through four challenges: alignment, efficient fusion, interaction characterization, and multimodal scaling.
Frames MI as inter-modal dependency, IB as task-relevant compression, and PID as the decomposition of information into redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy.
Introduces the Generalized Multimodal Information Lagrangian to position existing paradigms and highlight unexplored method families.
Interprets applications across healthcare, robotics, recommendation, affective computing, and wireless communications as validations of shared information principles.
Identifies open issues in scalable information estimation, standardized evaluation, multimodal PID complexity, and information-aware learning.

papers.title: Dependency, Compression, and Synergy: A Unified Information-Theoretic View of Multimodal Learning

papers.abstract: Clinical prognosis requires integrating structured measurements, physiological waveforms, longitudinal history, and population context. We introduce PRISM (Population-Retrieved Inference for Structured Multimodal Prognosis), a multimodal language model that combines per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted aggregation of longitudinal ECGs, and a dual-modality population memory bank. Retrieval operates in representation space: the model receives mean-pooled embeddings of similar training-cohort encounters, while no individual retrieved record enters the prompt. On the 1,443-task MDS-ED benchmark, PRISM achieves AUROCs of 86.2% for diagnosis, 93.1% for deterioration, 91.8% for ICU admission, and 92.8% for mortality. These results use a 96-hour pre-arrival window unavailable to reported baselines. With benchmark-window inputs only, PRISM reaches 0.8895 AUROC, compared with 0.8937 for UniPACT and 0.8889 for MDS-ED. A matched-input compact fusion model using the same five evidence streams and frozen encoders reaches 0.7652 AUROC, versus 0.9092 for PRISM. Replacing numerical EHR encoding with text serialization reduces AUROC by 3.66 points; removing pre-arrival history reduces it by 1.97 points; and zeroing retrieval reduces it by 0.99 points. Genuine retrieval outperforms random-neighbor retrieval by 0.97 macro-average points, although a paired task-level sign test does not establish a uniform advantage (p=0.067). On the external MC-MED cohort, supervised fine-tuning reaches 0.8611 AUROC, compared with 0.8227 for locally trained gradient boosting and 0.7841 for source-only PRISM. These results support structure-aware multimodal integration and supervised external adaptation.
bullets: Addresses clinical prognosis across diagnosis, deterioration, ICU admission, and mortality using heterogeneous evidence.
Uses per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted ECG history, and representation-space retrieval from a population memory bank without prompting individual records.
On MDS-ED, reports AUROCs of 86.2%–93.1% using a 96-hour pre-arrival window; with benchmark-window inputs, performance is comparable to reported baselines.

Ablations show declines from text-based numerical encoding, removing pre-arrival history, and removing retrieval; genuine retrieval improves average performance, though uniform superiority is not statistically established.
On external MC-MED data, supervised fine-tuning outperforms locally trained gradient boosting and source-only PRISM.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the PRISM architecture. Five modality streams (structured EHR, current ECG, longitudinal ECG history, retrieved EHR context, and retrieved ECG context) are independently encoded and projected as soft tokens into a shared sequence consumed by a LoRA-adapted MedGemma-4B decoder. The population memory bank (center) retrieves the k=3 nearest training-fold encounters from dual EHR and ECG indices constructed after Stage 1 and passes their mean-pooled embeddings, not their outcome labels, to the decoder. The temporal history aggregator (right) pools prior ECG embeddings under exponential recency weighting. Each task question is answered in one forward pass, via either the generative or the classification pathway, with no task-specific heads.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces PRISM, a multimodal language model for clinical prognosis that integrates heterogeneous evidence (waveforms, structured measurements) via a population memory bank and retrieval-augmented generation. This aligns with the 'Multimodal Foundation Models' topic, specifically the 'Multimodal Large Language Models' subtopic, as it extends LLMs to handle non-text modalities and retrieval-based context.
papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Model with Heterogeneous Evidence Integration for Clinical Prognosis
papers.tldr: PRISM integrates structured clinical data, waveforms, longitudinal history, and population retrieval to improve multimodal prognosis, with performance depending on input scope and supervised adaptation.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex voice agents make many small, closed decisions, which current systems answer by slow autoregressive decoding. We propose DuplexJev, which feeds ASR-encoder hidden states through a small connector into a frozen LLM and reads each question as a single-token distribution over its options. Nothing is decoded, and an 8-GPU node answers 80 decisions about eight utterances in about 0.1 s. With a last-layer connector, spoken QA stays close to reading the transcript (90% vs. 91%). DuplexJev also hears the speaker: gender and emotion accuracy both reach 90% (from 55% and 28%) with a cross-attention connector, whose spoken QA drops by only 1 point (83% to 82%). We train decisions with cross-entropy on the read-out answer token, instead of the usual transcript distillation, whose teacher never hears the voice, and keep distillation for content. Encoders and LLMs are interchangeable; we release weights, training recipe, a batched-inference pipeline for full-duplex serving and a bilingual spoken-QA set.
bullets: Maps ASR-encoder representations into a frozen LLM and reads each question as a single-token option distribution.
Uses answer-token cross-entropy for decision supervision while retaining distillation for speech content.
Handles spoken QA, speaker gender, and emotion, with cross-attention improving paralinguistic recognition while slightly reducing QA accuracy.
Batches 80 decisions over eight utterances in about 0.1 seconds on an 8-GPU node.
Provides interchangeable encoder/LLM components, released weights and recipe, a full-duplex inference pipeline, and a bilingual spoken-QA set.
