papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide limited support for sign language interaction. Unifying sign language translation (SLT) and generation (SLG) to enable sign language as both input and output can reduce switching between separate models during sign-text interaction. We present SignGPT, a unified, pose-based framework for gloss-free SLT and SLG. SignGPT integrates part-aware hierarchical representations of body, hand, and facial motion into a shared language model and employs asymmetric multi-token prediction and progressive training for bidirectional modeling. We evaluate SignGPT on How2Sign (ASL) and Phoenix-2014T (DGS) through benchmark comparisons, qualitative analyses, and component ablations. An exploratory study with 12 Deaf ASL signers assesses an LLM-mediated sign-to-sign response pipeline, highlighting the potential of unified modeling to support sign language conversation (SLC).
bullets: Targets limited LLM support for sign language and the need to combine translation and generation.
Uses part-aware hierarchical representations of body, hand, and facial motion within a shared language model.
Applies asymmetric multi-token prediction and progressive training for bidirectional modeling.
Evaluated on How2Sign (ASL) and Phoenix-2014T (DGS) with benchmark comparisons, qualitative analysis, and ablations.
A 12-person Deaf ASL signer study explores its potential for sign-to-sign conversational interaction.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of the Part-aware Hierarchical VQ-VAE (PHVQ) tokenizer. PHVQ combines bidirectional multi-scale temporal modeling with body-to-hand hierarchical quantization and encodes a full-body sign language motion sequence into three discrete streams: a body–face codebook 𝐵𝐵𝑜𝑑𝑦 , a left-hand codebook 𝐵𝐿𝐻 , and a right-hand codebook 𝐵𝑅𝐻 . Facial-expression features are encoded jointly with the body stream.

Fig. 2. Overview of SignGPT’s three training stages: (1) PHVQ discretizes continuous body and hand motion, with an optional text-alignment objective; (2) GHMLM is jointly trained on SLG and SLT and uses AMTP to decode text or part-aware motion tokens; and (3) instruction fine-tuning supports prompted translation and generation.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive generation of interleaved text and acoustic tokens is a common approach to spoken-response generation in speech large language models. Although this design enables streaming generation with explicit textual guidance, generated acoustic tokens become part of the context for subsequent text predictions. Given identical speech inputs, we observe markedly lower answer accuracy for the internal text generated in speech-to-text-and-speech (S2TS) mode than for speech-to-text (S2T) responses. We term this discrepancy the \emph{output-mode gap} (OMG). To reduce OMG, we propose \emph{Joint-Output On-Policy Distillation} (JO-OPD), which distills the model's stronger S2T policy into joint generation using student-generated S2TS trajectories. At each text position, the S2T teacher provides soft targets from a text-only projection of the student's preceding outputs, while the student predicts from the corresponding full interleaved history. A preservation objective further regularizes native non-text predictions. Experiments on Step-Audio-2-mini and Baichuan-Audio-Instruct reveal OMG across two interleaved generation architectures. On Step-Audio-2-mini, JO-OPD reduces OMG from 42.87 to 16.26 percentage points on Spoken-MQA and from 29.72 to 13.04 points on speech-rendered GSM8K, with little change in S2T accuracy and substantially larger reductions than matched SFT baselines. ASR-based evaluation further shows a 7.49-point improvement in spoken-answer accuracy on Spoken-MQA.
bullets: The output-mode gap arises because generated acoustic tokens remain in the context and degrade later text predictions.
JO-OPD uses student-generated S2TS trajectories and soft targets from an S2T teacher based on text-only histories.
A preservation objective regularizes the model’s native non-text predictions during distillation.
On Step-Audio-2-mini, the gap fell from 42.87 to 16.26 points on Spoken-MQA and from 29.72 to 13.04 points on speech-rendered GSM8K.
S2T accuracy changed little, while ASR evaluation showed a 7.49-point Spoken-MQA improvement; results cover two interleaved-generation architectures.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) allow a single model to perform clinical image analysis tasks ranging from diagnosis classification to report generation. However, joint adaptation is challenged by heterogeneous output formats, conflicting task gradients, and imbalanced training data. Hence, we present \textbf{Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA}, a framework built on MedGemma-1.5-4B. The framework uses a shared-specific Mixture-of-LoRA architecture comprising one shared LoRA and six task-specific expert LoRAs, together with a two-stage training procedure. In Stage 1, we jointly train the shared LoRA and all task-specific expert LoRAs on all tasks. In Stage 2, we first freeze the backbone, the shared LoRA, and all non-target experts, and refine one task expert at a time. Classification and regression then receive an additional modality-balanced continuation, in which smaller modality groups are repeated to match the largest group. In the FLARE 2026 Task 3 test sets, the proposed method achieves 0.85 balanced accuracy for classification, 0.48 micro-F1 for multi-label classification, 0.79 detection F1, and 17.39 regression MAE. Code is available at https://github.com/YuanYL03/MICCAI-FLARE-2026-Challenge-Task3-2D.
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous outputs, conflicting task gradients, and imbalanced data in joint medical VLM adaptation.
Uses one shared LoRA plus six task-specific expert LoRAs.
Jointly trains all adapters, then separately refines each task expert while freezing the others.
Adds modality-balanced continuation training for classification and regression.
On FLARE 2026 Task 3 test sets, reports 0.85 balanced accuracy, 0.48 micro-F1, 0.79 detection F1, and 17.39 regression MAE across task types.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA framework for medical vision-language tasks. In Stage 2, all six experts are independently refined while the backbone, shared LoRA, and non-target experts remain frozen. Classification and regression then receive an additional continuation using modality-balanced resampling.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina, the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data, a paired text--protein structure dataset of 1.8M structures and 50M+ captions describing global and residue-specific structural and functional properties. We adapt Proteina-Complexa, a pretrained structure generation model, through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their corresponding text. Prompteina outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions. In binder design, it leads baselines on at least 13 of 20 targets and improves interface confidence by 14\% over the strongest baseline. With iterative in silico feedback, Prompteina's gain over non-iterative generation is 57\% larger than the next-best baseline on the hardest targets. Finally, we experimentally validate Prompteina designs against GM2A, a target with no reported de novo binders. We identify nine binders, with the strongest at an apparent $K_{\mathrm{D}}$ of 107 nM. These results establish natural language as an effective and powerful conditioning interface for protein structure generation.
authors: Joseph Lee, Yanjing Li, Bo Qiang, Gregory Lau, Allyson Ettinger, Noah A. Smith, Rory Donovan-Maiye, David Baker, Hanna Hajishirzi, Pang Wei Koh
bullets: Addresses the limited range of objectives supported by protein design models requiring property-specific input representations.
Introduces Prompteina, an all-atom structure generator conditioned on natural-language descriptions of global and residue-specific properties.
Trains on Prompteina-Data, containing 1.8M protein structures and over 50M paired captions, with text–residue alignment.
Outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and leads on at least 13 of 20 binder-design targets; iterative feedback further improves performance.
Experimental validation against GM2A identified nine binders, with the strongest showing an apparent KD of 107 nM.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Experimental validation identifies diverse GM2A binders. (a) ESMFold2-Fast predictions of six sub-micromolar binders, ordered by apparent KD. Despite distinct agent-specified architectures, all six target the same GM2A face around W94 (GM2A, gray; W94, pink). (b) Agent reasoning and the design prompt for the strongest binder. (c) SPR sensorgrams for this binder across three replicates and five analyte concentrations, labeled with per-replicate apparent KD values.

Figure 1: Prompteina generates all-atom protein structures directly from natural language. (a) A single natural-language interface supports diverse design objectives spanning global and residuespecific properties. (b) In agentic binder design, an agent researches target biology and writes text prompts describing candidate binders. Prompteina then realizes these research-informed specifications directly in generated structures. Experimental validation against GM2A identifies nine diverse binders, with the best replicate at an apparent KD of 68.8 nM. (c) Across 20 targets, Prompteina achieves the highest interface confidence when the same agent specifies designs for every model.

Figure 2: Paired text–structure data and text-conditioned structure generation. (a) Structural and functional annotations are curated and (b) passed to a large language model for caption generation. (c) Residues are aligned to their corresponding caption text spans for supervised alignment finetuning. (d) Captions are embedded into pooled and per-token text representations, then projected to condition the structure generation model. (e) The denoiser is first trained on caption–structure pairs with a flow-matching objective, then fine-tuned with supervised text–residue alignment (§2.2).

Figure 3: Natural language controls global and residue-specific structural properties. Examples span global properties (shape, architecture, domain composition, and symmetry), residue-specific properties (disulfide and salt-bridge counts), and combinations of both (fold class with disulfide count). All structures match their captions and are designable (scRMSD < 2 Å).

papers.abstract: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.
bullets: Addresses the limits of book-by-book comics scholarship across vast American comics and Japanese manga archives.
Parses scans into panels, text, and bibliographic records, then applies codebook-guided vision-language annotation grounded in human checks.
Demonstrates three studies of political representation, visual form and artists’ styles, and speaking roles across comics traditions.

Potentially supports searchable archives, accessibility for blind and low-vision readers, preservation, and attribution of uncredited artists.

papers.abstract: How well can vision-language models (VLMs) reason about what is missing from an image? We study this question with OccludeBench, a manually curated benchmark for recovering fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains. OccludeBench distinguishes direct cases, where the hidden object must be recovered from a specific physical cue such as a shadow or reflection, from inferential cases, where it can be inferred from broader scene context. Across five VLMs, accuracy averages 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases, exhibiting a 20.0-point gap. Humans attain higher accuracies of 63.4% versus 68.5% for direct and inferential images, respectively, with no significant gap. To locate this failure, we introduce OccludeTrace, a four-stage diagnostic that isolates where the visual reasoning process breaks down. The bottleneck emerges when models must recover the relevant object from the projection within the full image: they succeed on only 50% of failed examples, compared with 91% of examples they answer correctly. Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting yield inconsistent improvements and do not reliably eliminate the gap. In contrast, an inpaint-then-confront intervention, which prompts models to first generate a candidate hidden object and then evaluate that hypothesis against the visible physical cue, reduces the gap to a statistically non-significant difference for both models with image-generation capabilities. Together, our results establish a tractable, controlled diagnostic for isolating how VLMs reason about visual content that is missing from an image.
authors: Jasin Cekinmez, Addison J. Wu, Ryo Mitsuhashi, Linrong Cai, Xingyu Fu, Zhuang Liu

OccludeTrace identifies recovering the hidden object from its projection in the full image as the main bottleneck.
Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting provide inconsistent improvements.
Inpaint-then-confront reduces the direct–inferential gap to a statistically non-significant difference for models with image-generation capabilities.

papers.abstract: Memes play a central role in modern online communication, especially in contexts of political conflict where visual and textual cues combine to convey persuasive messages. We study persuasive technique detection in Ukrainian memes using vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce UkrMeme, a dataset of 200 organically produced Ukrainian wartime memes annotated for persuasion techniques, and PTM-UA, a Ukrainian translation of a subset of the Propaganda 950 benchmark that preserves original visual content while translating meme text. We evaluate VLMs in a zero-shot prompting setup across image, text, and multimodal inputs using hierarchical F1 metrics. Finally, we compare Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and model-generated token attributions and analyze the semantic categories of evidence emphasized by each explanation method.

Analyzes which semantic evidence categories different explanation methods emphasize.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on speech-text tasks, but standard audio encoders produce hundreds of tokens for even short audio clips. Because self-attention scales quadratically in sequence length, this inflates inference-time compute substantially. Current training-free token compression methods prune or merge tokens based solely on coarse attention or feature similarity. However, treating audio tokens as generic, isotropic features smooths over spectral transitions, destroying fine-grained phonetic transitions essential for decoding speech. In contrast, speech signals exhibit highly structured temporal patterns where information density peaks at acoustic transitions. We propose AudioTETRIS, a training-free, two-stage framework that uses the audio encoder's representation geometry as an acoustic prior for token importance before applying attention-based compression. Instead of discarding encoder structure after the encoding stage, AudioTETRIS propagates this prior directly into the LLM decoder to compute a per-token fused score. This score drives progressive top-$k$ token selection across decoder layers without requiring additional training or auxiliary models. Evaluated on Qwen2-Audio-7B, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3, AudioTETRIS retains near-uncompressed performance on several speech tasks using only 25% of audio tokens, matches or surpasses full-token accuracy at moderate compression rates, and consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.
authors: Shreya Sajid, Anna Vettoruzzo, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Targets the high inference cost caused by hundreds of audio tokens and quadratic self-attention.
Uses encoder representation geometry to identify transition-rich, information-dense tokens.
Fuses acoustic-prior and decoder attention signals into per-token importance scores.
Progressively selects top-k tokens across decoder layers without training or auxiliary models.
Evaluated on three audio LLMs, it retains near-uncompressed speech-task performance and outperforms training-free baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of AudioTETRIS. A phoneme-transition-aware acoustic prior wt is computed from the audio encoder’s hidden states via the transitional distance dt = ∥ht − ht−1∥22, preserving phoneme transitions yhard (§4; left). Token pruning occurs in two stages: Stage 1 injects wt as a static acoustic prior from the encoder’s hidden states; Stage 2 computes a depth-adaptive LLM attention score, fusing intra-audio attention in early layers with cross-modal (text-to-audio) attention in later layers (right). The two scores are fused into a single importance score, and top-k selection retains the most salient tokens at each pruning layer ℓ.

Figure 8: Schematic of the phoneme-transition-aware prior pipeline. Top: audio waveform with forced-alignment phoneme segments. Second row: per-token encoder hidden states ht, colored by phoneme membership. Third row: raw derivative dt (bars) and the Gaussian-smoothed transition score bt (line). Bottom: ground-truth transition labels, shown as discrete spikes yhard and their Gaussian-smoothed form ysoft, used to compute rhard and rsoft.

Figure 4: Comparison of LibriSpeech WER (↓) and MMAU-mini accuracy (↑) at compression ratio 0.51, for Phi-4-Multimodal and Audio Flamingo 3. Error bars show standard deviation across runs. AUDIOTETRIS is highlighted in the darker shade.

Figure 3: Layer-wise diagnostics across Qwen2-Audio, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3. Top: Mean correlation between bt and ground-truth phoneme transitions (rsoft and rhard). Bottom: Kurtosis (κ) of the distance distribution dt. Both metrics identify an intrinsic mid-network sweet spot (shaded) where phonetic transitions are maximally accentuated.

Figure 2: Distribution of decoder attention mass allocated to audio tokens across model depth in Qwen2-Audio on LibriSpeech. Despite audio tokens comprising 84.98% of the input sequence (dashed ring), early layers are dominated by intra-audio attention (76.91%), which drops sharply in middle (46.73%) and late layers (40.60%) as attention shifts to text-conditioned representations. This shift motivates our layer-dependent pooling rule in Eq. 3.
Figure 6: Ablation of AudioTETRIS stages at compression ratio 0.51.

Figure 9: Layer-wise boundary correlation (rsoft, rhard) across Qwen2-Audio, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3, computed on CoVoST2 (top, MFA alignments generated in-house) and IEMOCAP (bottom, official released alignments). Shaded regions mark each backbone’s mid-network sweet spot, consistent with Figure 3. Dashed vertical lines and annotated values mark the peak layer for each curve.
Figure 5: WER/accuracy/BLEU across distance metrics for the transition score, at compression ratio 0.51. Error bars show standard deviation over runs.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs can fail to read text embedded in an image's coarse structure (text a human recovers by squinting) and report that no text is present. We name this class Squint Text and study it as a recognition deficiency, motivated by cases from a production moderation pipeline. We introduce SquintBench, comprising 1076 production-derived moderation images, and SquintCtrl, a controlled synthetic suite for mechanism diagnosis. Frozen-weight analysis shows that hidden text leaves a coarse signal while glyph identity is weakly represented; identity becomes substantially more accessible when the correct spatial regions are supplied, implicating spatial selection as a major bottleneck. Suppressing high-frequency content also improves reading at a fixed visual-token budget, while visual token count may also contribute. These findings motivate Squint OPSD: a frozen teacher receives a downscaled view and the ground-truth transcription as privileged context, and its token-level distributions supervise a student along on-policy trajectories. At inference, the student reads the original image alone. Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench, versus 26.50 for the unadapted backbone, 24.44 for the best general-purpose model on the original view, and 68.60 at best for an off-the-shelf model under a downscaled view. These results substantially narrow the gap between available visual evidence and its generated read-out without auxiliary views at inference.
authors: Chen Peng, Shan Huang, Jianbo Huang, Linrui Qin, Qibo Sun, Mengwei Xu
bullets: Introduces Squint Text: embedded text that humans can recover by squinting but MLLMs may report as absent.
Releases SquintBench with 1,076 production-derived moderation images and SquintCtrl for controlled diagnosis.
Finds that text location is a major bottleneck: supplying correct regions improves glyph identity, while suppressing high frequencies can help at fixed visual-token budgets.
Proposes Squint OPSD, which distills token-level supervision from a frozen teacher using privileged downscaled views and transcriptions, while the student uses only the original image at inference.
Achieves 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench, compared with 26.50 for the unadapted backbone and 68.60 for the best off-the-shelf model using a downscaled view.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit complementary capabilities, yet selecting the most suitable expert for a given image-question query remains challenging due to heterogeneous multimodal inputs and varying expert strengths. Existing routing approaches rely on text-based cues or static model profiles, failing to capture fine-grained visual evidence and expert-specific failure patterns. To address this, we propose MHR-Router, a multimodal heterogeneous retrieval-enhanced adaptive routing framework for VLM inference. It accurately dispatches each multimodal query to the most suitable VLM expert via local retrieval evidence. MHR-Router consists of two stages: (1) Multimodal Routing Representation, which fuses frozen multimodal features into a comprehensive query representation; and (2) Heterogeneous Retrieval-Enhanced Adaptive Routing, which retrieves expert-specific success and failure memories as local evidence and employs a shared scorer to adaptively select the optimal expert. Experiments show that MHR-Router effectively achieves heterogeneous modality routing and consistently improves accuracy over traditional baselines.
authors: Wenjuan Zhu, Zheming Yang, Yunqing Hu, Qi Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting among VLM experts with complementary strengths and heterogeneous failure patterns.
Fuses frozen multimodal features into a comprehensive representation of each query.
Retrieves expert-specific success and failure memories as local routing evidence.
Uses a shared scorer to select the expert best suited to the query.
Experiments report consistent accuracy improvements over traditional routing baselines.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) reveals versatility and convenience during VLM post-training, providing dense supervision for student from teacher. However, we observed an anomaly that the distilled VLM could still answer the questions accurately even when the related visual regions were masked or replaced with noise. Building on this observation, our quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that OPD, which uses the answer as a hint, has failed to teach students to genuinely seek out and rely on visual evidence. Our theoretical analysis suggests that this failure arises from a shortcut enabled by the lack of visual constraints during distillation. To address the issue, we introduce Contrastive Vision On-policy Distillation (CV-OPD), which compares teacher distributions induced by positive and negative crops while conditioning on the same student prefix and augments optimization with a margin-based contrastive constraint, which is modulated with discrepancy gating across token and sample level. Specifically, CV-OPD first introduces a negative teacher unrelated to the answer and designs a Contrastive Divergence Loss (CDL) that constrains the feature distribution of student by contrasting the positive and negative teachers, correcting how the student exploits visual regions. The CV-OPD introduces a Discrepancy Aware Gate (DAG) that uses token-level and sample-level discrepancies to select visually relevant tokens for optimization, directing the student's attention toward visual content. Extensive experiments across a broad range of fine-grained visual benchmarks demonstrate that CV-OPD substantially alleviates shortcut and consistently improves the visual reasoning capabilities of existing VLMs.
authors: Haowei Wang, Hao Lin, Qi Zhu, Jiayi Ji, Deyi Ji, Liujuan Cao, Rongrong Ji
bullets: OPD can produce accurate answers even when relevant image regions are masked or replaced with noise, revealing weak visual grounding.
CV-OPD contrasts teacher outputs from answer-relevant positive crops and unrelated negative crops under the same student prefix.
Its Contrastive Divergence Loss encourages students to distinguish useful from irrelevant visual features.
A Discrepancy Aware Gate selects visually relevant tokens using token- and sample-level discrepancies.
Experiments on broad fine-grained visual benchmarks show reduced shortcut behavior and improved visual reasoning in existing VLMs.

papers.abstract: Learning new tasks in multimodal continual instruction tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired knowledge. Although multi-expert LoRA distributes learning across experts, updates to a dense low-rank expert can still affect many output features. We introduce Monarch-MoE, which replaces the dense factors in LoRA experts with block-diagonal factors connected by a fixed permutation. This structure provides blockwise gradient isolation: individual block-pair updates affect only one output block, while connections between all input and output blocks are maintained. To make these compact experts practical on memory-limited hardware, we combine batched computation, fused forward operators, and an optimized backward pass. Across three continual-learning methods evaluated on MLLM-DCL and UCIT with LLaVA-1.5-7B, Monarch-MoE improves first-task retention while reducing adapter parameters by approximately 75% and 50%, respectively. In the main comparison, first-task forgetting is as low as 0.52 percentage points on MLLM-DCL and 0.10 on UCIT, with method-dependent trade-offs in final performance. Our implementation supports fine-tuning and inference on a single 24 GB RTX 4090, with lower measured memory use and competitive runtime in the evaluated settings. Together, these algorithmic and systems improvements make structured experts a practical option for continual adaptation on memory-limited hardware.
authors: Xi Zhang, Boyu Diao, Zesen Chen, Ruiqi Liu, Hangda Liu, Yongjun Xu
bullets: Targets catastrophic forgetting when learning new multimodal tasks.
Replaces dense LoRA factors with block-diagonal factors linked by a fixed permutation, isolating updates by output block while preserving global connectivity.

Across MLLM-DCL and UCIT with LLaVA-1.5-7B, reduces adapter parameters by approximately 75% and 50%, respectively, while improving first-task retention.
Runs fine-tuning and inference on a single 24 GB RTX 4090, with method-dependent trade-offs in final performance.

papers.abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models, its efficacy in long-horizon multimodal tasks remains underexplored. Visual Sudoku puzzles pose a representative challenge, requiring multi-step deductive reasoning over both local constraints and global dependency chains. To this end, we introduce FG-Sudoku, a fine-grained benchmark categorized by grid size and required deductive steps. Evaluations reveal that frontier MLLMs fail on complex long-range dependencies (e.g., 9*9 puzzles). During post-training, this near-zero success rate causes severe reward sparsity, halting standard RLVR. We propose Adaptive Curriculum Group Relative Policy Optimization (AdaC-GRPO) to overcome this. Unlike rigid or prior-based schedules, AdaC-GRPO dynamically constructs training batches by tracking the model's "Zone of Proximal Development" via online rollout accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that AdaC-GRPO enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach the performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash while bridging 62.2% of the overall accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro, with its generalizability further validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.
authors: Sida Li, Yuanxin Liu, Linli Yao, Shicheng Li, Xu Sun, Haoli Bai, Xiaohui Li

Enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach Gemini-2.5-Flash and close 62.2% of the accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro.
Generalization is validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. We introduce a black-box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2-4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model-dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language-prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal-grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.
bullets: LALMs may hallucinate absent sounds; Audio-Aware Decoding’s blank-audio comparison can be confounded by removing the entire clip.
The study localizes evidence with CLAP similarity, removes it via spectral gating, and compares it with random-window removal across multiple models and conditions.
After matching removal duration, localized ablation outperforms random removal, but raw detection behavior varies by model.
Combining blank and language-prior contrasts improves Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, outperforming AAD alone.
Grounding profiles do not transfer consistently between models; the study reports limitations and releases code.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes audio grounding and hallucination in large audio-language models, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
papers.tldr: A black-box causal audit shows that audio-grounding evidence and hallucination mitigation are model-dependent, while duration-controlled localization and combined contrastive decoding improve reliability in tested settings.

papers.abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.
authors: Yixuan Li, Minghao Lv, Xuenan Xu, Zihao Zheng, Mengyue Wu
bullets: Addresses coarse difficulty estimation in adaptive reasoning for large audio-language models.
Derives five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments.
Learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning across stages.
On MMAU-test-mini and MMAR, it improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens.
Shortens reasoning for easy instances while preserving performance on difficult ones.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our multi-dimensional difficulty-aware audio reasoning framework. (b) Structured SFT teaches the model to produce concise, rated reasoning traces. (c) Curriculum RL progresses from easy to hard while jointly optimizing task quality, format, rating-conditioned section-length rewards, and teacher-anchored rating calibration under reference-policy KL regularization. Offline annotators are used only during training.

papers.selection_reason: Difficulty-aware adaptive reasoning for audio-language models, relevant to multimodal LLMs and inference efficiency.
papers.title: SWEAR: Section-Wise Efficient Audio Reasoning via Self-Rated Difficulty
papers.tldr: SWEAR improves audio-language reasoning efficiency by allocating effort according to fine-grained, stage-specific difficulty.

papers.abstract: Radiology reports are essential for diagnostic reasoning and patient care, yet their manual preparation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding. Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) offers a scalable alternative, but existing models often produce lengthy, unstructured narratives that overlook diagnostic cues and multi-view information. We present Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation (CliQ-RRG), a unified two-stage framework for interpretable and clinically grounded reporting. In Stage 1, CliQ-RRG employs a Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment module that aligns image and text representations using predicted disease embeddings, reinforced by a Prior-Guided Attention Module (PrAM) to capture multi-view dependencies across current and prior scans. In Stage 2, GraphRAG-guided retrieval augments intermediate textual representations with graph-grounded clinical evidence, and a large language model restructures them into concise, interpretable question-answer (QA) pairs with diagnostic summaries. Experiments on two public chest X-ray benchmarks demonstrate that CliQ-RRG consistently outperforms prior methods across both lexical and clinical metrics, generating accurate and clinically coherent QA-style radiology reports. Code is available at: https://github.com/chandravardhan-singh-raghaw/CliQ-RRG.
authors: Chandravardhan Singh Raghaw, Shahid Shafi Dar, Arnav Nishith Sharma, Shrey Modi, Nagendra Kumar
bullets: Targets lengthy, unstructured reports that may miss diagnostic cues and multi-view information.
Stage 1 uses disease-aware visual-textual alignment and prior-guided attention to model current and prior scans.
Stage 2 applies GraphRAG-guided clinical retrieval and an LLM to produce QA pairs with diagnostic summaries.
On two public chest X-ray benchmarks, it outperforms prior methods on lexical and clinical metrics.
The approach is evaluated specifically for chest X-ray reporting and depends on clinical-knowledge retrieval.

papers.abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.
authors: Yongxin Zheng, Hao Wu, Fang Li, Hu Fu, Peiran Yin, Xudong Wang, Haozhe Hu, Xinghao Chen, Yunpu Ma, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Addresses high inference cost from repeated cross-view observations and processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer.
GeoSemZip builds compact 3D voxel-token representations using semantic saliency and spatial coverage, while retaining discarded information in contextual anchors.
GroupRoute uses late entry, early exit, and recoverable group-wise skipping to adapt visual computation to token relevance.
Using a 67K-sample compression-aware post-training set, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of dense-model performance on two 7B 3D VLMs.
It accelerates LLM prefill by 6.8× and 6.1×, demonstrating applicability to models with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of GeoGR. (1) Projector-level Compression: GeoSemZip consolidates crossview observations into 3D voxel tokens using depth and camera poses. Saliency-based selection preserves dominant tokens, while Morton-order sampling selects contextual anchors that aggregate unselected voxel features by cosine similarity. The compressed visual tokens are combined with text tokens to form the LLM input. (2) LLM-level Compression: GroupRoute confines visual computation to an intermediate-layer window through Late Entry and Early Exit. Within this window, Recoverable Group-wise Skipping routes query-conditioned token groups through or around complete LLM layers. Skipped tokens retain their hidden states and can resume computation after regrouping at subsequent anchor layers. Text tokens remain active throughout the LLM.

papers.selection_reason: Compresses 3D visual tokens and skips LLM layers for efficient 3D VLMs, directly relevant to token pruning and multimodal efficiency.
papers.title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
papers.tldr: GeoGR makes multi-view 3D vision-language models substantially faster by compressing redundant scene tokens and selectively routing visual tokens through LLM layers while preserving most performance.

papers.abstract: Visual interventions provide a training-free way to reduce hallucinations in multimodal large language models. However, an intervention may have little leverage at some layers and may damage a correct answer even when it changes the output. We investigate where visual interventions retain leverage and when they improve predictions. First, we apply the same visual-residual edit at successive decoder layers, matching its RMS strength across depth. Across six checkpoints from three model families, we observe a persistent drop in intervention effect and define its operational onset for this edit as the \textbf{Evidence Anchoring Boundary (EAB)}. With boundaries fixed on calibration queries, held-out effects on disjoint evaluation queries before EAB are $13.78\times$--$26.10\times$ larger than those after it. Comparison with intermediate readouts shows that the edit can lose leverage before answer preferences stabilize. Second, we compare counterfactual subtraction across presence, attribute, and relation questions. Subtraction can correct a misleading preference, leave a decision unchanged, or remove a preference supporting the correct answer. Based on these observations, we develop calibrated selective routing, which preserves the original prediction unless calibration supports an intervention for the question type. It improves full-set attribute accuracy by $1.56$--$1.81$ percentage points across three checkpoints, while universal subtraction is neutral or harmful.
authors: Qiji Zhou, Junyi Hu, Peiyu Wang, Yue Zhang
bullets: Visual-residual edits lose predictive leverage at later decoder layers, defining an operational Evidence Anchoring Boundary (EAB).
Across six checkpoints from three model families, pre-EAB held-out effects are 13.78×–26.10× larger than post-EAB effects.
Interventions can correct misleading preferences, have no effect, or disrupt preferences supporting the correct answer.
Calibrated selective routing improves full-set attribute accuracy by 1.56–1.81 percentage points across three checkpoints.
Universal counterfactual subtraction is neutral or harmful, highlighting the need for selective application.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes layer-wise visual interventions in multimodal LLMs to reduce hallucinations and proposes selective routing, directly relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: The Evidence Anchoring Boundary: Where Visual Interventions Matter and When They Help in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Visual interventions help multimodal LLMs mainly before an Evidence Anchoring Boundary, so calibrated, question-aware routing is safer than applying them universally.

papers.abstract: We introduce MVGraph, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) on multi-graph reasoning where the evidence required by a query is distributed across multiple interrelated visual graph views. Although such evidence commonly resides in source-specific graphs, temporal snapshots, or local observations, existing graph reasoning benchmarks remain confined to a single self-contained structure, assessing only graph perception and reasoning while leaving the alignment and composition of evidence across views underexplored. MVGraph comprises 8k instances spanning 8 \textit{graph-theoretic} tasks, abstracted from two multi-graph scenarios (partial and temporal graph views). Each problem is programmatically constructed and verified to be unsolvable from a single view. Beyond end-to-end evaluation, we decompose multi-graph reasoning into four complementary capabilities---Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning---and design 29 diagnostic tasks with 64k instances to probe each one, along with golden intermediate representations for evaluating the intermediate process. Across 15 LVLMs, we reveal the difficulty of multi-graph reasoning and identify cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as prominent bottlenecks through stage-oriented diagnostics. Meanwhile, temporal constraints and increasing view counts expose further capability boundaries. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AAAndy-Zhu/MVGraph.
authors: Yingjie Zhu, Han Cheng, Xuefeng Bai, Youcheng Pan, Yang Xiang, Kehai Chen
bullets: Introduces 8,000 benchmark instances covering 8 graph-theoretic tasks across partial and temporal multi-graph views.
Ensures each problem cannot be solved from any single view alone, isolating evidence-composition ability.
Decomposes performance into Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning using 29 diagnostic tasks and 64,000 instances.
Evaluates 15 LVLMs and identifies cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as key bottlenecks.
Temporal constraints and more numerous views further expose capability limits.

papers.abstract: Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect, can disagree, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is convex, and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy's own verifier-labeled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark. Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations, and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank.
authors: Yueying Li, Jingxuan Fan, Kiant\'e Brantley, Sham M. Kakade, Hanlin Zhang
bullets: Uses a linear head over a frozen Qwen3-VL intermediate layer, training original web captions to outrank perturbed versions.
Selecting the intermediate layer is critical, improving performance by 5.8 points over using the last layer.
A single recipe matches or exceeds GPT-4o across three benchmarks at 32B and leads VL-RewardBench by 6.6 points.
With equal pair budgets, perturbation-based training outperforms curated RLAIF-V pairs by 3–5 points.

Benchmark scores do not fully identify reward behavior: perturbation choice affects hallucination judgments, while verifier-driven bootstrapping improves CHAIR and image-generation pass rate despite lower benchmark scores.

papers.selection_reason: Unsupervised vision-language reward modeling on frozen VLM, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling
papers.tldr: An unsupervised intermediate-layer reward head trained on caption perturbations can provide low-cost, task-specific multimodal rewards without human preference labels.

papers.abstract: Modern video-language models are increasingly treated as general-purpose video reasoners, yet it remains unclear whether they robustly capture temporal dynamics in safety-critical settings such as driving. We study this question through controlled ego-motion tasks that require identifying actions from driving videos. Across video-language models, we find that standard prompting, visual prompting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought prompting remain unreliable and highly task- and model-dependent, with persistent class biases, although newer models show substantial task-specific few-shot gains. In contrast, lightweight LoRA finetuning and simple probes trained on intermediate visual features recover strong motion-discriminative performance, indicating that motion-relevant cues are often present inside the models but are not reliably used by the final video-to-language pathway. These results suggest that, in driving, current video-language models remain unreliable temporal reasoners and often behave more like frame-level, bias-driven recognizers than dependable temporal world models.
authors: Shiva Sreeram, Erfan Aasi, Tsun-Hsuan Wang, Alaa Maalouf, Daniela Rus
bullets: The study evaluates temporal understanding through controlled ego-motion action-identification tasks in driving videos.
Standard, visual, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting are unreliable and strongly dependent on the task and model.
Models exhibit persistent class biases, though newer systems can gain substantially from task-specific few-shot examples.
Lightweight LoRA finetuning and probes on intermediate visual features achieve strong motion discrimination.
Findings suggest final video-to-language pathways underuse temporal cues, causing models to act more like frame-level recognizers than temporal world models.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Pipeline for probing ego-motion understanding in video-language models. We evaluate increasingly structured approaches, from training-free prompting to lightweight learning-based probes. In standard prompting, the model directly classifies the vehicle’s motion. Visual prompting adds a green bounding box around a static reference object to test whether explicit spatial grounding improves motion inference. In fusion of visual and text, labeled few-shot video examples are provided before the query. Chain-of-thought prompting explicitly relates temporal changes in the reference object’s position or size to ego-motion. We then apply LoRA finetuning to test whether motion distinctions can be learned under lightweight supervision, and feature extraction to train simple classifiers on intermediate visual representations and examine where motion information remains decodable. Overall, prompt-level methods remain strongly model- and task-dependent, whereas learning-based approaches recover substantially stronger motion discrimination.

Fig. 3. Average ego-motion accuracy versus model release date. Standard and few-shot results are averaged across motion pairs. VideoLLaMA2 is excluded from the few-shot trend because its protocol is not comparable.
Fig. 2. Sim-to-real comparison of standard-prompting accuracy. The same class-level biases appear across CARLA and real-world videos. Overall class-level correlation is r = 0.957.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluation of temporal reasoning in video-language models for driving.
papers.title: Mind the Temporal Gap: Evaluating Video Models for Temporal Understanding in Driving
papers.tldr: Current video-language models often fail to reliably understand temporal dynamics in driving videos, despite containing motion-relevant information that lightweight adaptation can unlock.

papers.abstract: Small language models trained on a single local machine leave little room for architectural trial and error. Kairos combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention and sliding-window attention over shared projections (LiZAttention2), block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layer and a multi-scale byte-level codec, trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective over one byte space shared by text, image, audio, video, lidar and control streams; this report asks whether the combination optimizes at all before asking whether it is useful. We give code-derived algorithms for each component, including a cross-session recurrent-state memory gate, then run convergence sanity checks: overfittinga single 440-byte sentence at 1--15M parameters, text only, with three seeds for codec and attention choices and single-run sweeps for seven further factors. The two attention variants tested at 3\,000 steps (LiZAttention2 and window attention alone) reach a minimum loss near $10^{-3}$. After 600 steps, the mean minimum loss ranges from 0.018 (patch codec) to 0.354 (depthwise convolutional codec) with an identical ranking on three seeds. An apparent advantage of shared over separate attention projections closes with more steps or more diverse data and reverses when the projections are frozen: it is a convergence-speed effect, not a capacity effect. These checks suggest that the implementation optimizes; they say nothing about generalization, multimodal training or comparison with existing models, which a planned pretraining run is meant to address. The Discussion sizes a 200M-total/25M-active target analytically; none of its throughput figures is measured. Code is available at https://github.com/fabienfrfr/Kairos . Python package at https://pypi.org/project/kairos-fm/ .
bullets: Combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet and sliding-window attention, shared projections, block-wise attention-residual aggregation, sparse MoE layers, and a multi-scale byte codec.
Uses uniform-noise denoising across a shared byte space intended for text, images, audio, video, lidar, and control streams.
Convergence checks overfit one 440-byte sentence at 1–15M parameters; both tested attention variants reach minimum loss near 10⁻³ at 3,000 steps.
Codec choices produce different early optimization behavior, while the apparent shared-projection benefit is attributed to convergence speed rather than capacity.
Results do not establish generalization, multimodal training, model superiority, or the proposed throughput; larger pretraining is planned.

The ablation networks are far smaller than the notebook config, so ablation findings are not statements about the notebook config.

papers.selection_reason: Byte-level multimodal foundation model with linear attention and MoE; fits multimodal LLM and efficient attention interests.
papers.title: Kairos: Toward a Byte-Level Foundation Model for Every Modality
papers.tldr: Kairos proposes a byte-level multimodal foundation-model design and finds that its components can optimize on a tiny text-only memorization task, without yet demonstrating generalization or multimodal usefulness.

papers.abstract: Spatial coding agents significantly improve spatial reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by using external tools to generate verified execution traces. However, this paradigm inherently suffers from prohibitive inference-time overhead and external dependencies. In this paper, we explore whether an MLLM can internalize this agentic capability to operate entirely tool-free. We begin with a simple observation: prompting an MLLM with summarized execution traces of a spatial coding agent naturally unlocks the model's internal spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT). Motivated by this, we introduce SpatialOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework that internalizes spatial reasoning into a standalone MLLM by formulating verified agent traces as privileged information. To mitigate privileged-information leakage during distillation, we introduce Repetition-Aware Distillation, which combines repetition masking with unlikelihood regularization. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that self-distilling SpatialOPSD achieves higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO on both spatial and OOD datasets, exhibiting superior performance and generalization.
bullets: Targets the inference overhead and external dependencies of tool-using spatial coding agents.
Uses on-policy self-distillation to treat verified agent traces as privileged reasoning information.
Introduces Repetition-Aware Distillation with repetition masking and unlikelihood regularization to reduce privileged-information leakage.
Experiments report higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO across spatial and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
Scope: focuses on internalizing spatial reasoning in standalone MLLMs without external tools.

papers.selection_reason: Directly targets spatial reasoning in MLLMs via self-distillation from coding agent traces, fitting spatial intelligence and multimodal LLM subtopics.
papers.title: SpatialOPSD: Self-Distilling Spatial Intelligence from Verified Coding Agent Traces
papers.tldr: SpatialOPSD distills verified spatial coding-agent traces into an MLLM, enabling tool-free spatial reasoning with improved benchmark performance and generalization.

papers.abstract: Large audio language models answer questions about speech, sound, and music, yet their accuracy drops sharply on tasks that need fine-grained acoustic analysis. Judging which of two speakers has the higher pitch demands iterative signal-level reasoning that a content question does not. Current models spend the same computational depth on both. We introduce AdaLoop, a lightweight recurrent module that learns how many latent refinement steps a given audio--question pair requires. A shared transformer block iterates over the audio representation, guided by the question, while a learned halting mechanism exits the loop once the representation is ready. AdaLoop adds fewer than 3\% of the base model's parameters and plugs into any audio encoder--language model pair without modifying either component. Evaluated on three architecturally distinct models across MMSU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR, AdaLoop raises the average accuracy by 2.9 to 3.8 points, with the largest gains on perception-heavy subtasks where the model learns to apply deeper reasoning.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed reasoning depth and the varying acoustic-analysis demands of audio questions.
Uses a shared transformer block for question-guided recurrent refinement of audio representations.
A learned halting mechanism determines when further refinement is unnecessary.
Plugs into existing audio encoder–language model pairs without modifying either component.
Improves average accuracy by 2.9–3.8 points across three models and three benchmarks, with largest gains on perception-heavy subtasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of AdaLoop. The Recurrent Latent Block (dashed) applies question-guided cross-attention, scale-aware self-attention with four window sizes (w), and a feed-forward update. Shared parameters iterate K times; a halting unit conditioned on both the pooled audio state and the question decides when to stop.
Fig. 2. Average AdaLoop iterations by MMAR category on Qwen2.5Omni-7B. Signal-level tasks trigger the deepest reasoning.
Table 2. Ablations on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B. Each row changes one component of AdaLoop while keeping the training budget fixed. Base model Avg. is 59.3%.

papers.selection_reason: Extends audio language models with adaptive latent reasoning, fitting multimodal large language models with an additional audio modality.
papers.title: AdaLoop: Adaptive-Depth Latent Reasoning for Audio Language Models
papers.tldr: AdaLoop adaptively allocates iterative latent reasoning to audio questions, improving accuracy especially on fine-grained acoustic tasks with under 3% additional parameters.

papers.abstract: Continuous emotion control in text-to-image generation requires a model to improve affective alignment without changing the objects, layout, or scene described by the prompt. Existing supervised emotion-injection methods often optimize feature-space proxies and may therefore exhibit emotion-semantic drift, in which stronger emotional conditioning is accompanied by unintended content changes. We address this problem with a flow-matching image-generation framework that combines continuous valence-arousal (VA) conditioning, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and a neutral semantic anchor. The deterministic probability-flow ODE is converted into a marginal-preserving SDE, yielding non-degenerate transition densities for trajectory sampling and policy-ratio estimation. A frozen CLIP-based VA regressor supplies a terminal reward measuring the distance between the predicted and target VA coordinates, while an image generated from the same prompt under zero VA conditioning provides a feature-space reference for semantic preservation. A reduced denoising schedule is used for online RL sampling, whereas the original schedule is retained at inference. Experiments on 3,300 prompt-emotion combinations show substantially lower valence and arousal errors than the VA-conditioned baseline and an improved CLIPScore relative to EmotiCrafter, with a measurable trade-off in reference-free image quality. The results support anchor-regularized Flow-GRPO as a practical approach to balancing emotional alignment and semantic consistency in continuous-affect image synthesis.
bullets: Targets emotion-semantic drift, where stronger affect changes unintended image content.
Combines continuous valence-arousal conditioning, GRPO reinforcement learning, and a neutral semantic anchor.
Uses a frozen CLIP-based valence-arousal reward plus feature-space comparison with zero-emotion images.
Evaluated on 3,300 prompt-emotion combinations, achieving lower valence/arousal errors than a VA-conditioned baseline and improved CLIPScore versus EmotiCrafter.
Reports a measurable trade-off in reference-free image quality.

figures.caption: Fig. 5: Overview of the dataset statistics. The figures show neutral prompt length, arousal and valence values, and emotional prompt length for different data splits (Blue, Green, Red).

Fig. 9: Emotion variation across the valence–arousal (VA) space for a landscape prompt “A tranquil lake surrounded by golden autumn trees, misty morning.” Left: the baseline (EmotiCrafter) exhibits severe emotion–semantic drift. Right: our anchorconstrained GRPO method maintains consistent scene structure (lake, autumn trees, mist) across all VA conditions, while expressing emotion through controlled changes in color, illumination, and atmosphere.

In contrast, the blue curve (CLIPScore) exhibits a limited and mild decrease, reflecting the inherent trade-off between emotional expressiveness and semantic fidelity, where the anchor constraint effectively stabilizes semantic consistency during RL optimization.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses continuous emotion control in text-to-image generation using flow-matching and reinforcement learning, fitting multimodal generation.
papers.title: Balancing Emotional Alignment and Semantic Consistency in Image Generation via Reinforcement Learning with Valence-Arousal Anchoring
papers.tldr: Anchor-regularized Flow-GRPO improves continuous emotional control in text-to-image generation while preserving prompt semantics, though with a trade-off in reference-free image quality.

papers.abstract: Audio-based Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can generate detailed natural-language descriptions of complex acoustic scenes, yet it remains unclear which parts of the input audio support each generated token. This is particularly challenging because acoustic evidence is distributed across time and frequency, and concurrent sound events may overlap temporally while occupying different spectral regions. We introduce STAG, to our knowledge the first post-hoc framework for token-level spectro-temporal grounding of captions generated by audio-based MLLMs. STAG estimates the temporal support for each generated token using target-token-specific vocabulary projections of the encoded audio representations, measures frequency-band relevance through controlled spectral occlusion, and combines the two signals into a spectro-temporal relevance map. We evaluate STAG against ten post-hoc explanation methods across four grounding benchmarks, where it achieves the best event-localization performance on every dataset, and apply it to eight audio-language backbones without parameter updates. Counterfactual deletion further shows that removing the identified evidence selectively reduces confidence in the corresponding event and frequently removes it from the regenerated caption. These results provide behavioral support for the faithfulness and selectivity of the explanations.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of grounding token-level explanations when overlapping sounds occupy different spectral regions.
Combines target-token-specific temporal evidence from audio representations with frequency relevance from controlled spectral occlusion.
Evaluated against ten post-hoc methods across four grounding benchmarks, achieving the best event-localization performance on each dataset.
Applied to eight audio-language backbones without parameter updates.
Counterfactual deletion supports explanation faithfulness: removing identified evidence lowers confidence in the related event and often removes it from the caption.

papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc token-level spectro-temporal grounding for audio MLLMs; directly relevant to multimodal LLM interpretability.
papers.title: What Did the MLLM Hear? Token-Level Spectro-Temporal Grounding for Audio MLLM Explainability
papers.tldr: STAG explains audio-MLLM captions by locating the time–frequency regions that support each generated token.

papers.abstract: Ambiguity is often treated as a bug for AI systems to resolve---but in human communication and culture, ambiguity can also be a generative resource. From humour to politics to art, people express themselves in words and images that are open enough to invite different interpretations, yet constrained enough to be interpretable. We operationalise this notion of calibrated ambiguity with a task drawn from the parlour game Dixit. We compare differences in clues generated by human vs multimodal language models, based on a novel coding rubric for calibrated ambiguity, and find that models consistently exhibit ambiguity collapse (i.e., their outputs are over-specified, leaving no room for multiple legitimate interpretations). Unlike human clues, AI-generated clues also exhibit cultural flattening; they almost never make reference to culturally-situated knowledge, even when prompted to use allusion and figurative language.
bullets: The study examines ambiguity as a useful feature of communication rather than merely an error to eliminate.
It compares human and model-generated image clues using a novel coding rubric for calibrated ambiguity.
Models consistently show “ambiguity collapse,” reducing room for multiple legitimate interpretations.
Unlike humans, models rarely invoke culturally situated knowledge, even when prompted to use allusion and figurative language.

figures.caption: Figure 1: We use the parlour game Dixit as a paradigm for measuring calibrated ambiguity. The task requires a “storyteller” to generate a “clue” that ambiguously picks out a target card from a set of distractor—as judged by being correctly selected by some but not all of the other players. In this example, a human player constructs their clue around an allusion to a song from the movie Frozen—a widely-known cultural reference. Our results show how model-generated clues differ systematically from those given by humans. In this example, Gemma 3 offers a clue that is calibrated for ambiguity, but describes the image without reference to culturally-situated knowledge; while GLM-4.6V simply provides an unambiguously literal clue.

Figure 5: Models differ in their degree of ambiguity collapse, but all of them show evidence of cultural flattening. Each bank reflects analysis of 350 clues across six models under the minimal and the social cognition prompt, ordered by collapse under the minimal prompt. (a) Share of clues both coders rated Overspecified. (b) Share ratedMainstream or Niche on situatedness; note the 50% scale. Dashed lines: the human clues on the same rounds.

Figure 4: Formal linguistic features. (a) ROC AUC of each feature alone (95% CIs); dashed line: all twelve combined (Mahalanobis score, held out); inset: word-count distributions. (b) The same clues in the first two principal components; ellipses: 2 SD.

Table 4: Models differ in their degree of ambiguity collapse, but all of them show evidence of cultural flattening. Each bank reflects analysis of 350 clues across six models under the minimal and the social cognition prompt, ordered by collapse under the minimal prompt. (a) Share of clues both coders rated Overspecified. (b) Share rated Mainstream or Niche on situatedness; note the 50% scale. Dashed lines: the human clues on the same rounds.

Table 5: Example clues from all 6 model and 2 prompt permutations compared with humans for two boards, shown with their five cards (target in red). Cal.: coder-averaged calibration rating (1 Underspecified, 2 Calibrated, 3 Overspecified). min/soc: minimal / social cognition prompt.
